explanation.pearls: Never prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol) or high-potency atypicals in DLB - severe neuroleptic sensitivity can cause worsening parkinsonism, confusion, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome; low dose quetiapine is preferred if antipsychotic is unavoidable.

subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive in dementia (Austroads)
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 76 year old man 6 months after a diagnosis of mild Alzheimer disease was confirmed by a geriatrician. He drives a private vehicle only (no commercial licence). He lives with his wife who normally sits in the front passenger seat when he drives.

His MMSE is 24/30 with impairment in orientation and recall. Functional review by his wife reveals he now needs prompting to take his morning medications and has become lost driving home from the local supermarket twice in the last 2 months. He denies any recent motor vehicle collisions. His visual acuity is 6/9 corrected and he has no significant visual field deficit. His car has manual transmission and he wears reading glasses.

Examination shows no focal neurology. Vital signs are within normal limits. He asks you whether he can continue driving.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Cognition: MMSE 24/30; impairment in orientation and recall; needs prompting for medications; getting lost driving home twice in 2 months
data_table.Vision: 6/9 corrected; no significant visual field deficit
data_table.Licence: Private class only; drives with wife in front passenger seat

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding driving?

options.text: Recommend continued driving only when accompanied by his wife and only in daylight hours
options.rationale: A supervising passenger and daylight restriction have no basis in Austroads fitness to drive standards for dementia; conditional licences are decided by the licensing authority after formal assessment, not by informal restrictions negotiated in general practice (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

options.text: Reassure that mild cognitive impairment is compatible with unrestricted driving above MMSE 20
options.rationale: MMSE thresholds alone are not a driving decision tool per Austroads; functional impairment affecting driving safety (getting lost on familiar routes) mandates assessment regardless of MMSE score, and there is no MMSE cut-off that gives blanket unrestricted licence eligibility (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

options.text: Review him at the next annual dementia review before making any decision about driving
options.rationale: Waiting 12 months in a patient who has demonstrated navigational failure poses immediate risk to the patient and other road users; Austroads requires action at the time functional impairment is identified, not deferred review (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

options.text: Discharge from your care and advise him to arrange his own transport in future
options.rationale: Discharge does not discharge the doctor's duty to advise the patient of the driving implications of his condition; documented advice, driver notification, and consideration of statutory reporting remain professional responsibilities (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

options.text: Advise him to stop driving and arrange formal occupational therapy on-road assessment
options.rationale: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive states that a diagnosis of dementia with impairment of function affecting driving safety (getting lost on familiar routes is a specific example) makes a person not fit to hold an unconditional private licence and requires formal on-road driving assessment by an accredited occupational therapist. In NSW the treating doctor has a professional responsibility to advise the driver to stop and notify Transport for NSW; the driver has a legal obligation to notify (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive; Transport for NSW medical fitness to drive).
source_refs: Transport for NSW medical fitness to drive

explanation.summary: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive is the national medical standards resource for driver licensing in Australia. For dementia, the standard requires the treating health professional to advise the patient of the impact on driving and to consider notifying the licensing authority when the patient continues to drive against medical advice. Formal on-road assessment by an accredited occupational therapist is the definitive test of driving safety. Notification requirements vary by state - NSW requires the driver to self-notify Transport for NSW, and the doctor may notify in the public interest under health legislation. Functional impairments that specifically flag driving risk include getting lost in familiar areas, medication non-adherence, and impaired judgement.
key_points: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive is the national medical standard.
Dementia with functional impairment (e.g. getting lost) mandates on-road OT assessment.
Notification: driver must notify licensing authority in all states; doctor may notify in the public interest.
MMSE alone is not a driving decision tool - function is the metric.
explanation.pearls: Document in the notes the specific functional impairment that triggered your advice (e.g. getting lost driving home twice in 2 months), the advice given, and the driver's response - this protects both patient and doctor if a subsequent adverse event occurs.

sources.label: Transport for NSW medical fitness to drive

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barre syndrome immunotherapy choice
stem:
You are the medical registrar. A 54 year old man is admitted with 5 days of progressive ascending weakness starting in the feet and now involving the thighs, with paraesthesia in the fingertips developing today. He had gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhoea 3 weeks ago that self-resolved.

He cannot walk without support today; yesterday he could walk with a stick. He denies bladder or bowel dysfunction and has no back pain. He has no facial weakness or double vision.

Examination shows symmetrical lower limb weakness (MRC grade 3 hip flexion, grade 2 ankle dorsiflexion), absent knee and ankle reflexes, patchy sensory loss in a stocking distribution, and grade 4 grip strength bilaterally. Cranial nerves are intact. Forced vital capacity at the bedside is 32 mL/kg. Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8.

Investigations: CSF cell count 3 x10^6/L (less than 5), CSF protein 1.4 g/L (0.15-0.45), CSF glucose normal, culture negative. Nerve conduction studies show slowed motor conduction velocities and prolonged distal latencies with conduction block consistent with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. HIV serology negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative. He has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 128/76, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical LL weakness (hip flexion MRC 3, ankle dorsiflexion MRC 2); absent knee and ankle reflexes; stocking sensory loss; grip MRC 4; cranial nerves intact
data_table.History: 5 days progressive ascending weakness; gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhoea 3 weeks ago
data_table.Bedside: FVC 32 mL/kg; no bulbar or autonomic features
data_table.CSF: 3 x10^6/L (less than 5); protein 1.4 g/L (0.15-0.45); glucose normal; culture negative
data_table.NCS: Slowed motor conduction, prolonged distal latencies, conduction block (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy)
data_table.Serology: HIV, HBV, HCV negative; no known drug allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunotherapy?

options.text: High dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily tapered over 8 weeks total
options.rationale: Multiple randomised trials and Cochrane reviews show that corticosteroids alone do NOT hasten recovery in Guillain-Barre syndrome and may worsen outcome; this contrasts with CIDP where steroids are first line. Not prescribing steroids in GBS is a specific exam point (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Cochrane review corticosteroids in GBS).

options.text: High dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 consecutive days
options.rationale: Intravenous methylprednisolone is likewise not effective as monotherapy in GBS and does not improve outcome when combined with IVIG; this is a well-established negative trial finding (Source: Cochrane review corticosteroids in GBS).

options.text: Rituximab 375 mg per square metre intravenously weekly for 4 weeks
options.rationale: Rituximab has a role in some antibody-mediated autoimmune neurological diseases (MOG antibody disease, refractory myasthenia gravis, some IgG4-related conditions) but is not an established therapy for acute GBS; it lacks the evidence base of IVIG and plasma exchange (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days OR plasma exchange over 10 days
options.rationale: IVIG (2 g/kg total over 5 days) and plasma exchange are equally effective and are the two proven treatments for GBS when a patient cannot walk unaided (the standard treatment threshold). Combining them provides no additional benefit. IVIG is usually preferred for availability and side effect profile; PLEX is preferred when there is a contraindication to IVIG (severe IgA deficiency, hypersensitivity, hypercoagulability) (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
source_refs: Cochrane review IVIG and PLEX for GBS

options.text: Supportive care alone with physiotherapy and mechanical thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: Immunotherapy is indicated when a GBS patient cannot walk 10 metres unaided (the standard treatment threshold), as it reduces disability and time on ventilation; withholding immunotherapy in a non-ambulant patient does not meet standard of care (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, most commonly the acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP) subtype in Australia, often preceded by Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis (with bloody diarrhoea, as here) or viral illness. Diagnosis rests on progressive ascending symmetrical weakness with hypo/areflexia, cytoalbuminological dissociation in CSF (raised protein with normal cells), and characteristic nerve conduction findings. Immunotherapy - either IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days OR plasma exchange - is indicated when the patient cannot walk unaided and reduces disability and duration of ventilation. Corticosteroids are ineffective and should not be used. Monitoring for respiratory failure and autonomic instability is central.
key_points: GBS treatment: IVIG OR plasma exchange when patient cannot walk unaided.
Corticosteroids are INEFFECTIVE in GBS (contrast with CIDP where they are first line).
Monitor FVC, single breath count, and autonomic parameters serially.
Campylobacter jejuni (bloody diarrhoea) is the most common preceding infection.
explanation.pearls: Do not combine IVIG and PLEX in GBS - no added benefit and increased cost/harm; if a patient deteriorates after one course, discuss with neurology about a second IVIG course rather than switching to PLEX after IVIG has been given.

sources.label: Cochrane review IVIG and PLEX for GBS

subtopic_detail: Respiratory monitoring and ICU criteria in Guillain-Barre syndrome
stem:
You are the medical registrar covering the ward at 2 am. A 58 year old woman with Guillain-Barre syndrome (day 4 of admission, started IVIG yesterday) becomes anxious with increasing breathlessness and reports she cannot count higher than 15 on a single breath (was 30 yesterday).

She has no chest pain, no cough, and no fever. Nurses have called you because her forced vital capacity performed 30 minutes ago is 950 mL (weight 71 kg). She could walk with a frame yesterday afternoon; now she cannot lift her legs off the bed and her voice is quieter than earlier.

Examination shows use of accessory muscles at rest, paradoxical abdominal movement with each breath, weak cough, difficulty swallowing sips of water without coughing, MRC grade 2 in all four limbs, and no ptosis. Cardiac auscultation is unremarkable. Vital signs: pulse 118 irregular, blood pressure 168/102 (was 130/80 4 hours ago), respiratory rate 32, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.6.

Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.37, PaCO2 46 mmHg, PaO2 78 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L, base excess +1. Chest X-ray is clear. She has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 irregular, BP 168/102 (was 130/80 4 hours ago), RR 32, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Bedside respiratory: FVC 950 mL (weight 71 kg, so approx 13 mL/kg); single breath count 15 (was 30 yesterday); accessory muscle use; paradoxical abdominal movement; weak cough; coughing with sips of water
data_table.Neurology: Now MRC grade 2 all four limbs (was ambulating with frame yesterday); voice quieter; no ptosis
data_table.ABG (room air): pH 7.37; PaCO2 46 mmHg; PaO2 78 mmHg; HCO3 26 mmol/L; BE +1
data_table.Imaging: CXR clear
data_table.Treatment: Day 4 admission; IVIG started yesterday; no known allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start high flow nasal oxygen at 60 L/min FiO2 0.5 and repeat FVC in 4 hours
options.rationale: High flow nasal oxygen treats hypoxaemia but does not support the failing bellows - she has neuromuscular respiratory failure with a rising PaCO2 relative to her tachypnoea (ABG shows relative hypoventilation with PaCO2 46 mmHg despite RR 32, indicating fatigue and impending decompensation). Delaying 4 hours risks respiratory arrest (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Continuous positive airway pressure at 8 cmH2O with FiO2 0.4 on the medical ward
options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation is generally NOT recommended in Guillain-Barre syndrome because bulbar weakness increases aspiration risk (she is already coughing on sips), autonomic instability compromises tolerance, and progression to intubation is likely; ward-level NIV without ICU support is unsafe (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Give an additional IVIG loading dose 1 g/kg over 6 hours and observe with hourly obs
options.rationale: Additional IVIG may be considered after completion of the initial course if there is failure to improve, but it is not the immediate action for impending respiratory failure; airway and ventilation must be secured before further immunotherapy is escalated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Give intravenous salbutamol 250 mcg over 5 minutes and monitor peak expiratory flow
options.rationale: This is neuromuscular respiratory failure, not bronchospasm; peak expiratory flow reflects effort and airway calibre, not neuromuscular reserve, and salbutamol will not restore inspiratory muscle strength while potentially worsening tachyarrhythmia from her autonomic instability (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Urgent ICU review for intubation given FVC below 20 mL/kg and bulbar weakness
options.rationale: Standard criteria for intubation in GBS include FVC less than 20 mL/kg (she is 13 mL/kg), MIP less negative than -30 cmH2O, MEP less than 40 cmH2O (the 20/30/40 rule), rapidly falling FVC, bulbar weakness with aspiration risk, and autonomic instability. She meets multiple criteria. Elective intubation is preferred over emergency intubation. Suxamethonium is contraindicated for induction due to risk of life-threatening hyperkalaemia in denervating neuromuscular disease (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society statement).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society statement

explanation.summary: Approximately 25 to 30% of Guillain-Barre syndrome patients require mechanical ventilation, and elective intubation in a controlled setting is far safer than emergent intubation for respiratory arrest. The 20/30/40 rule triggers intubation consideration: FVC less than 20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure less negative than -30 cmH2O, or maximum expiratory pressure less than 40 cmH2O. Bulbar weakness with aspiration risk and autonomic dysfunction (labile blood pressure, arrhythmia) are additional intubation indicators. Serial bedside FVC or single breath count trending downwards, weak cough, paradoxical abdominal movement, and speech becoming quieter or more nasal all portend imminent respiratory failure. Rising PaCO2 is a late finding - do not wait for it. Suxamethonium is contraindicated for induction because of hyperkalaemic response.
key_points: 20/30/40 rule for GBS intubation: FVC less than 20 mL/kg, MIP less negative than -30, MEP less than 40 cmH2O.
Additional intubation triggers: bulbar weakness with aspiration risk, autonomic instability, rapidly falling FVC.
Non-invasive ventilation is generally NOT recommended in GBS.
Suxamethonium is contraindicated - use rocuronium for rapid sequence intubation.
explanation.pearls: Do serial bedside single breath counts (count to 20 in a single exhalation approximates FVC around 1.5 L) every 2 to 4 hours in GBS on the ward - a falling count is often the first bedside sign of impending respiratory failure before formal FVC drops below the 20 mL/kg threshold.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society statement

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis first line pharmacotherapy after minimal trauma fracture
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68 year old postmenopausal woman 6 weeks after she sustained a wrist fracture falling from standing height while carrying shopping. The fracture has been managed conservatively and is healing well.

She has never smoked, drinks 10 g of alcohol per day, and takes no regular medications. She has no history of malabsorption, coeliac disease, thyroid disease, or long term glucocorticoid use. Her mother sustained a hip fracture at age 78.

Examination shows a well-healed distal radius fracture and no kyphosis. Vital signs are within normal limits.

Investigations: DXA T-score lumbar spine -2.6, femoral neck -2.4, total hip -2.2. 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50 sufficient), corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 1.0 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), creatinine 68 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m^2, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), and normal full blood count. Serum protein electrophoresis and coeliac serology are negative. Dental review 4 months ago was normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well-healed distal radius fracture; no kyphosis
data_table.History: Minimal trauma wrist fracture 6 weeks ago; postmenopausal 68 yo; maternal hip fracture at 78; no smoking; 10 g alcohol/day; no glucocorticoid or malabsorption history
data_table.DXA: T-score lumbar spine -2.6; femoral neck -2.4; total hip -2.2
data_table.Bloods: 25-OH vitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50 sufficient); corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60); phosphate 1.0 mmol/L (0.8-1.5); creatinine 68 micromol/L with eGFR greater than 90; TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); FBC normal
data_table.Secondary workup: SPEP and coeliac serology negative; dental review normal 4 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Calcium 1000 mg and colecalciferol 25 mcg orally daily as sole prevention therapy
options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D alone are inadequate secondary prevention after minimal trauma fracture with T-score below -2.5; they support pharmacotherapy but do not substitute for antiresorptive therapy which reduces refracture risk by around 50% (Source: RACGP osteoporosis guideline).

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg orally weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: She has established osteoporosis by both a minimal trauma fracture at a major site AND a DXA T-score below -2.5. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines and the RACGP osteoporosis guideline recommend an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly) as first line pharmacotherapy in postmenopausal women with normal renal function and no upper gastrointestinal contraindications (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; RACGP osteoporosis guideline).

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months as first line antiresorptive therapy
options.rationale: Denosumab is effective and PBS-listed for osteoporosis but is not universally first line in Australia; it is preferred when oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated (upper gastrointestinal disease, oesophageal stricture) or when eGFR is less than 35 mL/min/1.73m^2. Its main issue is the rebound vertebral fracture risk if stopped abruptly (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneously daily as first line anabolic osteoporosis therapy
options.rationale: Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved for severe osteoporosis (typically T-score below -3.0 with multiple minimal trauma fractures, or fracture on antiresorptive therapy) and is subsidised on the PBS for these specific indications; it is not first line for a first minimal trauma fracture (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Menopausal hormone therapy with combined oestrogen and progestogen for fracture prevention
options.rationale: MHT reduces fracture risk but its risk profile (breast cancer, venous thromboembolism, stroke) makes it unsuitable as primary fracture prevention beyond age 60 in a woman with fracture already sustained; it is used for menopausal symptoms in appropriate candidates (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Osteoporosis is diagnosed either by DXA T-score at or below -2.5 at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip, OR by a minimal trauma (fragility) fracture at a major site (hip, vertebra, distal radius, proximal humerus) regardless of DXA. Secondary causes should be excluded with calcium, phosphate, 25-OH vitamin D, TSH, SPEP, coeliac serology, and (in men) testosterone. First line pharmacotherapy in Australia is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly), or IV zoledronic acid annually if oral therapy is not tolerated or adherence is poor. Denosumab is preferred when eGFR is less than 35 mL/min/1.73m^2 or oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated. Teriparatide is anabolic and reserved for severe or antiresorptive-failure disease. Adequate dietary calcium (1000-1300 mg/day) and vitamin D (25-OH-D greater than 50 nmol/L) support all antiresorptive therapy.
key_points: Osteoporosis dx: T-score at or below -2.5 OR minimal trauma fracture at major site.
First line: oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly, risedronate 35 mg weekly) OR IV zoledronic acid annually.
Denosumab if eGFR less than 35 or oral bisphosphonates contraindicated.
Exclude secondary causes: calcium, phosphate, 25-OH-D, TSH, SPEP, coeliac serology, (in men) testosterone.
explanation.pearls: Counsel on bisphosphonate dosing: swallow with a full glass of tap water on an empty stomach and remain upright for at least 30 minutes; this reduces oesophagitis and improves absorption which is less than 1% at baseline.

subtopic_detail: Denosumab discontinuation and rebound vertebral fracture risk
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar. A 73 year old woman has been on subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 7 years for postmenopausal osteoporosis. Her most recent DXA showed T-score lumbar spine -1.8, femoral neck -2.0, and total hip -1.9, all improved from baseline.

She has developed a slowly increasing serum creatinine and her estimated glomerular filtration rate is now 28 mL/min/1.73m^2. She has no history of minimal trauma vertebral fracture. Dental review last month was normal. She takes no glucocorticoids.

At her recent GP visit she was told her bone density is now good and denosumab could be stopped. Her next dose is due in 3 weeks. She has been referred to your clinic to discuss this. She has no back pain and no height loss. She is otherwise well. Vital signs are within normal limits.

Investigations today: corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 72 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone within reference range, and no evidence of vertebral fracture on lateral spine imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Denosumab history: Subcutaneous 60 mg every 6 months for 7 years; last DXA T-scores L-spine -1.8, femoral neck -2.0, total hip -1.9 (all improved from baseline)
data_table.Bloods: Corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.15-2.60); phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.5); 25-OH-D 72 nmol/L (greater than 50); PTH within reference range
data_table.Imaging: Lateral spine imaging: no vertebral fracture
data_table.Other: No back pain or height loss; no glucocorticoid use; dental review normal last month; next denosumab dose due in 3 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Stop denosumab now as T-scores have normalised and eGFR is less than 30
options.rationale: Discontinuing denosumab without follow-on antiresorptive therapy causes a rapid rebound in bone turnover with a rise in multiple vertebral fracture risk within 6 to 18 months, regardless of DXA improvement. eGFR less than 30 does not exempt her from rebound and mandates a plan (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Continue denosumab indefinitely at the standard 6 monthly dose without any change
options.rationale: Denosumab is not renally cleared and can be continued in advanced kidney disease, but hypocalcaemia risk rises markedly as eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m^2 requiring more intensive calcium and vitamin D monitoring; indefinite continuation without addressing renal-adjusted monitoring is not best practice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Continue denosumab; intensify calcium and vitamin D monitoring; specialist review
options.rationale: In a woman on 7 years denosumab with declining renal function, the immediate priorities are avoiding a missed dose (which triggers rebound within 6 months) and mitigating hypocalcaemia risk. Denosumab is not renally cleared so it can be continued in advanced CKD but hypocalcaemia risk rises sharply below eGFR 30; corrected calcium is checked 2 to 4 weeks after each dose. Zoledronic acid is contraindicated at eGFR less than 35, so any transition off denosumab requires specialist input (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Endocrine Society denosumab position statement).

options.text: Stop denosumab and give intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg as follow-on antiresorptive therapy
options.rationale: Zoledronic acid is contraindicated at eGFR less than 35 mL/min/1.73m^2 in Australia because of risk of acute kidney injury and hypocalcaemia; her eGFR of 28 excludes this option (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Stop denosumab and switch to teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneously daily as anabolic therapy
options.rationale: Teriparatide is actually contraindicated as sequential therapy after denosumab because it causes worsening cortical bone loss and does not protect against rebound vertebral fracture in this specific sequence; it is used after bisphosphonate, not after denosumab (Source: Endocrine Society denosumab position statement).

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a fully reversible RANKL inhibitor with rapid onset and rapid offset - within 6 to 12 months of a missed dose, bone turnover markers rebound above pre-treatment levels and multiple vertebral fracture risk rises sharply, particularly in patients who have been on denosumab for longer periods. Consequently, denosumab is either continued indefinitely (with attention to atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw at the long end, and hypocalcaemia risk at low eGFR) or transitioned with careful antiresorptive follow-on. In advanced CKD (eGFR less than 35) IV zoledronic acid is contraindicated, oral bisphosphonates have limited data, and specialist-directed strategies (continued denosumab with intensified monitoring, or raloxifene bridging) are the norm. Teriparatide after denosumab worsens cortical bone loss and does not prevent rebound vertebral fracture on its own.
key_points: Denosumab discontinuation causes rebound vertebral fracture within 6-18 months if no follow-on antiresorptive.
Missed doses (beyond 7 months) trigger rebound - never simply stop.
Zoledronic acid contraindicated at eGFR less than 35; oral bisphosphonate absorption poor in CKD.
Teriparatide after denosumab causes cortical bone loss - not a suitable follow-on.
explanation.pearls: Corrected calcium should be checked 2 to 4 weeks after each denosumab dose in patients with eGFR less than 30 - severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia is the most immediate risk and requires prompt oral or IV replacement with active vitamin D.

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated adult female urinary tract infection
stem:
You are the general practitioner. A 32 year old non-pregnant woman presents with 2 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever, no back pain, no vaginal discharge, and no nausea or vomiting.

She has had 2 uncomplicated urinary tract infections in the past 5 years, both successfully treated with a short antibiotic course. She has no history of pyelonephritis, no known urological anomaly, and no diabetes. She is sexually active with a regular male partner, uses condoms, and has no recent hospital admission or urinary catheterisation.

Examination shows suprapubic tenderness only. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Vital signs are within normal limits.

Urinalysis is positive for leukocytes and nitrites; midstream urine has been sent for culture. She has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Suprapubic tenderness only; no CVA tenderness; no vaginal discharge
data_table.History: 2 days dysuria, frequency, suprapubic discomfort; 2 previous uncomplicated UTIs in 5 years; not pregnant; no diabetes; no urological anomaly; no catheter or recent hospitalisation
data_table.Urinalysis: Leukocytes and nitrites positive; MSU sent for culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days as first line agent
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days is the current Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic first line empirical treatment for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women in Australia. It concentrates in urine, has good E. coli activity, and preserves fluoroquinolone and cephalosporin activity for more serious infections. It is contraindicated in eGFR less than 45 mL/min/1.73m^2 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally 12 hourly for 3 days as empirical treatment
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are second or third line in Australia for uncomplicated cystitis; the TGA and Therapeutic Guidelines restrict fluoroquinolones because of adverse effects (tendinopathy, aortic aneurysm/dissection, dysglycaemia, QT prolongation) and to preserve activity for serious infections (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally 12 hourly for 5 days as first line antibiotic
options.rationale: Cefalexin is a reasonable alternative when nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim are contraindicated, but it has higher rates of vaginal candidiasis, poorer eradication than nitrofurantoin, and broader spectrum than needed for uncomplicated cystitis; it is not first line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 500/125 mg orally 8 hourly for 5 days empirically
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate has poor coverage for E. coli in many Australian regions (resistance rates approaching 20%) and is not recommended empirically for cystitis; it may be used based on culture and susceptibility results (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Fosfomycin 3 g orally as a single dose without further follow-up antibiotic
options.rationale: Fosfomycin single dose is a reasonable alternative in some settings and internationally recommended, but in Australia Therapeutic Guidelines list it as second line where first line agents are contraindicated or where resistance patterns favour it; nitrofurantoin remains first line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated urinary tract infection in a non-pregnant, non-diabetic, catheter-naive woman without upper tract features (fever, flank pain, nausea/vomiting) can be treated empirically without waiting for culture. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic first line is nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days OR trimethoprim 300 mg orally nocte for 3 days. Nitrofurantoin is preferred where trimethoprim resistance is high and eGFR is above 45 mL/min/1.73m^2. Send MSU only for recurrent, complicated, or treatment-failure UTI (women); routinely for all men, pregnant women, and children. Reserve fluoroquinolones for pyelonephritis or documented multi-resistant organisms.
key_points: First line for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women: nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6 hourly x 5 days OR trimethoprim 300 mg nocte x 3 days.
Nitrofurantoin contraindicated at eGFR less than 45 mL/min/1.73m^2.
Reserve fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins for pyelonephritis, complicated UTI, or documented multi-resistance.
Send MSU for pregnancy, men, children, recurrent, or complicated UTI - routine culture not needed for isolated uncomplicated female cystitis.
explanation.pearls: Counsel that nitrofurantoin can cause brown-orange discolouration of the urine (harmless), avoid taking with milk (reduces absorption), and to complete the full 5 day course even if symptoms resolve within 48 hours.

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis empirical intravenous therapy
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 42 year old woman presents with 24 hours of right flank pain, high fever, rigors, nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has had dysuria and urinary frequency for 3 days beforehand.

She is not pregnant, has no diabetes, has no urinary catheter, and has no history of recurrent UTI or urological surgery. She has not recently travelled overseas or had recent hospital or aged care admission. She takes no antibiotics regularly.

Examination shows right costovertebral angle tenderness, dry mucous membranes, and mild suprapubic tenderness. Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 39.4.

Investigations: haemoglobin 128 g/L (120-160), white cells 18.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 320 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), urinalysis 3+ leukocytes 3+ nitrites 1+ blood no ketones. Urine and blood cultures have been drawn but no results yet. Bedside renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis or renal calculi. She has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 96/58, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.4
data_table.Examination: Right costovertebral angle tenderness; dry mucous membranes; mild suprapubic tenderness
data_table.History: 24 h right flank pain, high fever, rigors, nausea, one vomit; 3 days preceding dysuria and frequency; not pregnant; no diabetes; no catheter; no recent hospitalisation or overseas travel
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (120-160); WCC 18.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); platelets 320 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110); lactate 3.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
data_table.Urine: 3+ leukocytes, 3+ nitrites, 1+ blood, no ketones; cultures pending
data_table.Imaging: Bedside renal US: no hydronephrosis or calculi

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg 12 hourly for 7 days with GP review the next day
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate in a hypotensive tachycardic patient with lactate 3.2 mmol/L and vomiting; she meets sepsis criteria and needs IV antibiotics after cultures, IV fluids, and admission per CEC SEPSIS KILLS pathway (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; CEC SEPSIS KILLS NSW).

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6 hourly as empirical monotherapy
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is reserved for hospital-acquired urinary sepsis, patients with prior ESBL colonisation, or complicated UTI with sepsis unresponsive to first line; empirical use in community-acquired pyelonephritis is excessive spectrum and drives antimicrobial resistance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin plus metronidazole as empirical cover for pyelonephritis
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers gram positives (including MRSA) and metronidazole covers anaerobes; neither reliably covers the gram negative enteric organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) that dominate community-acquired pyelonephritis, so this regimen misses the target pathogens (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous meropenem 1 g 8 hourly as empirical monotherapy for pyelonephritis
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for suspected or confirmed extended-spectrum beta-lactamase infection, severe sepsis with recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, or previous ESBL colonisation; empirical use in community-acquired pyelonephritis drives carbapenem resistance and is not first line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: IV amoxicillin 2 g 6 hourly plus single dose gentamicin per AMH weight-adjusted schedule
options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic empirical regimen for adult community-acquired pyelonephritis in a septic patient is amoxicillin (or ampicillin) 2 g IV 6 hourly PLUS gentamicin at a weight-adjusted dose given as a single initial dose. Amoxicillin covers enterococci and the gentamicin covers gram negative enteric organisms including most community E. coli. Gentamicin is reviewed at 24 to 48 hours based on culture and creatinine; oral step-down at 48 to 72 hours if improving, for total 10 to 14 days (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; CEC SEPSIS KILLS NSW).

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis with sepsis physiology (hypotension, tachycardia, raised lactate) requires admission, IV fluid resuscitation per the hour-1 sepsis bundle, cultures, and empirical IV antibiotics. Australian first line for community-acquired pyelonephritis in a systemically unwell adult without recent healthcare contact or ESBL risk is amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin, targeting enterococci and gram negative enteric organisms. Gentamicin is single dose initially and reviewed at 24 to 48 hours; extended aminoglycoside courses require close monitoring for nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Oral step-down to a culture-guided oral agent (trimethoprim, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or ciprofloxacin) at 48 to 72 hours if clinical improvement, for total 10 to 14 days. Imaging with CT urogram is indicated if obstructing calculus, abscess, or ongoing sepsis despite 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics.
key_points: Septic pyelonephritis: admit, IV fluids, cultures, empirical IV antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines.
Empirical: amoxicillin (or ampicillin) 2 g IV 6 hourly PLUS single dose gentamicin.
Review gentamicin at 24-48 h; oral step-down at 48-72 h if improving; total 10-14 days.
Escalate to piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for suspected ESBL or hospital-acquired sepsis.
explanation.pearls: In pyelonephritis with sepsis, obtain a bedside renal ultrasound early in the emergency department to exclude obstruction - an obstructed infected kidney is a urological emergency requiring urgent decompression by percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteric stent regardless of antibiotic choice.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle and vasopressor initiation
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department. A 66 year old man presents with 12 hours of productive cough, fever, and progressive breathlessness. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 10 years ago and takes metformin only.

On arrival he is drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only. He has crackles and bronchial breathing at the right base. He has no chest pain, no calf pain, and no urinary symptoms. He has no known drug allergies.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 78/44, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 91% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 39.1. Peripheries are cool and capillary refill is 4 seconds. His qSOFA is 3.

Investigations drawn at arrival 20 minutes ago: haemoglobin 132 g/L (135-175), white cells 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110) (baseline 82), lactate 4.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0), venous blood gas pH 7.28, glucose 14.2 mmol/L, blood and sputum cultures drawn. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. IV access is established with 2 large bore cannulae. The first 30 mL/kg (approximately 2.1 L) crystalloid bolus has just completed over 45 minutes; his blood pressure is now 88/52 with pulse 122. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g plus azithromycin has been given. A central venous line is being placed.

data_table.Vital signs at arrival: Pulse 128, BP 78/44, RR 30, SpO2 91% on 6 L/min Hudson mask, temperature 39.1
data_table.After fluid bolus: BP 88/52, pulse 122 following 30 mL/kg crystalloid over 45 min
data_table.Examination: Drowsy oriented to person only; right basal crackles and bronchial breathing; cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 sec
data_table.Bloods: Hb 132 g/L (135-175); WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 82); lactate 4.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0); VBG pH 7.28; glucose 14.2 mmol/L
data_table.Cultures: Blood and sputum cultures drawn at arrival
data_table.Imaging: CXR right lower lobe consolidation
data_table.Given: IV ceftriaxone 2 g + azithromycin; 30 mL/kg crystalloid; central line being placed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in resuscitation?

options.text: Give further 2 L crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes before considering any vasopressor
options.rationale: He has already received 30 mL/kg with inadequate mean arterial pressure response (MAP 64 remains below 65 target); further large-volume crystalloid without vasopressor support risks worsening pulmonary oedema in septic cardiomyopathy and is not the SEPSIS KILLS pathway when hypotension persists post-bolus (Source: CEC SEPSIS KILLS NSW; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Commence intravenous dopamine 10 microgram/kg/minute peripherally as first line vasopressor
options.rationale: Dopamine is no longer recommended as first line vasopressor in septic shock (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) because of higher arrhythmia rates and higher mortality in randomised comparison with noradrenaline; noradrenaline is preferred (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg 6 hourly and hold vasopressor pending response
options.rationale: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (in divided doses or infusion) is added when catecholamine-refractory shock persists despite adequate vasopressor and fluid; it is not the immediate next step and does not replace vasopressor initiation (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Commence intravenous noradrenaline titrated to MAP at least 65 mmHg; involve ICU; repeat lactate
options.rationale: This is fluid-refractory septic shock (lactate greater than 4, persistent MAP less than 65 after 30 mL/kg crystalloid). The CEC SEPSIS KILLS NSW pathway and Surviving Sepsis Campaign both recommend noradrenaline as first line vasopressor titrated to MAP at least 65 mmHg, escalated oxygen support, ICU involvement, source control review, and lactate reassessment in 2 to 4 hours. Noradrenaline can be started peripherally through a large bore cannula while central access is placed (Source: CEC SEPSIS KILLS NSW; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Broaden antibiotic cover to meropenem plus vancomycin and defer further haemodynamic resuscitation
options.rationale: His antibiotic cover is appropriate for community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis and does not require empirical broadening in the first hour without a specific risk (recent hospitalisation, immunosuppression, ESBL colonisation); haemodynamic resuscitation cannot be deferred while considering antibiotic changes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

explanation.summary: The CEC SEPSIS KILLS NSW hour-1 bundle for septic shock is: measure lactate, take blood and other cultures before antibiotics if this does not delay them, give empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, give 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid for hypotension or lactate greater than 4 mmol/L, and start vasopressors if hypotension persists after fluid to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg. Noradrenaline is first line vasopressor; vasopressin can be added when catecholamine dose is escalating. Adrenaline is second line. IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day is added for catecholamine-refractory shock. Reassess lactate at 2 to 4 hours; if not clearing, review source control (drainage of abscess, removal of infected line, urinary obstruction relief). Corticosteroids do not replace vasopressor.
key_points: CEC SEPSIS KILLS hour-1: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor if persistent hypotension.
First line vasopressor: noradrenaline (not dopamine) titrated to MAP at least 65 mmHg.
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for catecholamine-refractory shock.
Reassess lactate 2-4 hourly and review source control if not clearing.
explanation.pearls: Noradrenaline can safely be started through a large bore peripheral cannula in a proximal vein (antecubital or larger) for up to a few hours while central access is being obtained - do not delay vasopressor start waiting for the central line.

subtopic_detail: Initial gait and balance assessment after a single non-syncopal fall
stem:
A 79-year-old woman attends your general practice after catching her foot on a rug at home last week. She landed on her hands and got up without help; she did not hit her head.

She lives alone in a single-storey house and manages her own shopping. Her only regular medicine is perindopril. She describes no light-headedness or blackout around the time of the fall.

Heart sounds are dual and her visual acuity is 6/9 in each eye with her glasses on. She steadies herself on the furniture as she walks across the consulting room. Both knees show crepitus and reduced range of movement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min regular, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg supine and 136/76 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol 1 g as required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial assessment?

options.text: Arrange a non-contrast CT brain to exclude an intracranial cause of falling
options.rationale: Imaging the brain is not indicated when there was no head strike, no loss of consciousness and no focal neurological sign; it would be appropriate if she were anticoagulated and had struck her head. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Request a 24-hour ambulatory electrocardiogram to look for an intermittent arrhythmia
options.rationale: Rhythm monitoring is reserved for falls with syncope, palpitations or an abnormal resting electrocardiogram; a witnessed trip with no prodrome does not meet that threshold. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Perform a timed up-and-go test with direct observation of her gait
options.rationale: Observed gait and balance testing is the first-line bedside assessment after a fall and takes under a minute; a timed up-and-go beyond 12 seconds identifies the mobility impairment that her furniture-walking already suggests and directs her to a strength and balance program. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Refer her for bone densitometry before undertaking any further clinical assessment
options.rationale: Densitometry addresses fracture risk, not fall risk, and does not change the immediate assessment; it is worth arranging later but it is not the initial step. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on comprehensive geriatric assessment)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on comprehensive geriatric assessment

options.text: Arrange an echocardiogram to assess her for structural valvular heart disease
options.rationale: Echocardiography is driven by an abnormal cardiac examination or syncope, and her heart sounds are normal with no murmur. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

explanation.summary: About a third of Australians over 65 fall each year, and a fall is a sentinel event that should trigger assessment even when no injury occurs. The initial assessment is clinical and bedside: gait and balance observation, lying and standing blood pressure, vision, footwear, medication review and a check for cognitive impairment. Investigations are added only when the history or examination points to a specific cause, such as syncope or focal neurology. Supervised strength and balance training is the intervention with the strongest evidence for reducing falls in community-dwelling older people. In context, a fall in an older person is a clinical event to be assessed at the bedside first, with investigations reserved for the features that the history and examination actually raise.
key_points: Observed gait and balance testing is the first step after any fall in an older person
A timed up-and-go beyond 12 seconds flags impaired mobility and predicts further falls
Investigations follow the history and examination; they do not replace them
Osteoarthritis and lower limb weakness are common, modifiable contributors to tripping falls
explanation.pearls: A timed up-and-go over 12 seconds identifies an older person who needs a supervised strength and balance program of at least 50 hours total to reduce fall rates.

sources.label: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls
ANZSGM position statement on comprehensive geriatric assessment

subtopic_detail: Primary prevention of delirium in a high-risk surgical admission
stem:
You are the admitting resident for an 83-year-old woman who has fractured the neck of her right femur after a fall at home. She is booked for hemiarthroplasty tomorrow afternoon.

Her daughter reports that she has been forgetting appointments for the past two years but still manages at home with prompting. She wears glasses and two hearing aids, neither of which came in with the ambulance. She has never had an episode of confusion in hospital before.

On assessment she is orientated to time, place and person, and her abbreviated mental test score is 8 out of 10. She has received one dose of intravenous morphine in the emergency department and reports her hip pain as 3 out of 10 at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, urea and creatinine all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action to reduce her risk of delirium?

options.text: Start a multicomponent program addressing orientation, sleep, mobility and sensory aids
options.rationale: Multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention is the only intervention shown to reduce incident delirium, cutting it by around a third in at-risk hospitalised older people; retrieving her glasses and hearing aids is part of that bundle. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Prescribe regular oral haloperidol 0.5 mg twice daily until after her operation
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no established role in preventing delirium and carry extrapyramidal, cardiac and mortality risk in older people; haloperidol is reserved for severe distress or risk of harm during established delirium. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Prescribe melatonin 2 mg nightly from admission until the day of discharge
options.rationale: Melatonin is sometimes used for sleep-wake disturbance but the prevention evidence is inconsistent and it is not a substitute for the multicomponent program. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Order a non-contrast CT brain and screen for occult infection before theatre
options.rationale: Investigations look for precipitants of an established delirium; she is currently cognitively intact and there is no clinical pointer to infection or intracranial pathology. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

options.text: Restrict her analgesia to paracetamol alone to avoid opioid-induced confusion after theatre
options.rationale: Undertreated pain is itself one of the strongest precipitants of postoperative delirium after hip fracture; the aim is adequate analgesia, ideally opioid-sparing with a regional block, not opioid avoidance. (Source: ACSQHC Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: ACSQHC Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard

explanation.summary: Delirium complicates up to half of hip fracture admissions in older people and is associated with longer stay, functional decline and increased mortality. Prevention is far more effective than treatment, and the evidence base sits with multicomponent programs that target the modifiable precipitants together: sensory aids, orientation, sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, hydration, bowel and bladder care, and pain control. Pharmacological prophylaxis, including antipsychotics and cholinesterase inhibitors, has not been shown to work. Surgery within 48 hours and regional analgesia both reduce delirium risk in hip fracture. In context, prevention bundles outperform every drug studied for delirium, and their components are cheap, ward-level and available on the day of admission.
key_points: Pre-existing cognitive impairment and sensory impairment are the dominant delirium risk factors
Multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention reduces incident delirium by roughly one third
No drug is recommended for delirium prophylaxis
Untreated pain precipitates delirium; opioid avoidance is not a prevention strategy
explanation.pearls: Getting a patient's own glasses and hearing aids to the bedside within the first 24 hours is one of the highest-yield single actions in delirium prevention, and applies before any drug is considered.

sources.label: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people
ACSQHC Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard

subtopic_detail: Hypoactive presentation misattributed to low mood
stem:
An 81-year-old man is on day 4 of treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. The nursing staff ask you to review him because he has become withdrawn, is eating very little and takes a long time to answer questions. They wonder whether he has become depressed since his wife died last year.

His daughter tells you he was managing his own finances and driving to bowls twice a week until this admission, and that he seemed himself when she visited on the day he came in.

At the bedside he is drowsy and loses the thread mid-sentence, but the nursing notes record him as alert and chatting at 8 am. He denies feeling sad and says he simply feels tired.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night and review his mood again in two weeks
options.rationale: Starting an antidepressant labels a fluctuating attentional disturbance as depression and adds a sedating drug that will worsen it; mirtazapine would be reasonable only once delirium has been excluded and low mood persists. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

options.text: Start regular quetiapine 12.5 mg at night to settle his fluctuating daytime state
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and are not indicated for the hypoactive form, where the patient is not distressed or at risk of harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an inpatient psychiatry consultation for assessment of a major depressive disorder
options.rationale: Referral defers the assessment that can be done at the bedside now, and psychomotor slowing with fluctuating attention is far more commonly delirium than depression in this setting. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Delirium)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Delirium

options.text: Screen for delirium at the bedside and review his precipitants and medications
options.rationale: Fluctuating attention with an acute change from his baseline in an unwell older inpatient is delirium until proven otherwise; a short validated screen such as the 4AT plus a search for precipitants, including hypoxaemia and newly charted drugs, is the correct immediate step. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Arrange an MRI brain and formal neuropsychological testing before any further treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is reserved for focal signs, head injury or unexplained failure to improve, and formal cognitive testing is invalid while attention fluctuates. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

explanation.summary: Hypoactive delirium is the most common form in older inpatients and the most frequently missed, because a quiet, withdrawn patient causes no trouble on the ward. It is routinely misread as depression, fatigue or dementia, and carries a worse prognosis than the hyperactive form. The discriminating features are acuity of onset, fluctuation through the day and inattention, which is why a structured screen at the bedside outperforms clinical impression. Once identified, management is to find and fix precipitants: infection, hypoxaemia, pain, constipation, urinary retention, dehydration and culprit medicines. In context, any acute change in an older inpatient's alertness or engagement deserves a structured attention test before it is given a psychiatric label.
key_points: Inattention plus acute onset and fluctuation defines delirium regardless of psychomotor activity
Hypoactive delirium is commonly mislabelled as depression in older inpatients
A collateral history establishes the cognitive baseline and the time course
Treatment is finding and correcting precipitants, not prescribing a sedative
explanation.pearls: The 4AT takes about two minutes, needs no special training, and a score of 4 or more indicates probable delirium; a score of 1 to 3 suggests cognitive impairment warranting further assessment.

sources.label: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people
RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Delirium

subtopic_detail: Searching for a reversible precipitant before sedating an agitated postoperative patient
stem:
You are the night resident called to an 84-year-old man on day 2 after a hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. Since midnight he has been pulling at his intravenous cannula and trying to climb over the bed rails. He was calm and orientated at the evening ward round.

He answers questions in single words and keeps reaching towards his lower abdomen. His indwelling catheter was removed at 10 am and the fluid balance chart records no urine output since.

His analgesia chart shows regular paracetamol only; the oxycodone charted in recovery was ceased when the spinal block wore off.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 156/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (<5), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give haloperidol 0.5 mg orally now, repeating in two hours if he remains agitated
options.rationale: Sedation without a search for the precipitant treats the observer's problem rather than the patient's, and an antipsychotic will worsen urinary retention through its anticholinergic effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Assess him for pain and urinary retention, including a bedside bladder scan
options.rationale: Retention and undertreated pain are the two most common and most rapidly reversible precipitants of postoperative delirium, and both are signposted here by the 14 hours without voiding and the ceased opioid; a bladder scan settles the first within minutes. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Give lorazepam 0.5 mg sublingually and nurse him in a low-stimulus single room
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines prolong and deepen delirium except when it is caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal, and add to his fall risk on a fresh hip. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

options.text: Send a urine culture and start empirical oral trimethoprim for presumed infection
options.rationale: He is afebrile with a normal white cell count and a postoperative C-reactive protein rise, so treating a presumed urinary infection risks anchoring on a positive dipstick that reflects colonisation. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Apply a physical restraint and arrange one-to-one nursing observation through the night
options.rationale: Physical restraint increases injury, delirium duration and mortality; one-to-one observation is a supportive measure but does not address the cause. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

explanation.summary: Agitation after hip surgery in an older person is delirium until proven otherwise, and the clinical task is to find the precipitant rather than to suppress the behaviour. The highest-yield reversible causes at the bedside are pain, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxaemia, and recently charted or recently ceased drugs. Non-pharmacological measures come first; an antipsychotic is reserved for severe distress or behaviour that puts the patient or others at risk, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Postoperative inflammatory markers rise predictably and should not be read as evidence of infection. In context, agitation in an older surgical patient is a signal to examine the patient rather than a prescription cue.
key_points: Pain and urinary retention are the two quickest reversible precipitants to exclude
Anticholinergic and sedative drugs both worsen delirium and retention
A positive urine dipstick in an afebrile older inpatient is usually colonisation
Physical restraint worsens outcomes and is not a management step
explanation.pearls: A post-void residual above 300 mL on bedside bladder scan warrants catheterisation, and relieving retention can settle postoperative agitation within the hour without any sedative.

sources.label: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

subtopic_detail: Palliative emergency with evolving cord signs
stem:
A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents to the emergency department with five days of mid-thoracic back pain that is worse when he lies flat and wakes him at night. For the past two days his legs have felt heavy and he has needed both arms to push himself out of a chair.

He takes slow-release morphine 20 mg twice daily, which has not helped the back pain, and abiraterone with prednisolone.

Power is 4 out of 5 for hip flexion on both sides with normal upper limb power. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. He last passed urine nine hours ago and says his bladder feels full.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 142/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), prostate specific antigen rising over three months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent CT of the lumbar spine and review it in the morning
options.rationale: CT is insensitive for epidural disease and the wrong region has been chosen given the thoracic pain and upper motor neurone signs; delay of a further night risks irreversible paraplegia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Increase his slow-release morphine and arrange an outpatient MRI within a fortnight
options.rationale: Escalating analgesia alone treats the symptom and ignores an evolving neurological deficit; outpatient timing is far outside the window in which function can be preserved. (Source: Palliative Care Australia)

options.text: Refer directly for urgent radiotherapy planning without further imaging of the spine
options.rationale: Radiotherapy is a definitive treatment here but cannot be planned without imaging to define the level and extent of disease. (Source: eviQ Radiation Oncology: Bone metastases (palliative))

options.text: Request urgent neurosurgical review after plain radiographs of the whole spine today
options.rationale: Plain films miss epidural compression in a substantial minority of cases and a normal film would falsely reassure; surgical review is appropriate but follows the MRI. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Give dexamethasone 16 mg orally now and arrange urgent MRI of the whole spine
options.rationale: High-dose corticosteroid started immediately reduces peritumoural oedema while whole-spine MRI, the definitive investigation, is arranged; whole-spine imaging is required because a third of patients have disease at more than one level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Metastatic epidural spinal cord compression affects around 5 per cent of patients with advanced cancer and is most common in prostate, breast and lung primaries. Back pain that is worse lying flat or at night precedes neurological signs by weeks, and that window is the opportunity to preserve function. Once weakness or sphincter disturbance appears, treatment is measured in hours: corticosteroid immediately, urgent whole-spine MRI, then radiotherapy or surgical decompression depending on stability, prognosis and radiosensitivity. Ambulatory status at the time of treatment is the single strongest predictor of walking afterwards. In context, a new neurological symptom in a patient with bone metastases compresses the timeline from weeks to hours.
key_points: Nocturnal or supine-worse back pain in known malignancy is the warning sign, not the weakness
Whole-spine MRI is required because multilevel disease is common
Dexamethasone is given before imaging, not after it
Function at the time of treatment predicts function afterwards
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 16 mg daily is started at the moment cord compression is suspected in cancer, and whole-spine MRI should be obtained within 24 hours because up to one third of patients have compression at a second level.

subtopic_detail: Responding to a family request for artificial hydration in the last days of life
stem:
An 88-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer is in a palliative care unit and is recognised to be in her last days of life. She has taken only sips of water for three days and has been unrousable since yesterday morning.

Her son has driven from interstate and is distressed. He asks you to start a drip, saying he cannot bear the thought of his mother dying thirsty.

Her lips and tongue are dry, she is not grimacing or restless, and there has been no jerking of her limbs. She is on a continuous subcutaneous infusion of morphine that has kept her settled for the past 48 hours, with no breakthrough doses required overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, SpO2 not measured, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema and no added breath sounds

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start subcutaneous fluid at one litre over 24 hours and review the effect daily
options.rationale: Subcutaneous fluid does not relieve the sensation of dry mouth and, in a dying patient with falling albumin, adds to respiratory secretions and peripheral oedema; a short trial is defensible only when dehydration is contributing to a reversible delirium. (Source: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit)
source_refs: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit

options.text: Start intravenous fluid at 80 mL per hour and monitor her for peripheral oedema
options.rationale: Intravenous access in a dying patient adds an invasive procedure without symptom benefit, and this rate exceeds what a failing circulation will distribute. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Provide regular mouth care and sips as tolerated, with explanation for family
options.rationale: The sensation of thirst in the dying is driven by dry oral mucosa rather than by circulating volume, so frequent mouth care relieves it while artificial hydration does not; explaining this to the family is part of the intervention, not an alternative to it. (Source: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit)
source_refs: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube for hydration and continue it until she is more alert
options.rationale: Nasogastric hydration is burdensome, carries aspiration risk in an unrousable patient, and the premise that she will become more alert is not realistic at this stage. (Source: Palliative Care Australia)

options.text: Check her urea and electrolytes and decide on fluid once the results are back
options.rationale: Blood tests in the last days of life do not change symptom-directed management and the venepuncture itself is a burden; investigation here substitutes for a conversation. (Source: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit)
source_refs: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit

explanation.summary: Requests for fluid at the end of life are usually requests for reassurance that the patient is not suffering, and they are best answered by addressing the symptom rather than the biochemistry. Randomised evidence in advanced cancer shows no improvement in thirst, delirium or survival with subcutaneous hydration, while fluid loading worsens respiratory secretions, oedema and vomiting in bowel obstruction. Mouth care every one to two hours, lip balm and ice chips are the effective treatment for dry mouth. A time-limited trial of subcutaneous fluid remains reasonable when dehydration is a plausible contributor to a potentially reversible delirium, with agreed review points. In context, a family's request at the end of life is usually a request for reassurance, and the answer is to treat the symptom and explain the reasoning rather than to order the intervention.
key_points: Thirst at the end of life correlates with dry mucosa, not with hydration status
Artificial hydration does not improve thirst, delirium or survival in advanced cancer
Excess fluid worsens secretions, oedema and obstructive vomiting
Explaining the reasoning to family is an essential part of the management
explanation.pearls: Mouth care every one to two hours with an oral sponge and lip balm relieves end-of-life thirst more reliably than a litre of subcutaneous fluid, and can be taught to family members who want to help.

sources.label: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit

subtopic_detail: Rationalising the medication chart when swallowing is lost in the last days of life
stem:
You visit a 90-year-old man in his residential aged care facility. He has metastatic lung cancer and over the past week has become bed-bound and drowsy, rousing only briefly when his daughter speaks to him. The facility staff report that this morning he coughed and spluttered on his crushed tablets and refused any further medicines.

His current chart is perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, alendronate 70 mg weekly, metformin 500 mg twice daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, slow-release morphine 20 mg twice daily and a daily macrogol sachet.

He grimaces when the staff roll him. His daughter and the facility both wish him to remain there rather than return to hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Rouses briefly to voice, unable to swallow safely, no urine output recorded for 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication plan?

options.text: Cease the whole oral regimen and chart subcutaneous morphine with as-required medicines
options.rationale: When swallowing is lost in the last days, medicines with no symptom benefit in that timeframe are stopped and essential symptom control is converted to the subcutaneous route, with as-required medicines charted in advance for pain, breathlessness, nausea, secretions and agitation. (Source: caring@home (palliative care subcutaneous medicines project))

options.text: Continue all his current medicines by crushing them and giving them in thickened fluid
options.rationale: Crushing in thickened fluid risks aspiration in a patient who is already coughing on his medicines, and none of the preventive agents will benefit him in the days remaining. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Palliative and end-of-life care)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Palliative and end-of-life care

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube so that his oral regimen can be continued without change
options.rationale: A nasogastric tube is a burdensome intervention to deliver drugs whose time to benefit is measured in years, and it conflicts with the plan to keep him where he is. (Source: Palliative Care Australia)

options.text: Cease only the statin and the bisphosphonate and continue the other oral medicines
options.rationale: Stopping the two longest time-to-benefit drugs is a step in the right direction but leaves him swallowing tablets he cannot manage and leaves his pain relief on an unusable route. (Source: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing)
source_refs: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing

options.text: Chart subcutaneous morphine but continue his oral cardiac and diabetes medicines unchanged
options.rationale: This gets the analgesic route right but retains antihypertensive and glucose-lowering agents that now risk symptomatic hypotension and hypoglycaemia in a patient with negligible intake. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Recognising dying triggers a specific set of prescribing decisions: stop what cannot help in the time remaining, convert what is still needed to a usable route, and chart anticipatory medicines before the symptom appears so that nobody has to wait for a doctor at 3 am. In Australian residential aged care the subcutaneous route is the standard alternative when swallowing fails, delivered by intermittent injection through an indwelling subcutaneous cannula or by continuous infusion. Statins, bisphosphonates, antihypertensives, oral hypoglycaemics and antiplatelets all have time to benefit far longer than the prognosis and are ceased. Anticipatory prescribing is what most often prevents an avoidable transfer to hospital. In context, recognising that a patient is dying is itself a prescribing decision, and every drug on the chart is then judged against the time that remains.
key_points: Time to benefit is the test for continuing any preventive medicine at the end of life
Loss of swallowing is the trigger to convert essential symptom medicines to subcutaneous
Anticipatory as-required medicines cover pain, breathlessness, nausea, secretions and agitation
Continuing antihypertensives and hypoglycaemics in a dying patient causes symptoms, not benefit
explanation.pearls: An indwelling subcutaneous cannula sited in the upper chest or abdomen can be left in place for up to seven days and lets aged care staff give as-required symptom medicines without repeated needle insertions.

sources.label: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Palliative and end-of-life care
Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing

subtopic_detail: Predictable procedure-related pain on a stable background opioid
stem:
A 74-year-old woman with locally advanced breast cancer attends the community palliative care clinic. Her chest wall wound is dressed twice weekly by the district nurses.

For the past month her background pain has been controlled on her current slow-release opioid, and she has used no more than one breakthrough dose a week. She reads and gardens between dressing changes and is not drowsy.

During each dressing change she cries out and asks the nurses to stop, and she is tearful for the rest of the visit. Within 20 minutes of the dressing being finished she is comfortable again and back to her usual self.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Slow-release morphine 30 mg twice daily, immediate-release morphine 10 mg as required, macrogol daily, paracetamol 1 g four times daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her analgesia?

options.text: Increase her slow-release morphine to 60 mg twice daily and review weekly
options.rationale: Doubling the background dose to cover two brief episodes a week will sedate her for the 165 hours in between, when her pain is already controlled. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

options.text: Add regular paracetamol four times daily and continue her current opioid regimen
options.rationale: She is already taking regular paracetamol, so this changes nothing and leaves the procedural pain untreated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add slow-release oxycodone 10 mg twice daily alongside her current morphine dose
options.rationale: Running two long-acting opioids together compounds the background dose and makes future titration and conversion unsafe; if a rotation were indicated, one drug would replace the other. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

options.text: Give an immediate-release morphine dose half an hour before each dressing
