explanation.summary: Infection of ascitic fluid without a surgically treatable source occurs in a substantial minority of cirrhotic patients admitted with ascites and carries a mortality of 20 to 30 per cent even when treated. It presents non-specifically with fever, abdominal pain, worsening encephalopathy, renal impairment or simply clinical deterioration, so any cirrhotic patient with ascites who deteriorates gets a diagnostic tap before antibiotics. The diagnosis rests on an ascitic polymorphonuclear count of 250 per cubic millimetre or more, and culture in blood culture bottles at the bedside improves yield but remains negative in many cases. Intravenous albumin at 1.5 g per kg on day one and 1 g per kg on day three reduces hepatorenal syndrome and death in those with a creatinine above 88 micromol/L, urea above 10.7 mmol/L or bilirubin above 68 micromol/L. After recovery, long term quinolone prophylaxis is indicated and the patient should be assessed for transplantation.
key_points: A tap before antibiotics is mandatory in any deteriorating cirrhotic with ascites
A neutrophil count of 250 or more makes the diagnosis regardless of culture
Culture is negative in around 40 per cent of genuine episodes
Albumin reduces renal failure and death in those with impaired renal or hepatic markers
Secondary quinolone prophylaxis follows every treated episode
explanation.pearls: A neutrophil count at or above 250 per cubic millimetre with more than one organism on Gram stain, a protein above 10 g/L, glucose below 2.8 mmol/L or a raised lactate dehydrogenase suggests a perforated viscus instead, and that combination needs urgent imaging and a surgical opinion rather than antibiotics alone.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management, medical

subtopic_detail: Three centimetre adrenal nodule with low unenhanced attenuation found incidentally on imaging for renal colic in a normotensive man
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52 year old man who had a computed tomogram last week for left sided loin pain. He passed a 4 mm stone and the pain has settled, but the report also describes a 3 cm nodule in the right adrenal gland with an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units and a smooth margin.

He feels well. He has never had hypertension and his blood pressure today is normal, and he has had no episodes of sweating, headache or palpitations. He has not gained weight, has no striae and no proximal weakness, and there is no easy bruising. He has never had a cancer diagnosis and has never smoked. His potassium and renal function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg per square metre, no supraclavicular fat pad, no purple striae, no proximal myopathy, no hirsutism, no palpable abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography showing a 3 cm right adrenal nodule with an unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units and smooth margins, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange image guided percutaneous biopsy of the nodule to obtain a tissue diagnosis
options.rationale: Biopsy of an adrenal nodule before catecholamine excess has been excluded can provoke a hypertensive crisis, and it cannot distinguish an adenoma from an adrenocortical carcinoma in any case. It is reserved for suspected metastasis in a patient with a known primary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic adrenalectomy because the nodule measures more than 3 cm
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated for a functioning nodule or for radiological features suggesting malignancy, with size thresholds usually set around 4 cm alongside those features. A smooth 3 cm lesion with low attenuation has benign imaging characteristics. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adrenal incidentaloma)

options.text: Screen for hormone excess with an overnight dexamethasone test and metanephrines
options.rationale: Every adrenal nodule found incidentally needs assessment of whether it secretes, and the minimum screen is a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test for cortisol excess and plasma free or urinary metanephrines for catecholamine excess, with an aldosterone to renin ratio added only if there is hypertension or hypokalaemia. Both of his relevant clinical prompts are absent, but function still has to be excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Repeat the computed tomogram in twelve months with no biochemical testing now
options.rationale: Imaging follow up alone misses the subclinical cortisol excess that is present in a meaningful minority and that carries measurable cardiovascular and bone consequences. The near pair is that surveillance is part of the plan but never a substitute for the functional screen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange positron emission tomography to characterise the nodule before further testing
options.rationale: Functional imaging is used when the lesion has indeterminate attenuation or when metastatic disease is suspected, since it addresses malignancy rather than hormone secretion. Attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units already indicates a lipid rich benign lesion. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Adrenal incidentaloma)

explanation.summary: Adrenal nodules are found on around four per cent of abdominal computed tomograms and the proportion rises with age, so the practical question is never whether the lesion is there but whether it secretes and whether it is malignant. Unenhanced attenuation answers most of the malignancy question, since a value at or below 10 Hounsfield units indicates a lipid rich adenoma with a very high negative predictive value, while higher attenuation, irregular margins, size above 4 cm and rapid growth all raise concern. The functional question is answered biochemically in every case, because mild autonomous cortisol secretion is frequently present without any of the classical physical signs and is associated with hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis and increased mortality. Catecholamine excess must be excluded before any biopsy or operation, and mineralocorticoid screening is added when there is hypertension or hypokalaemia.
key_points: Attenuation of 10 Hounsfield units or less indicates a lipid rich adenoma
Every incidental nodule needs a functional screen regardless of symptoms
Mild autonomous cortisol secretion occurs without classical physical signs
Exclude catecholamine excess before any biopsy or operation
Mineralocorticoid screening is added only with hypertension or hypokalaemia
explanation.pearls: A serum cortisol above 50 nanomoles per litre the morning after 1 mg of dexamethasone indicates failure of suppression, and this finding in an apparently asymptomatic patient predicts a higher rate of vertebral fracture and cardiovascular events over the following decade.

subtopic_detail: Abrupt severe hypertension with rising creatinine, fragmented red cells and a bland urinary sediment weeks after starting moderate dose corticosteroid for early diffuse skin thickening
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 44 year old woman admitted with a three day headache and blurred vision. Her hands and forearms have become tight and thickened over the past eight months and she has had cold painful colour changes in her fingers for a year.

Her rheumatologist started prednisolone 20 mg daily five weeks ago for troublesome joint pain. She has no fever, no rash and no recent diarrhoea. Her blood pressure was 126/78 mmHg at her clinic visit two months ago and is now 214/122 mmHg. Her creatinine has risen from 68 to 212 micromol/L over three weeks. The blood film shows fragmented red cells and her platelet count has fallen, while her urinalysis shows no casts and only a trace of protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 214/122 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Skin thickening over the fingers, hands and forearms extending above the elbows, digital pitting scars, bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy, no rash, no synovitis, chest clear, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 212 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 68 three weeks ago, haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-155), platelets 84 x10^9/L (150-450), blood film with fragmented red cells, lactate dehydrogenase 620 units per litre (120-250), urinalysis with trace protein and no red cell casts, ADAMTS13 activity 62 per cent, antinuclear antibody positive with a nucleolar pattern

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Start an intravenous labetalol infusion and titrate against the blood pressure response
options.rationale: Beta blockade lowers the pressure without addressing the renin driven mechanism and may worsen the digital vasospasm, and controlling the number by another route does not protect the kidney. The near pair is that both lower blood pressure but only one alters the disease process. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic sclerosis)

options.text: Start oral captopril and increase the dose rapidly against the blood pressure response
options.rationale: Abrupt severe hypertension with a rising creatinine and a microangiopathic blood picture in early diffuse skin disease, particularly after corticosteroid exposure, is treated with a short acting angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor titrated aggressively, and this is the intervention that changed the outcome of the condition from almost uniformly fatal. A rising creatinine after starting it is expected and is not a reason to stop. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic sclerosis)

options.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and increase her maintenance prednisolone
options.rationale: Corticosteroid at doses of 15 mg daily or more is a recognised precipitant of this complication rather than a treatment for it, and escalating the dose compounds the problem. The steroid should be reduced as fast as her other disease allows. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic sclerosis)

options.text: Start daily plasma exchange and give intravenous methylprednisolone alongside it
options.rationale: Plasma exchange treats thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which is suggested by fragmented cells and thrombocytopenia but requires severely deficient ADAMTS13 activity below 10 per cent. Her activity of 62 per cent excludes it, which is the finding that redirects the whole assessment. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic microangiopathy)

options.text: Start intravenous cyclophosphamide and arrange urgent percutaneous renal biopsy
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is used for progressive interstitial lung disease in this condition and has no role in the renal complication, and biopsy in the setting of severe hypertension and thrombocytopenia carries substantial bleeding risk. The diagnosis is clinical and treatment must not wait for tissue. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic sclerosis)

explanation.summary: Renal crisis complicates diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis in around one in ten patients and clusters in the first four to five years of disease, when the skin changes are progressing most rapidly. The classical picture is the abrupt onset of accelerated hypertension with an acute rise in creatinine, often accompanied by a microangiopathic anaemia with thrombocytopenia, headache, visual disturbance and sometimes seizures or pulmonary oedema. The urinary sediment is characteristically bland, which separates it from a glomerulonephritis, and the microangiopathy leads many to consider thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura until ADAMTS13 activity comes back normal. Corticosteroid exposure at 15 mg of prednisolone daily or more is the best established precipitant, which is why steroids are used sparingly and at the lowest effective dose in early diffuse disease. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibition, titrated rapidly regardless of an initial rise in creatinine, transformed the prognosis, though a proportion still require dialysis, and recovery of renal function can occur over many months.
key_points: Risk is highest in early diffuse skin disease within the first five years
Prednisolone at 15 mg daily or more is the best established precipitant
A bland urinary sediment separates this from glomerulonephritis
Normal ADAMTS13 activity excludes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Continue the inhibitor despite an early rise in creatinine
explanation.pearls: Patients with early diffuse disease should be taught to check their blood pressure at home two or three times a week, because the hypertension precedes symptoms and a reading above 150/90 in this group is an indication to present the same day rather than to wait for the next clinic.

subtopic_detail: Uniform swelling of an entire toe with asymmetric large joint involvement, nail pitting and negative rheumatoid serology after six weeks of an anti-inflammatory drug
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar seeing a 38 year old man referred with four months of joint pain. His left second toe is swollen along its whole length rather than at one joint, his right knee has been swollen for six weeks, and the terminal joints of two fingers on his left hand are painful and swollen.

He has an hour of stiffness in the morning. He has had scaly patches behind both ears for years that he treats with a cream from the pharmacy, and his nails have small pits and lifting at the free edge. He has taken naproxen twice daily for six weeks with only partial relief and continues to miss work as a carpenter. He has no back pain and no eye symptoms, and he has had no diarrhoea or urethral discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uniform swelling of the entire left second toe, swollen right knee with an effusion, synovitis of two distal interphalangeal joints on the left hand, nail pitting and onycholysis of four fingernails, scaly erythematous plaques behind both ears and at the umbilicus, no sacroiliac tenderness, no conjunctival injection
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 42 mm/h (less than 20), C reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), rheumatoid factor negative, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative, urate 0.32 mmol/L (0.20-0.45), radiographs of the hands and feet with soft tissue swelling and no erosion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue the anti-inflammatory drug at a higher dose and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Anti-inflammatory drugs relieve symptoms but do not alter progression, and six weeks of an adequate dose with continuing synovitis and time off work has already defined the failure. Escalating the dose buys nothing while joint damage accrues. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor as the first disease modifying treatment
options.rationale: Biological therapy is highly effective and is the right answer for predominant axial disease or for failure of conventional agents, and Australian subsidy requires a documented trial of conventional therapy first. The near pair is that both are disease modifying, but only one is the entry point here. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis)

options.text: Start weekly methotrexate with folic acid and review his response in eight weeks
options.rationale: Persistent peripheral synovitis with whole digit swelling and skin and nail disease that has failed six weeks of an anti-inflammatory drug requires a disease modifying agent, and methotrexate is the usual Australian first choice because it treats both the joints and the skin. Early treatment prevents the erosive damage that has not yet appeared on his films. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis)

options.text: Start allopurinol after checking his renal function and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy treats crystal arthritis, which presents with recurrent acute attacks resolving between episodes rather than persistent swelling of an entire digit, and his urate is mid range. Chronic synovitis with nail and skin changes is a different process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Inject the swollen knee with corticosteroid and review his joint symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Intra-articular injection is a useful adjunct for a dominant single joint and will help the knee, but it leaves the toe, the finger joints and the skin untreated. Systemic disease needs systemic treatment. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis)

explanation.summary: Inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis affects up to a third of people with the skin disease and often presents before the skin is recognised, particularly when the plaques are hidden behind the ears, at the umbilicus, in the natal cleft or on the scalp. Its distinguishing features are asymmetry, involvement of the terminal finger joints, uniform swelling of an entire digit from combined joint and tendon sheath inflammation, inflammation at tendon insertions, nail pitting and onycholysis, and negative rheumatoid serology. Presentations range from an oligoarticular peripheral pattern through a symmetrical polyarthritis to predominantly spinal disease, and each pattern drives a different treatment choice. Conventional agents including methotrexate, leflunomide and sulfasalazine are used for peripheral disease, while axial disease responds poorly to them and moves directly to biological therapy. Screening for the arthritis in every patient with psoriasis matters because delay of even six months is associated with worse radiographic and functional outcomes.
key_points: Uniform swelling of a whole digit reflects joint and tendon sheath inflammation
Terminal finger joint involvement and nail changes are characteristic
Rheumatoid serology is typically negative in this condition
Conventional agents work for peripheral but not for axial disease
Hidden plaques behind the ears or at the umbilicus are easily missed
explanation.pearls: Nail involvement is present in about 80 per cent of people with this arthritis compared with roughly 40 per cent of those with skin psoriasis alone, so pitting and onycholysis in a patient with joint pain should raise the diagnosis even before the plaques are found.

subtopic_detail: Large unilateral exudative pleural effusion in a former power station worker that has recurred after drainage with malignant cells not found on two separate fluid samples
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old man with three months of increasing breathlessness and a constant dull ache in the right side of his chest that does not change with breathing. He worked as a fitter at a power station through the 1970s and 1980s and has never smoked.

He has lost 5 kg. A right sided effusion was drained four weeks ago, 1.4 litres came off and he felt better for a fortnight, but it has reaccumulated. Fluid sent on that occasion and again last week was exudative by protein and lactate dehydrogenase criteria, with no organisms on culture and no malignant cells on cytology on either sample. His chest computed tomogram shows nodular thickening of the pleura with involvement of the mediastinal surface.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Reduced expansion on the right with stony dullness to the mid zone and absent breath sounds, trachea central, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid protein 48 g/L with serum protein 68 g/L, pleural lactate dehydrogenase 420 units per litre with serum 240 units per litre, fluid cytology negative on two occasions, fluid culture and acid fast bacilli negative, computed tomography showing nodular circumferential pleural thickening including the mediastinal pleura with a moderate effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Refer for local anaesthetic thoracoscopy with direct biopsy of the thickened pleura
options.rationale: Cytology is negative in around half of pleural malignancies of this type, so two negative samples do not exclude it and repeated taps waste months, while nodular mediastinal pleural thickening on imaging demands tissue. Thoracoscopy gives the highest diagnostic yield and allows pleurodesis at the same sitting. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Refer for a third large volume aspiration with cytology on a larger fluid sample
options.rationale: Sending more fluid raises the yield only marginally after two adequate negative samples and the near pair is that both approaches sample the same disease, one from the fluid and one from the pleura itself. A third negative result would leave him where he started weeks later. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Refer for blind percutaneous pleural biopsy using an Abrams needle at the bedside
options.rationale: Blind sampling has a much lower yield for malignant disease because the involvement is patchy, and it retains a place mainly where tuberculous pleuritis is likely and the pleura is diffusely involved. Image guided or direct vision sampling has superseded it. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Refer for bronchoscopy with washings and transbronchial biopsy of the right lower lobe
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is useful when there is a mass or collapse suggesting an endobronchial lesion, and his imaging shows pleural rather than parenchymal disease. It would sample the wrong compartment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Refer for talc pleurodesis through an intercostal catheter without further sampling
options.rationale: Pleurodesis controls recurrent fluid and will be needed, but performing it without a diagnosis removes the effusion that makes further sampling possible and forecloses treatment decisions and compensation claims. Tissue first, then palliation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

explanation.summary: A unilateral exudative effusion with weight loss and non-pleuritic chest wall pain in someone with a history of asbestos exposure should be pursued to a tissue diagnosis, because cytology alone misses a large proportion of pleural malignancy and is particularly insensitive for mesothelial tumours. Australia has among the highest rates of asbestos related disease in the world and the latency from exposure is typically 30 to 40 years, so occupational histories from decades earlier remain relevant, including trades, power generation, shipbuilding, construction and home renovation. Computed tomography features that raise concern are circumferential nodular pleural thickening, thickening greater than 1 cm, involvement of the mediastinal pleural surface and volume loss on the affected side. Thoracoscopy under local anaesthetic combines the highest diagnostic yield with the opportunity to perform pleurodesis, and a confirmed diagnosis matters not only for treatment but for access to Australian statutory compensation schemes.
key_points: Pleural fluid cytology misses around half of mesothelial malignancies
Nodular, mediastinal or over 1 cm pleural thickening indicates malignancy
Latency after asbestos exposure is typically thirty to forty years
Thoracoscopy has the highest yield and allows simultaneous pleurodesis
A tissue diagnosis underpins access to compensation schemes
explanation.pearls: Chest wall pain that is constant and dull rather than pleuritic, in a patient with an effusion, points towards pleural infiltration rather than inflammation, and it is the symptom most often present at the first presentation of asbestos related pleural malignancy.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease
BMJ Best Practice: Malignant pleural mesothelioma

subtopic_detail: New firm persistent unilateral parotid enlargement over three months in a woman with established sicca syndrome, a falling C4 and a new paraprotein
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 57 year old woman with an eight year history of dry eyes and dry mouth, anti Ro antibodies and a previous labial gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic infiltration. She manages with artificial tears and frequent sips of water.

For the past three months her left parotid has been enlarging. It is not painful, it does not fluctuate with meals, and it has not settled with a course of antibiotics from her general practitioner. She has had drenching night sweats twice in the last month and has lost 3 kg. Her complement C4 has fallen from 0.22 to 0.08 g/L over a year and a small monoclonal band has appeared on serum electrophoresis that was not present previously.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Firm non-tender 4 cm left parotid enlargement with no overlying erythema and no facial nerve weakness, right parotid normal, no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable, spleen tip palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, dry buccal mucosa with dental caries
data_table.Investigations: Complement C4 0.08 g/L (0.15-0.45) fallen from 0.22, complement C3 0.94 g/L (0.80-1.80), small immunoglobulin M kappa monoclonal band on serum electrophoresis that was absent a year ago, anti Ro antibody positive, rheumatoid factor positive at high titre, lactate dehydrogenase 310 units per litre (120-250), full blood count with lymphocytes 1.1 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a further course of antibiotics with sialogogues and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Bacterial infection of the gland is painful, tender and erythematous, often with pus expressible from the duct, and it responds to antibiotics within days. Three months of painless firm enlargement that has already failed antibiotics is a different problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start hydroxychloroquine for her underlying disease and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine helps fatigue and arthralgia in this condition but has no effect on glandular swelling of this kind, and the near pair is that treating the autoimmune disease feels responsive while the actual concern goes unassessed for a quarter of a year. Systemic symptoms and a new band demand explanation first. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone at a moderate dose and review the size of the gland in one month
options.rationale: Corticosteroid shrinks lymphoid tissue temporarily and can obscure the histology if biopsy follows, making the tissue diagnosis harder to obtain. It also treats the wrong process if the swelling is neoplastic. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Arrange a repeat labial salivary gland biopsy to reassess the degree of infiltration
options.rationale: Minor gland biopsy is used to establish the original diagnosis and would simply reconfirm what is already known, since it samples a different site from the enlarging gland. Sampling must target the abnormal tissue. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent imaging of the gland with biopsy of the enlarged parotid tissue
options.rationale: Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement in this condition, especially with a falling C4, a new monoclonal band, splenomegaly and systemic symptoms, is the recognised presentation of lymphoma arising in the gland, and tissue is required to make that diagnosis. Imaging maps the gland and the biopsy is taken with care for the facial nerve. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

explanation.summary: Primary Sjogren syndrome carries a risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma some 15 to 20 times that of the general population, the highest of any autoimmune rheumatic disease, and the tumour most often arises in the affected salivary tissue as a marginal zone lymphoma. The predictors that should prompt vigilance are persistent or recurrent parotid enlargement, palpable purpura, low complement C4, cryoglobulins, a monoclonal band, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and lymphopenia, and they accumulate over years rather than appearing suddenly. Because the risk is lifelong, these features are checked at annual review rather than only when the patient complains. Ordinary glandular swelling in the condition is usually bilateral, episodic and modest, so a unilateral gland that keeps growing over months is the presentation that changes the diagnosis. Treatment of the underlying dryness remains symptomatic with tear and saliva substitutes, muscarinic agonists and meticulous dental care.
key_points: Lymphoma risk is roughly fifteen to twenty times the background rate
Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement is the classic warning sign
Low C4, cryoglobulins and a monoclonal band are validated predictors
Corticosteroid before biopsy can obscure the histological diagnosis
Annual review should actively look for these predictors
explanation.pearls: A falling complement C4 in this condition is not a marker of disease activity in the way it is in lupus but a predictor of lymphoma, so a C4 that drifts down over successive annual reviews should trigger examination of the glands, nodes and spleen rather than an increase in immunosuppression.

subtopic_detail: Enlarging hands and feet with new snoring, carpal tunnel symptoms and difficult to control diabetes and hypertension in a man in his forties
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46 year old man whose wedding ring had to be cut off last year and who has gone up three shoe sizes in a decade. He has come today about numbness in both hands that wakes him at night.

His wife says he has begun snoring heavily and stops breathing at times. His blood pressure has needed a third agent this year and his glycated haemoglobin has risen from 7.1 to 8.4 per cent despite metformin and good adherence. He has a persistent headache most mornings and has noticed his teeth feel further apart. Photographs from ten years ago show a visibly different face with finer features and a less prominent jaw.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Broad spade like hands with doughy soft tissue, prominent supraorbital ridges and mandible with interdental separation, macroglossia, Tinel sign positive at both wrists, visual fields full to confrontation, no galactorrhoea, skin tags over the neck
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 8.4 per cent, fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), calcium and thyroid function within normal limits, prolactin 620 milliunits per litre (less than 500)

lead_in: Which investigation should be performed first?

options.text: Measure a random serum growth hormone level on a morning fasting blood sample
options.rationale: Pulsatile secretion means a random level can be low in someone with the disease and high in someone without it, so it neither confirms nor excludes anything. The near pair matters because both tests interrogate the same axis but only one gives an integrated measure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 against an age matched reference range
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses and a single random level is uninterpretable, whereas insulin like growth factor 1 integrates secretion over days and is the recommended initial screening test, compared against an age matched range because the normal value falls with age. An elevated result then leads to a suppression test and imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure growth hormone during a 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test this week
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress during a glucose load is the confirmatory test, performed after an elevated integrated marker rather than as the entry point, and it is cumbersome in a man whose glucose control is already poor. Sequence matters here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: Imaging localises a lesion once excess secretion is proven biochemically, and performed first it will find incidental pituitary lesions in around one in ten people, committing him to surgery for a possibly irrelevant finding. Biochemistry precedes anatomy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography to quantify the severity of his sleep disordered breathing
options.rationale: A sleep study will be needed because obstructive sleep apnoea affects most patients with this condition and contributes to the hypertension, but it characterises a consequence rather than the cause. Treating the apnoea alone leaves the driving process untouched. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Obstructive sleep apnoea)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Obstructive sleep apnoea

explanation.summary: Growth hormone excess in adults develops so gradually that the median delay from first symptom to diagnosis is close to a decade, and patients usually present with a consequence rather than with the appearance, most often carpal tunnel syndrome, sleep apnoea, difficult hypertension, new or worsening diabetes, arthropathy or headache. Serial photographs are among the most useful bedside tools because the facial change is invisible to those who see the person daily. The biochemical sequence is an integrated marker first, then failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 microgram per litre during an oral glucose load, then pituitary imaging, and roughly a third of tumours co-secrete prolactin so a modestly raised prolactin fits rather than contradicts the diagnosis. Treatment is transsphenoidal surgery in the first instance, with somatostatin analogues, dopamine agonists, a growth hormone receptor antagonist and radiotherapy available for residual disease, and the excess mortality is largely reversed when hormone levels are normalised. Colonoscopy is recommended at diagnosis because of the increased incidence of colonic neoplasia.
key_points: Presentation is usually via a complication rather than the appearance itself
Old photographs demonstrate the change better than any examination finding
Insulin like growth factor 1 is the screening test, not random growth hormone
Failure to suppress during a glucose load is the confirmatory test
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation because incidental lesions are common
explanation.pearls: A modestly raised prolactin supports rather than argues against the diagnosis, because about a third of these tumours co-secrete prolactin or compress the stalk, and treating the raised prolactin as the primary problem is a well described route to a missed diagnosis.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Obstructive sleep apnoea

subtopic_detail: Palpable purpura on the legs with arthralgia and a mildly abnormal sensory examination in a man with untreated chronic hepatitis C, a low C4 and a positive rheumatoid factor
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 55 year old man with six months of crops of raised purple spots over both shins that come and go, leaving brown staining behind. He also has aching in both wrists and a numb patch over the outer side of the left calf.

He was diagnosed with hepatitis C fifteen years ago after injecting drug use, has never been treated and has not injected for twelve years. He has no ascites, no encephalopathy and no varices on a gastroscopy last year, and his transient elastography reading was in the mild fibrosis range. His creatinine is normal and his urine shows no blood or protein. He takes no regular medication and has had no recent infection or new drug exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over both shins with haemosiderin staining, no ulceration or digital infarcts, wrists tender with no synovitis, reduced pinprick sensation over the left lateral calf with normal power and reflexes, no hepatosplenomegaly, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis C antibody positive with detectable hepatitis C ribonucleic acid at 1.2 million international units per millilitre, genotype 1a, complement C4 0.04 g/L (0.15-0.45), C3 0.98 g/L (0.80-1.80), rheumatoid factor positive at high titre, cryoglobulins detected, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), urinalysis with no blood or protein, albumin 39 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.9-1.3), platelets 186 x10^9/L (150-450)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start rituximab infusions first and add antiviral therapy once the vasculitis settles
options.rationale: Antibody depleting therapy is added for rapidly progressive kidney involvement, ulcerating skin disease or severe neuropathy, none of which he has, and the near pair matters because both treat the same disease at different levels of severity. His creatinine is normal with a bland urinalysis. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis C treatment)

options.text: Start high dose oral prednisolone alone and taper it over the next several months
options.rationale: Corticosteroid alone suppresses the inflammation while leaving viral replication unchecked and can increase the viral load, so it is used only as short term adjunctive therapy in severe disease. It also carries metabolic and bone costs over months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start pegylated interferon with ribavirin for a twenty four week treatment course
options.rationale: Interferon based regimens were superseded in Australia in 2016 by all oral direct acting agents, which are better tolerated, shorter and far more effective. Interferon can also aggravate the neuropathy. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis C treatment)

options.text: Start direct acting antiviral therapy for the underlying chronic viral infection
options.rationale: The vasculitis is driven by immune complexes containing the virus, so clearing the virus resolves the skin, joint and nerve involvement in the majority, and direct acting agents achieve cure rates above 95 per cent with a short oral course. With normal renal function and no organ threatening disease, antiviral therapy alone is the first step. (Source: ASHM: Hepatitis C treatment)

options.text: Start colchicine with graduated compression stockings and review him in three months
options.rationale: Colchicine and compression are symptomatic measures for cutaneous small vessel inflammation of unclear cause, and they do nothing for the antigen driving the immune complexes. His nerve involvement also indicates disease beyond the skin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Chronic hepatitis C causes disease well beyond the liver, and the best characterised extrahepatic manifestation is a small vessel vasculitis driven by circulating immune complexes containing the virus, rheumatoid factor and immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold. The clinical triad is palpable purpura, arthralgia and fatigue, with peripheral neuropathy and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis marking more extensive disease, and the laboratory signature is a strikingly low complement C4 with a relatively preserved C3 and a positive rheumatoid factor in someone who does not have rheumatoid arthritis. All Australians with chronic hepatitis C are eligible for subsidised direct acting antiviral therapy prescribed in general practice with cure rates above 95 per cent, and eradication resolves the vasculitis in most, though a minority have persistent disease requiring immunosuppression. Severe organ threatening presentations receive rituximab, with or without plasma exchange and corticosteroid, alongside or ahead of antiviral treatment.
key_points: A very low C4 with a preserved C3 is the characteristic complement pattern
Positive rheumatoid factor without rheumatoid arthritis is a useful clue
Purpura, arthralgia and fatigue form the classic triad
Clearing the virus resolves the vasculitis in most patients
Rituximab is reserved for organ threatening kidney, skin or nerve disease
explanation.pearls: Blood for cryoglobulins must reach the laboratory in a prewarmed tube kept at 37 degrees Celsius until the serum is separated, because a sample allowed to cool in transit precipitates the protein into the clot and returns a false negative, which is the commonest reason this diagnosis is missed.

subtopic_detail: Rings and linear furrows seen at endoscopy for a food bolus obstruction in a young man with atopy and no biopsies taken
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 24 year old man the morning after an emergency endoscopy for a steak bolus that had been stuck for four hours. The bolus was pushed through and he is now eating without difficulty.

On questioning he tells you he has cut steak and crusty bread out of his diet over the past two years, always drinks water with meals and is usually the last to finish. He has asthma, hay fever and childhood eczema. The endoscopy report describes concentric rings and fine longitudinal furrows through the whole oesophagus, with no stricture, no ulceration and no mass, and records that no biopsies were taken.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well and comfortable, body mass index 23 kg per square metre, abdomen soft and non tender, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count shows an eosinophil count of 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, C reactive protein within normal limits, endoscopy reports concentric rings and linear furrows throughout the oesophagus with no stricture, ulceration or mass and no biopsies taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and review his symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Acid suppression is a legitimate treatment for this condition, but starting it before biopsies are taken suppresses the mucosal eosinophilia and can make the histology uninterpretable for months. Treatment follows the tissue diagnosis rather than preceding it. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)

options.text: Arrange a barium swallow and review once the study has been reported
options.rationale: Contrast radiology can show a narrowed or ringed oesophagus but cannot establish a diagnosis that is defined histologically, and the endoscopic appearance is already known. It adds a step without answering the question. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)

options.text: Repeat endoscopy and biopsy the proximal and distal oesophagus
options.rationale: The diagnosis rests on finding at least 15 eosinophils per high power field, and because the infiltrate is patchy, multiple biopsies from both the proximal and distal oesophagus are needed rather than distal samples alone. Endoscopic appearances of rings and furrows are suggestive but are neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or exclude the condition. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)

options.text: Arrange oesophageal manometry and review once it has been reported
options.rationale: Manometry investigates a motility disorder, which would present with dysphagia to liquids as well as solids rather than with solid food impaction and dietary adaptation. Motility abnormalities can occur here but do not define the disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Start a topical corticosteroid and review his symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Swallowed topical corticosteroid is effective first line therapy once the diagnosis is confirmed, but giving it first removes the histological evidence needed to confirm it. The near pair here is that this becomes the right answer at the visit after the biopsies return. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is now the commonest cause of food bolus obstruction in young adults, and the history is typically one of years of silent adaptation, with patients cutting out meat and bread, chewing excessively, drinking with every mouthful and eating slowly, long before they present acutely. Most patients have a personal or family history of atopy, and a peripheral eosinophilia is common but neither sensitive nor specific. Diagnosis requires at least 15 eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy in a patient with symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction, and because the infiltrate is patchy and can spare the distal oesophagus, several biopsies are taken from both proximal and distal sites. Treatment options are a proton pump inhibitor, swallowed topical corticosteroid, or an elimination diet, with dilatation reserved for fibrostenotic strictures, and each is assessed by repeat histology rather than by symptoms alone.
key_points: Dietary adaptation over years often precedes the first bolus obstruction
Endoscopic rings and furrows are suggestive but not diagnostic
At least 15 eosinophils per high power field is the histological threshold
Patchy involvement means proximal and distal biopsies are both required
Acid suppression before biopsy can render the histology uninterpretable
explanation.pearls: Response to treatment in this condition is judged on repeat histology rather than on symptoms, because patients who feel better frequently have persistent mucosal eosinophilia that goes on to produce the fibrotic strictures responsible for long term dysphagia.

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of dysphagia to solids and liquids together with regurgitation of undigested food and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 52 year old woman with eighteen months of food sticking behind the sternum. She says it has been just as hard to get water down as bread from the very beginning, and that she has to stand up and arch her back to make things go through.

She brings up undigested food from hours earlier, sometimes onto her pillow, and has lost 6 kg. A proton pump inhibitor prescribed by her general practitioner made no difference. Endoscopy performed last week showed retained food and saliva in the oesophagus with a snug but passable gastro-oesophageal junction, normal mucosa and no mass, and gastric and duodenal biopsies were normal. A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly to a narrow segment at the junction.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg per square metre having fallen from 23, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non tender, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, endoscopy shows retained food and saliva with normal mucosa, a passable gastro-oesophageal junction and no mass, gastric and duodenal biopsies normal, barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly at the junction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset with regurgitation of undigested food and a smoothly tapering junction on contrast study points to a motility disorder, and high resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard, demonstrating failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter with absent peristalsis. Manometry also assigns the subtype, which determines which treatment is likely to work. (Source: GESA: Achalasia clinical update)

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and review her symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: She has already had an adequate trial without benefit, which is expected because the obstruction is functional rather than acid related. Repeating an ineffective treatment delays the diagnosis while she continues to lose weight. (Source: GESA: Achalasia clinical update)

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic myotomy without further physiological testing
options.rationale: Manometric subtype predicts the response to myotomy, and operating without it risks a poor outcome in the subtype that responds least well. Definitive treatment follows rather than replaces the physiological diagnosis. (Source: GESA: Achalasia clinical update)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest and abdomen, then reassess
options.rationale: Weight loss and a narrowed junction do raise the possibility of a tumour producing the same picture, but endoscopy with a normal mucosa and normal biopsies has already addressed that. Imaging is added when the history is short, the patient older, or the endoscopist finds the junction difficult to traverse. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Achalasia)

options.text: Refer for oesophageal dilatation at the next available endoscopy list
options.rationale: Pneumatic dilatation is one of the definitive treatments but it carries a perforation risk and should not be undertaken before the diagnosis and subtype are established. The near pair here is a peptic stricture, where dilatation without manometry would be entirely appropriate. (Source: GESA: Achalasia clinical update)

explanation.summary: The single most useful discriminator in dysphagia is whether liquids are affected from the beginning, since a mechanical obstruction narrows progressively and therefore troubles solids first, whereas a motility disorder impairs transit of both from the outset. Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, so the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and peristalsis is lost, producing dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain and weight loss over months to years. Endoscopy is performed in every case to exclude pseudoachalasia, in which a tumour at the junction reproduces the picture, and a short history, older age or a junction that is difficult to pass should raise that suspicion. High resolution manometry confirms the diagnosis and classifies it into three subtypes, which matters because the subtype predicts response to pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic myotomy and peroral endoscopic myotomy.
key_points: Dysphagia to liquids from the outset indicates a motility rather than mechanical cause
Failure to respond to acid suppression is expected in this condition
Endoscopy is mandatory to exclude a tumour mimicking the disorder
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and assigns the subtype
Subtype predicts which definitive treatment is likely to succeed
explanation.pearls: Patients with achalasia carry a small but lifelong increased risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma from chronic stasis, and this risk persists after successful myotomy, so new or changed dysphagia in a treated patient warrants repeat endoscopy rather than an assumption that the myotomy has failed.

subtopic_detail: An incidental immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein of 12 g per litre with a normal free light chain ratio and normal end organ markers
stem:
You are the physician reviewing a 68 year old man referred after a paraprotein was found on blood tests ordered because of a raised total protein on a routine panel. He feels entirely well, walks 5 km most days and has kept his weight steady.

He reports no bone pain and no night sweats. On examination the lymph node areas, the abdomen and the axial skeleton are unremarkable, and pinprick and vibration sense are intact in both feet. Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation identifies an immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein of 12 g/L, the serum free light chain ratio is within the normal range, and his haemoglobin, calcium and creatinine are all normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bony tenderness, no peripheral neuropathy on testing pinprick and vibration sense, no macroglossia
data_table.Investigations: Immunoglobulin G kappa paraprotein 12 g/L, serum free light chain ratio within the normal range, haemoglobin 142 g/L (130 to 180), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110), immunoglobulin A and immunoglobulin M within normal limits, urine protein electrophoresis shows no Bence Jones protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for bone marrow biopsy and skeletal survey before further review
options.rationale: Marrow examination and imaging are indicated when the paraprotein is 15 g/L or more, is not immunoglobulin G, or the free light chain ratio is abnormal, or where there is any evidence of end organ damage, none of which applies here. Investigating a low risk finding exposes him to an invasive procedure with a very low yield. (Source: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement)
source_refs: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement

options.text: Start bortezomib based therapy and refer to the haematology clinic
options.rationale: Treatment is directed at symptomatic myeloma defined by anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment or bone lesions, and he has none of these. Treating an asymptomatic paraprotein exposes him to toxicity without evidence of benefit. (Source: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement)
source_refs: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement

options.text: Arrange whole body magnetic resonance imaging and review in six months
options.rationale: Whole body imaging is used to detect occult bone disease in smouldering myeloma or where risk features are present, and it is not part of the assessment of a low risk paraprotein. The near pair here is a patient with the same paraprotein but bone pain, in whom imaging would be essential. (Source: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement)
source_refs: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement

options.text: Repeat the paraprotein, blood count and renal function in six months
options.rationale: An immunoglobulin G paraprotein below 15 g/L with a normal free light chain ratio and no end organ damage carries none of the three recognised risk factors, so this is low risk monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and the management is surveillance without marrow examination. Repeating at six months confirms stability, after which the interval extends to annually, because the risk of progression is only about 1 per cent per year. (Source: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement)
source_refs: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement

options.text: Reassure him that no further monitoring of any kind will be needed
options.rationale: The risk of progression is low but it is cumulative and lifelong rather than disappearing with time, so discharge without surveillance is not appropriate. Patients who stop being monitored typically present later with established end organ damage. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance

explanation.summary: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is present in around 3 per cent of people over 50 and rises steeply with age, so it is a common incidental finding rather than a rare one. Risk of progression to myeloma or a related disorder is stratified on three factors, namely a paraprotein of 15 g/L or more, a non immunoglobulin G isotype, and an abnormal serum free light chain ratio, with progression risk rising from about 1 per cent per year when none is present to substantially higher when all three are. Patients with no risk factors and no evidence of end organ damage do not need a bone marrow biopsy or skeletal imaging, and are monitored with periodic blood tests, whereas anyone with a risk factor or any suggestion of damage is referred for full staging. The end organ features that define myeloma are hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and bone lesions, and any of them converts surveillance into urgent investigation.
key_points: Risk stratification uses paraprotein size, isotype and free light chain ratio
Low risk disease needs neither marrow biopsy nor skeletal imaging
Progression risk is about 1 per cent per year and is lifelong
Hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia or bone lesions define myeloma
Surveillance intervals lengthen once stability has been demonstrated
explanation.pearls: An immunoglobulin M paraprotein progresses to Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma rather than to myeloma, so the isotype changes not only the risk but which disease is being watched for and therefore which symptoms are asked about at review.

sources.label: HSANZ: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance position statement
BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance

subtopic_detail: A haematocrit of 0.58 with itching after a hot shower and a palpable spleen in a man whose oxygen saturation is normal
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 58 year old man referred because three separate blood counts over four months have shown a haemoglobin around 190 g/L. He mentions in passing that he has developed intense itching for about half an hour after a hot shower, which he has been treating with moisturiser.

He has never smoked, sleeps well without snoring and his partner has not noticed any pauses in his breathing. He is not on testosterone or any other medication. His oxygen saturation is 98 per cent breathing room air, both at rest and after walking briskly along the corridor. On examination his face is plethoric and the splenic edge is palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Plethoric facies, conjunctival suffusion, splenic edge palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin, no hepatomegaly, no clubbing, no cyanosis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 192 g/L (130 to 180), haematocrit 0.58 (0.40 to 0.52), white cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 512 x10^9/L (150 to 400), ferritin 18 micrograms/L (30 to 300), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, oxygen saturation 98 per cent at rest and on exertion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry on 2 consecutive nights and review the report
options.rationale: Nocturnal hypoxaemia is a genuine cause of secondary erythrocytosis but does not explain a raised white cell count, a raised platelet count or splenomegaly. He also has no snoring, no witnessed apnoeas and normal daytime saturations. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Measure serum erythropoietin and test for the JAK2 V617F mutation
options.rationale: A raised haematocrit accompanied by leucocytosis, thrombocytosis, splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus and a low ferritin points to a primary marrow disorder rather than a hypoxic drive, and a suppressed erythropoietin with the JAK2 V617F mutation confirms it. That mutation is present in around 95 per cent of cases, so the pair of tests both establishes the diagnosis and excludes the secondary causes in which erythropoietin is normal or raised. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Arrange renal tract ultrasound and review once it has been reported
options.rationale: An erythropoietin secreting renal lesion is a rare secondary cause worth excluding when erythropoietin is inappropriately raised, but imaging before measuring the hormone inverts the sequence. It also would not account for the splenomegaly or the other cell lines. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Polycythaemia vera)

options.text: Start venesection of 450 mL and review his blood count in four weeks
options.rationale: Venesection is the mainstay of treatment once the diagnosis is made, and it is urgent where there is hyperviscosity or thrombosis, but starting it before the cause is established removes the diagnostic information the counts carry. The near pair here is a patient presenting with a thrombotic event, in whom venesection would proceed alongside the diagnostic testing. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

options.text: Repeat the full blood count in three months and review him after that
options.rationale: Three counts over four months have already established that the elevation is persistent rather than a transient or apparent change from dehydration. Further delay leaves him at ongoing thrombotic risk without a diagnosis. (Source: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management)
source_refs: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

explanation.summary: A persistently raised haematocrit is separated into apparent erythrocytosis from a reduced plasma volume, secondary erythrocytosis driven by erythropoietin, and primary disease of the marrow. The clinical features that point to primary disease are involvement of more than one cell line, splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus, and a low ferritin reflecting iron consumption by an expanded red cell mass in someone who is not bleeding. Testing a suppressed erythropoietin alongside JAK2 mutation analysis distinguishes these efficiently, since secondary causes such as chronic hypoxaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, high altitude, smoking, testosterone use and erythropoietin secreting tumours all leave erythropoietin normal or raised. The clinical importance lies in thrombosis, which is the main cause of morbidity and death, and treatment combines venesection to a target haematocrit below 0.45, low dose aspirin, and cytoreduction for those at higher risk.
key_points: Involvement of more than one cell line argues against a secondary cause
A low ferritin without bleeding reflects consumption by an expanded red cell mass
Aquagenic pruritus is a characteristic and often overlooked symptom
Suppressed erythropoietin separates primary from secondary erythrocytosis
Thrombosis is the dominant clinical risk and drives treatment decisions
explanation.pearls: The target for venesection is a haematocrit below 0.45, and iron should not be replaced even though the ferritin falls, because iron deficiency is the mechanism by which venesection restrains red cell production.

sources.label: HSANZ: Myeloproliferative neoplasms diagnosis and management

subtopic_detail: An acutely hot swollen knee in a seventy six year old with chondrocalcinosis on radiograph and a temperature of 37.8 degrees
stem:
You are the physician called to see a 76 year old woman who developed a painful swollen right knee overnight. She has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each settling over a week or so with anti inflammatory tablets.

She takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and has stage 3 chronic kidney disease. There has been no injury and no recent travel. The knee is warm, swollen and tense with a large effusion, and she will not let you flex it beyond 20 degrees. A radiograph taken in the emergency department shows fine linear calcification within the meniscal cartilage of both knees. Her temperature is 37.8 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee warm and swollen with a tense effusion and patellar tap, flexion limited to 20 degrees by pain, overlying skin intact with no break or cellulitis, no other joint involved, no tophi
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 118 mg/L (less than 5), serum urate 0.34 mmol/L (0.16 to 0.42), creatinine 128 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 42 mL/min/1.73m2, knee radiograph shows linear calcification of the meniscal cartilage in both knees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Aspirate the joint for cell count, culture and polarised light microscopy
options.rationale: A hot swollen joint with fever and a C reactive protein of 118 must be sampled, because crystal arthritis and infection are clinically indistinguishable and can coexist, and the fluid provides the cell count, the Gram stain and culture, and the crystal identification in a single procedure. Aspiration also relieves the pressure of a tense effusion and is done before antibiotics wherever possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start oral colchicine and review her again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Colchicine is a reasonable treatment for the crystal arthritis suggested by the radiograph, but treating without sampling risks masking a septic joint that destroys cartilage within days. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate of 42 also requires dose reduction and makes toxicity more likely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone and review her again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is effective for crystal arthritis in a patient with renal impairment, but giving it before the joint is sampled both obscures the diagnosis and would worsen an unrecognised infection. The near pair here is that this becomes the treatment of choice once infection has been excluded on the fluid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin and review her response overnight
options.rationale: Antibiotics before aspiration substantially reduce the yield of synovial culture, leaving her on a prolonged empirical course with no organism and no drainage. Treatment for infection begins immediately after the sample is taken rather than instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee and then reassess
options.rationale: Imaging cannot distinguish an infected effusion from a sterile inflammatory one, which is the question that must be answered tonight. It also delays a procedure that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease produces acute attacks that closely resemble gout, most often in the knee or wrist of an older patient, and chondrocalcinosis on a radiograph supports it but is a common incidental finding with age and does not prove that it is the cause of the current attack. The essential principle in any acutely hot swollen joint is that septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically, that crystals and infection can coexist in the same joint, and that the joint is therefore aspirated before treatment. Synovial fluid is sent for cell count and differential, Gram stain and culture, and polarised light microscopy, where rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals identify pyrophosphate and needle shaped strongly negatively birefringent crystals identify urate. Treatment once infection is excluded is with a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug, colchicine or a corticosteroid given orally or into the joint, chosen according to comorbidity, and an underlying metabolic association such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism or hypomagnesaemia should be considered in younger patients or polyarticular disease.
key_points: Chondrocalcinosis supports but does not prove crystal arthritis as the current cause
Crystal arthritis and septic arthritis can occur in the same joint
Aspiration answers the infective and the crystal question in one procedure
Antibiotics and corticosteroids both obscure the diagnosis if given first
Renal impairment restricts the choice of anti inflammatory treatment
explanation.pearls: Chondrocalcinosis appearing in a patient under 55, or affecting several joints, should prompt testing for haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia, since in that age group the deposition is far more likely to be secondary to a metabolic disorder than age related.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

subtopic_detail: A magnetic wide based gait with urinary urgency and ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy in a seventy four year old
stem:
You are the geriatrician seeing a 74 year old man whose wife says that over eighteen months he has begun to walk as though his feet are stuck to the floor, taking small shuffling steps and turning in several small movements rather than one.

He has had three falls and now uses a walking frame. He has started to reach the toilet too late, which distresses him greatly. His wife reports that he is slower to answer questions and has lost interest in the newspaper, but he still recognises visitors, manages his own medications with a dosette box and has had no visual hallucinations. There is no resting tremor and no rigidity, and his arm swing is preserved. Computed tomography of the brain reports enlarged lateral ventricles with an Evans index of 0.36 and only mild cortical sulcal widening.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop
data_table.Examination: Wide based short stepped gait with reduced foot clearance and en bloc turning, preserved arm swing, no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, power and reflexes normal, plantar responses downgoing, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 23 out of 30 with losses in executive and attention items
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, syphilis serology negative, computed tomography of the brain reports an Evans index of 0.36 with mild cortical sulcal widening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and review his cognition in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are used in Alzheimer disease and in dementia with Lewy bodies, in which memory or visual hallucinations dominate and gait disturbance appears late. Here gait came first and the cognitive change is executive rather than amnestic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer directly for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion without further tests
options.rationale: Only a proportion of patients with this radiological and clinical picture improve after shunting, and the operation carries risks of infection, subdural haemorrhage and shunt failure. Predicting response before committing to surgery is what the preliminary testing is for. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start an anticholinergic for the urinary symptoms and review in three months
options.rationale: Treating the bladder in isolation addresses one element of a triad while leaving the gait and cognition untouched, and anticholinergic agents worsen cognition in an older patient with existing impairment. The near pair here is isolated overactive bladder without gait or cognitive change, where this would be reasonable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange a large volume lumbar puncture with gait assessment before and after
options.rationale: Removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid and comparing timed gait measures before and afterwards is the standard way of predicting which patients will benefit from shunting, and a clear improvement identifies the group most likely to respond. Objective timed testing rather than global impression is used because the improvement can be modest and short lived. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange carotid duplex ultrasound and review once it has been reported
options.rationale: Carotid imaging is directed at stroke risk in a patient with a territorial ischaemic event or carotid bruit, neither of which is present, and asymptomatic carotid disease would not produce this gradually progressive triad. It does not address the question being asked. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with a triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment, and it matters disproportionately because it is one of the few causes of cognitive decline in older people that can be substantially improved by treatment. Gait is characteristically the first and most prominent feature, described as magnetic, wide based and short stepped with turning en bloc, and the pattern in which gait clearly precedes cognitive change is the most useful clinical discriminator from Alzheimer disease and from dementia with Lewy bodies. Imaging shows ventricular enlargement disproportionate to cortical atrophy, usually quantified by an Evans index above 0.3, but this appearance alone is neither sufficient nor specific. Selection for surgery therefore rests on demonstrating a response to cerebrospinal fluid removal, either by a high volume lumbar puncture with objective gait timing or by extended lumbar drainage, since gait is the domain most likely to improve after shunting while cognition responds least.
key_points: Gait disturbance precedes and dominates the cognitive change
The gait is wide based and magnetic with en bloc turning
An Evans index above 0.3 supports but does not establish the diagnosis
Response to cerebrospinal fluid removal predicts response to shunting
Gait improves most after shunting and cognition least
explanation.pearls: Preserved arm swing with a short stepped shuffling gait distinguishes this condition from Parkinson disease, where arm swing is reduced early, and it is the reason the gait has been described as a lower body parkinsonism that spares the upper limbs.

sources.label: Dementia Australia: Diagnosis and assessment of dementia
BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness and bone pain with an alkaline phosphatase of 340 and a bone density T score of minus 2.8 in a housebound woman
stem:
You are the physician seeing a 64 year old woman referred after a bone density scan requested by her general practitioner returned a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.8. The referral asks you to start treatment for osteoporosis.

She has been largely housebound for three years since a stroke left her with a mild left hemiparesis, and she goes outside only for appointments. She describes aching in her hips and thighs and says she now has to push up on the arms of the chair to stand. Her gait is waddling when she walks with her stick. She takes no calcium or vitamin D supplement and eats little dairy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild residual left hemiparesis, proximal weakness of hip flexion and shoulder abduction graded 4 out of 5 bilaterally, waddling gait, tenderness on firm pressure over both anterior tibiae and the sternum, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.08 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50), alkaline phosphatase 340 U/L (30 to 110), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 11 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone markedly elevated, creatinine 74 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2, liver function tests otherwise within normal limits, bone density lumbar spine T score minus 2.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start alendronate weekly and review her bone density in two years
options.rationale: Starting an antiresorptive agent in a patient with profound vitamin D deficiency and a calcium at the lower limit risks precipitating symptomatic hypocalcaemia, and the low bone density here reflects defective mineralisation rather than the bone loss that bisphosphonates treat. Vitamin D status must be corrected before any antiresorptive is considered. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm

options.text: Start denosumab six monthly and review her bone density in two years
options.rationale: Denosumab carries the same hypocalcaemia hazard as other antiresorptive agents and a greater one, since its effect cannot be withdrawn once the injection is given. Correcting vitamin D and calcium before starting it is a specific requirement of its use. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm

options.text: Replace vitamin D and calcium, then reassess before any antiresorptive
options.rationale: Proximal myopathy, bone pain, a low calcium and phosphate, a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase and a 25 hydroxyvitamin D of 11 nmol/L describe osteomalacia, in which the bone is undermineralised rather than reduced in quantity, and repletion alone improves symptoms, biochemistry and measured bone density. Reassessment after repletion determines whether any residual bone density deficit warrants specific osteoporosis treatment. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management algorithm

options.text: Start teriparatide daily and review her bone density in eighteen months
