You are the nephrology registrar seeing a 24 year old man referred after three episodes of visibly bloody urine over two years. He describes the urine as being the colour of cola, and on each occasion it began on the second day of a sore throat and cleared within four days.

He is well between episodes with no oedema, no rash and no joint pain. His blood pressure today is 142/88 mmHg on two readings. Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts. His protein excretion is 1.2 g per day, creatinine is 96 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 88 mL/min/1.73m2, and his albumin is within normal limits. Complement C3 and C4 are both within normal limits, antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are negative, hepatitis B and C serology are negative, and his antistreptolysin O titre is not raised. Renal ultrasound shows two normal sized kidneys with no structural abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No peripheral or periorbital oedema, no rash or purpura, no synovitis, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft with no renal angle tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, urinary protein 1.2 g per day, creatinine 96 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73m2, albumin within normal limits, complement C3 and C4 within normal limits, antinuclear antibody negative, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative, antistreptolysin O titre not raised, renal ultrasound showing two normal sized kidneys

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start high dose prednisolone and cyclophosphamide without delay
options.rationale: Aggressive immunosuppression is the treatment for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescents and falling renal function, and his function is preserved with a two year history of intermittent episodes. Commencing cyclophosphamide before histology risks substantial toxicity including infertility and malignancy for a disease that may not require it. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Arrange cystoscopy and computed tomography urography to exclude a tumour
options.rationale: Urological imaging and cystoscopy are the pathway for non-glomerular bleeding, and dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts and proteinuria localise the bleeding to the glomerulus. Urothelial malignancy would also be very unlikely at 24 with no smoking history or risk factors. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Start renin angiotensin blockade and refer for renal biopsy
options.rationale: Recurrent visible haematuria synchronous with upper respiratory infection, glomerular red cells with casts, proteinuria above 1 g per day, hypertension and normal complement is the classic presentation of immunoglobulin A nephropathy, and biopsy is indicated because proteinuria at this level with hypertension identifies a patient at risk of progression whose histological features guide immunosuppression. Renin angiotensin blockade is started immediately with a blood pressure and proteinuria target, since it is the intervention that most reduces long term progression. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Give a course of penicillin and repeat his urinalysis in six weeks
options.rationale: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows a pharyngitis by one to three weeks with a low C3 and a raised antistreptolysin O titre, whereas his haematuria begins within a day or two of the sore throat with normal complement and no serological evidence of streptococcal infection. That latency difference is the classic discriminator between the two conditions. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Reassure him and arrange annual urinalysis and blood pressure checks
options.rationale: Annual surveillance is appropriate for isolated microscopic haematuria with normal blood pressure, no proteinuria and normal renal function, and he fails all three of those conditions. Proteinuria above 1 g per day with hypertension marks him as being at genuine risk of progressive loss of function. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of glomerulonephritis)

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and typically presents in young adults either with recurrent visible haematuria coinciding with mucosal infection or, more insidiously, with microscopic haematuria and proteinuria found incidentally. The characteristic timing of synpharyngitic haematuria, beginning within a day or two of an upper respiratory infection, distinguishes it from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows a latent period of one to three weeks and is accompanied by a depressed C3 and serological evidence of recent streptococcal infection. The initial task with any haematuria is to establish whether it is glomerular, and dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and proteinuria settle that question and redirect the patient away from urological investigation. Prognosis is far from uniformly benign, with a substantial minority progressing to end stage kidney disease over decades, and the adverse markers are proteinuria above 1 g per day, hypertension, reduced function at presentation and specific histological features. Management centres on optimised supportive care with renin angiotensin blockade titrated to reduce proteinuria, blood pressure control, sodium restriction and sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibition, with immunosuppression reserved for those at high risk of progression despite this.
key_points: Haematuria within a day or two of pharyngitis suggests immunoglobulin A nephropathy
Post-streptococcal disease has a one to three week latency and a low C3
Dysmorphic red cells with casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Proteinuria above 1 g per day with hypertension predicts progression
Renin angiotensin blockade titrated to proteinuria is the mainstay of treatment
explanation.pearls: Proteinuria is both the strongest prognostic marker and the treatment target, and reducing it below 1 g per day, ideally towards 0.5 g, is associated with markedly better long term outcomes, which is why the dose of renin angiotensin blockade is titrated to the proteinuria rather than to blood pressure alone.

subtopic_detail: Eight loose motions a day with abdominal cramping six weeks into pembrolizumab for melanoma, with negative stool cultures
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 64 year old man in the oncology day unit who has had six weeks of pembrolizumab for metastatic melanoma. Over the past five days he has developed increasingly frequent loose motions, now eight a day including two overnight, with cramping lower abdominal pain.

He reports a small amount of blood mixed through the stool yesterday. He has not travelled, has taken no antibiotics and no one else at home is unwell. His vital signs are pulse 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. His abdomen is soft with generalised tenderness but no guarding or rebound, and bowel sounds are present. Stool cultures and Clostridioides difficile toxin testing are negative, his C reactive protein is 68 mg/L (less than 5), and computed tomography of the abdomen shows diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and no perforation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness, no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds present, mucous membranes slightly dry, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Stool culture negative, Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, stool viral panel negative, C reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 32 g/L (35 to 50), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), creatinine 94 micromol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, morning cortisol within normal limits, computed tomography of the abdomen showing diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement and no perforation or free gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start oral vancomycin empirically and repeat the toxin assay in 48 hours
options.rationale: Empirical treatment for Clostridioides difficile is not justified when the toxin assay is negative, he has had no antibiotic exposure, and a non-infective cause is strongly supported by the timing and imaging. Repeat testing would delay effective treatment of the actual pathology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for urgent colonoscopy with biopsies before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Endoscopy is useful to confirm the diagnosis and assess severity and can be performed once treatment is under way, but it carries perforation risk in an inflamed colon and should not delay corticosteroid therapy in a patient with grade 3 disease. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is most valuable where the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain or the response to steroids is poor. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management

options.text: Replace potassium, give intravenous fluids and reassess him in 24 hours
options.rationale: Correcting hypokalaemia and volume depletion is necessary supportive care but as the sole plan it leaves the immune mediated inflammation untreated for a further day during which perforation can occur. Supportive measures accompany rather than substitute for immunosuppression. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management

options.text: Give loperamide regularly and continue his immunotherapy as scheduled
options.rationale: Antimotility agents mask the severity of immune mediated colitis and delay recognition of a condition that can progress to perforation, so they are avoided once colitis is suspected. Loperamide is appropriate for mild grade 1 diarrhoea without abdominal pain, blood or raised inflammatory markers. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management

options.text: Withhold the immunotherapy and start high dose corticosteroid treatment
options.rationale: Eight stools a day with abdominal pain, blood and radiological colitis on a checkpoint inhibitor, with infection excluded, is grade 3 immune mediated colitis requiring the drug to be withheld and corticosteroid started at 1 to 2 mg/kg of prednisolone equivalent, usually intravenously with admission at this severity. Infliximab or vedolizumab is added if there is no response within about three days, and a rapid steroid taper over at least four to six weeks follows improvement. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management

explanation.summary: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have transformed the treatment of melanoma, lung and renal cancers and other tumours, and their characteristic toxicities arise from loss of immune tolerance rather than from cytotoxicity, so they behave like autoimmune disease and respond to immunosuppression. Colitis is among the commonest and most dangerous, more frequent with cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 blockade such as ipilimumab than with programmed cell death protein 1 blockade, and more frequent again with combination therapy, and it can occur weeks to many months after treatment starts or even after it has stopped. Severity is graded by stool frequency above baseline together with abdominal pain, blood and systemic features, and management is graded in parallel: supportive measures for mild disease, oral corticosteroid with drug interruption for moderate disease, and admission with high dose parenteral corticosteroid for severe disease, escalating to infliximab or vedolizumab if there is no response within about three days. Infection must always be excluded first because the treatments diverge completely, and a steroid taper of at least four to six weeks is needed since rapid withdrawal produces relapse. The other immune related toxicities to consider in any unwell patient on these agents are hypophysitis, thyroid dysfunction, adrenal insufficiency, hepatitis, pneumonitis, nephritis and myocarditis.
key_points: Exclude infection first, since treatment for colitis and for infection diverge entirely
Antimotility agents mask severity and are avoided in suspected immune colitis
Grade 3 colitis needs drug interruption and corticosteroid at 1 to 2 mg/kg
Escalate to infliximab or vedolizumab if no response within about three days
Taper corticosteroid over at least four to six weeks to prevent relapse
explanation.pearls: Immune related adverse events can appear months after the last dose because the drugs act on immune memory rather than persisting in the circulation, so a patient who stopped pembrolizumab three months ago and presents with bloody diarrhoea still has immune colitis high on the differential.

sources.label: eviQ: Immune related adverse events management
BMJ Best Practice: Immune checkpoint inhibitor toxicity

subtopic_detail: Jaundice and a tender enlarged liver three weeks after a heavy drinking period with a bilirubin of 280 and an international normalised ratio of 1.9
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 47 year old man who has become progressively jaundiced over three weeks following several months of drinking around 20 standard drinks daily. He stopped drinking eight days ago.

He has anorexia and a dull ache under the right ribs. His vital signs are pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air and temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius. He is deeply jaundiced with a smooth tender liver palpable 4 cm below the costal margin and mild ascites. He is fully oriented with no asterixis. His bilirubin is 280 micromol/L (less than 20), aspartate aminotransferase is 186 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase is 74 U/L (less than 40), international normalised ratio is 1.9, creatinine is 88 micromol/L and white cell count is 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0). His chest radiograph is clear, blood and urine cultures are negative at 48 hours, an ascitic tap shows 120 neutrophils per mm3, and viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune markers are negative. His abdominal ultrasound with Doppler shows a coarse echotexture with patent hepatic and portal veins and no biliary dilatation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Deep jaundice, smooth tender liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, mild ascites with shifting dullness, spider naevi over the upper chest, fully oriented with no asterixis, Glasgow Coma Scale 15
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 280 micromol/L (less than 20), aspartate aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110), albumin 26 g/L (35 to 50), international normalised ratio 1.9, creatinine 88 micromol/L (60 to 110), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150 to 400), ascitic fluid 120 neutrophils per mm3 with negative culture, blood and urine cultures negative at 48 hours, chest radiograph clear, hepatitis A B C and E serology negative, antinuclear and anti smooth muscle antibodies negative, ultrasound with Doppler showing coarse hepatic echotexture with patent hepatic and portal veins and no biliary dilatation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Give a 21 hour N-acetylcysteine infusion and monitor liver function
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol hepatotoxicity, which produces transaminases in the thousands with a relatively low bilirubin early on, the opposite of this pattern of modest transaminases with deep jaundice. There is no history of paracetamol ingestion here. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Start prednisolone 40 mg daily with nutritional support and thiamine
options.rationale: Jaundice developing within weeks of heavy drinking with an aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio above 2, a bilirubin of 280 micromol/L and an international normalised ratio of 1.9 indicates severe alcohol related hepatitis, and prednisolone 40 mg daily is indicated at this severity once sepsis and gastrointestinal bleeding have been excluded, alongside intensive nutritional support, thiamine and abstinence. Response is assessed at day 7 using the Lille score, and corticosteroid is stopped in non-responders because continuing it adds infection risk without benefit. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily for bacterial peritonitis
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of 250 per mm3 or more, and his count is 120 with negative cultures, so the threshold is not met. The raised white cell count and low grade fever are themselves features of the inflammatory syndrome rather than proof of infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent transjugular liver biopsy before considering any treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is not required when the clinical and biochemical picture is characteristic and competing causes have been excluded serologically and on imaging, and delaying treatment for it costs time in a condition with high short term mortality. Transjugular biopsy is reserved for genuine diagnostic uncertainty, particularly where an alternative cause remains plausible. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease

options.text: Give lactulose 30 mL three times daily and restrict dietary protein
options.rationale: Treatment for hepatic encephalopathy is not indicated in a patient who is fully oriented with no asterixis, and protein restriction is now specifically discouraged in liver disease because it worsens the sarcopenia that drives poor outcomes. Adequate protein intake of around 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg daily is part of correct management. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease

explanation.summary: Alcohol related hepatitis is a distinct syndrome of acute hepatic inflammation superimposed on chronic alcohol use, presenting with jaundice developing over weeks in someone drinking heavily up to or close to presentation, and it carries a short term mortality of up to 30 to 50 per cent in its severe form. The biochemical signature is a modest transaminase rise with an aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio above 2 alongside a disproportionately high bilirubin and a prolonged international normalised ratio, which differentiates it from viral and ischaemic hepatitis and from paracetamol toxicity where transaminases dominate. Severity is quantified using the Maddrey discriminant function or the model for end stage liver disease, and severe disease is the group in whom corticosteroid is considered, with prednisolone 40 mg daily conferring a modest short term survival benefit provided sepsis, active gastrointestinal bleeding and uncontrolled renal failure have been excluded. Response is formally reassessed at day 7 with the Lille score so that non-responders can be spared further immunosuppression. The interventions that matter most across the whole cohort are aggressive nutritional support with adequate protein and thiamine, vigilance for infection and acute kidney injury, and sustained abstinence with addiction support, since abstinence determines long term survival far more than any drug.
key_points: Aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio above 2 with deep jaundice is the signature
Severity scores identify the minority who may benefit from corticosteroid
Exclude sepsis and gastrointestinal bleeding before starting corticosteroid
Reassess response at day 7 and stop steroid in non-responders
Protein restriction is harmful; nutrition and abstinence drive long term outcome
explanation.pearls: An ascitic neutrophil count of 250 per mm3 is the threshold for treating spontaneous bacterial peritonitis regardless of culture result, so a count of 120 does not warrant antibiotics while a count of 300 with a sterile culture does.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol related liver disease
BMJ Best Practice: Alcohol related hepatitis

subtopic_detail: Morning confusion relieved by orange juice with a glucose of 2.1, raised insulin and C-peptide and a negative sulfonylurea screen
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 39 year old woman with six months of episodes in which she becomes confused, sweaty and tremulous, mostly before breakfast or if a meal is delayed. Her husband says she becomes vague and cannot follow a conversation, and that a glass of orange juice reverses it within minutes.

She has gained 7 kg because she now eats every two hours to prevent episodes. She has no diabetes, works as a florist, and no one in the household has diabetes or access to insulin or tablets for it. During a supervised 72 hour fast she became symptomatic at 14 hours with a plasma glucose of 2.1 mmol/L. Samples taken at that moment show insulin inappropriately detectable, C-peptide raised, proinsulin raised and beta hydroxybutyrate suppressed. Her sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen is negative, her morning cortisol is within normal limits and her insulin antibodies are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits between episodes
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, no hyperpigmentation, no hepatomegaly, no abdominal mass, normal neurological examination between episodes, no lipohypertrophy or injection sites
data_table.Investigations: At the point of symptomatic hypoglycaemia during supervised fasting: plasma glucose 2.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8), insulin inappropriately detectable, C-peptide raised, proinsulin raised, beta hydroxybutyrate suppressed; sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen negative; insulin antibodies negative; morning cortisol within normal limits; short synacthen test normal; liver function tests and creatinine within normal limits; HbA1c 4.7 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure her and advise frequent small meals with a bedtime snack
options.rationale: Dietary measures are what she is already doing and they have produced weight gain without preventing episodes, and reassurance is unsafe once fasting hypoglycaemia with inappropriate insulin secretion has been documented. Frequent meals are appropriate for postprandial reactive symptoms with normal fasting studies. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start diazoxide and review her symptom diary again in three months
options.rationale: Agents that suppress insulin secretion such as diazoxide are used for symptom control in patients whose lesion cannot be localised or who are unfit for surgery, not as an alternative to establishing the anatomy in a fit 39 year old. Medical therapy also leaves a potentially malignant lesion in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure insulin like growth factor 2 and screen for an occult malignancy
options.rationale: Non-islet cell tumour hypoglycaemia is mediated by incompletely processed insulin like growth factor 2 and characteristically suppresses insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin rather than raising them. Her raised C-peptide and proinsulin establish that the hypoglycaemia is insulin mediated and exclude that mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange pancreatic imaging to localise the lesion for surgical resection
options.rationale: Endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia is established by a raised insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin with suppressed ketones at a glucose of 2.1 mmol/L and a negative sulfonylurea screen, which points to an insulinoma, so the next step is localisation with pancreatic protocol computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging, adding endoscopic ultrasound or somatostatin receptor imaging when cross sectional imaging is negative. Surgical enucleation or resection is curative in the great majority, and screening for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is considered given her age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Begin hydrocortisone replacement for probable adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycaemia by loss of counter-regulation and would show a suppressed insulin and C-peptide with an inadequate cortisol response, whereas her morning cortisol and short synacthen test are both normal. Treating a normal adrenal axis would add iatrogenic harm without addressing the insulin excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Hypoglycaemia in a person without diabetes is investigated by documenting Whipple triad, symptoms with a low plasma glucose relieved by correcting it, and then by taking a critical sample at the moment of hypoglycaemia, because a normal insulin measured when the glucose is normal is uninterpretable. That sample sorts the differential decisively: insulin mediated hypoglycaemia shows detectable insulin with suppressed ketones, and within that group a raised C-peptide indicates endogenous secretion from an insulinoma, nesidioblastosis or a sulfonylurea, while a suppressed C-peptide indicates exogenous insulin administration. A drug screen therefore matters as much as the hormone panel, since surreptitious or accidental sulfonylurea exposure exactly mimics an insulinoma biochemically, while non-islet cell tumour hypoglycaemia mediated by insulin like growth factor 2 and counter-regulatory failure from adrenal insufficiency both suppress all the insulin related measures. Once endogenous hyperinsulinism is established, localisation precedes surgery, which cures most patients, and around 5 to 10 per cent of insulinomas arise in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, where lesions are multiple and younger patients are affected.
key_points: The critical sample must be taken at the moment of documented hypoglycaemia
Detectable insulin with suppressed ketones indicates insulin mediated hypoglycaemia
Raised C-peptide means endogenous secretion; suppressed means exogenous insulin
A sulfonylurea screen is essential because it mimics insulinoma exactly
Around 5 to 10 per cent of insulinomas occur in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
explanation.pearls: Proinsulin is the measure that most reliably separates an insulinoma from a sulfonylurea effect, because tumour cells secrete incompletely processed hormone and proinsulin is disproportionately raised, whereas a sulfonylurea drives release of normally processed insulin from healthy beta cells.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Evaluation of hypoglycaemia in adults

subtopic_detail: Creatinine rising from 98 to 186 ten days after perindopril was started in a smoker with bruits over both flanks
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 71 year old man referred by his general practitioner because of a rise in creatinine. He has hypertension that has needed four agents to control, peripheral vascular disease with bilateral calf claudication, and a 50 pack year smoking history.

Ten days ago perindopril was added because his blood pressure remained at 168/94 mmHg despite amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide and prazosin. He feels well and has not had diarrhoea, vomiting or reduced oral intake, and takes no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. On examination he is not volume depleted, with a jugular venous pressure visible at 2 cm and no postural drop, and there are audible bruits over both flanks and absent foot pulses. His creatinine has risen from 98 to 186 micromol/L with potassium 5.4 mmol/L, and his urinalysis shows no blood, no protein and no casts. Renal ultrasound reports a right kidney of 11.2 cm and a left kidney of 8.4 cm with increased cortical echogenicity on the left.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/90 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure visible at 2 cm with no postural blood pressure drop, chest clear, audible bruits over both flanks, absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally, no peripheral oedema, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 186 micromol/L, up from 98 micromol/L four weeks ago (60 to 110), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), bicarbonate 21 mmol/L (22 to 32), urinalysis showing no blood, no protein and no casts, renal ultrasound with a right kidney 11.2 cm and left kidney 8.4 cm with increased left cortical echogenicity, full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Give intravenous fluids for presumed prerenal acute kidney injury
options.rationale: He is clinically euvolaemic with a visible jugular venous pressure, no postural drop and no history of fluid loss, so there is no volume deficit to replace and fluid loading risks pulmonary oedema. Volume expansion is the right answer when history and examination indicate depletion. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

options.text: Stop the perindopril and arrange imaging of the renal arteries
options.rationale: A sharp creatinine rise within two weeks of starting renin angiotensin blockade in a vasculopath with resistant hypertension, flank bruits and asymmetric kidney sizes points to critical renal artery stenosis, in which glomerular filtration depends on angiotensin mediated efferent arteriolar tone, so the drug is withdrawn and the anatomy defined with computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography. Bland urinalysis excludes an intrinsic glomerular or interstitial process and supports a haemodynamic mechanism. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

options.text: Continue the perindopril and repeat his biochemistry in four weeks
options.rationale: A rise of up to about 30 per cent in creatinine after starting renin angiotensin blockade is expected and acceptable, but his creatinine has risen by 90 per cent with hyperkalaemia, which exceeds that threshold and requires action. Watchful continuation applies to the smaller expected rise. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

options.text: Start high dose prednisolone for probable acute interstitial nephritis
options.rationale: Interstitial nephritis typically produces white cells, white cell casts or eosinophils in the urine, often with rash and eosinophilia, and his urinalysis is entirely bland with a normal C reactive protein. Corticosteroid would add harm without treating the haemodynamic cause. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

options.text: Refer for renal biopsy to establish the cause before changing his drugs
options.rationale: Biopsy is invasive and carries bleeding risk, and it is not needed when a clear temporal drug association and supportive imaging explain the picture. It becomes appropriate where the urinalysis is active, an intrinsic renal disease is suspected and function does not recover after removing the precipitant. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury guidance)

explanation.summary: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and receptor blockers reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole, which is precisely why they protect the kidney in proteinuric disease and also why they precipitate a functional fall in filtration where perfusion pressure is already critically dependent on that tone. A creatinine rise of up to around 30 per cent after initiation is expected, is not a reason to stop, and is associated with better long term outcomes, but a larger or progressive rise with hyperkalaemia signals that the drug has unmasked a haemodynamically significant lesion. Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is the classic cause and should be suspected in an older vasculopath with resistant hypertension, asymmetric kidney sizes, flank bruits, recurrent flash pulmonary oedema or a bland urinalysis alongside the creatinine rise. Diagnosis is by computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography, and the important therapeutic nuance is that randomised trials have not shown revascularisation to be better than optimal medical therapy for most patients, so stenting is reserved for those with refractory hypertension despite maximal treatment, progressive renal impairment, recurrent pulmonary oedema or stenosis affecting a solitary functioning kidney.
key_points: A creatinine rise up to about 30 per cent after starting the drug is expected
A larger rise with hyperkalaemia suggests a critical perfusion dependent lesion
Bland urinalysis separates a haemodynamic cause from intrinsic renal disease
Asymmetric kidney size, flank bruits and resistant hypertension support the diagnosis
Revascularisation is reserved for refractory cases, not offered routinely
explanation.pearls: Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema with preserved left ventricular function in a hypertensive vasculopath is the presentation most specific for bilateral renal artery stenosis, and it is one of the few indications where revascularisation clearly outperforms medical therapy.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Renal artery stenosis

subtopic_detail: Ringing ears, deep rapid breathing and agitation after a large ingestion of tablets for arthritis, with a pH of 7.44 and a bicarbonate of 12
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34 year old woman brought in four hours after taking an unknown number of tablets from a bottle of her mother's arthritis medication. She is agitated, complains of ringing in her ears and says she feels hot.

Her vital signs are pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air and temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius. She is breathing deeply and is diaphoretic, restless and confused but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 14, and she has no focal neurological signs. Her arterial blood gas shows pH 7.44, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L and lactate 2.6 mmol/L. Her sodium is 140 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, glucose 4.6 mmol/L and creatinine 96 micromol/L. Her paracetamol level is undetectable and her salicylate level is 720 mg/L (therapeutic 150 to 300), rising from 640 mg/L an hour earlier.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and confused but rousable with Glasgow Coma Scale 14, deep rapid respiration, diaphoretic with warm peripheries, tinnitus reported, no focal neurological deficit, pupils equal and reactive, no clonus or rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.44, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L; sodium 140 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), chloride 102 mmol/L (95 to 110), bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22 to 32), glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45 to 90); salicylate 720 mg/L rising from 640 mg/L one hour earlier (therapeutic 150 to 300); paracetamol undetectable; electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia with a QTc of 420 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Intubate and ventilate her now to protect the airway given her confusion
options.rationale: Intubation is the most dangerous intervention available here, because paralysis removes the compensatory hyperventilation that is maintaining her pH and the resulting respiratory acidosis drives salicylate across the blood brain barrier, with cardiac arrest reported after induction. If ventilation becomes unavoidable, hyperventilation must be maintained and alkalinisation continued throughout. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give activated charcoal and repeat the salicylate level in four hours
options.rationale: Activated charcoal has a genuine role and may be given even at this interval because salicylate delays gastric emptying and can form concretions, but it is wholly insufficient as the sole response to a rising level above 700 mg/L with confusion. Charcoal alone would be reasonable for an asymptomatic patient with a low and falling level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Start intravenous sodium bicarbonate and defer dialysis until the pH falls
options.rationale: Alkalinisation is correct and urgent, but waiting for the pH to fall before referring for dialysis misreads the trajectory, since a normal or alkalotic pH in salicylate poisoning reflects intact respiratory compensation that fails abruptly as the patient tires. Deferring until acidaemia appears means intervening after deterioration rather than before it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Start sodium bicarbonate with potassium replacement and refer for dialysis
options.rationale: A salicylate level above 700 mg/L that is still rising, together with confusion, marks severe poisoning, so urinary alkalinisation with a sodium bicarbonate infusion is started immediately while the renal team is contacted for urgent haemodialysis, which clears salicylate and corrects the acid base disturbance. Potassium must be replaced aggressively because hypokalaemia prevents the kidney from excreting an alkaline urine, and the neurological features rather than the pH are what mandate extracorporeal removal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous fluids with active cooling and observe her in the department
options.rationale: Volume resuscitation and temperature control are supportive measures that accompany definitive treatment, and hyperthermia here reflects uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation rather than an infective or environmental cause. Observation without alkalinisation or dialysis in a confused patient with a rising level risks rapid deterioration to seizures and cardiac arrest. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Salicylate poisoning produces a characteristic mixed acid base disturbance that is easy to misread: direct stimulation of the respiratory centre causes a primary respiratory alkalosis, while uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation and accumulation of organic acids produce a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, so the measured pH depends entirely on which process is currently winning. In this patient the anion gap is raised at 26 mmol/L while the pH remains 7.44, which means respiratory compensation is intact and is doing the work of keeping her alive; a normal pH is therefore reassuring only in the way that a normal blood pressure is reassuring in compensated shock. The clinical features that determine severity are neurological rather than biochemical, since confusion, agitation, seizures and coma indicate central nervous system salicylate penetration, which is promoted by acidaemia because only the non-ionised form crosses the blood brain barrier. This mechanism explains the two management principles that candidates most often get wrong: alkalinisation is given to trap salicylate in the extracellular space and the urine rather than simply to correct a number, and intubation is hazardous because paralysis abolishes the hyperventilation, acidaemia follows, and drug floods into the brain. Indications for haemodialysis are a level above roughly 700 mg/L, altered mental state, seizures, pulmonary oedema, renal impairment or refractory acidosis, and they are assessed on the trajectory rather than on a single value.
key_points: The disturbance is mixed respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap metabolic acidosis
A normal pH reflects intact compensation, not a mild poisoning
Neurological features rather than pH determine severity and dialysis need
Hypokalaemia prevents alkaline urine and must be corrected aggressively
Intubation removes compensatory hyperventilation and can precipitate arrest
explanation.pearls: Salicylate is a weak acid with a pKa near 3, so raising urine pH to between 7.5 and 8.5 converts it to the ionised form that cannot be reabsorbed by the renal tubule and increases elimination several fold; this cannot be achieved while the patient is hypokalaemic, because the distal tubule then exchanges potassium for hydrogen and acidifies the urine regardless of how much bicarbonate is infused.

sources.label: Australian Poisons Information Centre: Salicylate poisoning guidance

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids with regurgitation and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 42 year old woman referred with eighteen months of food sticking. She describes the sensation behind the lower sternum and says it happens just as much with water as with steak, and that she now eats standing up and drinks fizzy water to push food down.

She brings up undigested food on the pillow at night and has lost 5 kg. She was treated for reflux with esomeprazole for six months with no benefit. She has never smoked and takes no other medicines.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non tender with no mass, no oral candidiasis
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy reporting retained saliva and food residue in the oesophagus, a normal oesophageal mucosa with no rings, furrows or stricture, and mild resistance on passing the scope through the gastro-oesophageal junction that yields with gentle pressure, biopsies from the distal oesophagus showing no eosinophilic infiltrate, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry with assessment of relaxation at the gastro-oesophageal junction
options.rationale: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset, with regurgitation of undigested food and a normal mucosa, points to a motility disorder, and manometry is the test that establishes failure of relaxation at the junction with absent peristalsis and subclassifies the pattern. That subclassification matters because it predicts the response to dilatation, myotomy and botulinum toxin. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

options.text: Twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH and impedance monitoring off acid suppressing therapy
options.rationale: Ambulatory reflux monitoring quantifies acid exposure and correlates symptoms with reflux episodes, which is useful for refractory heartburn or before antireflux surgery. It does not assess peristalsis or junction relaxation and would not explain dysphagia to liquids. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen with intravenous contrast to look for an infiltrating lesion
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is used when malignancy at or near the junction is suspected, typically with rapid progression over weeks in an older patient and a mucosal abnormality at endoscopy. It has a place later if manometry shows a pattern suggesting an infiltrating tumour mimicking a primary motility disorder. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

options.text: A further eight week course of a high dose proton pump inhibitor taken twice daily before meals
options.rationale: She has already failed six months of acid suppression, and retained food with dysphagia to liquids is not a reflux pattern. Repeating a failed therapeutic trial delays a diagnosis that has now been symptomatic for eighteen months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: A timed barium swallow with fluoroscopic screening of the oesophagus and gastro-oesophageal junction
options.rationale: A barium study can show a dilated oesophagus with a tapered bird beak appearance and is a useful adjunct, particularly for assessing emptying before and after treatment, but a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis and it cannot subclassify the disorder. Manometry remains the reference standard. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

explanation.summary: Achalasia is a primary oesophageal motility disorder in which the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and oesophageal peristalsis is lost, producing dysphagia that is present for liquids as well as solids from the outset, regurgitation of undigested food, chest discomfort and weight loss. This liquid and solid pattern is the key discriminator from a mechanical stricture or tumour, which typically causes solid food dysphagia first. Endoscopy is performed in every patient to exclude mucosal disease and pseudoachalasia from a tumour infiltrating the junction, and retained food with mild resistance at the junction is a supportive but non specific finding. High resolution manometry confirms the diagnosis and defines the subtype, which guides treatment between pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy with fundoplication, peroral endoscopic myotomy and, in those unfit for procedures, botulinum toxin injection. Long standing disease carries a small increased risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, and treatment relieves obstruction without restoring peristalsis, so reflux management after myotomy is part of ongoing care.
key_points: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset suggests a motility disorder rather than a mechanical obstruction.
Endoscopy is done first to exclude mucosal disease and a tumour infiltrating the junction.
High resolution manometry is the reference standard and subclassifies the disorder to guide treatment.
Barium studies support the diagnosis and assess emptying but cannot exclude it or subtype it.
Failure to respond to an adequate trial of acid suppression argues against reflux as the explanation.
explanation.pearls: Pseudoachalasia from a tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction is suggested by symptoms of under six months, weight loss out of proportion to the dysphagia, and age over sixty, and in that combination cross sectional imaging or endoscopic ultrasound follows manometry even when the mucosa looked normal.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Dysphagia clinical update

subtopic_detail: Recurrent food bolus obstruction in a young atopic man planned for endoscopy after spontaneous passage
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 26 year old man in clinic after his second presentation to the emergency department with meat lodged in his oesophagus, which passed spontaneously after an hour both times.

Between episodes he eats slowly, chews carefully and avoids bread and steak at restaurants. He has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid, hay fever each spring, and had eczema as a child. Acid suppression for three months made no difference to his swallowing. You are booking his gastroscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, chest clear with no wheeze, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no oral lesions, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count with eosinophils 0.6 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), previous gastroscopy report from another centre describing linear furrows and concentric rings with no stricture and no biopsies taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange a timed barium swallow to define the calibre of the oesophagus before any further endoscopic procedure
options.rationale: A barium study can outline a narrow calibre oesophagus but cannot make a diagnosis that depends on counting eosinophils in tissue. It is reserved for assessing strictures and planning dilatation rather than for establishing the diagnosis. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

options.text: Proceed to gastroscopy and take at least six oesophageal biopsies from both the proximal and the distal oesophagus
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires at least fifteen eosinophils per high power field in oesophageal tissue, disease is patchy, and the yield rises with the number of biopsies, so six or more specimens from two levels is the standard sampling strategy. Biopsies are taken even when the mucosa looks normal, because up to a fifth of affected patients have no endoscopic abnormality. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

options.text: Refer him for skin prick testing to common foods and start an elimination diet based on the results obtained
options.rationale: Allergy testing performs poorly at predicting which foods drive this condition, and dietary therapy is guided by empirical elimination of common trigger groups with endoscopic reassessment rather than by test results. Diet is also a treatment decision that follows histological confirmation. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Eosinophilic oesophagitis

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to assess peristalsis and relaxation at the gastro-oesophageal junction
options.rationale: Manometry investigates dysphagia to liquids as well as solids with regurgitation, a pattern typical of achalasia, whereas his obstruction occurs only with solid boluses and his previous endoscopy showed rings and furrows. Motility testing would not detect the mucosal disease being tested for. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

options.text: Start a topical swallowed corticosteroid preparation now and reassess his symptoms in the clinic after eight weeks
options.rationale: Swallowed topical corticosteroid is an established first line treatment but starting it before biopsies are taken removes the histological evidence needed to confirm the diagnosis and to judge response. Treatment follows tissue confirmation in this condition. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic immune mediated disease that has become the commonest cause of food bolus obstruction in young adults, typically men with a personal or family history of atopy. Symptoms are solid food dysphagia and bolus impaction, often with years of adaptive behaviours such as eating slowly, over chewing, drinking with meals and avoiding dense foods, which patients rarely volunteer unless asked. Diagnosis requires symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction with at least fifteen eosinophils per high power field on biopsy, and because the infiltrate is patchy the standard is six or more biopsies taken from proximal and distal levels, including when the mucosa appears normal. Treatment options are proton pump inhibitors, swallowed topical corticosteroids such as budesonide or fluticasone preparations, empirical dietary elimination, and dilatation for fibrotic strictures, with repeat biopsy used to confirm histological remission because symptoms alone underestimate ongoing inflammation. Untreated inflammation leads to subepithelial fibrosis and a narrow calibre oesophagus over years, so maintenance therapy is the rule rather than the exception.
key_points: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is the commonest cause of food bolus obstruction in young adults and is strongly associated with atopy.
Diagnosis needs at least fifteen eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy.
Disease is patchy, so at least six biopsies are taken from proximal and distal oesophagus, even if the mucosa looks normal.
Peripheral eosinophilia is neither sensitive nor specific and cannot substitute for tissue sampling.
Symptoms underestimate inflammation, so histological reassessment guides maintenance therapy.
explanation.pearls: Adaptive eating behaviours are the most useful history in this condition: a young man who cuts food into tiny pieces, always has a glass of water at the table and lets everyone else finish first has had oesophageal narrowing for years even if he denies dysphagia.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Eosinophilic oesophagitis clinical update
Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Eosinophilic oesophagitis

subtopic_detail: Progressive magnetic gait with urinary urgency and mild cognitive slowing alongside ventriculomegaly on imaging
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 76 year old man referred with eighteen months of unsteadiness. His wife says his feet seem stuck to the floor when he starts to walk and he has had three falls in six months.

He has become slower in conversation and now has to hurry to the toilet, with two episodes of incontinence. He has no tremor, his handwriting is unchanged, and he has never had a stroke or head injury. He takes perindopril and atorvastatin only.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Examination: Broad based shuffling gait with reduced step height and difficulty initiating, turning by small steps taking five steps to turn, arm swing preserved, no resting tremor, tone normal without cogwheeling, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 24 out of 30 with losses in executive and attention items, no focal weakness, reflexes symmetrical, plantar responses flexor
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showing symmetrically enlarged lateral ventricles with an Evans index of 0.37, narrowed callosal angle and tight high convexity sulci with only mild cortical atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer him directly for insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt on the basis of his symptoms and imaging findings
options.rationale: Shunting is the definitive treatment but carries risks of infection, subdural haematoma and overdrainage, so patient selection rests on demonstrating that cerebrospinal fluid removal actually improves gait rather than on imaging appearances alone. Imaging findings like these are also seen in people who do not respond to shunting. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Commence a trial of levodopa with carbidopa and assess his gait and turning after four weeks of treatment
options.rationale: A levodopa trial is used when the picture suggests parkinsonism, which typically brings asymmetric bradykinesia, rigidity with cogwheeling, reduced arm swing and a resting tremor, none of which he has. Gait apraxia with preserved arm swing and normal tone points elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange a large volume lumbar puncture with timed gait testing before and after the cerebrospinal fluid is removed
options.rationale: Removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid and formally measuring gait speed and a timed walk before and several hours after is the standard test of whether this gait will respond to shunting, and a clear improvement predicts benefit. It also excludes raised opening pressure and allows cerebrospinal fluid analysis for alternative causes. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor for his cognitive impairment and review his cognition and function in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors treat Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies and have no role in a potentially reversible hydrocephalic picture, and his cognitive deficits are executive rather than amnestic. Starting one here would delay a treatable diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer him for urodynamic studies and start an antimuscarinic agent for his urinary urgency and incontinence
options.rationale: Treating the bladder in isolation ignores the unifying explanation for gait, cognition and continence, and antimuscarinics worsen cognition in older adults. Urinary symptoms in this syndrome improve when the underlying problem is treated. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a potentially reversible cause of gait disturbance in older people, characterised by the triad of a magnetic apraxic gait, urinary urgency and incontinence, and subcortical cognitive slowing, with gait usually the earliest and most shunt responsive feature. Imaging shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to cortical atrophy, commonly quantified by an Evans index above 0.3, with a narrowed callosal angle and crowded sulci at the high convexity. Because ventricular enlargement also accompanies cerebral atrophy and other neurodegenerative disease, imaging alone cannot select patients for surgery, and a supplementary test of cerebrospinal fluid removal is used: a large volume lumbar puncture with objective gait measurement before and after, or extended external lumbar drainage in equivocal cases. Patients who improve after fluid removal have substantially higher rates of benefit from ventriculoperitoneal shunting, with gait improving most reliably and cognition least. The main differentials are vascular parkinsonism, Parkinson disease, and cervical myelopathy, and the practical error is attributing a treatable gait disorder to age or to dementia.
key_points: Gait disturbance is the earliest and most shunt responsive element of the triad.
Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, with a narrowed callosal angle, supports the diagnosis.
Imaging cannot select surgical candidates, so a cerebrospinal fluid removal test is performed.
Objective timed gait measurement before and after the tap is what makes the test interpretable.
Preserved arm swing with normal tone argues against Parkinson disease as the cause.
explanation.pearls: Measure the gait formally with a timed ten metre walk and a timed up and go before the tap and again three to four hours afterwards, because subjective impressions from the patient and family after a lumbar puncture are unreliable and a documented improvement of around twenty per cent is what drives the neurosurgical referral.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

subtopic_detail: Persistent watery diarrhoea after stopping the implicated drug in a woman whose colonoscopy was macroscopically normal
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 68 year old woman eight weeks after her colonoscopy. She has had six months of watery diarrhoea, six to eight times a day including at night, with urgency but no blood.

Her colonoscopy looked normal to the eye and random biopsies showed a thickened subepithelial collagen band with a lymphocytic infiltrate. She stopped the diclofenac she had been taking for knee pain the day after the procedure and has had no improvement in eight weeks. Her weight is stable and she has coeliac serology that was negative with a normal immunoglobulin A.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender with no mass, no perianal disease, no oedema, no goitre, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, faecal calprotectin within normal limits, stool culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, colonic biopsies showing a thickened subepithelial collagen band with chronic inflammation and preserved crypt architecture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Commence mesalazine 3 g daily and review her stool frequency and inflammatory markers after 8 weeks
options.rationale: Mesalazine performs poorly in this condition compared with budesonide in randomised comparisons and is not recommended as first line. Its established role is in ulcerative colitis, in which the mucosa is macroscopically abnormal and crypt architecture is distorted. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

options.text: Prescribe loperamide 2 mg titrated to stool frequency and review her in the outpatient clinic in 3 months
options.rationale: Antidiarrhoeal therapy is a reasonable adjunct and is sometimes sufficient for mild disease, but it controls the symptom without treating the mucosal inflammation in a woman whose nocturnal diarrhoea is disrupting her life. It is generally used alongside or after the agent that induces remission. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

options.text: Arrange a repeat colonoscopy with extensive random biopsies from the right and left colon to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: The diagnosis is already secure on histology from a macroscopically normal colon, which is exactly how this condition is identified. Repeating the procedure exposes her to risk and delays treatment. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

options.text: Commence oral budesonide at 9 mg daily for eight weeks and then taper according to her symptomatic response
options.rationale: Budesonide is the treatment with the strongest randomised evidence for inducing remission in microscopic colitis, with response rates around eighty per cent, and its high first pass metabolism limits systemic corticosteroid effects. Treatment is indicated here because withdrawal of the implicated drug alone has not worked over an adequate interval. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

options.text: Commence a bile acid sequestrant and arrange a selenium homocholic acid taurine scan if she does not respond
options.rationale: Bile acid diarrhoea is an important cause of chronic watery diarrhoea and coexists with this condition in some patients, so sequestrants are used as second line therapy. It does not explain the histological findings already documented on her biopsies. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

explanation.summary: Microscopic colitis is a common and underdiagnosed cause of chronic watery non bloody diarrhoea, particularly in women over fifty, and comprises collagenous colitis, defined by a thickened subepithelial collagen band, and lymphocytic colitis, defined by increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. The colon looks normal at colonoscopy, which is why random biopsies from the right and left colon are mandatory in the investigation of chronic diarrhoea even when the mucosa appears unremarkable. Nocturnal diarrhoea, urgency and faecal incontinence are typical and distinguish it clinically from irritable bowel syndrome, and it is associated with coeliac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease and with drugs including non steroidal anti inflammatory agents, proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and statins. Management begins with stopping implicated drugs, and budesonide is the first line agent for inducing remission with response rates around eighty per cent, although relapse after withdrawal is common and some patients need maintenance therapy. Second line options include bile acid sequestrants, and immunomodulators or biologic therapy are reserved for refractory disease.
key_points: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy requires random biopsies to make the diagnosis.
Nocturnal diarrhoea and urgency point away from irritable bowel syndrome.
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and statins are recognised triggers.
Budesonide is first line for induction, with response rates around eighty per cent and limited systemic effects.
Relapse after stopping treatment is common and some patients require maintenance therapy.
explanation.pearls: Check coeliac serology in every patient diagnosed with microscopic colitis, because coeliac disease coexists in up to one in five and diarrhoea that fails to respond to budesonide is frequently explained by untreated gluten sensitive enteropathy.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic diarrhoea clinical update

subtopic_detail: Postprandial vomiting of recognisable food with erratic glucose readings in long standing type 1 diabetes and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 38 year old woman with type 1 diabetes of twenty two years who has four months of fullness after a few mouthfuls, nausea and vomiting of recognisable food several hours after eating.

Her continuous glucose monitor shows lows two hours after her meal boluses and highs four to six hours later, and she has stopped bolusing before meals because of the lows. She takes no opioid or anticholinergic medicine and has never used a glucagon like peptide 1 agonist. Her most recent haemoglobin A1c was 9.4 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, abdomen soft with a succussion splash and no organomegaly or mass, absent ankle reflexes with reduced vibration sense to the mid shin bilaterally, background diabetic retinopathy on fundoscopy, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy reporting retained food in the stomach with no ulcer, stricture or outlet obstruction, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, haemoglobin A1c 9.4 per cent (target under 7.0 per cent), urine albumin creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol (less than 2.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast to exclude a mechanical cause for her symptoms
options.rationale: Mechanical obstruction has already been excluded at endoscopy, which visualised the pylorus and duodenum directly and found retained food without a stricture. Cross sectional imaging is reserved for cases where endoscopy is incomplete or an extrinsic compressing lesion is suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: A twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH study performed after her acid suppressing therapy has been withheld
options.rationale: Reflux monitoring addresses heartburn and regurgitation of acid rather than vomiting of recognisable food hours after a meal with a succussion splash. It measures oesophageal acid exposure and says nothing about gastric emptying. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Antroduodenal manometry to characterise the contractile pattern of the gastric antrum and the proximal small bowel
options.rationale: Antroduodenal manometry is a specialised test used in tertiary centres to investigate suspected generalised intestinal dysmotility when simpler tests are unhelpful. It is not the initial test for suspected delayed gastric emptying. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: A urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori with repeat gastroscopy and antral biopsies if the breath test is positive
options.rationale: Helicobacter pylori causes ulcer disease and dyspepsia rather than retained food with a succussion splash, and her endoscopy showed no ulceration. Eradication would not alter symptoms driven by impaired gastric motor function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Solid phase gastric emptying scintigraphy performed over four hours with her glucose in the target range on the day
options.rationale: Four hour solid phase scintigraphy is the reference standard for delayed gastric emptying and is the test that converts a clinical suspicion into a diagnosis that justifies prokinetic therapy and insulin timing changes. Acute hyperglycaemia itself slows emptying, so the study is performed with glucose reasonably controlled to avoid a falsely abnormal result. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes complications position statement)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes complications position statement

explanation.summary: Diabetic gastroparesis is a manifestation of autonomic neuropathy that typically appears after many years of diabetes and is usually accompanied by other evidence of neuropathy such as absent ankle reflexes, retinopathy or albuminuria. The characteristic story is early satiety, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting of food eaten hours earlier, together with the distinctive glycaemic signature of hypoglycaemia soon after a meal bolus followed by later hyperglycaemia as delayed absorption occurs. Endoscopy is done first to exclude mechanical obstruction and ulceration, and four hour solid phase scintigraphy then confirms delayed emptying, performed with glucose reasonably controlled because acute hyperglycaemia slows emptying in its own right and drugs including opioids, anticholinergics and glucagon like peptide 1 agonists must be withheld beforehand. Management combines small frequent low fat low fibre meals, optimisation of glycaemic control, a short course of a prokinetic such as metoclopramide with attention to its extrapyramidal risk on prolonged use, antiemetics, and adjustment of insulin timing to match delayed absorption. Refractory cases are referred for consideration of enteral feeding beyond the stomach or specialist interventions.
key_points: Gastroparesis usually occurs with other evidence of autonomic and peripheral neuropathy after long standing diabetes.
Postprandial hypoglycaemia followed by later hyperglycaemia is a characteristic glycaemic pattern.
Endoscopy first excludes mechanical obstruction; scintigraphy then confirms delayed emptying.
Acute hyperglycaemia and drugs such as opioids and glucagon like peptide 1 agonists slow emptying and must be accounted for before testing.
Treatment combines dietary modification, glycaemic optimisation, prokinetics and insulin timing adjustment.
explanation.pearls: Metoclopramide carries a cumulative risk of tardive dyskinesia and Australian practice limits it to short courses, so a prokinetic is prescribed for defined periods with review rather than added to a repeat prescription indefinitely.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes complications position statement

subtopic_detail: A shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus with oedema and pigmentation in a woman with palpable foot pulses
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old woman with a shallow ulcer above the inner ankle that has been present for ten weeks. It weeps clear fluid, aches at the end of the day and eases when she puts her legs up.

She has hypertension and a body mass index of 34 kg/m2, and she had a deep vein thrombosis in that leg after a knee replacement twelve years ago. A practice nurse has been dressing it weekly with a foam dressing and has asked you whether antibiotics are needed.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Shallow ulcer of 4 cm by 3 cm above the medial malleolus with a flat granulating base and irregular sloping edges, surrounding brown pigmentation with induration of the gaiter area, pitting oedema to the mid calf, varicose veins in the great saphenous distribution, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable bilaterally, normal sensation to monofilament testing, no surrounding warmth beyond the ulcer margin and no purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin A1c 5.4 per cent (under 6.0 per cent), full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), wound swab growing mixed skin flora

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for seven days on the basis of the mixed growth from her wound swab
options.rationale: All chronic ulcers are colonised, and mixed skin flora on a swab from a wound without spreading erythema, increasing pain, purulence or systemic features does not indicate infection. Antibiotics for colonisation drive resistance without accelerating healing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe pentoxifylline and continue the current weekly dressing regimen with review of the ulcer in six weeks
options.rationale: Pentoxifylline has modest evidence as an adjunct to compression but no role as a substitute for it, and continuing dressings alone leaves the venous hypertension that is causing the ulcer untreated. Adjuncts are considered once compression is established. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Refer her for a split skin graft to the ulcer bed and arrange the procedure through the plastic surgery service
options.rationale: Grafting is considered for large or refractory ulcers after compression has failed, and a graft applied without correcting venous hypertension will break down. Definitive treatment of the underlying haemodynamic problem comes first. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Measure the ankle brachial pressure index and commence graduated multilayer compression bandaging
options.rationale: Compression is the intervention that heals venous ulcers, roughly doubling healing rates compared with dressings alone, and the ankle brachial pressure index is measured first because significant arterial disease makes full compression unsafe. Palpable pulses are reassuring but are not a substitute for the measurement in an older patient with cardiovascular risk factors. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Arrange a punch biopsy of the ulcer edge to exclude malignancy before any compression therapy is commenced
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for an ulcer with rolled or everted edges, atypical appearance or failure to heal despite three months of adequate compression, because squamous cell carcinoma can arise in chronic ulcers. A typical venous ulcer that has not yet had compression does not warrant biopsy first. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

explanation.summary: Venous leg ulcers account for the large majority of chronic lower limb ulcers and arise from sustained venous hypertension, often after deep vein thrombosis or with superficial venous incompetence and obesity. The typical ulcer sits in the gaiter area, most often above the medial malleolus, is shallow with sloping edges and a granulating base, and is surrounded by haemosiderin pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis and oedema, with pain relieved by elevation. Graduated multilayer compression is the treatment that heals them, and an ankle brachial pressure index is measured beforehand because compression is unsafe in significant arterial disease, with an index below about 0.8 prompting modified compression or vascular referral and an index below 0.5 contraindicating it. Wound swabs are not taken routinely because all chronic ulcers are colonised, and antibiotics are reserved for clinical infection with spreading erythema, increasing pain, purulence or systemic features.
