Adjuncts include leg elevation, exercise of the calf pump, weight management, pentoxifylline, and referral for assessment of superficial venous incompetence, which reduces recurrence, and ulcers failing to heal after three months of adequate compression are biopsied to exclude malignancy.
key_points: Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area with pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis and oedema, and ease with elevation.
Graduated compression is the definitive treatment and roughly doubles healing rates compared with dressings alone.
An ankle brachial pressure index is measured before compression because arterial disease makes it unsafe.
Swabs grow colonising flora, and antibiotics are reserved for clinical signs of infection.
An ulcer that has not healed after three months of adequate compression is biopsied for malignancy.
explanation.pearls: An ankle brachial pressure index above 1.3 is as concerning as a low one, because incompressible calcified vessels in diabetes and chronic kidney disease produce a falsely high reading, and in that situation toe pressures or a waveform assessment are used before compression is applied.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers
BMJ Best Practice: Venous leg ulcer

subtopic_detail: Macrocytic anaemia with neutropenia and dysplastic changes on the film in an older man with normal vitamin levels
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 78 year old man referred with four months of increasing breathlessness on walking to his letterbox. He has had two courses of antibiotics for chest infections this winter.

He drinks two beers on a Friday, takes perindopril and atorvastatin, and has had no melaena, rectal bleeding or weight loss. His colonoscopy two years ago for bowel screening was normal apart from two small hyperplastic polyps.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bruising or petechiae, no glossitis, chest clear on auscultation, neurological examination with normal vibration and proprioception and normal gait
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 84 g/L (130 to 180), mean cell volume 106 fL (80 to 100), white cell count 3.1 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L, platelets 92 x10^9/L (150 to 400), reticulocytes 22 x10^9/L (20 to 100), blood film showing hypogranular neutrophils with bilobed nuclei and occasional macro-ovalocytes with no blasts, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, ferritin 210 micrograms/L (30 to 300), direct antiglobulin test negative, erythropoietin 180 IU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence intramuscular hydroxocobalamin and oral folate, and repeat the full blood count in six weeks
options.rationale: Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin deficiency is excluded by normal B12 and folate levels with normal neurological examination, and empirical replacement would simply delay diagnosis. Hypersegmented neutrophils rather than hypogranular bilobed forms would be the film finding in deficiency. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

options.text: Arrange upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy to identify a source of occult blood loss causing his anaemia
options.rationale: Endoscopy is the pathway for iron deficiency anaemia, which is microcytic with a low ferritin and low transferrin saturation, whereas his indices are macrocytic with a normal ferritin. The neutropenia and thrombocytopenia also point to a production problem rather than to blood loss. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells and arrange a repeat full blood count with clinical review in three months
options.rationale: Transfusion relieves symptoms and will be part of his supportive care, but it does not explain a trilineage abnormality with a dysplastic film, and three months of transfusion alone allows iron loading and leaves the diagnosis unmade. Transfusion accompanies the diagnostic pathway rather than replacing it. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and perindopril as likely causes of his cytopenias, and recheck his blood count in one month
options.rationale: Drug induced cytopenias are worth considering, but neither of these agents typically produces macrocytosis with dysplastic morphology across three lineages. Stopping them delays a diagnosis that a marrow examination would establish now. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer him for bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with cytogenetic and molecular studies through haematology
options.rationale: Macrocytic anaemia with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, dysplastic neutrophils on the film and normal vitamin levels describe a marrow production disorder, and bone marrow examination with cytogenetics and molecular testing is what confirms myelodysplastic syndrome and assigns the risk group. Risk stratification determines whether he receives supportive care, erythropoiesis stimulating therapy or a hypomethylating agent. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

explanation.summary: Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal disorders of haematopoietic stem cells that mainly affect people over seventy and present with cytopenias arising from ineffective haematopoiesis, most often a macrocytic or normocytic anaemia with a low reticulocyte response, sometimes accompanied by neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. The blood film provides the first clue, showing dysplastic features such as hypogranular neutrophils, the bilobed pseudo Pelger Huet form, macro-ovalocytes and giant or hypogranular platelets. Reversible causes are excluded first, including vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, alcohol, thyroid disease, liver disease, haemolysis, copper deficiency and drugs, and the diagnosis is then confirmed with bone marrow aspirate and trephine including cytogenetics and molecular studies. Risk stratification using the revised international prognostic scoring system drives management, which ranges from transfusion support and erythropoiesis stimulating agents in lower risk disease to hypomethylating agents and, in fit younger patients, allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Progression to acute myeloid leukaemia occurs in a minority, and iron chelation is considered for transfusion dependent patients with a reasonable life expectancy.
key_points: Unexplained cytopenias in an older person with a macrocytic anaemia and a low reticulocyte count suggest marrow failure.
Hypogranular neutrophils with bilobed nuclei on the film are strongly suggestive of dysplasia.
Reversible causes including vitamin deficiency, alcohol, thyroid and liver disease and drugs are excluded first.
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics confirms the diagnosis and enables risk stratification.
Management ranges from supportive care in lower risk disease to hypomethylating agents or transplantation in higher risk disease.
explanation.pearls: A serum erythropoietin level below about 500 IU/L in lower risk disease predicts a worthwhile response to an erythropoiesis stimulating agent, which is why it is measured before transfusion rather than after, since transfusion suppresses the endogenous level and makes the result uninterpretable.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

subtopic_detail: An incidental sustained lymphocytosis of twenty two in a well man with no lymphadenopathy or cytopenias
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 67 year old man whose blood count was taken as part of a preoperative check before a cataract operation. He feels entirely well, plays golf twice a week and has lost no weight.

He has had no fevers, drenching night sweats or unusual infections. A count taken eight weeks ago showed a lymphocyte count of 19 x10^9/L, and today's shows 22 x10^9/L. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine and no other medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No cervical, axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy, no hepatomegaly, spleen not palpable, no pallor, no bruising or petechiae, no skin lesions, tonsils not enlarged
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130 to 180), white cell count 26.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with lymphocytes 22.1 x10^9/L and neutrophils 3.6 x10^9/L, platelets 212 x10^9/L (150 to 400), blood film showing small mature lymphocytes with scattered smudge cells and no blasts, lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Peripheral blood flow cytometry to immunophenotype the circulating lymphocytes and confirm clonality
options.rationale: A sustained monoclonal lymphocytosis with small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells is diagnosed by immunophenotyping on peripheral blood, which demonstrates the characteristic surface marker pattern and light chain restriction without any need for tissue sampling. Establishing the diagnosis this way avoids an invasive procedure in a man who is otherwise well. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

options.text: Excisional lymph node biopsy of an accessible node with histology and immunohistochemistry to classify the lymphoid disorder
options.rationale: Node biopsy is the procedure for a lymphadenopathic presentation or where transformation to a high grade lymphoma is suspected, signalled by rapid node growth, systemic symptoms and a rising lactate dehydrogenase. He has no palpable nodes to sample. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with cytogenetic studies to assess the degree of marrow infiltration present
options.rationale: Marrow examination is not required for diagnosis when the peripheral blood immunophenotype is characteristic, and it is reserved for unexplained cytopenias or for assessing an unclear response to treatment. Performing it first adds risk and discomfort without adding information. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

options.text: Computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast to stage the extent of nodal involvement
options.rationale: Routine staging imaging is not recommended for an asymptomatic patient in whom treatment is not being contemplated, because it does not change management and delivers radiation. Imaging is used at the point of treatment decisions or when bulky disease or transformation is suspected. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

options.text: Repeat the full blood count with a film in twelve months and refer him only if the lymphocyte count has risen further
options.rationale: Simple observation without characterisation cannot distinguish this from mantle cell lymphoma in leukaemic phase or another lymphoproliferative disorder with a very different prognosis and treatment. Watchful waiting is appropriate after the diagnosis is established, not instead of establishing it. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

explanation.summary: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is the commonest leukaemia in Australian adults and is increasingly found incidentally on a blood count taken for another reason, in a person who feels entirely well. The diagnosis requires a monoclonal B lymphocyte count of at least 5 x10 to the power of 9 per litre in the peripheral blood with a characteristic immunophenotype, and peripheral blood flow cytometry is therefore the diagnostic test, making marrow examination and node biopsy unnecessary in a typical case. The important mimic is mantle cell lymphoma in leukaemic phase, which shares a mature B cell appearance but has a markedly worse prognosis and is separated by immunophenotype and cyclin D1 or translocation testing. Most patients with early stage disease need no treatment, and observation with periodic clinical review and blood counts is the standard, with treatment triggered by progressive marrow failure, bulky or symptomatic lymphadenopathy, massive splenomegaly, rapid lymphocyte doubling or constitutional symptoms. Complications include hypogammaglobulinaemia with recurrent infection, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia, and transformation to high grade lymphoma, so vaccination and infection awareness are part of long term care.
key_points: Peripheral blood flow cytometry establishes the diagnosis without marrow or node sampling in typical cases.
Smudge cells with small mature lymphocytes on the film are characteristic but not by themselves diagnostic.
Mantle cell lymphoma in leukaemic phase is the key mimic and is separated by immunophenotype.
Routine staging imaging is not recommended when treatment is not being contemplated.
Treatment is triggered by marrow failure, symptomatic bulk, rapid doubling or constitutional symptoms, not by the count alone.
explanation.pearls: A lymphocyte doubling time of less than twelve months is one of the recognised triggers for treatment, which is why the date and value of every previous blood count matter more than any single result at referral.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement
eviQ Cancer Treatments Online: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
BMJ Best Practice: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia

subtopic_detail: Acute kidney injury with a very high creatine kinase after an older man spent a night on the floor
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar receiving an 82 year old man found by his daughter on his bathroom floor this morning. He had fallen after getting up in the night and had been unable to get up, and thinks he had been there since about eleven o'clock.

He has not passed urine since being found. He takes perindopril, atorvastatin and pantoprazole and has no history of kidney disease. His blood pressure has responded to an initial litre of fluid given by the ambulance service.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/64 mmHg after the prehospital fluid, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in room air, temperature 35.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tender swollen left thigh and buttock with intact overlying skin, no compartment tightness and pain not disproportionate on passive stretch, dry mucous membranes, no focal neurological deficit, hip radiographs showing no fracture, urinary catheter draining 15 mL of dark tea coloured urine
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 42000 U/L (less than 200), creatinine 218 micromol/L (60 to 110) with a value of 84 micromol/L six months ago, potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), sodium 146 mmol/L (135 to 145), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22 to 32), corrected calcium 2.02 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60), phosphate 1.9 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), urine dipstick strongly positive for blood with no red cells seen on microscopy, electrocardiogram showing sinus rhythm with peaked T waves in the anterior leads

lead_in: What is the single most important step in his management after the immediate treatment of his hyperkalaemia?

options.text: Commence an infusion of sodium bicarbonate titrated to a urinary pH above 6.5 as the primary means of protecting his kidneys
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation is a debated adjunct that has never been shown to be superior to sodium chloride alone, and it risks worsening the hypocalcaemia that already accompanies rhabdomyolysis. Volume repletion is the intervention with the evidence behind it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous mannitol as an osmotic diuretic to flush pigment casts through the tubules and increase urine flow
options.rationale: Mannitol has no demonstrated benefit over adequate crystalloid resuscitation and can itself cause acute kidney injury and volume overload, particularly in an oliguric patient. It is not part of standard Australian practice for this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide to convert his oliguric kidney injury to a non oliguric state and improve fluid balance
options.rationale: Loop diuretics do not improve renal outcomes in acute kidney injury and giving one to a volume depleted patient worsens the injury by reducing renal perfusion further. Diuretics are used for established fluid overload once the patient is replete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride at a high rate, titrated to a urine output target with close fluid monitoring
options.rationale: Aggressive isotonic crystalloid resuscitation is the single intervention that reduces the risk of pigment induced acute kidney injury, and it is titrated to a urine output target of around 200 to 300 mL per hour with frequent reassessment for fluid overload in an older patient. Nephrotoxic drugs including his angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor are withheld at the same time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis through a vascular access catheter to clear myoglobin before further renal damage occurs
options.rationale: Dialysis is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, volume overload or uraemic complications, and it does not usefully clear myoglobin. Starting it before a trial of volume repletion in a patient whose blood pressure has responded to fluid is premature. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury guidance)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury guidance

explanation.summary: Rhabdomyolysis after a long lie is a common cause of acute kidney injury in older people, produced by pressure necrosis of muscle with release of myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase, and by sequestration of fluid into damaged muscle that compounds the dehydration of lying immobile for hours. The characteristic biochemical signature is a markedly raised creatine kinase with hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and a urine dipstick strongly positive for blood in the absence of red cells on microscopy, which reflects myoglobin rather than haematuria. Kidney injury results from renal vasoconstriction, tubular obstruction by pigment casts and direct tubular toxicity, and early aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation is the only intervention with consistent evidence for preventing it. Additional priorities are treating hyperkalaemia, withholding nephrotoxic drugs, checking for compartment syndrome in a tense painful limb, and looking for the reason for the fall including arrhythmia, stroke, sepsis and medication effects. Hypocalcaemia is generally not corrected unless symptomatic or accompanying severe hyperkalaemia, because calcium released from damaged muscle during recovery frequently produces rebound hypercalcaemia.
key_points: Dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy indicates myoglobinuria.
Early high volume isotonic crystalloid titrated to urine output is the intervention that protects the kidneys.
Hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia accompany muscle breakdown and are monitored closely.
Bicarbonate, mannitol and loop diuretics have no established advantage over adequate crystalloid.
Assess for compartment syndrome and for the underlying cause of the fall, not just the muscle injury.
explanation.pearls: Resist correcting the hypocalcaemia unless the patient is symptomatic or needs calcium for cardiac membrane stabilisation, because calcium deposited in injured muscle is released during recovery and treated patients frequently swing into rebound hypercalcaemia in the second week.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury guidance

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of fever with headache and hepatitic liver enzymes in an abattoir worker with culture negative blood
stem:
You are the general physician admitting a 45 year old man from a regional town with three weeks of daily fevers, drenching sweats and a severe retro-orbital headache. He has lost 4 kg and feels exhausted.

He has worked on the killing floor of a sheep and goat abattoir for six years and helps at a friend's farm during lambing. He has taken no antibiotics, has not travelled overseas and has no ticks or rash. He was told about a vaccine when he started the job but never followed it up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Unwell and diaphoretic, no rash, no eschar, no lymphadenopathy, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin and mildly tender, spleen not palpable, no heart murmur, no splinter haemorrhages, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 132 x10^9/L (150 to 400), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110), bilirubin within normal limits, three sets of blood cultures with no growth at five days, chest radiograph with a small area of right lower lobe consolidation, malaria thick and thin films negative, hepatitis A, B and C serology negative, transthoracic echocardiogram with no vegetation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and repeat the blood cultures after 48 hours of treatment
options.rationale: This combination targets the usual bacterial causes of sepsis and endocarditis, and three negative culture sets with a normal echocardiogram make that unlikely. Neither agent covers the intracellular organism suggested by this exposure and illness pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone for a presumed inflammatory hepatitis and arrange autoimmune liver serology and liver biopsy
options.rationale: Corticosteroid given empirically to a man with an undiagnosed febrile illness and an occupational zoonotic exposure risks disseminating an untreated infection. Autoimmune hepatitis would not explain three weeks of daily fever with drenching sweats and lung consolidation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Start oral azithromycin for an atypical community acquired pneumonia and review his response after five days of therapy
options.rationale: Macrolides cover Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila and Legionella, and a short course would not treat the organism that this abattoir exposure points to, for which doxycycline is the agent of choice. Treating for the wrong atypical pathogen also risks partially masking the illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a positron emission tomography scan for a fever of unknown origin and withhold antimicrobial therapy meanwhile
options.rationale: Functional imaging is used when a systematic first line workup including targeted serology has not produced a diagnosis, and here a specific exposure history points directly to a testable pathogen. Delaying treatment while awaiting imaging prolongs a debilitating illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send Coxiella burnetii serology with a convalescent sample planned, and start oral doxycycline while awaiting the result
options.rationale: Abattoir and lambing exposure with prolonged fever, headache, hepatitis and culture negative blood is the classic Australian presentation of acute Q fever, which is diagnosed serologically because the organism does not grow in routine blood culture bottles and requires paired acute and convalescent samples. Doxycycline is started empirically because early treatment shortens the illness and reduces the risk of chronic infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Q fever national guidelines

explanation.summary: Q fever, caused by Coxiella burnetii, is an occupational zoonosis of abattoir workers, farmers, shearers, veterinarians and people living downwind of livestock, and Australia has one of the highest reported incidences in the world. Acute infection presents with abrupt high fever, severe headache that is often retro-orbital, myalgia and sweats, frequently with hepatitis and sometimes with atypical pneumonia, and characteristically with negative routine blood cultures because the organism is intracellular and does not grow in standard media. Diagnosis is serological using phase II antibodies in acute infection, with paired acute and convalescent samples taken two to three weeks apart, and polymerase chain reaction on blood is useful in the first fortnight before antibodies appear. Doxycycline for two weeks is the treatment and is started empirically on clinical suspicion, with complications including chronic Q fever endocarditis in those with valvular disease, vascular grafts or immunosuppression, and a post Q fever fatigue syndrome. Australia has a licensed vaccine, which requires pre-vaccination skin testing and serology because giving it to someone with prior exposure can cause a severe local reaction.
key_points: Abattoir, farm, shearing and veterinary work are the classic Australian exposures.
Routine blood cultures are negative because the organism is intracellular and does not grow in standard media.
Diagnosis is serological with paired acute and convalescent samples; polymerase chain reaction helps in the first two weeks.
Doxycycline for two weeks is the treatment and is started empirically on clinical suspicion.
Valvular heart disease, vascular grafts and immunosuppression greatly increase the risk of chronic infection.
explanation.pearls: Anyone diagnosed with acute Q fever who has a known valvular abnormality should have an echocardiogram and prolonged serological follow up, because chronic Q fever endocarditis develops in a substantial minority of that group and can appear months to years after the acute illness.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Q fever national guidelines

subtopic_detail: A rapidly enlarging painful leg ulcer with a violaceous undermined border that worsened after surgical debridement
stem:
You are the general physician asked to review a 52 year old woman with ulcerative colitis whose shin ulcer has trebled in size over three weeks. She rates the pain at nine out of ten and it wakes her at night.

The lesion began as a small tender pustule after she knocked her leg on a trailer. She completed ten days of flucloxacillin without change, and the ulcer expanded rapidly in the week after a surgical team debrided its edges. Her bowel symptoms have been quiescent on azathioprine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Ulcer of 7 cm on the left shin with a violaceous undermined border overhanging a boggy necrotic base, surrounding erythematous halo without warmth extending beyond it, exquisite tenderness on light contact, fresh linear ulceration along the line of the recent debridement incision, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable, normal monofilament sensation
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 48 mg/L (less than 5), wound swab and tissue culture with no significant growth including no mycobacteria or fungi, haemoglobin A1c 5.3 per cent (under 6.0 per cent), ankle brachial pressure index 1.05, skin biopsy from the ulcer edge showing a dense neutrophilic infiltrate with no vasculitis and no organisms on special stains

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange further surgical debridement of the necrotic base and apply negative pressure wound therapy afterwards
options.rationale: Surgical trauma provokes further ulceration in this condition through pathergy, which is exactly what followed the first debridement, so operating again reliably enlarges the wound. Surgery is contemplated only under immunosuppressive cover and when debridement is unavoidable. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

options.text: Commence systemic corticosteroid therapy at an immunosuppressive dose and avoid further surgical intervention
options.rationale: A rapidly expanding painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border, a sterile neutrophilic infiltrate on biopsy, an associated inflammatory bowel disease and clear pathergy after debridement describes pyoderma gangrenosum, for which high dose systemic corticosteroid is the standard first line treatment and usually produces a response within days. Ciclosporin is an alternative first line agent and a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor is used where inflammatory bowel disease also needs control. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

options.text: Commence intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam for a deep soft tissue infection and obtain repeat tissue cultures
options.rationale: Broad spectrum antibiotics are appropriate when there is spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis or a positive culture, and her tissue cultures including mycobacterial and fungal specimens were negative after a failed course of an antistaphylococcal agent. Continuing to treat for infection delays the immunosuppression that this ulcer needs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply multilayer graduated compression bandaging and arrange weekly dressings through the community nursing service
options.rationale: Compression treats venous ulceration, which sits in the gaiter area with pigmentation and oedema and is relatively painless, whereas this ulcer is on the shin with an undermined violaceous border and extreme pain. Compression alone would not halt an inflammatory ulcer that is expanding daily. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Refer her for hyperbaric oxygen therapy and continue the current dressing regimen while awaiting the first session
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is used for selected hypoxic wounds such as diabetic foot ulcers and osteoradionecrosis and has no established role as primary therapy here. Her palpable pulses and normal ankle brachial pressure index also indicate that the wound is not ischaemic. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

explanation.summary: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis that produces rapidly enlarging, exquisitely painful ulcers, classically on the lower legs, with a violaceous undermined border and a necrotic base, and it is associated in around half of cases with inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritis or a haematological disorder. It is a diagnosis of exclusion supported by a compatible clinical picture, a sterile neutrophilic infiltrate on biopsy taken from the ulcer edge, negative cultures including mycobacterial and fungal, and exclusion of vasculitis, infection, malignancy and vascular causes. Pathergy, in which minor trauma or surgery provokes new or expanded ulceration, is characteristic and is the reason debridement and grafting are avoided unless the patient is immunosuppressed. First line treatment is high dose systemic corticosteroid or ciclosporin, with tumour necrosis factor inhibitors particularly useful when inflammatory bowel disease requires treatment as well, alongside potent topical or intralesional corticosteroid for small lesions, generous analgesia and non adherent wound care. The commonest clinical error is to interpret the ulcer as infected and to debride it repeatedly, which converts a treatable dermatosis into a catastrophic wound.
key_points: A painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border that enlarges rapidly should raise pyoderma gangrenosum.
Pathergy, with ulceration triggered or worsened by trauma or surgery, is characteristic and contraindicates debridement.
Biopsy shows a sterile neutrophilic infiltrate and serves mainly to exclude infection, vasculitis and malignancy.
Around half of cases occur with inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritis or a haematological disorder.
High dose systemic corticosteroid or ciclosporin is first line, with biologic therapy when bowel disease also needs control.
explanation.pearls: Pain out of proportion to the appearance of the wound is the single most useful bedside discriminator, and an ulcer that hurts at nine out of ten with an undermined edge after a failed antibiotic course should prompt a biopsy from the edge rather than another trip to theatre.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum
Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

subtopic_detail: Sudden profound proximal weakness on waking with a potassium of two point zero and a suppressed thyrotropin
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar called to a 28 year old man who woke unable to lift himself out of bed. He had eaten a large plate of fried rice and several beers late the previous night after a heavy session at the gym.

He has had three milder episodes over six months, each lasting a few hours and each resolving by itself, and he had put them down to overtraining. He has lost 6 kg without dieting, sweats through his shirts and has noticed his hands shaking when he holds a coffee. He has had no diarrhoea, no vomiting and takes no diuretic, laxative or supplement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Power 2 out of 5 in hip flexion and shoulder abduction with 4 out of 5 distally, reflexes reduced symmetrically, sensation fully intact, no bulbar or respiratory weakness with a normal single breath count, fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist palms, small diffuse goitre without a bruit, no proptosis or lid lag
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 2.0 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), magnesium 0.86 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.80 to 1.50), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 to 32), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110), creatine kinase 220 U/L (less than 200), thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) with free thyroxine 38 pmol/L (10 to 20), spot urine potassium to creatinine ratio low, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia with flattened T waves and prominent U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his weakness?

options.text: Give a large oral potassium load followed by an intravenous potassium infusion until the serum level exceeds 4.0 mmol/L
options.rationale: Total body potassium is normal in this syndrome because the deficit is a shift into cells, so aggressive replacement is followed by rebound hyperkalaemia in up to two thirds of patients as the potassium moves back out. Replacement is deliberately small and cautious with frequent monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give an intravenous infusion of glucose with insulin to shift potassium and correct the electrocardiographic changes
options.rationale: Insulin and glucose drive potassium into cells and would deepen the very shift causing the paralysis, and a carbohydrate load is one of the recognised triggers of an attack. This treatment belongs to hyperkalaemia, not to this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give small doses of intravenous potassium with a non selective beta blocker under continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Cautious potassium replacement corrects the dangerous hypokalaemia while a non selective beta blocker such as propranolol blocks the adrenergic drive on the sodium potassium pump that is shifting potassium into cells, shortening the attack and reducing rebound. Continuous monitoring is required because both the initial hypokalaemia and the rebound hyperkalaemia carry arrhythmic risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate and withhold potassium replacement until the magnesium level has been normalised
options.rationale: Magnesium repletion is essential in hypokalaemia driven by renal or gastrointestinal loss, because deficiency perpetuates urinary potassium wasting, but his magnesium is already within the reference interval. Withholding potassium in a man with profound weakness and prominent U waves would be unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give oral carbimazole immediately and defer potassium replacement until the thyroid function results have been repeated
options.rationale: Antithyroid therapy is essential to prevent further attacks and is started during the admission, but it takes weeks to restore euthyroidism and does nothing for a potassium of 2.0 mmol/L today. Definitive treatment follows the acute correction rather than replacing it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is an uncommon but dramatic complication of hyperthyroidism, disproportionately affecting young men of Asian background, in which excess thyroid hormone amplifies sodium potassium adenosine triphosphatase activity and an adrenergic or insulin stimulus drives potassium abruptly into cells. Attacks characteristically follow a high carbohydrate meal, alcohol or strenuous exercise and strike on waking, producing symmetrical proximal weakness with preserved sensation, reduced reflexes and sparing of the respiratory and bulbar muscles in most cases. The critical insight is that total body potassium is normal, so the hypokalaemia is a distribution problem rather than a deficit, and this is supported by a low urinary potassium excretion, a normal acid base status and the absence of vomiting, diarrhoea or diuretic use. Management combines cautious low dose potassium replacement, which prevents arrhythmia while minimising the rebound hyperkalaemia that occurs in a majority of aggressively replaced patients, with a non selective beta blocker such as propranolol that addresses the underlying shift. Definitive treatment is restoration of euthyroidism, after which attacks cease, and patients are counselled to avoid high carbohydrate loads and alcohol until then.
key_points: Hypokalaemia here reflects a shift into cells, not a total body deficit, so replacement is cautious.
Attacks are triggered by carbohydrate loads, alcohol and exercise, and typically occur on waking.
A low urinary potassium with normal acid base status distinguishes a shift from renal or gastrointestinal losses.
Non selective beta blockade counteracts the adrenergic drive on the sodium potassium pump and shortens attacks.
Rebound hyperkalaemia occurs in a majority of aggressively replaced patients, hence continuous monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Familial hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is the main differential and is separated by a normal thyroid function test and a history that usually begins in the first two decades, whereas thyrotoxic periodic paralysis presents in the twenties to forties and disappears permanently once euthyroidism is restored.

subtopic_detail: Eight months of abdominal pain relieved by opening the bowels with alternating stool form and a normal faecal calprotectin
stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman referred with eight months of lower abdominal cramping. She tells you the pain eases once she has opened her bowels and that her motions swing between hard pellets and loose stools from week to week, often with bloating that worsens through the day.

She has not lost weight, has never woken at night with the pain and has never seen blood. Nobody in her family has had bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. She has brought printouts about bowel cancer and wants a colonoscopy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2 with no documented weight change, abdomen soft with mild non localised tenderness and no mass, no perianal disease, no clubbing, no mouth ulcers, no abdominal distension on examination
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30 to 200), coeliac serology negative with a normal total immunoglobulin A, faecal calprotectin 26 micrograms/g (less than 50), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her for colonoscopy to exclude an organic cause before committing to any symptomatic treatment for her abdominal symptoms
options.rationale: Colonoscopy in a woman under fifty with no alarm features, normal inflammatory markers and a normal calprotectin has a diagnostic yield little different from the background population and carries procedural risk. It is indicated for rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, a family history of bowel cancer or symptom onset after fifty. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Arrange a gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude coeliac disease despite the negative serology and reassess her symptoms afterwards
options.rationale: Negative coeliac serology with a normal total immunoglobulin A makes coeliac disease very unlikely, so biopsy adds risk without meaningful yield. Biopsy despite negative serology is reserved for patients already on a gluten free diet or with immunoglobulin A deficiency. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Explain the positive diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome and refer her to a dietitian for a supervised trial of a low fermentable carbohydrate diet
options.rationale: Pain related to defaecation with a change in stool form and frequency, in the absence of alarm features and with normal screening tests, meets the criteria for irritable bowel syndrome, which is a positive diagnosis rather than one of exclusion. A dietitian supervised low fermentable carbohydrate diet improves symptoms in around three quarters of patients and includes a structured reintroduction phase. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and review her abdominal pain and bloating in the clinic once the course is complete
options.rationale: Acid suppression does not treat pain that is relieved by defaecation and has no effect on stool form or bloating. A proton pump inhibitor trial is appropriate for epigastric burning or reflux symptoms, which she does not describe. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Request a faecal occult blood test and repeat it in three months to provide her with reassurance about the possibility of bowel cancer
options.rationale: Immunochemical faecal testing is a population screening tool for asymptomatic people and is not validated for investigating symptoms, so a negative result cannot be used as reassurance in a symptomatic patient. Symptomatic patients meeting referral criteria go to colonoscopy directly rather than to stool testing. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

explanation.summary: Irritable bowel syndrome affects around one in seven Australians and is diagnosed positively on recurrent abdominal pain related to defaecation or associated with a change in stool frequency or form, present for at least six months. A limited screening panel of full blood count, C-reactive protein, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin is sufficient in a young patient without alarm features, and normal results make inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease very unlikely. Alarm features that shift the approach are unintentional weight loss, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, a family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and onset after the age of fifty. Treatment begins with explanation and dietary modification, with the low fermentable oligosaccharide, disaccharide, monosaccharide and polyol approach developed in Australia having the strongest dietary evidence, delivered with dietitian supervision because of the risk of nutritional inadequacy and disordered eating if the restriction phase is prolonged. Second line options are directed at the predominant symptom, and gut brain neuromodulators and gut directed hypnotherapy help refractory pain.
key_points: The diagnosis is positive, based on pain related to defaecation with a change in stool form or frequency.
A normal calprotectin with normal inflammatory markers makes inflammatory bowel disease very unlikely.
Alarm features include weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms and onset after fifty.
A dietitian supervised low fermentable carbohydrate diet is the dietary treatment with the best evidence.
Faecal immunochemical testing is a screening tool and is not validated for symptomatic patients.
explanation.pearls: Keep the restriction phase of a low fermentable carbohydrate diet to two to six weeks and insist on structured reintroduction, because prolonged restriction reduces beneficial colonic bacteria and calcium and fibre intake, and is a recognised trigger for disordered eating patterns.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome
Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines
NICE: Irritable bowel syndrome in adults

subtopic_detail: Two years of recurrent painful lumps in both armpits and the groin with rope like scarring and discharging tunnels
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 24 year old woman referred after four courses of flucloxacillin in the past year. She describes painful lumps in both armpits and her groin that swell, burst and discharge, then come back in a slightly different spot a few weeks later.

She has stopped wearing sleeveless tops and has taken sick leave because of the pain and the smell. She smokes fifteen cigarettes a day. She has no fever and feels systemically well between episodes.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, multiple tender inflammatory nodules in both axillae and both groins with several double headed open comedones, rope like scarring across the left axilla and two sinus tracts discharging on gentle pressure, no involvement of the face or trunk, no fever
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5), swab from a discharging lesion growing mixed skin flora, fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further two week course of flucloxacillin and advise her to return promptly if the lesions recur again after treatment
options.rationale: Short antistaphylococcal courses treat the disorder as recurrent boils, which is why she has relapsed four times, and the swab growing mixed flora reflects colonisation rather than a primary infection. Flucloxacillin is the right drug for a genuine staphylococcal abscess in previously normal skin. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

options.text: Refer her directly for wide surgical excision of both axillae and both groins as the definitive treatment for her recurrent lesions
options.rationale: Wide excision has a role in burnt out fibrotic disease at Hurley stage three but is disfiguring and does not address active inflammation elsewhere. Medical therapy is offered first, with surgery reserved for localised persistent tracts once inflammation is controlled. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

options.text: Arrange incision and drainage of each fluctuant lesion under local anaesthetic and review her in the surgical clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Simple incision and drainage gives brief relief but the lesions recur at the same sites and the procedure adds to the scarring burden, so it is not a treatment for the disease. It is appropriate for acute pain relief of a tense abscess alongside, never instead of, disease modifying therapy. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

options.text: Prescribe topical mupirocin to both axillae and the groin and arrange nasal decolonisation for her and her household contacts
options.rationale: Decolonisation targets recurrent staphylococcal furunculosis, which does not produce sinus tracts, double headed comedones or the characteristic scarring seen here. It would be the right approach to genuinely recurrent boils with a consistent staphylococcal isolate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence oral doxycycline for at least three months with smoking cessation support and refer her to a dermatology service for ongoing care
options.rationale: Double headed comedones with sinus tracts and rope like scarring in both axillae and groins is hidradenitis suppurativa at Hurley stage two, for which a tetracycline given for three months or longer is the standard systemic first line treatment in Australian practice. Smoking is the strongest modifiable driver of severity and cessation support belongs in the initial plan rather than as an afterthought. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

explanation.summary: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic inflammatory disease of the follicular unit in apocrine bearing skin, affecting around one per cent of the population with a strong female preponderance and a typical onset in the twenties. It is very commonly misdiagnosed as recurrent boils, and the average delay to correct diagnosis remains around seven years, during which patients receive repeated short antibiotic courses and incision and drainage procedures that do nothing to alter the disease. The diagnostic triad is typical lesions including nodules, abscesses, double headed comedones and sinus tracts, in typical locations of axillae, groin, inframammary and perianal skin, with a chronic relapsing course. Severity is staged by the Hurley system, with stage one being isolated nodules, stage two recurrent lesions with tracts and scarring separated by normal skin, and stage three diffuse interconnected tracts across an entire area. Smoking and obesity are the major modifiable factors, topical clindamycin suits stage one, tetracyclines are first line systemic therapy, and biologic therapy with adalimumab is available for moderate to severe disease that fails conventional treatment.
key_points: Double headed comedones and sinus tracts distinguish the disease from recurrent boils.
Typical sites are axillae, groin, inframammary and perianal skin.
Repeated short antibiotic courses and drainage procedures do not modify the disease.
Tetracyclines given for three months or longer are first line systemic therapy.
Smoking and obesity are the strongest modifiable drivers of severity.
explanation.pearls: Screen every patient with hidradenitis suppurativa for depression and for inflammatory bowel disease, since rates of suicidal ideation are around twice those of other dermatological patients and Crohn disease is several times more common than in the general population and shares the perianal phenotype.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

subtopic_detail: Isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with a warm bowed shin and progressive hearing loss in a man in his seventies
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 72 year old man referred with an abnormal blood test found when his general practitioner investigated tiredness. He mentions a dull ache in his right shin that has been present for about a year and is worse at night, and says he has needed the television louder over the past two years.

He has no history of cancer and has not lost weight. He takes no regular medications and drinks two standard drinks a week.

data_table.Examination: Anterior bowing of the right tibia with skin over it warmer than the left, no localised bony tenderness to percussion over the spine, conductive pattern hearing loss on the right with Rinne negative on that side, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, normal power and sensation in both legs
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 412 U/L (30 to 110), gamma glutamyl transferase 24 U/L (less than 60), bilirubin and transaminases within normal limits, corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 72 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60 to 110), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum parathyroid hormone to establish whether the bone turnover is being driven by parathyroid overactivity
options.rationale: Hyperparathyroidism raises alkaline phosphatase but does so with hypercalcaemia and a low or low normal phosphate, and his calcium, phosphate and vitamin D are all normal. Parathyroid hormone is the right test when calcium is abnormal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Request serum and urine protein electrophoresis with serum free light chains to look for a monoclonal paraprotein as the underlying cause
options.rationale: Myeloma characteristically produces a normal or low alkaline phosphatase because its lesions are purely lytic with suppressed osteoblastic activity, so a markedly raised level argues against it. Electrophoresis is warranted with anaemia, renal impairment, hypercalcaemia or unexplained bone pain with lytic lesions. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase

options.text: Request plain radiographs of the symptomatic tibia together with a whole body radionuclide bone scan to define the distribution of disease
options.rationale: An isolated rise in alkaline phosphatase with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase confirms a bony rather than hepatic source, and bowing with overlying warmth alongside hearing loss is Paget disease of bone, in which plain films characterise the lesion and a bone scan maps every affected site. Mapping the distribution matters because asymptomatic skull or vertebral involvement changes management. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to search for a primary malignancy with skeletal metastatic disease
options.rationale: Metastatic bone disease is the important differential but it would be unusual to produce a year of localised pain with bowing of a long bone and no weight loss, anaemia or known primary. Cross sectional imaging becomes appropriate if the bone scan shows a pattern inconsistent with Paget disease. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase

options.text: Commence oral alendronate weekly and recheck the alkaline phosphatase level in three months to confirm a response to treatment
options.rationale: Starting treatment before imaging leaves the diagnosis unconfirmed and the extent of disease unknown, and oral weekly bisphosphonate dosing is an osteoporosis regimen rather than the intensive dosing used in Paget disease. Treatment follows confirmation, and a single zoledronic acid infusion is the usual Australian choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of excessive and disorganised bone remodelling that affects perhaps two per cent of Australians over fifty five and is most often found incidentally through an isolated rise in alkaline phosphatase or an abnormal radiograph. The first step in any raised alkaline phosphatase is to establish its source, and a normal gamma glutamyl transferase points away from the liver and towards bone. Common sites are the pelvis, femur, tibia, skull and lumbar spine, and the clinical features follow from expanded, vascular and structurally weak bone: bone pain, warmth over the affected area, deformity such as tibial bowing, deafness from skull involvement, and pathological fracture. A radionuclide bone scan is the most sensitive way to map all affected sites while plain films confirm the characteristic appearance of cortical thickening, trabecular coarsening and expansion. Treatment with a single intravenous zoledronic acid infusion normalises turnover in most patients for years and is indicated for symptomatic disease or for disease at sites where complications threaten, such as the skull base, weight bearing bones or adjacent to major joints.
key_points: A normal gamma glutamyl transferase confirms that a raised alkaline phosphatase is of bony origin.
Bone pain, warmth, deformity and deafness are the characteristic clinical features.
A radionuclide bone scan maps all affected sites and plain films confirm the appearance.
Alkaline phosphatase is normal or low in myeloma, which helps exclude it.
A single zoledronic acid infusion is the usual treatment for symptomatic or high risk disease.
explanation.pearls: A sudden increase in pain or a rapidly enlarging soft tissue mass at a known pagetic site should raise the possibility of osteosarcoma, which complicates well under one per cent of cases but accounts for most Paget related mortality and requires urgent imaging rather than escalation of analgesia.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase
BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone

subtopic_detail: Fasting triglycerides above 20 mmol/L found incidentally in a man with poorly controlled diabetes and heavy alcohol use
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 45 year old man in a diabetes clinic. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin alone and admits he has not been taking it consistently for the past year.

He drinks six standard drinks most evenings. He has no abdominal pain now and has never been admitted with pancreatitis, and he has no personal or family history of cardiovascular disease. The laboratory has telephoned because his fasting lipid sample was grossly lipaemic.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, waist circumference 112 cm, eruptive xanthomata over both elbows and the extensor surfaces of the forearms, no hepatomegaly, no abdominal tenderness, no corneal arcus, no tendon xanthomata
data_table.Investigations: Fasting triglycerides 22.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), total cholesterol 9.8 mmol/L (less than 5.5), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.7 mmol/L (greater than 1.0), low density lipoprotein cholesterol not calculable, glycated haemoglobin 10.2 per cent (less than 7.0 for treated diabetes), lipase 38 U/L (less than 60), liver function tests showing an alanine aminotransferase of 68 U/L (less than 40), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management of his lipid abnormality?

options.text: Refer him urgently for therapeutic plasma exchange to clear the circulating triglycerides before starting any oral lipid lowering therapy
options.rationale: Plasma exchange removes triglycerides rapidly but is invasive, resource intensive and reserved for severe hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, particularly with organ failure or in pregnancy. He has no abdominal pain and a normal lipase, so there is no acute indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence a high intensity statin as the sole lipid lowering agent and reassess his full lipid profile again in three months
options.rationale: Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and will not bring a level above 20 mmol/L out of the pancreatitis range, although one is eventually indicated for his cardiovascular risk as a man with diabetes. A statin alone is the correct choice once triglycerides are below about 5 mmol/L and low density lipoprotein cholesterol is the target. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence ezetimibe and review whether his total cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations have fallen when he returns in three months
options.rationale: Ezetimibe blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption and has almost no effect on triglycerides, so it does not address the abnormality that threatens his pancreas. It is used as an add on to a statin when low density lipoprotein cholesterol targets are not met. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence a high dose omega 3 fatty acid preparation as the only agent and review his triglyceride level again in three months
options.rationale: Omega 3 preparations lower triglycerides usefully but less reliably than a fibrate at this magnitude of elevation, and using one alone in a man at immediate risk of pancreatitis is insufficient. They are a reasonable adjunct where a fibrate is not tolerated or the response is incomplete. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence a fibrate alongside intensified glycaemic control and a structured plan to reduce his alcohol intake substantially
options.rationale: At triglyceride concentrations above about 10 mmol/L the immediate danger is acute pancreatitis rather than atherosclerosis, and a fibrate is the most effective triglyceride lowering agent while uncontrolled diabetes and alcohol are the two drivers that must be corrected simultaneously. Lipid lowering alone will not succeed while the glycated haemoglobin remains above 10 per cent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia in adults is almost always the product of a genetic predisposition unmasked by acquired factors, of which uncontrolled diabetes, alcohol, obesity, hypothyroidism, renal disease, oestrogen therapy, and drugs such as isotretinoin and second generation antipsychotics are the commonest. The clinical priority shifts at around 10 mmol/L, above which the risk of acute pancreatitis rises steeply and becomes the dominant concern, whereas below that level treatment is driven by cardiovascular risk. Eruptive xanthomata, lipaemia retinalis and a grossly lipaemic sample are the physical correlates of very high concentrations, and laboratory interference means the low density lipoprotein cholesterol cannot be calculated. Treatment combines removal of the acquired drivers with a fibrate, supported by dietary fat restriction, and insulin is added in diabetes both to control glycaemia and because it activates lipoprotein lipase directly. Once triglycerides fall below about 5 mmol/L, attention returns to low density lipoprotein cholesterol and a statin for cardiovascular protection.
key_points: Above about 10 mmol/L the dominant risk is acute pancreatitis rather than atherosclerosis.
Uncontrolled diabetes and alcohol are the two commonest acquired drivers in adults.
Fibrates are the most effective triglyceride lowering agents at this magnitude.
Statins and ezetimibe have little effect on very high triglyceride concentrations.
Once triglycerides fall below about 5 mmol/L, cardiovascular risk reduction resumes priority.
explanation.pearls: Serum lipase can be falsely normal in hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis because the lipaemic sample interferes with the assay, so a patient with severe abdominal pain and triglycerides above 10 mmol/L should be treated as having pancreatitis on clinical and imaging grounds regardless of the enzyme result.

subtopic_detail: Bruising and mouth bleeding in a young adult with pancytopenia, a very low reticulocyte count and no organomegaly
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 22 year old university student referred with three weeks of tiredness and easy bruising. She says her gums bleed when she brushes her teeth and that she has bruises on her legs she cannot account for.

She takes no regular medications, has taken no new supplements and has not travelled. She has had no fevers at home and feels well enough to have attended her lectures this week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pallor of the conjunctivae, scattered petechiae over both shins and two large bruises on the thighs, blood crusting at the gingival margins, no lymphadenopathy anywhere, no hepatomegaly and no splenomegaly, no bone tenderness over the sternum
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 76 g/L (115 to 165) with a mean cell volume of 94 fL (80 to 100), white cell count 1.9 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with a neutrophil count of 0.6 x10^9/L (2.0 to 7.5), platelets 11 x10^9/L (150 to 400), reticulocyte count 6 x10^9/L (20 to 100), blood film showing no blasts and no dysplastic forms, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for presumed immune destruction of the blood cells and review her counts in the clinic in one week
options.rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia affects platelets alone and would not explain the anaemia, neutropenia and profoundly suppressed reticulocyte count, and starting steroids before a marrow diagnosis can obscure the histology. Steroids are appropriate once an immune mechanism has been established. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and platelets and arrange outpatient haematology review with repeat blood counts in two weeks
options.rationale: Transfusing without a diagnosis and sending her home leaves a profoundly neutropenic young woman exposed to overwhelming infection and delays a diagnosis that determines urgent treatment. Transfusion support is given alongside, not instead of, same day specialist assessment. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

options.text: Start oral iron and a multivitamin preparation and repeat her full blood count and iron studies again in four weeks
options.rationale: Nutritional deficiency does not cause a pancytopenia with this degree of reticulocytopenia, and her mean cell volume, vitamin B12 and folate are all normal. Haematinic replacement is the right answer when a single deficient nutrient is demonstrated. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

options.text: Arrange same day haematology assessment for bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics, alongside transfusion and neutropenic precautions
options.rationale: Pancytopenia with a reticulocyte count this low indicates failure of marrow production rather than peripheral destruction, and only a marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetic studies will separate aplastic anaemia from hypoplastic myelodysplasia or an infiltrative process. The severity of the neutropenia makes this a same day rather than an outpatient problem. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

options.text: Request a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to search for an occult malignancy causing her blood count abnormalities
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging cannot diagnose a disorder of marrow production and delays the test that will, particularly with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly to pursue. Staging imaging follows a tissue diagnosis when lymphoma or another malignancy is confirmed. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

explanation.summary: Pancytopenia is approached by asking whether the marrow is failing to produce cells or the periphery is destroying them, and the reticulocyte count is the single most informative discriminator, since a marrow responding appropriately to anaemia raises it. A very low reticulocyte count alongside an absence of organomegaly, lymphadenopathy and circulating blasts points towards acquired aplastic anaemia, an immune mediated destruction of haematopoietic stem cells that peaks in young adults and again in later life. The diagnosis requires a bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing a hypocellular marrow without fibrosis or infiltration, with cytogenetics and flow cytometry to exclude hypoplastic myelodysplastic syndrome and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Severity is graded on the neutrophil, platelet and reticulocyte counts, and severe disease is a medical emergency because untreated it carries very high mortality from infection and bleeding. Treatment is either allogeneic stem cell transplantation, favoured in younger patients with a matched sibling donor, or immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin and ciclosporin, increasingly with eltrombopag added.
key_points: The reticulocyte count separates failure of production from peripheral destruction.
Absent organomegaly, lymphadenopathy and blasts point away from leukaemia and lymphoma.
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics is required to make the diagnosis.
Severe aplastic anaemia is a medical emergency because of infection and bleeding risk.
Treatment is stem cell transplantation or immunosuppression depending on age and donor availability.
explanation.pearls: Avoid transfusing blood products donated by family members in any young person with suspected marrow failure, because alloimmunisation to related donor antigens measurably worsens the outcome of a subsequent allogeneic stem cell transplant from that same family.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia
National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Four months of dry tickly cough in a man with a clear chest and normal spirometry who began a blood pressure tablet last year
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 58 year old man referred with four months of a dry tickly cough that he describes as a constant need to clear his throat. It troubles him most when he lies down and when he talks on the telephone at work.

He produces no sputum, has never wheezed and has no heartburn or acid taste. He has smoked five cigarettes a day for thirty years and has not lost weight. His blood pressure medication was changed eleven months ago and he had no cough before that.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation with no wheeze or crackles, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, oropharynx normal with no cobblestoning or postnasal discharge, no ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph reported as normal with clear lung fields, spirometry showing a forced expiratory volume in one second of 92 per cent predicted with a ratio of 0.78 and no bronchodilator response, full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor twice daily for eight weeks and review whether his cough has settled at the end of the course
options.rationale: Reflux related cough is a genuine cause and can occur without heartburn, but it should not be pursued ahead of a drug cause that has a clear temporal relationship and is reversible within weeks. Acid suppression is the next step once the medication has been changed and the cough persists. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest to exclude a malignancy given his smoking history and the duration of the cough
options.rationale: Chronic cough in a smoker always deserves a thought about malignancy, but he has a normal chest radiograph, no haemoptysis, no weight loss and no clubbing or lymphadenopathy, and a reversible drug cause that is easily tested. Computed tomography is warranted if the cough persists after the drug is withdrawn or if any red flag emerges. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Commence a trial of inhaled corticosteroid for eight weeks on the basis that cough variant asthma is the likeliest explanation
options.rationale: Cough variant asthma produces a nocturnal or exercise related cough with variable airflow obstruction or bronchodilator responsiveness, and his spirometry is normal with no response. An inhaled corticosteroid trial, ideally with sputum eosinophil counts, belongs later in the pathway. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Substitute his angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker and reassess his cough after four weeks
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor cough affects up to one in ten users, is characteristically dry and tickly, and can begin anywhere from hours to a year after the drug is started, which makes the delayed onset here entirely consistent. Angiotensin receptor blockers do not cause the cough because they do not inhibit bradykinin breakdown, so substitution both tests and treats the hypothesis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe an intranasal corticosteroid with an oral antihistamine for upper airway cough syndrome and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Upper airway cough syndrome is a leading cause of chronic cough but is suggested by postnasal discharge, throat cobblestoning or nasal symptoms, none of which he has. It is the reasonable next trial once a drug cause has been excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Chronic cough is defined as a cough lasting more than eight weeks and, in a non smoker with a normal chest radiograph, is dominated by three causes: upper airway cough syndrome, asthma or eosinophilic bronchitis, and gastro oesophageal reflux. Before working through that triad, the single most rewarding step is to review the medication list, because angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are among the most widely prescribed drugs in Australia and cause cough in up to a tenth of those taking them. The mechanism is accumulation of bradykinin and substance P in the airway rather than any structural change, which explains why the cough is dry and tickly, why examination and investigations are normal, and why angiotensin receptor blockers are a safe substitute. The characteristic that trips clinicians up is the timing, since onset ranges from the first dose to a year of uneventful use, so a long period of tolerance does not exclude the drug. Resolution usually begins within one to four weeks of withdrawal but occasionally takes up to three months, so the trial must be given adequate time before the cause is dismissed.
key_points: Review the medication list before working through the chronic cough triad.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor cough affects up to ten per cent of users.
Onset ranges from hours to a year after starting, so delayed onset does not exclude the drug.
Angiotensin receptor blockers do not cause cough and are a direct substitute.
Resolution usually occurs within one to four weeks but can take up to three months.
