explanation.pearls: Allow up to three months after withdrawal before concluding that an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor was not the cause of a chronic cough, because a minority of patients take that long to settle and rechallenging or investigating too early sends them down an unnecessary diagnostic pathway.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

subtopic_detail: Severe wet season pneumonia in a Top End man with diabetes and heavy alcohol use growing a Gram negative bacillus
stem:
You are the general medical registrar in a Darwin hospital in February admitting a 52 year old man with five days of fever, productive cough and increasing breathlessness. He works maintaining irrigation lines on a market garden and has been out in heavy rain and mud most of the week.

He has type 2 diabetes with a glycated haemoglobin of 11.4 per cent and drinks heavily. He was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin in the emergency department twelve hours ago and has deteriorated since, now requiring 8 litres per minute of oxygen. The laboratory has telephoned to say both blood culture bottles are growing a Gram negative bacillus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 91 per cent on 8 litres per minute of oxygen, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breathing at the right upper zone with coarse crackles bilaterally, no skin abscess or ulcer found on full skin survey, no neck stiffness, no joint effusion, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph showing right upper lobe consolidation with a developing cavity, white cell count 18.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 342 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60 to 110), lactate 3.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glycated haemoglobin 11.4 per cent (less than 7.0 for treated diabetes), blood cultures growing a Gram negative bacillus with bipolar staining

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Continue ceftriaxone and add oral doxycycline to cover atypical and zoonotic causes of community acquired pneumonia in this region
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is unreliable against the organism suggested here and doxycycline has no role in the intensive phase of treatment, so this leaves a rapidly progressive infection inadequately covered. Doxycycline is relevant to other tropical zoonoses such as Q fever, leptospirosis and rickettsial infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Change to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate once he is afebrile and continue it for a total course of three weeks after discharge
options.rationale: Oral therapy has no place in the intensive phase of a severe cavitating pneumonia with bacteraemia and shock, and amoxicillin with clavulanate is inferior for this organism. It is sometimes used as a second line eradication agent in pregnancy or intolerance, after the intravenous phase is complete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Change to intravenous gentamicin combined with amoxicillin to broaden Gram negative cover while awaiting formal identification and sensitivities
options.rationale: Aminoglycosides and amoxicillin are both ineffective against this organism, which is intrinsically resistant to gentamicin, and this combination would be actively harmful in a man with acute kidney injury. Gentamicin remains useful for other Gram negative sepsis where renal function permits. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Change to intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam as broad spectrum cover for a Gram negative bacteraemia with a pulmonary source
options.rationale: Piperacillin with tazobactam covers most Gram negative organisms but is not recommended for this infection, where carbapenem or ceftazidime therapy is supported by mortality data from Australian trials. It is a reasonable empirical choice for healthcare associated Gram negative sepsis without this epidemiological picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Change to intravenous meropenem and plan a prolonged intensive phase followed by months of oral eradication therapy
options.rationale: Wet season cavitating pneumonia with septic shock in a Top End man with diabetes and soil exposure, growing a bipolar staining Gram negative bacillus, is melioidosis, and Burkholderia pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to the usual community acquired pneumonia regimens. Treatment requires an intensive phase of at least two weeks with meropenem or ceftazidime followed by at least three months of oral eradication therapy to prevent relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental saprophyte of soil and surface water across northern Australia and South East Asia, and cases cluster sharply in the monsoonal wet season when the organism is brought to the surface and aerosolised. Diabetes is the single strongest risk factor, followed by hazardous alcohol use, chronic lung disease, chronic kidney disease and immunosuppression, and around four fifths of patients have at least one. Pneumonia is the commonest presentation and may cavitate and progress rapidly to septic shock, while other presentations include skin abscesses, genitourinary infection, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, parotid abscess in children and central nervous system disease. The organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, gentamicin and most cephalosporins other than ceftazidime, which is why standard community acquired pneumonia regimens fail. Treatment has two phases: an intensive intravenous phase of at least two weeks with meropenem or ceftazidime, extended for deep seated infection, followed by at least three months of oral eradication therapy with trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, and relapse follows incomplete eradication.
key_points: Wet season presentation with soil or water exposure in northern Australia is the epidemiological signature.
Diabetes and hazardous alcohol use are the dominant host risk factors.
The organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, gentamicin and most cephalosporins.
Intensive phase is at least two weeks of meropenem or ceftazidime intravenously.
Eradication requires at least three months of oral therapy to prevent relapse.
explanation.pearls: Extend the intravenous intensive phase to four weeks for deep seated disease and to eight weeks for central nervous system, bone or joint involvement, because relapse rates rise sharply when a fourteen day course is applied to infection at these sites.

subtopic_detail: Vomiting with yellow green visual disturbance and bradycardia in an older woman weeks after two new cardiac drugs were added
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 78 year old woman brought in by her daughter with four days of nausea, vomiting and poor appetite. Her daughter says she has been muddled since yesterday and complains that everything looks as though it has a yellow green haze over it.

She has taken digoxin for atrial fibrillation for six years without trouble. Three weeks ago her general practitioner added two new tablets for her blood pressure and heart. She has not taken any extra digoxin tablets and the packet count matches her prescription.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 42 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable and orientated to person only, dry mucous membranes, heart sounds dual with no murmur, chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 6.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), creatinine 194 micromol/L (45 to 90) risen from 92 micromol/L three months ago, sodium 134 mmol/L (135 to 145), serum digoxin concentration 4.6 nanomol/L (0.5 to 1.0), electrocardiogram showing bradycardia with frequent ventricular ectopy and short runs of bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilise the cardiac membrane against the effects of her raised serum potassium concentration
options.rationale: Calcium is the standard first move in hyperkalaemia but is traditionally avoided in acute digoxin toxicity, where intracellular calcium is already high and further loading is thought to risk refractory contracture. The hyperkalaemia here is a consequence of the poisoning and resolves as the toxin is neutralised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give an intravenous insulin and dextrose infusion as the sole treatment for the hyperkalaemia and repeat her potassium in two hours
options.rationale: Shifting potassium into cells treats a marker of severity while leaving the poisoning that produced it entirely untreated, so the arrhythmia risk persists. Insulin and dextrose is appropriate for hyperkalaemia from other causes or as an adjunct while antidote is being prepared. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Insert a temporary transvenous pacing wire to protect against her bradycardia while the drug is cleared over the next several days
options.rationale: Pacing wire insertion in a digoxin poisoned myocardium can provoke ventricular fibrillation and does not treat the toxicity, so it is avoided where antidote is available. Temporary pacing is reserved for haemodynamically significant bradycardia when digoxin immune Fab cannot be obtained. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis to clear the drug from her circulation and to correct the raised potassium concentration at the same time
options.rationale: Digoxin has a very large volume of distribution and is bound extensively within tissue, so dialysis removes a negligible fraction of the body burden. Dialysis is useful for toxins with small volumes of distribution such as lithium, salicylate and toxic alcohols. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous digoxin specific antibody fragments and monitor her rhythm and potassium closely as the toxicity reverses
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia in chronic digoxin toxicity indicates poisoning of the sodium potassium pump and is an indication for digoxin specific antibody fragments, as are bidirectional ventricular tachycardia and haemodynamically significant bradycardia. The antidote reverses all these effects within an hour and the potassium falls as the pump recovers. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

explanation.summary: Chronic digoxin toxicity in older people is usually precipitated by a fall in renal clearance or by an interacting drug rather than by an overdose, and the two tablets commonly added for blood pressure and rate control, an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and a diuretic or amiodarone, do both. The clinical picture is dominated by gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric symptoms with the characteristic yellow green visual disturbance, and the electrocardiogram shows a wide range of bradyarrhythmias and ventricular ectopy, with bidirectional ventricular tachycardia being close to pathognomonic. Hyperkalaemia arises because digoxin inhibits the sodium potassium adenosine triphosphatase pump, and in acute poisoning the potassium concentration predicts mortality better than the drug concentration does. Digoxin specific antibody fragments bind the drug and are indicated for life threatening arrhythmia, significant bradycardia unresponsive to atropine, hyperkalaemia attributable to the poisoning, or a very high concentration with symptoms. After the antidote is given, standard serum assays measure both bound and free drug and become uninterpretable, so treatment is guided by clinical response.
key_points: Chronic toxicity is usually precipitated by renal impairment or an interacting drug.
Yellow green visual disturbance and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia are characteristic.
Hyperkalaemia reflects poisoning of the sodium potassium pump and predicts severity.
Digoxin specific antibody fragments reverse arrhythmia, bradycardia and hyperkalaemia.
Dialysis is ineffective because of the very large volume of distribution.
explanation.pearls: Serum digoxin concentrations become uninterpretable for days after digoxin specific antibody fragments are given, because routine assays measure antibody bound drug as well as free drug, so repeat levels must not be used to judge whether further antidote is required.

subtopic_detail: Shock with a raised blood glucose after a large modified release calcium channel blocker ingestion unresponsive to calcium and atropine
stem:
You are the general medical registrar in the emergency department managing a 32 year old man who took around thirty modified release verapamil tablets three hours ago after an argument. He is alert and talking to you but looks grey.

He has received 2 litres of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent, atropine 1.2 mg and two doses of intravenous calcium gluconate without meaningful improvement. He has taken nothing else and the Poisons Information Centre has been contacted. Whole bowel irrigation has been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38 beats per minute, blood pressure 72/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated with cool peripheries and a capillary refill of 5 seconds, chest clear with no crackles, jugular venous pressure not elevated, abdomen soft, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 13.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5) with no history of diabetes, lactate 4.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), corrected calcium 2.74 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60) after the calcium given, creatinine 96 micromol/L (60 to 110), electrocardiogram showing a junctional bradycardia with a normal QRS duration, bedside echocardiography showing preserved left ventricular contractility with a dilated inferior vena cava

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Give repeated further boluses of intravenous calcium gluconate targeting a corrected serum calcium concentration well above the normal range
options.rationale: Calcium is a reasonable early measure but its effect is transient and incomplete in significant calcium channel blocker poisoning, and his calcium is already above the reference range without response. Persisting with it risks hypercalcaemia while delaying the treatment that works. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Commence an intravenous lipid emulsion infusion as the primary circulatory rescue therapy for this lipophilic drug overdose
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is a salvage therapy for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity and is considered in cardiac arrest from other lipophilic drugs, but the evidence in calcium channel blocker poisoning is weak and it interferes with laboratory assays and extracorporeal circuits. It is not the treatment to reach for while a patient still has a perfusing rhythm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Commence an adrenaline infusion titrated to blood pressure as the sole additional therapy and admit him to the intensive care unit
options.rationale: Catecholamines are used as adjuncts but frequently fail to restore perfusion alone in significant poisoning because the underlying problem is impaired calcium mediated excitation contraction coupling and myocardial glucose utilisation. A vasopressor is a supportive measure alongside, not instead of, the definitive therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Commence high dose insulin euglycaemic therapy with dextrose and close monitoring of his glucose and potassium concentrations
options.rationale: High dose insulin with dextrose is the definitive therapy for significant calcium channel blocker poisoning because it restores myocardial carbohydrate utilisation and has a positive inotropic effect that catecholamines and calcium cannot reproduce. The hyperglycaemia in a non diabetic patient reflects blocked pancreatic insulin release and is itself a marker of severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give a single dose of activated charcoal by mouth and observe him closely on the resuscitation bay for the next four hours
options.rationale: Decontamination remains relevant for modified release preparations and whole bowel irrigation has already started, but it does nothing for the shock in front of you and observation alone in a patient with this degree of hypoperfusion is not tenable. Charcoal is an adjunct in a patient with a protected airway, never a substitute for circulatory support. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

explanation.summary: Calcium channel blocker poisoning is among the most lethal of common pharmaceutical overdoses, and verapamil and diltiazem are particularly dangerous because they depress both conduction and contractility, whereas dihydropyridines such as amlodipine produce predominantly vasodilatory shock. Modified release preparations are a specific hazard because absorption continues for many hours and patients who look well on arrival can deteriorate abruptly, which is why whole bowel irrigation and prolonged monitoring are recommended. Hyperglycaemia in a patient without diabetes is a useful early marker of severity, arising because calcium channel blockade inhibits pancreatic insulin release and shifts the myocardium away from its usual free fatty acid metabolism at exactly the moment it needs carbohydrate. High dose insulin euglycaemic therapy exploits that mechanism and has become the definitive treatment, given as a bolus followed by a high rate infusion with dextrose and close monitoring of glucose and potassium, since hypokalaemia is expected and is largely a shift rather than a deficit. Refractory cases proceed to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and early discussion with a toxicologist and the intensive care team is essential.
key_points: Verapamil and diltiazem depress conduction and contractility, unlike dihydropyridines.
Modified release preparations cause delayed and prolonged toxicity requiring extended monitoring.
Hyperglycaemia without diabetes reflects blocked insulin release and marks severity.
High dose insulin euglycaemic therapy is the definitive treatment and is inotropic.
Refractory shock is an indication for early extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
explanation.pearls: Expect and tolerate a falling serum potassium during high dose insulin euglycaemic therapy, replacing it only to keep the concentration above about 2.5 mmol/L, because the fall is an intracellular shift rather than a true deficit and aggressive replacement produces dangerous rebound hyperkalaemia when the insulin is weaned.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Calcium channel blocker poisoning
BMJ Best Practice: Calcium channel blocker overdose

subtopic_detail: Severe cramping pain, sweating and hypertension developing half an hour after a barely noticed sting off a north Queensland beach
stem:
You are the medical registrar at a Cairns hospital in January seeing a 28 year old backpacker brought in by ambulance. She was swimming beyond the stinger net and felt what she describes as a small scratch on her shoulder that she barely noticed at the time.

About thirty minutes later she developed severe cramping pain in her lower back and abdomen, began vomiting and told the paramedics she felt certain she was about to die. Vinegar has been applied to the sting site. She is restless and drenched in sweat, and has had 5 mg of intravenous morphine without much effect.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 188/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Restless and agitated with piloerection and profuse sweating, a faint 3 cm patch of erythema over the right shoulder with no tentacle marks and no weals, chest clear with no crackles, abdomen soft with generalised discomfort but no guarding, no rash elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic change, troponin pending, chest radiograph clear, potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45 to 90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Administer box jellyfish antivenom intravenously and repeat the dose if her pain and cardiovascular signs do not settle
options.rationale: Box jellyfish antivenom is raised against Chukia fleckeri and has no established role in this syndrome, in which there is no antivenom available. Antivenom is given for major Chukia fleckeri envenomation, which presents immediately with severe skin pain, characteristic ladder pattern weals and rapid cardiovascular collapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Apply a pressure immobilisation bandage to the affected limb and keep her still while awaiting resolution of her symptoms
options.rationale: Pressure immobilisation is used for snake and funnel web spider envenomation and is specifically not recommended for jellyfish stings, where it may worsen local venom discharge from adherent nematocysts. Vinegar to the sting site is the appropriate local measure in tropical Australian waters. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council: Envenomation guidelines)

options.text: Immerse the affected limb in hot water at 45 degrees Celsius for twenty minutes as the primary treatment for her severe pain
options.rationale: Hot water immersion is the standard treatment for bluebottle and stonefish stings, where the pain is local and the venom is heat labile, but her pain is systemic and generalised rather than confined to the sting. Local measures cannot address a catecholamine driven systemic syndrome. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council: Envenomation guidelines)

options.text: Give escalating doses of intravenous opioid analgesia with an antiemetic and monitor for pulmonary oedema and myocardial injury
options.rationale: Irukandji syndrome is a catecholamine surge for which no antivenom exists, so treatment is titrated intravenous opioid in doses that are often far larger than expected, with antiemetics, and close observation for the cardiomyopathy and pulmonary oedema that complicate severe cases. The delayed onset after a trivial sting with generalised pain and a sense of impending doom is the defining picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline for a presumed severe allergic reaction to the marine sting and observe her for four hours afterwards
options.rationale: Adding a catecholamine to a syndrome already driven by excess endogenous catecholamine release will worsen her hypertension and the risk of myocardial injury and pulmonary oedema. Adrenaline is correct for anaphylaxis, which presents with urticaria, airway compromise or hypotension rather than severe hypertension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

explanation.summary: Irukandji syndrome follows envenomation by Carukia barnesi and several related small carybdeid jellyfish found in tropical Australian waters, most often between November and May. The sting itself is trivial and frequently goes unnoticed, and the syndrome begins after a characteristic latent period of roughly twenty to forty minutes with severe generalised muscle cramps, back and abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, sweating, piloerection, restlessness, hypertension and an intense sense of impending doom. The mechanism is massive endogenous catecholamine release, which explains both the clinical picture and the two serious complications, namely stress cardiomyopathy with acute pulmonary oedema and, rarely, intracranial haemorrhage from severe hypertension. There is no antivenom, so treatment is supportive with generous titrated intravenous opioid analgesia, antiemetics and observation, and magnesium has been used but a randomised trial did not confirm benefit. Severe or persistent hypertension is managed with a short acting vasodilator such as a glyceryl trinitrate or phentolamine infusion, and patients need troponin measurement and echocardiography if cardiac features develop.
key_points: A latent period of twenty to forty minutes after a trivial sting is characteristic.
Generalised cramping pain, sweating, hypertension and a sense of doom define the syndrome.
The mechanism is massive endogenous catecholamine release.
No antivenom exists, so treatment is generous titrated opioid analgesia and supportive care.
Watch for stress cardiomyopathy with pulmonary oedema and for hypertensive complications.
explanation.pearls: Measure troponin and arrange echocardiography in any patient whose Irukandji symptoms last beyond a few hours or who develops breathlessness, because catecholamine mediated cardiomyopathy with acute pulmonary oedema typically appears four to twelve hours after the sting, well after the pain has begun to settle.

subtopic_detail: Unclottable blood one hour after a garden bite in a well patient with a correctly applied first aid bandage still in place
stem:
You are the medical registrar at a rural Victorian hospital seeing a 43 year old man bitten on the right ankle while clearing long grass an hour ago. He did not see the snake clearly. The ambulance service applied a broad elasticated bandage over the bite site and along the whole limb with a splint, and he has been kept still since.

He feels well, with no headache, no abdominal pain, no double vision and no difficulty swallowing. He is not bleeding from anywhere and the bandage has not been disturbed. The nearest tertiary hospital is two hours away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pressure bandage and splint intact over the right leg, no ptosis, full eye movements with no ophthalmoplegia, normal power in all limbs, no muscle tenderness, no bleeding from the gums or cannula sites, no lymphadenopathy in the groin
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio greater than 12 (0.8 to 1.2), activated partial thromboplastin time greater than 180 seconds (25 to 38), fibrinogen not detected, D-dimer markedly elevated, platelets 186 x10^9/L (150 to 400), creatine kinase 142 U/L (less than 200), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60 to 110), initial coagulation profile taken on arrival was within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Remove the pressure bandage now and observe him with repeat coagulation studies every six hours while he remains free of bleeding
options.rationale: Removing the bandage releases a bolus of venom into the systemic circulation and must not be done until antivenom is immediately available in a resuscitation area with adrenaline drawn up. Observation alone ignores a complete venom induced consumption coagulopathy that carries a real risk of intracranial haemorrhage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Transfuse fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate first to correct the coagulopathy, and reserve antivenom for any patient who bleeds
options.rationale: Giving clotting factors while venom is still circulating simply provides more substrate for the procoagulant toxin to consume, so factor replacement is given only after antivenom and only if bleeding is clinically significant. Antivenom neutralises the toxin and allows the patient's own factors to recover over hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Send a blood sample for venom detection so that the appropriate monovalent antivenom can be selected before any treatment is given
options.rationale: The venom detection kit is validated on a swab of the bite site or on urine and is unreliable on blood, and in any case its role is to guide antivenom choice rather than to decide whether antivenom is given. Geographical distribution and the clinical syndrome are the primary guides to antivenom selection in Australia. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council: Envenomation guidelines)

options.text: Arrange immediate road transfer to the tertiary hospital with the bandage in place and defer antivenom until he arrives there
options.rationale: A two hour transfer with an untreated consumption coagulopathy exposes him to catastrophic haemorrhage in a vehicle, and antivenom is stocked in and given from rural hospitals precisely to avoid this. Transfer is arranged after antivenom has been administered and the patient stabilised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give antivenom in a resuscitation area with adrenaline prepared, leaving the bandage until the infusion is running and he is being monitored
options.rationale: A complete venom induced consumption coagulopathy is definite systemic envenomation and mandates antivenom, given where anaphylaxis can be managed immediately, with the pressure bandage left undisturbed until the infusion is under way. This sequence prevents a further systemic venom bolus at the moment the patient is least protected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

explanation.summary: Australian snakebite management rests on pressure immobilisation first aid applied over the bite and the whole limb, observation in a hospital with antivenom, and serial testing to detect systemic envenomation, which is defined by coagulopathy, neurotoxicity, myotoxicity, acute kidney injury or a systemic syndrome of headache, vomiting and collapse. Brown snakes are the commonest cause of serious envenomation and characteristically produce an isolated venom induced consumption coagulopathy with an unrecordable international normalised ratio, undetectable fibrinogen and a grossly elevated D-dimer, often in a patient who otherwise looks entirely well. Coagulation studies and creatine kinase are repeated at one, six and twelve hours after the bite and before discharge, because the first set can be normal, as it was here. Antivenom is the treatment for systemic envenomation and is given in a monitored area with adrenaline available, since anaphylaxis is the main risk, and the pressure bandage is left in place until the infusion is running. Factor replacement is reserved for significant bleeding after antivenom, and the venom detection kit is used on a bite site swab rather than blood.
key_points: Systemic envenomation is defined by coagulopathy, neurotoxicity, myotoxicity or kidney injury.
Brown snake envenomation typically produces an isolated consumption coagulopathy in a well patient.
Repeat coagulation studies and creatine kinase at one, six and twelve hours after the bite.
Give antivenom in a resuscitation area and leave the pressure bandage until the infusion is running.
Factor replacement follows antivenom and only when bleeding is clinically significant.
explanation.pearls: Use the venom detection kit on a swab of the bite site rather than on blood or urine where a bite site is available, and never delay antivenom waiting for the result, because in most Australian regions only one or two snake types occur and geography plus syndrome already determine the choice.

subtopic_detail: Ringing ears, fever and confusion with a mixed acid base disturbance six hours after an uncounted analgesic ingestion
stem:
You are the general medical registrar in the emergency department managing a 19 year old woman brought in by her housemate six hours after she was found with an empty bottle of aspirin tablets of unknown count. She has vomited three times.

She tells you her ears are ringing and that she cannot hear you properly, and she is breathing deeply and continuously. Over the past hour she has become increasingly muddled and is no longer able to tell you the day. The intensive care registrar is on the phone asking whether to come and intubate her for her altered conscious state.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confused and agitated with a Glasgow coma scale of 13, deep sighing respirations, warm and diaphoretic, pupils equal and reactive, no neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Arterial pH 7.41 (7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 20 mmHg (35 to 45), bicarbonate 13 mmol/L (22 to 32), sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 3.3 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45 to 90), salicylate concentration 4.9 mmol/L (therapeutic less than 2.2) having risen from 3.6 mmol/L two hours earlier, paracetamol not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Proceed to rapid sequence intubation for airway protection and ventilate her using standard lung protective tidal volumes and rates
options.rationale: Her compensatory hyperventilation is what is keeping the salicylate ionised in plasma and out of the brain, and intubation with standard ventilator settings abolishes it, causing an abrupt fall in pH and a surge of drug into the central nervous system that has repeatedly proved fatal. Intubation is undertaken only when unavoidable, by the most experienced operator, with bicarbonate loading and matched high minute ventilation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give repeated doses of activated charcoal and repeat her salicylate concentration in a further four hours before deciding on any escalation
options.rationale: Multiple dose charcoal does reduce ongoing absorption and is a useful adjunct, but it does nothing about the drug already distributed into tissue in a patient who is confused with a rising concentration. Charcoal alone is adequate for an asymptomatic patient with a low and falling concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give a sodium chloride 0.9 per cent infusion with potassium replacement and repeat the salicylate concentration in a further six hours
options.rationale: Rehydration and potassium replacement are necessary but insufficient, because neither enhances elimination nor addresses the central nervous system toxicity that her confusion already demonstrates. Fluid and electrolyte correction alone suits a mildly symptomatic patient whose concentration is falling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous acetylcysteine according to the standard weight based protocol and continue it while her conscious state is monitored
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning and has no role in salicylate toxicity, and paracetamol was not detected on her screen. It would be indicated had this been a combination analgesic preparation containing paracetamol above the treatment line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

options.text: Start a sodium bicarbonate infusion with potassium replacement and refer her immediately for haemodialysis while avoiding intubation
options.rationale: Altered mental state in salicylate poisoning indicates central nervous system penetration and is an indication for haemodialysis regardless of the concentration, and a rising level above about 7.2 mmol/L with acidosis or renal impairment independently qualifies. Bicarbonate with potassium replacement traps salicylate in plasma and urine while dialysis is arranged, and intubation is avoided because losing her hyperventilation would be catastrophic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)

explanation.summary: Salicylate poisoning produces a characteristic mixed acid base disturbance in which direct stimulation of the respiratory centre causes a primary respiratory alkalosis while uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation generates a primary high anion gap metabolic acidosis, so the arterial pH may sit deceptively within the normal range while both processes are severe. Tinnitus, hyperventilation, vomiting, hyperthermia and hypoglycaemia are the classic features, and confusion signals that salicylate has crossed into the central nervous system, which is the point at which mortality rises steeply. Only the un-ionised fraction crosses the blood brain barrier, so maintaining alkalaemia with a bicarbonate infusion keeps the drug ionised in plasma and enhances its renal excretion, and potassium must be replaced aggressively because hypokalaemia prevents effective urinary alkalinisation. Cerebrospinal fluid glucose can be low despite a normal serum value, so dextrose is given to any confused patient regardless of the blood glucose. The most dangerous intervention available is intubation, because a period of apnoea or an inadequate ventilator minute volume collapses the respiratory compensation and drives the drug into the brain, and dialysis is the definitive treatment for severe poisoning.
key_points: The picture is a mixed respiratory alkalosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis with a near normal pH.
Confusion signals central nervous system penetration and is itself an indication for dialysis.
Bicarbonate keeps salicylate ionised in plasma and urine, and requires aggressive potassium replacement.
Intubation abolishes protective hyperventilation and can be rapidly fatal.
Give dextrose to any confused patient because central nervous system glucose can be low with a normal serum value.
explanation.pearls: Give dextrose to a confused salicylate poisoned patient even when the blood glucose is normal, because salicylate drives cerebral glucose consumption and cerebrospinal fluid glucose can be profoundly low while the serum value looks reassuring.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Salicylate poisoning

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis after eighteen months of an antiarrhythmic where the gland shows absent vascularity and no antibodies
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 64 year old man referred with six weeks of palpitations, tremor and a 7 kg weight loss. He has been taking amiodarone for eighteen months for symptomatic atrial fibrillation after other agents failed, and his rhythm has been well controlled until now.

He has no eye symptoms and no neck discomfort. He has never had thyroid disease and has no family history of it. He has not had a computed tomography scan or any other contrast study.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 148/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm sweaty palms, no palpable goitre and no thyroid bruit, no lid lag, no proptosis, no pretibial changes, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free thyroxine 46 pmol/L (10 to 20), free triiodothyronine 14 pmol/L (3.5 to 6.5), thyroid peroxidase and thyrotropin receptor antibodies both negative, thyroid ultrasound reporting a normal sized gland with absent vascularity on colour flow Doppler, interleukin 6 elevated, C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (less than 5), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence carbimazole at a high dose and titrate it downwards according to thyroid function tests repeated every four weeks
options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and are the treatment for the iodine induced hyperthyroidism of type one disease, but they achieve nothing where the gland is not synthesising hormone and is instead releasing preformed hormone as it is destroyed. The absent vascularity and negative antibodies are what separate the two types. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer him for radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid gland once his cardiovascular symptoms have been controlled with a beta blocker
options.rationale: The enormous iodine load carried by amiodarone saturates the gland and suppresses radioiodine uptake to near zero for many months, so ablation cannot work. Radioiodine remains a good option for Graves disease or a toxic nodule in a patient who has never taken amiodarone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Add potassium perchlorate to a thionamide to block further iodine uptake by the gland and reassess his thyroid function in six weeks
options.rationale: Perchlorate with a thionamide is the intensified regimen for type one disease, in which excess iodine is driving synthesis in an abnormal gland. Applying it to destructive thyroiditis treats a mechanism that is not operating and delays the treatment that works. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the amiodarone alone and observe his thyroid function over the coming months while controlling his symptoms with a beta blocker
options.rationale: Stopping the drug is reasonable to discuss but its half life is measured in months, so withdrawal has little short term effect and leaves severe thyrotoxicosis untreated in a man with atrial fibrillation. Cessation is also a cardiological decision, since he reached amiodarone only after other agents failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence high dose oral corticosteroid therapy and discuss with cardiology whether the amiodarone can be continued or ceased
options.rationale: Absent vascularity on Doppler with negative antibodies, no goitre and a raised interleukin 6 identifies type two disease, a destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone, which responds to corticosteroid, often within one to two weeks. Whether to continue amiodarone is decided jointly with cardiology, because the arrhythmia risk may outweigh the thyroid problem and the drug persists for months either way. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains around 37 per cent iodine by weight and a single 200 mg tablet delivers many times the recommended daily intake, which is why thyroid dysfunction affects a substantial minority of those taking it and can appear months after the drug is stopped given its half life of fifty to a hundred days. Two mechanisms of thyrotoxicosis are described. Type one is iodine induced excess synthesis in a gland with underlying pathology such as a nodule or latent Graves disease, and it shows a goitre, sometimes positive antibodies and normal or increased vascularity on colour Doppler, and it responds to thionamides with or without perchlorate. Type two is a destructive thyroiditis in a previously normal gland, releasing preformed hormone, and it shows no goitre, negative antibodies, absent vascularity and often a raised interleukin 6, and it responds to corticosteroid. Radioiodine is useless in either type because the iodine load suppresses uptake, mixed forms occur and are treated with both thionamide and steroid, and thyroidectomy is the fallback for refractory disease or when the arrhythmia demands that amiodarone continue.
key_points: Amiodarone carries a large iodine load and has a half life of fifty to a hundred days.
Type one arises in an abnormal gland with normal or increased vascularity and responds to thionamides.
Type two is destructive thyroiditis with absent vascularity and responds to corticosteroid.
Radioiodine is ineffective in both types because the iodine load suppresses uptake.
Mixed presentations are treated with both a thionamide and a corticosteroid.
explanation.pearls: Thyroidectomy under local or regional anaesthesia is the definitive option for amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis that fails medical therapy in a patient with poor cardiac reserve, and outcomes are better when it is done early rather than after months of uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis has further compromised the heart.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Amiodarone induced thyroid dysfunction

subtopic_detail: Two exacerbations in a year on dual bronchodilator therapy with blood eosinophils of 0.4
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a sixty six year old retired shearer with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has smoked forty pack years and stopped two years ago.

He has had two exacerbations in the past twelve months, each needing prednisolone and antibiotics, with one overnight hospital stay. He takes a combined long acting muscarinic antagonist and long acting beta agonist inhaler and you have watched him use it correctly today. He walks more slowly than people his age on the flat and stops after about two hundred metres. He has completed pulmonary rehabilitation and is up to date with influenza and pneumococcal vaccination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Barrel shaped chest with reduced expansion, quiet breath sounds with a prolonged expiratory phase, no wheeze at rest, no peripheral oedema, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Post bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in one second 45 per cent predicted with a ratio of 0.58, blood eosinophils 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alpha one antitrypsin within normal limits, chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without focal change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his inhaled therapy?

options.text: Continue the current inhaler and add long term azithromycin three times weekly after checking the corrected QT interval and hearing
options.rationale: Macrolide prophylaxis is an option for continued exacerbations despite optimised inhaled therapy, particularly in former smokers, but it comes after triple therapy rather than before it. It also carries risks of hearing loss, arrhythmia and resistance. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

options.text: Change to a combined inhaled corticosteroid and long acting beta agonist inhaler, stopping the long acting muscarinic antagonist component he now takes
options.rationale: Withdrawing the muscarinic antagonist removes a bronchodilator with proven exacerbation reduction in this disease and would represent a step backwards. Escalation means adding the steroid, not exchanging one component for another. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Change to a single inhaler containing an inhaled corticosteroid with both a long acting muscarinic antagonist and a long acting beta agonist
options.rationale: Adding an inhaled corticosteroid to dual bronchodilator therapy reduces exacerbations in people with frequent exacerbations and a blood eosinophil count at this level, and a single device preserves adherence. The eosinophil count is the biomarker that identifies who benefits. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

options.text: Continue the current inhaler and add regular oral prednisolone at a low maintenance dose to reduce the frequency of further exacerbations
options.rationale: Maintenance oral corticosteroid causes osteoporosis, diabetes, myopathy and skin fragility without reducing exacerbation frequency, and it has no place in stable disease. Steroid exposure here belongs in the airway rather than the bloodstream. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

options.text: Continue the current inhaler and add regular oral theophylline with periodic measurement of the serum concentration to guide the dose
options.rationale: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, numerous interactions and modest benefit, so it sits well down the escalation sequence. It would be considered only after inhaled options have been optimised. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

explanation.summary: Australian management of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease follows the COPD-X framework, in which non pharmacological measures including smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and a written action plan carry as much weight as inhaled therapy. Pharmacological escalation moves from a short acting reliever, to a single long acting bronchodilator, to dual long acting bronchodilators, with inhaled corticosteroid added for people who continue to exacerbate. The blood eosinophil count predicts who benefits from the inhaled corticosteroid, with little benefit below about zero point one five and progressively greater benefit above zero point three, so it is the biomarker used to make this decision. Inhaled corticosteroid in this disease raises the risk of pneumonia, which is why it is targeted rather than given to everyone. Before escalating, adherence, inhaler technique and the diagnosis itself are checked, and where exacerbations continue on triple therapy the options include long term macrolide therapy or referral for specialist assessment.
key_points: Escalate to triple therapy when exacerbations continue on dual bronchodilators.
Blood eosinophil count identifies those who benefit from an inhaled corticosteroid.
Inhaled corticosteroid in this disease increases pneumonia risk, so it is targeted.
Check adherence and inhaler technique before every escalation.
Maintenance oral corticosteroid has no role in stable disease.
explanation.pearls: A single combination device is preferred to two or three separate inhalers wherever possible, because each additional device roughly halves the chance of correct daily use, and mixed device types with different inspiratory flow requirements are a common hidden cause of apparent treatment failure.

sources.label: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

subtopic_detail: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder and weight loss in a seventy year old
stem:
You are the physician seeing a seventy year old woman referred by her general practitioner with three weeks of yellow eyes. She has no abdominal pain and no fever, but describes itching that keeps her awake, dark urine and pale stools.

She has lost 7 kg over two months without trying and her appetite has fallen. She drinks minimal alcohol, takes no regular medications and has had no previous abdominal surgery. Her abdominal ultrasound reports a dilated common bile duct and intrahepatic ducts with a distended gallbladder and no stones seen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Deeply jaundiced with scratch marks over the arms, smooth non tender palpable gallbladder below the right costal margin, liver edge not enlarged, no ascites, no palpable lymph nodes
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 210 micromol/L (less than 20), alkaline phosphatase 620 units per litre (30-110), gamma glutamyl transferase 480 units per litre (5-35), alanine aminotransferase 96 units per litre (5-35), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.9-1.3), ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts with no stones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy to establish a tissue diagnosis, with staging imaging arranged once the histological result is available for review
options.rationale: Biopsying the liver in obstructive jaundice yields only the secondary changes of obstruction unless a metastasis is targeted, and a coagulopathy from prolonged cholestasis adds bleeding risk. Tissue, when needed, is best obtained by endoscopic ultrasound guided sampling after staging. (Source: GESA: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen using a pancreatic protocol with arterial and portal venous phases, before any attempt at biliary intervention
options.rationale: A dedicated multiphase study defines the mass, its relationship to the mesenteric vessels and the presence of metastases, and this staging determines whether the disease is resectable. Stenting first introduces duct wall inflammation and air that degrade the staging images. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines

options.text: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with brushings and placement of a biliary stent to relieve the obstruction and the associated itch
options.rationale: Drainage before staging compromises the imaging that determines operability and adds pancreatitis and cholangitis risk, and preoperative stenting is not routinely required when surgery can proceed promptly. It is appropriate for cholangitis or when surgery will be delayed. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines

options.text: Repeat abdominal ultrasound after an overnight fast with attention to the distal duct, to look for a stone that may have been missed on the first study
options.rationale: Ultrasound is poor at visualising the distal duct behind bowel gas and has already established that the obstruction is distal. Repeating it delays definitive imaging in a patient with weight loss and painless jaundice. (Source: GESA: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Serum tumour marker measurement including carbohydrate antigen 19 point 9 and carcinoembryonic antigen, with imaging arranged according to those results
options.rationale: These markers rise with any biliary obstruction and lack the specificity to diagnose or exclude malignancy, so they cannot direct imaging. They are used for monitoring after a diagnosis has been established. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines

explanation.summary: Painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss in an older patient is pancreatic head or periampullary malignancy until proven otherwise, and the palpable distended gallbladder described by Courvoisier makes stone disease unlikely because a chronically inflamed stone bearing gallbladder is usually fibrotic and does not distend. The pattern of liver tests, with alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamyl transferase raised out of proportion to the transaminases, confirms cholestasis. The correct next step is a multiphase pancreatic protocol computed tomography scan, which identifies the primary lesion, defines the relationship between tumour and the superior mesenteric and coeliac vessels, and detects metastatic disease, thereby determining resectability. Endoscopic drainage before staging degrades those images and is reserved for cholangitis, severe symptomatic itch or a planned delay before surgery such as neoadjuvant therapy. Tissue diagnosis is obtained by endoscopic ultrasound guided fine needle sampling when required, and all cases are discussed in a multidisciplinary meeting at a centre with hepatobiliary surgical expertise.
key_points: Painless jaundice with weight loss in an older adult suggests pancreatic or periampullary malignancy.
A palpable distended gallbladder argues against stone disease as the cause.
Multiphase pancreatic protocol computed tomography is the staging investigation of choice.
Biliary stenting before staging degrades imaging and is not routinely required before surgery.
Tumour markers cannot diagnose or exclude the condition and are used for monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Check the international normalised ratio and give vitamin K before any procedure in prolonged cholestasis, because absent bile salts prevent absorption of fat soluble vitamins and produce a coagulopathy that corrects within a day of parenteral vitamin K but causes serious bleeding if it is overlooked.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines

subtopic_detail: Eligibility for lung cancer screening in a current smoker with a thirty five pack year history
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a fifty eight year old woman for a routine review. She smokes fifteen cigarettes a day and has done so since she was seventeen, giving about thirty five pack years, and she has tried to quit twice.

She has no cough, no haemoptysis, no chest pain and no weight loss, and she is otherwise well with no significant medical history. Her sister was recently diagnosed with lung cancer and she has read that scans are now available to detect it early. She asks what she should do and whether a chest X ray would be enough.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation with no wheeze, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, body mass index 26 kg/m2, no hoarseness
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function and liver function within normal limits, spirometry shows a ratio of 0.74 with a forced expiratory volume in one second of 88 per cent predicted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: She should have an annual chest radiograph instead, since it involves less radiation exposure and is more accessible in general practice than a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Chest radiography was tested in large randomised trials and did not reduce lung cancer mortality, because tumours are usually well advanced by the time they appear on a plain film. Lower radiation from a test that does not work is not an advantage. (Source: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines)
source_refs: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines

options.text: She is not eligible for screening because she has no respiratory symptoms, so she should be reviewed if cough, weight loss or haemoptysis develops
options.rationale: Screening by definition applies to asymptomatic people, and symptomatic patients require diagnostic investigation rather than screening. Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of early detection. (Source: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines)
source_refs: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines

options.text: She should be referred for sputum cytology and a serum tumour marker panel, with computed tomography arranged only if either of those results is abnormal
options.rationale: Sputum cytology and tumour markers have poor sensitivity for early disease and are not screening tests for this cancer. Using them as gatekeepers would miss most of the small peripheral lesions that screening is designed to find. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: She should be referred directly to a respiratory physician for bronchoscopy given her family history, with imaging arranged by the specialist afterwards
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is an invasive diagnostic procedure for a suspected central lesion, not a screening tool, and family history does not change the screening pathway for this cancer. Referral without imaging inverts the diagnostic sequence. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: She is eligible for low dose computed tomography through the national screening program, and you should also offer her structured smoking cessation support
options.rationale: The Australian program uses age, pack year history and current or recent smoking as its criteria, and she satisfies all three, with screening repeated at defined intervals while she remains eligible. Cessation support is offered alongside because it remains the single most effective risk reduction available to her. (Source: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines)
source_refs: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines

explanation.summary: Lung cancer causes more cancer deaths in Australia than any other malignancy, largely because most cases present at an advanced stage. Australia commenced a National Lung Cancer Screening Program in July 2025, offering biennial low dose computed tomography to asymptomatic people aged fifty to seventy without symptoms suggestive of lung cancer, who have a smoking history of at least thirty pack years and who currently smoke or have quit within the past ten years. The evidence comes from randomised trials showing a mortality reduction of around twenty per cent with low dose computed tomography, while chest radiography showed no benefit in equivalent trials. Results are reported using a structured nodule classification system that determines the interval to the next scan or referral for assessment, which limits investigation of the many benign nodules found. Screening is offered together with smoking cessation support, since cessation delivers a larger reduction in risk than screening does and the two are complementary rather than alternatives.
key_points: Eligibility rests on age, a smoking history of at least thirty pack years, and current or recent smoking.
Screening applies only to asymptomatic people, since symptoms require diagnostic workup.
Low dose computed tomography reduces mortality whereas chest radiography does not.
Structured nodule reporting determines the interval to the next scan or referral.
Cessation support is offered alongside screening and reduces risk more than screening alone.
explanation.pearls: Quitting is worth raising at every screening visit, because a screening participant who continues to smoke retains most of their excess risk, and the period around a scan is a recognised teachable moment when quit attempts are substantially more likely to succeed.

sources.label: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines
Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

subtopic_detail: Postural dizziness and two falls in a frail older man taking eleven regular medicines
stem:
You are the physician seeing an eighty eight year old man in the outpatient clinic after two falls at home in the past month, both when getting up from a chair. He lives alone with support from his daughter and walks with a stick.

He takes perindopril, amlodipine, furosemide, metoprolol, doxazosin, mirtazapine, temazepam, oxybutynin, atorvastatin, aspirin and pantoprazole. His blood pressure was measured in a supine and standing position today. He has no chest pain, palpitations or blackouts, and his daughter says his memory is slightly worse over the past year. There is no history of Parkinson disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/70 mmHg lying and 106/58 mmHg after three minutes standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Frail with reduced muscle bulk, timed up and go test prolonged, no focal neurological deficit, no resting tremor or rigidity, cardiac examination normal with no murmur, lying and standing pressures as recorded
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 42 mL/min/1.73m2, haemoglobin 118 g/L (130-175), electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain and carotid ultrasound to investigate the falls, and review his medicines once those results have been reviewed
options.rationale: Falls occurring on standing with a documented postural drop and a long list of culprit drugs do not require neurovascular imaging, and carotid disease does not cause falls of this pattern. Investigation of this kind delays the intervention that will actually help. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention

options.text: Withdraw the medicines contributing to postural hypotension and falls in a staged plan, reviewing symptoms and blood pressure after each change
options.rationale: Several of his medicines act directly on the mechanisms that maintain standing blood pressure or impair balance and cognition, and staged withdrawal with review is the approach that identifies which changes help without destabilising him. Deprescribing has the strongest evidence of any intervention for drug related falls. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people)
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.text: Start fludrocortisone to support the standing blood pressure and continue his current regimen, reviewing him again in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Adding a mineralocorticoid to counteract drugs that could simply be stopped compounds the polypharmacy and risks fluid overload, hypokalaemia and supine hypertension. Removing the cause precedes any pharmacological support. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people)
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.text: Prescribe graduated compression stockings and advise him to rise slowly from sitting, continuing all current medicines and reviewing in three months
options.rationale: Physical measures help at the margins but are poorly tolerated by frail older people and do not address a drop of this magnitude driven by five contributing drugs. Delaying review for three months leaves him at risk of a fracture in the interim. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention

options.text: Refer him for consideration of a permanent pacemaker given the sinus bradycardia, with medication review deferred until after the cardiology assessment
options.rationale: The bradycardia is explained by a beta blocker in a man with no syncope and no conduction disease, so it is a medication effect rather than an indication for pacing. Referral would expose him to a procedure that treats an iatrogenic finding. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people)
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

explanation.summary: Falls in frail older people are multifactorial, and medication is the most readily modifiable contributor, with risk rising steeply as the number of regular medicines increases. This man is taking four antihypertensives including an alpha blocker and a diuretic, a sedating antidepressant, a benzodiazepine and an anticholinergic agent for bladder symptoms, and together these explain both the postural drop and the impaired recovery when he stands. Deprescribing proceeds in stages rather than all at once, prioritising the drugs with the clearest link to the presenting harm, with each change followed by review of symptoms, blood pressure and function, and with the patient and family involved in the decisions. Anticholinergic burden deserves particular attention because it contributes to cognitive impairment as well as falls, and the bladder anticholinergic here is a frequent culprit. Comprehensive assessment also covers vision, footwear, home hazards, vitamin D and strength and balance exercise, which has the best evidence of any non pharmacological falls intervention.
key_points: Medication review is the highest yield intervention for drug related falls.
Antihypertensives, alpha blockers, sedatives and anticholinergics are the usual contributors.
Withdraw in stages with review after each change rather than all at once.
Anticholinergic burden contributes to cognitive impairment as well as to falls.
Strength and balance exercise has the best evidence among non drug measures.
explanation.pearls: Measure the blood pressure after three minutes of standing rather than immediately, since the delayed drop is the one that causes falls on walking away from the chair, and an early reading taken at thirty seconds regularly misses it.

sources.label: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention

subtopic_detail: Large primary spontaneous pneumothorax with minimal symptoms in a stable young man
stem:
You are the emergency physician seeing a twenty three year old university student with left sided chest discomfort that came on suddenly while he was sitting at his desk four hours ago. He is tall and slim, smokes occasionally and has never had this before.

He walked into the department unaided and is comfortable at rest, describing mild pleuritic discomfort and no breathlessness when sitting. He has no underlying lung disease, no recent trauma and no diving history. His chest radiograph shows a left pneumothorax with a rim of about 3 cm at the level of the hilum and no mediastinal shift. He lives ten minutes away with two housemates and has reliable transport.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Comfortable at rest and speaking in full sentences, reduced breath sounds at the left apex, trachea central, no surgical emphysema, no distended neck veins, chest wall not tender
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph shows a left sided pneumothorax with an interpleural rim of about 3 cm at the hilum, no mediastinal shift, no effusion, no underlying parenchymal abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer him for video assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis during this admission to prevent recurrence, since the pneumothorax is large
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated for a persistent air leak, a second ipsilateral event, a first contralateral event or occupational reasons such as flying or diving, not for a first uncomplicated episode. Operating now would over treat a condition that often resolves without intervention. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

options.text: Admit him for high flow oxygen by mask for twenty four hours with a repeat radiograph the next morning before deciding whether drainage is required
options.rationale: Supplemental oxygen modestly accelerates resorption and is used in admitted patients, but admitting a comfortable young man purely for oxygen is unnecessary when observation and outpatient review are safe. The admission adds cost without adding benefit. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

options.text: Observe him for several hours and arrange outpatient review with a repeat radiograph, giving written advice about symptoms that require immediate return
options.rationale: Conservative management is supported for a stable patient with minimal symptoms regardless of the size of the pneumothorax, with a randomised trial showing non inferior lung reexpansion and fewer adverse events than intervention. Safe discharge depends on proximity, reliable transport and clear return advice. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

options.text: Insert a large bore intercostal catheter connected to an underwater seal drain and admit him to the ward until the lung has fully reexpanded
options.rationale: A large bore tube causes more pain and more complications than smaller alternatives and is reserved for tension, haemopneumothorax or ventilated patients. Routine drainage of a stable primary pneumothorax has been superseded. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

options.text: Perform needle aspiration in the department, and if the lung reexpands discharge him with follow up and advice about symptoms requiring return
options.rationale: Aspiration remains an accepted option and was the previous default for a large pneumothorax, but it offers no advantage over observation in a patient with minimal symptoms and introduces a procedural risk. It is chosen when symptoms warrant active intervention. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in people without known lung disease, characteristically tall slim young men, and smoking substantially raises the risk. Management has shifted over the past decade from size based algorithms toward a symptom based approach, after a randomised trial demonstrated that conservative management of moderate to large primary pneumothorax was non inferior to interventional management for lung reexpansion at eight weeks, with fewer adverse events and fewer days in hospital. A stable patient with minimal symptoms can therefore be observed and reviewed as an outpatient, provided they can return quickly and have been given clear advice about worsening breathlessness. Intervention, by aspiration or small bore catheter, is reserved for significant symptoms, physiological compromise, or secondary pneumothorax in a patient with underlying lung disease, in whom the threshold is much lower. Smoking cessation halves the recurrence risk, and patients are advised not to fly until resolution is confirmed and never to dive again unless definitive surgical management has been undertaken.
key_points: Management is guided by symptoms and stability rather than by radiographic size alone.
Conservative management is non inferior for a stable patient with minimal symptoms.
Intervention is reserved for significant symptoms, instability or secondary pneumothorax.
Surgery follows persistent air leak, recurrence or occupational indications.
Smoking cessation substantially reduces the recurrence risk.
explanation.pearls: Diving is contraindicated for life after a spontaneous pneumothorax unless definitive surgical pleurectomy has been performed and cleared by a diving medicine specialist, and flying is deferred until resolution is radiologically confirmed, usually about a week afterwards.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia with a raised parathyroid hormone and preserved renal function
stem:
You are the physician seeing a fifty two year old primary school teacher referred with a high calcium level found when she was investigated for tiredness. She describes constipation, low mood and two episodes of loin pain over the past year, the second of which passed a stone she collected.

She takes no supplements, no thiazide diuretic and no lithium. Her mother had a parathyroid operation in her sixties. A bone density scan performed last month showed a T score of minus 2.1 at the distal third of the radius. She has had no fractures.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well appearing with no palpable neck mass, no bony tenderness, no proximal weakness, abdomen soft with no renal angle tenderness, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.90 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), parathyroid hormone 11.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, twenty four hour urinary calcium raised, vitamin D 68 nmol/L (above 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observe with annual calcium, renal function and bone density measurement, advising generous fluid intake and avoidance of calcium supplements
options.rationale: Surveillance is appropriate for asymptomatic disease that fails to meet operative criteria, and she meets them on two counts. Continuing to observe accepts further stones and bone loss that surgery would prevent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start an oral bisphosphonate to protect her skeleton and review the calcium in three months before deciding whether any further treatment is required
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates improve bone density in this condition but leave the hypercalcaemia and stone risk untreated, so they are an adjunct for patients who cannot have surgery. They do not address the underlying adenoma. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Check the urinary calcium to creatinine clearance ratio and reassure her if it is low, since this pattern suggests a benign familial condition needing no treatment
options.rationale: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is an important differential and the ratio is the right test for it, but her urinary calcium excretion is already known to be raised. Her stone disease also argues strongly against that diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer her for parathyroidectomy after localisation imaging, since she has symptomatic disease with a kidney stone and reduced bone density
options.rationale: A documented kidney stone is an operative criterion in its own right, and she also has symptoms attributable to the hypercalcaemia, so surgery offers cure where medical therapy does not. Localisation with ultrasound and sestamibi scanning guides a targeted operation rather than establishing the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start cinacalcet to lower the calcium level and monitor her calcium and renal function every six months in the outpatient clinic thereafter
options.rationale: Cinacalcet lowers calcium but does not improve bone density or prevent stones, and it is reserved for people in whom surgery is contraindicated or has failed. Using it in an operable patient trades cure for indefinite medical therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the community and is usually detected incidentally on a biochemistry panel. The diagnosis rests on a raised or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone in the presence of hypercalcaemia, typically with a low phosphate and raised urinary calcium excretion, and the main differential is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, which is distinguished by a low urinary calcium to creatinine clearance ratio and which needs no treatment.
