data_table.Examination: Four hertz right hand rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist with contralateral activation, decrementing finger tapping, reduced right arm swing
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, no hallucinations
data_table.Medications: No antiemetic, antipsychotic or other dopamine blocking drug

lead_in: Which initial symptomatic therapy would you recommend?

options.text: A monoamine oxidase B inhibitor such as rasagiline as monotherapy at the standard daily dose
options.rationale: This class gives a genuine but modest benefit and is a reasonable choice for mild symptoms not yet affecting function. It is unlikely to restore the fine motor precision that his clock repair work demands. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Deferring drug therapy with physiotherapy and review in six months given his preserved gait
options.rationale: Deferring is defensible while symptoms are not interfering with function, but he has told you they now interfere with the work he values. Exercise should accompany drug therapy rather than replace it once function is affected. (Source: Parkinson's Australia: Clinical Information)

options.text: Levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor, titrated slowly from a low starting dose
options.rationale: Levodopa gives the largest and most reliable motor benefit and is the preferred first agent in patients over about seventy, where the neuropsychiatric and impulse control risks of dopamine agonists outweigh their dyskinesia sparing advantage. His symptoms already impair skilled work, which is the trigger to treat rather than observe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: A non-ergot dopamine agonist such as pramipexole, titrated slowly from a low starting dose
options.rationale: Agonists are considered in younger patients to defer motor complications, but in this age group they cause substantially more somnolence, hallucinations, oedema and impulse control disorder for less motor benefit. The distinguishing consideration is age and cognitive reserve rather than tremor severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: An anticholinergic such as benzhexol, titrated slowly from a low starting dose for the tremor
options.rationale: Anticholinergics can help rest tremor but are avoided beyond middle age because of confusion, urinary retention and constipation, and they do nothing for bradykinesia or rigidity. His shrinking handwriting and decrementing finger taps are the disabling features. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antiparkinson Drugs)

explanation.summary: Asymmetric rest tremor with cogwheel rigidity, decrementing repetitive movement and reduced arm swing, in the absence of red flags such as early falls, vertical gaze palsy, cerebellar signs or prominent autonomic failure, is straightforward idiopathic parkinsonism. The decision to treat rests on functional impact, and skilled fine motor work that he can no longer perform meets that bar. In patients over about seventy, levodopa is preferred first line because dopamine agonists carry markedly higher rates of somnolence, hallucination and impulse control disorder with less motor benefit. Anticholinergics are avoided in this age group and address only tremor.
key_points: Treat when symptoms interfere with function, not at an arbitrary disease stage
Levodopa is first line above roughly seventy years of age
Dopamine agonists defer dyskinesia but cause more neuropsychiatric harm in older patients
Anticholinergics treat tremor only and are poorly tolerated beyond middle age
Absent red flags such as early falls or vertical gaze palsy support the idiopathic diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Contralateral activation, asking the patient to tap the opposite hand while you assess wrist tone, unmasks subtle cogwheel rigidity that is undetectable at rest and is the most useful bedside manoeuvre in early disease. Warn every patient starting levodopa that nausea in the first fortnight is managed with domperidone rather than metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, because the latter two cross the blood brain barrier and block the very receptors you are trying to stimulate.

subtopic_detail: sequencing haematinic replacement when macrocytic anaemia is accompanied by posterior column signs and both vitamin levels are low
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman in the assessment unit with three months of tiredness and unsteadiness that is worse in the dark. She has vitiligo and treated hypothyroidism and follows a strict vegan diet begun eleven years ago.

She describes pins and needles in both feet that has crept up to mid-calf. On examination vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at the knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes, and Romberg is positive. Reflexes are brisk at the knees with extensor plantar responses. Her haemoglobin is 96 g/L (115-155) with a mean cell volume of 112 fL (80-100), and the film shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum vitamin B12 is 84 pmol/L (150-700) and red cell folate is 220 nmol/L (>360). Thyroid function is within normal limits on her current thyroxine dose and there is no alcohol history.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Absent ankle vibration sense, impaired great toe joint position sense, positive Romberg, brisk knee reflexes with extensor plantars
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 112 fL (80-100), hypersegmented neutrophils on film, vitamin B12 84 pmol/L (150-700), red cell folate 220 nmol/L (>360)
data_table.Background: Vegan diet for eleven years, vitiligo, treated hypothyroidism with normal thyroid function

lead_in: How should you start replacement?

options.text: High dose oral cyanocobalamin now with oral folic acid added after the first week of treatment
options.rationale: High dose oral cobalamin works well through passive absorption for uncomplicated deficiency, including dietary and pernicious causes, but the parenteral route is preferred when neurological signs are present. The distinguishing factor is the cord involvement rather than the underlying cause of the deficiency. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Vitamin B12)

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells now and commence both vitamins once the haemoglobin is safe
options.rationale: A haemoglobin of 96 g/L in a woman who has adapted over months does not meet a transfusion threshold, and transfusion in severe megaloblastic anaemia risks fluid overload for no benefit. The reticulocyte response to cobalamin begins within days. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Patient Blood Management)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Patient Blood Management

options.text: Withhold both vitamins until intrinsic factor antibody and gastroscopy results clarify the cause
options.rationale: Establishing whether there is an autoimmune gastritis matters for lifelong therapy and cancer surveillance, but the samples can be taken now and treatment started the same day. Delaying replacement for investigation risks irreversible cord damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin now with oral folic acid added only after the cobalamin is running
options.rationale: When both are deficient, cobalamin must be replaced first or started simultaneously, because folate alone restores erythropoiesis while allowing the neurological lesion to progress. The parenteral route is chosen because she has neurological involvement, where reliable and rapid repletion matters more than convenience. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Oral folic acid 5 mg daily now with cobalamin added once the blood count has begun to respond
options.rationale: Giving folate first is the classic and genuinely harmful error, because it corrects the megaloblastic anaemia and removes the haematological warning sign while subacute combined degeneration of the cord advances. The cord lesion, not the anaemia, is what determines her long term function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, dorsal column signs and upper motor neurone reflexes is subacute combined degeneration of the cord from cobalamin deficiency. When folate is also low, the sequencing of replacement is the whole exam point: folate given alone drives haematopoiesis using the remaining cobalamin and accelerates neurological deterioration while making the blood count look better. Cobalamin is therefore given first or at the same time, and the parenteral route is preferred whenever neurological features are present. Her vegan diet plus vitiligo and autoimmune thyroid disease means both dietary insufficiency and autoimmune gastritis should be pursued, but investigation never delays treatment.
key_points: Replace cobalamin before or with folate, never folate alone, when both are deficient
Neurological involvement makes the parenteral route preferred over high dose oral therapy
Hypersegmented neutrophils and a mean cell volume above 110 fL point to megaloblastic rather than other macrocytosis
Brisk reflexes with extensor plantars plus dorsal column loss localise to the cord, not a peripheral neuropathy
Vitiligo with autoimmune thyroid disease raises the prior probability of autoimmune gastritis
explanation.pearls: Check potassium two to four days after starting cobalamin, because the burst of erythropoiesis drives potassium into new cells and can produce a clinically significant fall in a patient who was not hypokalaemic at baseline. Neurological recovery correlates with the duration of symptoms before treatment, so deficits present for more than six months frequently leave a permanent residue even with perfect replacement.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Patient Blood Management

subtopic_detail: headache with papilloedema in a young woman on a drug that is itself a recognised precipitant of raised pressure
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman referred by her optometrist. She has had a daily headache for seven weeks that is worse on waking and when she bends forward, and twice this week her vision has greyed out completely for a few seconds when she stood up quickly. She also describes a rhythmic whooshing in her right ear that matches her pulse.

Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she started oral isotretinoin for acne four months ago. Fundoscopy shows bilateral disc swelling with blurred margins and loss of spontaneous venous pulsation. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye and formal perimetry shows an enlarged blind spot bilaterally with no other field defect. There is no focal neurological deficit and no fever. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with venography is reported as showing no mass lesion, no hydrocephalus and patent dural venous sinuses.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema with absent venous pulsation, visual acuity 6/6 both eyes, no focal deficit, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Perimetry: bilateral enlarged blind spot only
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance brain with venography: no mass, no hydrocephalus, patent dural venous sinuses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start acetazolamide and arrange outpatient neurology review in six weeks without further testing
options.rationale: Acetazolamide is the right drug once the diagnosis is secure, but starting it without a measured opening pressure leaves the diagnosis presumptive and a treatable alternative unexcluded. Normal imaging alone does not confirm raised pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Stop the isotretinoin and review the discs in three months with repeat visual field testing
options.rationale: Withdrawing the retinoid is an essential part of management because it is a recognised precipitant, but observation over three months risks permanent field loss while the pressure remains untreated. The drug is stopped in parallel with, not instead of, establishing the diagnosis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Retinoids)

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
options.rationale: Sinus thrombosis is the key structural mimic and must always be excluded, but magnetic resonance venography has already done so and repeating the question with a different modality adds radiation without information. The near pair remains worth remembering because it can present identically with headache, papilloedema and pulsatile tinnitus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for optic nerve sheath fenestration now given the presence of bilateral disc swelling
options.rationale: Surgical decompression is reserved for rapidly progressive visual loss that fails medical therapy, and her acuity is 6/6 with only enlarged blind spots. Operating at this stage exposes her to surgical risk that the visual findings do not justify. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Papilloedema)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Papilloedema

options.text: Lumbar puncture with measurement of the opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid analysis
options.rationale: With imaging that excludes a mass and confirms patent sinuses, the diagnosis of raised intracranial pressure without a structural cause requires a documented elevated opening pressure with normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents. That measurement both establishes the diagnosis and guides how urgently vision must be protected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Daily headache worse on waking and on bending, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus and bilateral papilloedema in a young woman with a raised body mass index describes idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The diagnosis is one of exclusion and requires neuroimaging with venography to rule out a mass and sinus thrombosis, followed by a lumbar puncture documenting a raised opening pressure with normal constituents. Isotretinoin, tetracyclines, excess vitamin A and withdrawal of corticosteroids are recognised precipitants and must be identified and stopped. Acuity is typically preserved until late, so an enlarged blind spot with normal acuity is reassuring but not a reason to defer diagnosis.
key_points: Imaging with venography comes first, then lumbar puncture for opening pressure and constituents
Pulsatile tinnitus with transient visual obscurations is the characteristic symptom pairing
Retinoids, tetracyclines and vitamin A excess are recognised drug precipitants
Normal visual acuity with an enlarged blind spot is the usual early field finding
Surgical decompression is reserved for progressive visual loss despite medical therapy
explanation.pearls: An opening pressure above 25 cmH2O in a non-obese adult, or above 28 cmH2O when measured in a sedated or obese patient, supports the diagnosis provided the fluid constituents are normal. Track the condition with formal perimetry rather than acuity, because central vision is preserved until very late and relying on the Snellen chart is how patients lose peripheral field irreversibly.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Papilloedema

subtopic_detail: separating a delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity from the epidermal detachment syndromes when both a rash and a fever follow a new anticonvulsant
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 33-year-old man admitted with fever and a rash. He was started on lamotrigine five weeks ago after a first unprovoked seizure and the dose was escalated over that period.

He has a confluent morbilliform eruption covering about 70 per cent of his body surface with marked facial swelling, particularly periorbital. The rash is not tender, Nikolsky sign is negative, and there are no erosions on the lips, conjunctivae or genitals. His pulse rate is 106 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air and temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius. Bloods show white cells 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 384 units/L (5-40), alkaline phosphatase 180 units/L (30-110), creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110) and atypical lymphocytes on the film. There is bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform rash over 70 per cent body surface, marked periorbital and facial oedema, negative Nikolsky sign, no mucosal erosions, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cells 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 384 units/L (5-40), creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110), atypical lymphocytes on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start systemic corticosteroid with organ monitoring for at least several weeks
options.rationale: Facial oedema, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy and hepatitis five weeks into a new anticonvulsant define the delayed multiorgan hypersensitivity reaction, which is treated by immediate withdrawal of the culprit and systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper. Prolonged monitoring is required because relapse and late thyroiditis are characteristic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and transfer to a burns unit for management of epidermal detachment
options.rationale: The epidermal detachment syndromes are excluded here by a negative Nikolsky sign, absent mucosal erosions and a non-tender rash, and they do not produce eosinophilia or facial oedema. The distinguishing relationship is that one is a delayed eosinophilic multiorgan reaction and the other is keratinocyte apoptosis with skin loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Continue lamotrigine at a reduced dose with antihistamine and emollient for a benign drug rash
options.rationale: A simple morbilliform drug eruption has no fever, no organ involvement and no eosinophilia, and can sometimes be treated through. Organ dysfunction in two systems makes continuing the drug at any dose unsafe. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antiepileptics)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start intravenous immunoglobulin as the primary immunomodulatory therapy
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has been used in severe epidermal detachment and in refractory cases, but it is not the first line immunomodulator for this syndrome and the evidence for it here is weak. Corticosteroid remains the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and treat empirically for acute Epstein-Barr virus infection with supportive care
options.rationale: Atypical lymphocytes and lymphadenopathy do suggest a viral illness, and reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 or Epstein-Barr virus genuinely occurs within this syndrome, but that reactivation is part of the reaction rather than an alternative diagnosis. Supportive care alone leaves the hepatitis and renal impairment untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: The combination of a late onset rash two to eight weeks after a new anticonvulsant, facial oedema, fever, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy and hepatitis is the delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity syndrome. It is distinguished from the epidermal detachment syndromes by a negative Nikolsky sign, absent mucosal erosion, a non-tender eruption and the presence of eosinophilia, and from a benign morbilliform eruption by fever and organ involvement. Management is immediate cessation of the culprit drug and systemic corticosteroid with a prolonged taper, because abrupt withdrawal of steroid commonly triggers relapse. Herpesvirus reactivation occurs within the syndrome and is not an alternative explanation.
key_points: Onset two to eight weeks after the drug distinguishes this from an immediate hypersensitivity reaction
Facial oedema with eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes is the recognisable signature
Negative Nikolsky sign and intact mucosae argue against epidermal detachment syndromes
Systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper over weeks is first line, not immunoglobulin
Aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides and vancomycin are the usual culprits
explanation.pearls: Recheck thyroid function at three months after recovery, because autoimmune thyroiditis develops in up to a fifth of patients and appears long after the rash has cleared. Label the culprit in the allergy record along with its cross-reacting relatives: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital and lamotrigine cross-react frequently enough that sodium valproate or levetiracetam should be chosen for future seizure control.

subtopic_detail: managing a catecholamine crisis precipitated in a patient already taking a beta blocker before the diagnosis was suspected
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward. A 49-year-old woman admitted yesterday for investigation of episodic palpitations, drenching sweats and headaches was started on metoprolol 50 mg twice daily last night by the covering doctor for a presumed tachyarrhythmia. She had a computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast this morning.

Thirty minutes after returning from the scan she became acutely unwell with a crushing headache, pallor and vomiting. Her pulse rate is 128 per minute, blood pressure 248/142 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 92 per cent on room air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. She has bibasal crackles and a third heart sound. The scan report describes a 5 cm right adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units and marked heterogeneous enhancement. Her plasma free metanephrines, sent yesterday, have just returned at more than six times the upper limit of normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 per minute, blood pressure 248/142 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 92 per cent room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic, bibasal inspiratory crackles, third heart sound, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines more than six times the upper limit of normal
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography abdomen: 5 cm right adrenal mass, unenhanced attenuation 38 Hounsfield units, heterogeneous enhancement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?

options.text: Start an intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion alone and withhold any further adrenergic blockade
options.rationale: Nitrate will lower the pressure transiently but does nothing about the receptor level problem, so the pressure oscillates as catecholamine release continues. Leaving the beta blocker in place without alpha cover perpetuates the underlying mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start intravenous phentolamine and continue the beta blocker once alpha blockade is established
options.rationale: Beta blockade given before alpha blockade leaves alpha mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which is what has converted her episodic symptoms into a crisis with pulmonary oedema. The correction is immediate alpha blockade with a short acting intravenous agent, after which beta blockade can safely continue to control the reflex tachycardia. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Increase the metoprolol dose and add intravenous furosemide for the pulmonary congestion present
options.rationale: More beta blockade worsens the unopposed alpha stimulation that is driving the crisis, and the pulmonary oedema here is a consequence of extreme afterload rather than primary fluid overload. This is the specific escalation that has caused deaths in reported cases. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Start intravenous labetalol, relying on its combined alpha and beta receptor blocking activity
options.rationale: Labetalol looks attractive because it blocks both receptors, but its beta to alpha potency ratio is roughly seven to one, so in practice it behaves like a beta blocker in this setting and can worsen the crisis. The distinguishing point is the ratio, not the presence of alpha activity. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Start oral phenoxybenzamine and arrange surgical resection of the adrenal mass within the week
options.rationale: Oral phenoxybenzamine is the right agent for the elective ten to fourteen day preoperative preparation, but it is too slow for a patient with a systolic pressure of 248 mmHg and pulmonary oedema now. Operating in the middle of an uncontrolled crisis carries a very high mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Episodic headache, palpitations and sweating with a heterogeneous adrenal mass of high unenhanced attenuation and grossly raised metanephrines is a catecholamine secreting tumour. Introducing a beta blocker before alpha blockade removes beta mediated vasodilatation while leaving alpha mediated vasoconstriction intact, and contrast administration can trigger release, which together explain the crisis. Immediate treatment is intravenous alpha blockade with a short acting agent such as phentolamine, with the beta blocker retained once the alpha receptor is covered. Oral phenoxybenzamine and surgery belong to the elective pathway after the crisis is controlled.
key_points: Alpha blockade always precedes beta blockade in catecholamine excess
Beta blockade first leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate crisis
Labetalol is predominantly a beta blocker and is unsuitable as sole therapy here
Unenhanced attenuation above 10 Hounsfield units makes a benign adenoma unlikely
Elective surgery follows ten to fourteen days of oral alpha blockade, never a crisis
explanation.pearls: Prepare elective patients with phenoxybenzamine titrated until a postural drop appears and the haematocrit falls, and liberalise salt and fluid intake in the final days, because the intravascular volume is chronically contracted and collapse after tumour devascularisation is the main intraoperative danger. Any adrenal incidentaloma with unenhanced attenuation above 10 Hounsfield units should have biochemical exclusion of catecholamine excess before any biopsy or procedure is contemplated.

subtopic_detail: deciding on timing of valve surgery when embolic and haemodynamic indications conflict with a very recent cerebral event
stem:
You are the medical registrar on the cardiology ward. A 52-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve has been on intravenous benzylpenicillin for six days for viridans streptococcal endocarditis, and his blood cultures cleared after forty eight hours. He has remained afebrile for four days.

This morning he developed sudden left arm and leg weakness. Computed tomography of the brain performed two hours ago shows a right middle cerebral artery territory infarct of about 2 cm with no haemorrhagic transformation. His pulse rate is 104 per minute, blood pressure 108/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 94 per cent on room air and temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. He has a new early diastolic murmur, bibasal crackles and a raised jugular venous pressure. Transoesophageal echocardiography today shows a 16 mm mobile aortic vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation with premature mitral valve closure, and no abscess. His weakness has not progressed and he is fully alert.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 per minute, blood pressure 108/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 94 per cent room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, left hemiparesis four out of five, new early diastolic murmur, bibasal crackles, raised jugular venous pressure
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography brain: 2 cm right middle cerebral artery infarct without haemorrhagic transformation
data_table.Echocardiography: 16 mm mobile aortic vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation with premature mitral valve closure, no abscess

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation about valve surgery?

options.text: Avoid valve surgery altogether and add therapeutic anticoagulation to prevent further embolism
options.rationale: Anticoagulation does not prevent vegetation embolism and substantially raises the risk of haemorrhagic transformation of a fresh infarct. It is continued only where there is an independent indication such as a mechanical prosthesis. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis

options.text: Delay valve surgery for seventy two hours and repeat brain imaging to confirm infarct stability
options.rationale: A short delay for repeat imaging is reasonable when the haemodynamics are stable and the neurological picture is uncertain, but this patient has pulmonary congestion with premature mitral valve closure and cannot safely wait. The near pair is the neurologically stable patient with moderate regurgitation, where a brief delay is entirely appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Proceed to valve surgery now, since a non-haemorrhagic small infarct does not require postponement
options.rationale: Severe aortic regurgitation with premature mitral valve closure and pulmonary congestion is a haemodynamic indication for early surgery that outweighs the small ischaemic stroke, and current guidance is that a non-haemorrhagic infarct without extensive damage or coma does not mandate delay. A large mobile vegetation after a first embolic event adds a second indication. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis

options.text: Delay valve surgery for four weeks after the stroke to avoid haemorrhagic transformation on bypass
options.rationale: A four week delay applies to haemorrhagic stroke, not to a small bland infarct, and premature mitral valve closure signals acute severe regurgitation that patients do not survive for four weeks. The distinguishing factor is the presence or absence of intracranial blood, not the presence of a stroke as such. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis

options.text: Delay valve surgery until the full six week antibiotic course is finished with repeat cultures taken
options.rationale: Completing antibiotics before operating is a common misconception, and surgery is not contraindicated by an incomplete course when a haemodynamic indication exists. Cultures have already cleared, which lowers the risk of prosthetic seeding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Three separate indications for surgery in endocarditis are heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection, and prevention of embolism from a large mobile vegetation, and the first of these is the most urgent. Premature mitral valve closure on echocardiography indicates acute severe aortic regurgitation with left ventricular end diastolic pressure exceeding left atrial pressure, which is a surgical emergency rather than a finding to monitor. A small ischaemic infarct without haemorrhagic transformation, in an alert patient whose deficit is not progressing, does not require surgery to be postponed. Delay of around four weeks applies specifically to intracranial haemorrhage, and completing the antibiotic course first is not required.
key_points: Heart failure from valve destruction is the most urgent surgical indication in endocarditis
Premature mitral valve closure signals acute severe aortic regurgitation and imminent decompensation
A small bland infarct in an alert patient does not mandate postponing surgery
Haemorrhagic stroke, not ischaemic stroke, drives the four week delay
Anticoagulation does not prevent septic embolism and risks haemorrhagic transformation
explanation.pearls: Vegetations larger than 10 mm that have already embolised, and any vegetation larger than 15 mm, justify early surgery for embolic prevention even when the haemodynamics are stable, with most embolic events occurring in the first two weeks of antibiotic therapy. Obtain cerebral imaging in every left sided endocarditis before surgery even without neurological signs, because a clinically silent mycotic aneurysm changes both the timing and the anticoagulation plan.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis

subtopic_detail: responding to a sodium rise that has exceeded the safe daily limit partway through correction of chronic hyponatraemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old woman admitted eighteen hours ago. She had been drinking heavily for years, eating little, and taking a thiazide started three months ago. Her admission sodium was 104 mmol/L (135-145) with a serum osmolality of 228 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 96 mmol/kg and urine sodium 12 mmol/L. She was confused but had no seizure.

She was given a single 100 mL bolus of hypertonic saline for confusion, the thiazide was ceased, and she then received 1 litre of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent. Over the past few hours her urine output has risen to 380 mL per hour and is dilute. Her sodium is now 121 mmol/L, having risen 17 mmol/L in eighteen hours. She is alert and orientated with no focal neurological deficit, her observations are within normal limits, and her potassium and glucose are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no focal neurological deficit, mucous membranes moist, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Admission sodium 104 mmol/L (135-145), current sodium 121 mmol/L, serum osmolality 228 mmol/kg on admission, urine osmolality 96 mmol/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L
data_table.Fluid balance: Urine output 380 mL per hour and dilute over the past few hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Give a further 100 mL bolus of hypertonic saline because the sodium remains below 125 mmol/L
options.rationale: Hypertonic boluses are for active neurological emergency such as seizure or obtundation, not for a number below an arbitrary line in an alert patient. Further sodium loading here compounds the overcorrection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Restrict fluid to 800 mL daily and recheck the sodium in six hours without other intervention
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is the treatment for the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, but her admission biochemistry with dilute urine and a low urine sodium indicates a hypovolaemic and low solute picture instead. Restriction would accelerate the rise rather than slow it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a tolvaptan dose to control the free water handling and recheck the sodium in four hours
options.rationale: Vasopressin receptor antagonists promote free water excretion and would drive the sodium higher still, which is the opposite of what is needed. The near pair is euvolaemic hyponatraemia resistant to restriction, where a short course can be justified under close monitoring. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Tolvaptan)

options.text: Give desmopressin with 5 per cent dextrose to relower the sodium toward the intended daily target
options.rationale: A rise of 17 mmol/L in eighteen hours far exceeds the 8 to 10 mmol/L daily ceiling and places her at real risk of osmotic demyelination, which typically appears days later and is often irreversible. The established rescue is desmopressin to stop the aquaresis together with electrolyte free water, deliberately bringing the sodium back down into the intended range. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Continue the current plan unchanged because she is alert with no neurological deficit at present
options.rationale: Normal neurology now is expected and reassures nobody, because osmotic demyelination characteristically declares itself two to six days after the overcorrection with dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis. Waiting for symptoms means waiting until the injury is done. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Chronic hyponatraemia must be corrected no faster than about 8 to 10 mmol/L in any twenty four hour period, and slower still when risk factors such as alcohol use, malnutrition, hypokalaemia or a sodium below 105 mmol/L are present. Removing the cause, here a thiazide and low solute intake, characteristically unleashes a brisk water diuresis once vasopressin is suppressed, and the sodium then overshoots without anyone giving more sodium. The rescue is to stop the aquaresis with desmopressin while replacing electrolyte free water with dextrose, relowering the sodium into the intended range. Normal neurology at the time of overcorrection is the rule rather than the exception, because osmotic demyelination is delayed by days.
key_points: Correction limit is 8 to 10 mmol/L per twenty four hours, and 8 mmol/L in high risk patients
Autocorrection by water diuresis is the usual mechanism of accidental overcorrection
Desmopressin plus 5 per cent dextrose is the standard relowering rescue
Osmotic demyelination presents two to six days later and is frequently irreversible
Dilute urine with low urine sodium separates this picture from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis
explanation.pearls: In a patient with sodium below 110 mmol/L plus alcohol use or malnutrition, consider proactive desmopressin clamping from the outset with hypertonic saline titrated against it, which controls the rate rather than chasing it. Measure sodium every two hours during active correction, because urine output above 200 mL per hour with dilute urine predicts an overshoot several hours before the serum value shows it.

subtopic_detail: sequencing adjunctive corticosteroid against the first antibiotic dose in suspected adult bacterial meningitis awaiting imaging
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department at 3 am. A 54-year-old man has been brought in by his wife with 12 hours of headache, fever and neck stiffness, and she says he has become progressively harder to rouse over the past two hours.

He opens his eyes to voice, is confused in his speech, and localises to pain. He has no rash, no focal limb weakness and no papilloedema on fundoscopy, but given his reduced conscious level the department protocol requires computed tomography of the head before a lumbar puncture, and the radiographer has been called in from home with an expected delay of about 40 minutes. He takes no immunosuppressive medication, has no history of central nervous system disease and has had no recent overseas travel. Blood cultures have been taken and two cannulas are in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 12, neck stiffness present, no rash, no focal neurological deficit, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 248 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2), blood cultures taken
data_table.Logistics: Computed tomography of the head required before lumbar puncture, expected delay approximately 40 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Await the computed tomography and lumbar puncture results before giving any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Every hour of delay in this condition increases mortality, and cerebrospinal fluid cell count, protein, glucose and polymerase chain reaction remain informative for hours after antibiotics have started. The imaging requirement exists to make the tap safe, not to postpone treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give ceftriaxone with intravenous aciclovir now and withhold corticosteroid entirely
options.rationale: Aciclovir is a reasonable addition where encephalitic features such as seizures, personality change or focal deficits are present, and may well be added here, but omitting dexamethasone discards a treatment with a mortality benefit. Ceftriaxone alone also leaves Listeria uncovered in an adult over 50. (Source: eTG: Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

options.text: Give vancomycin with meropenem now and add dexamethasone after the lumbar puncture is performed
options.rationale: This broader regimen is reserved for healthcare associated meningitis, neurosurgical patients or regions with high cephalosporin resistant pneumococcus, and it is unnecessarily broad for community acquired disease in Australia. Deferring the steroid until after the tap repeats the timing error that removes its benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give dexamethasone with the first dose of ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin now
options.rationale: Antibiotics must not be delayed for imaging or lumbar puncture when meningitis is suspected and the conscious level is falling, and adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis when given before or with the first dose. Benzylpenicillin is added to ceftriaxone in Australian practice to cover Listeria monocytogenes, which is intrinsically cephalosporin resistant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin now and add dexamethasone once the culture confirms the organism
options.rationale: Starting antibiotics promptly is right but the steroid loses most of its benefit once the inflammatory cascade triggered by bacterial lysis is underway, which is why the timing relative to the first dose matters more than the organism. Waiting for culture would place it 24 to 48 hours too late. (Source: eTG: Acute Bacterial Meningitis)

explanation.summary: Community acquired bacterial meningitis in Australian adults is most often pneumococcal or meningococcal, with Listeria monocytogenes contributing in those over 50, pregnant women, and the immunosuppressed, which is why empirical therapy pairs a third generation cephalosporin with benzylpenicillin in those groups. The classical triad of fever, neck stiffness and altered mental state is present in fewer than half of cases, but nearly all have at least two of fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered mental state. Imaging before lumbar puncture is indicated for a reduced or fluctuating conscious level, focal neurological signs, new seizures, papilloedema or immunosuppression, and in every one of those situations antibiotics are given before the scan. Adjunctive dexamethasone blunts the inflammatory response to bacterial lysis and reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal disease, but only if given before or with the first antibiotic dose. Public health notification and clearance antibiotics for close contacts follow for confirmed meningococcal disease.
key_points: Give antibiotics before imaging whenever imaging would delay treatment.
Add benzylpenicillin to ceftriaxone for Listeria cover in adults over 50, pregnancy and immunosuppression.
Dexamethasone must be given before or with the first antibiotic dose to retain its benefit.
Indications for imaging first are reduced conscious level, focal signs, seizures, papilloedema or immunosuppression.
Cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction remains positive for hours to days after antibiotics begin.
explanation.pearls: Adjunctive dexamethasone is given as 10 mg intravenously every six hours for four days, and it is stopped if cultures identify an organism other than Streptococcus pneumoniae, since the mortality benefit is confined to pneumococcal disease.

subtopic_detail: choosing the imaging modality for suspected inflammatory back pain in a young adult whose plain films are normal
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 26-year-old man referred with four years of lower back pain that his previous doctor treated as a mechanical injury from his job as a scaffolder.

He says the pain is worst when he wakes and that his back is stiff for about an hour before it loosens, that it eases once he starts moving around on site, and that it wakes him in the second half of the night so he gets up and walks around. Rest over the Christmas break made it worse rather than better. He had a painful red eye treated with drops by an optometrist last year and has intermittent loose stools that he puts down to diet. His C reactive protein is 9 mg/L (less than 5) and his erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 22 mm/h (less than 15). Radiographs of the lumbar spine and pelvis taken last month are reported as normal with no sacroiliac erosion or sclerosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced lumbar flexion with a modified Schober measurement of 3.5 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, chest expansion 4.5 cm, no peripheral synovitis, no psoriasis or nail changes
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 9 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 22 mm/h (less than 15), full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Radiographs of lumbar spine and pelvis reported as normal with no sacroiliac erosion or sclerosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints to assess for erosion and joint space narrowing
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows established bone damage better than plain films but is blind to the active inflammation that precedes it, so a normal study would not exclude early disease. It also delivers a substantial gonadal radiation dose to a young man for information that does not change the next step. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Human leucocyte antigen B27 typing to establish or exclude the diagnosis on genetic grounds
options.rationale: This marker is a useful contributor within the classification criteria but cannot make or exclude the diagnosis alone, since it is carried by around 8 per cent of the Australian population and a minority of carriers ever develop disease. It is interpreted alongside imaging rather than in place of it. (Source: ASAS: Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis)
source_refs: ASAS: Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to assess for disc protrusion and nerve root compression
options.rationale: Imaging the lumbar spine looks for the mechanical pathology his previous doctor assumed, and degenerative changes found incidentally would reinforce that label, but his pain improves with activity and worsens with rest, which is the reverse of a discogenic pattern. The sacroiliac joints are where this disease begins and are frequently not covered adequately on a lumbar spine protocol. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Radionuclide bone scan of the whole skeleton to identify areas of increased osteoblastic activity
options.rationale: Scintigraphy lacks both the sensitivity and the specificity required at the sacroiliac joints, where degenerative change and normal variation both produce uptake. It has largely been superseded for this indication by cross sectional imaging. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints including short tau inversion recovery sequences
options.rationale: His features meet the accepted definition of inflammatory back pain, namely onset before 45, insidious onset, morning stiffness beyond 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, and night pain that improves on rising, and structural change on plain films takes years to appear. Magnetic resonance imaging detects the active bone marrow oedema of sacroiliitis before any radiographic change, which is what allows the non-radiographic form to be diagnosed and treated. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)
source_refs: ASAS: Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis

explanation.summary: Axial spondyloarthritis is characteristically diagnosed eight to ten years after symptoms begin, because young adults with back pain are assumed to have mechanical injury and the plain radiographic changes that define the classical ankylosing form take years to develop. The clinical screen is inflammatory back pain, defined by onset before age 45, insidious onset, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not rest, and pain in the second half of the night that eases on getting up. Associated features that raise the probability substantially include anterior uveitis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, a family history, and a good response to non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Recognising the non-radiographic form matters because treatment is the same, beginning with regular exercise and a non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, and progressing to a tumour necrosis factor or interleukin 17 inhibitor when disease activity persists. Inflammatory markers are normal in a substantial minority, so a normal C reactive protein never excludes the diagnosis.
key_points: Inflammatory back pain improves with exercise and worsens with rest, the reverse of mechanical pain.
Structural radiographic change lags symptom onset by years, so normal films exclude nothing.
Magnetic resonance imaging with fluid sensitive sequences detects active sacroiliitis before radiographic change.
Human leucocyte antigen B27 supports the diagnosis but neither confirms nor excludes it alone.
Anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are the extra-articular features to ask about.
explanation.pearls: A dramatic response to a full dose non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug within 48 hours is itself a diagnostic clue in axial spondyloarthritis, and it is written into the classification criteria as a feature rather than merely a treatment.

sources.label: ASAS: Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis

subtopic_detail: deciding anticoagulation duration after a first pulmonary embolism with no identifiable provoking factor
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 47-year-old man in clinic three months after a segmental pulmonary embolism. He has completed three months of apixaban and is asking whether he can stop.

His embolism followed no surgery, no immobilisation, no long haul flight, no trauma and no hospital admission, and he had no active malignancy on a thorough review including up to date bowel screening. He has had no bleeding on treatment, is fully active and back at work as an electrician, and his exercise tolerance has returned to normal. His full blood count, renal and liver function are within normal limits. There is no family history of venous thromboembolism. His echocardiogram at diagnosis showed a normal right ventricle and he has no residual breathlessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no calf swelling or tenderness, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal and liver function within normal limits; no bleeding events on treatment
data_table.Event details: First segmental pulmonary embolism with no surgery, immobilisation, travel, trauma or malignancy identified; normal right ventricle on echocardiography

lead_in: What would you recommend about the duration of his anticoagulation?

options.text: Continue extended anticoagulation indefinitely with periodic review of bleeding risk and benefit
options.rationale: A first unprovoked pulmonary embolism carries a recurrence risk of roughly 10 per cent in the first year and 30 per cent at five years after stopping, and extended anticoagulation reduces that by more than 80 per cent at a low bleeding cost in a patient with no risk factors for haemorrhage. Extended means indefinite with periodic reassessment rather than a fixed further course, because the risk does not fall with time. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines

options.text: Stop anticoagulation now, since three months is a complete course for a first event
options.rationale: Three months is the complete course for an event provoked by a transient major risk factor such as surgery, where the provoking factor has resolved and recurrence risk falls to around 1 per cent per year. The near pair distinction is entirely whether the event was provoked, which determines whether the risk resolves with the trigger. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines

options.text: Extend anticoagulation to a total of six months and then stop without further review
options.rationale: Trials comparing six or twelve months against three months show that recurrence is deferred rather than prevented, with the rate after cessation the same whenever treatment stops. A fixed longer course therefore buys time without changing the eventual risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Stop anticoagulation and perform a full thrombophilia screen to guide any further treatment
options.rationale: Thrombophilia testing rarely changes management after an unprovoked event, because the decision to continue already rests on the unprovoked nature of the event, and results are unreliable while a patient is anticoagulated or soon after a thrombosis. Testing is reserved for selected cases such as suspected antiphospholipid syndrome. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines

options.text: Stop anticoagulation and commence aspirin 100 mg daily as long term secondary prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces recurrence by only around a third compared with more than 80 per cent for a direct oral anticoagulant, so it is a substantially weaker option that is reserved for patients who decline or cannot take anticoagulation. Its bleeding risk is also not negligible, which narrows the apparent advantage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Deciding how long to anticoagulate after venous thromboembolism turns on a single classification: whether the event was provoked by a major transient risk factor, provoked by a persistent one, or unprovoked. Events after surgery, major trauma or prolonged immobilisation resolve with their trigger and are treated for three months, while events associated with active cancer or another persistent risk factor continue while that factor persists. Unprovoked events carry a recurrence risk that does not decline with time off treatment, so extended anticoagulation is offered indefinitely, with a reduced dose of apixaban or rivaroxaban after the initial treatment period providing efficacy with less bleeding. The decision is reviewed periodically against bleeding risk, patient preference, and any change in circumstances, and male sex, a raised D-dimer after cessation and residual vein thrombosis all shift the balance towards continuing. Patients who stop should be taught the symptoms of recurrence and advised on prophylaxis during future high risk periods.
key_points: Three months completes treatment for an event provoked by a major transient risk factor.
Unprovoked events carry roughly 30 per cent recurrence at five years and warrant extended treatment.
Extended anticoagulation means indefinite with periodic review, not a fixed longer course.
Reduced dose apixaban or rivaroxaban is used for the extended phase after the initial months.
Thrombophilia testing rarely alters management and is unreliable during anticoagulation.
explanation.pearls: Extended phase dosing drops apixaban from 5 mg to 2.5 mg twice daily and rivaroxaban from 20 mg to 10 mg daily after the first six months, retaining most of the protection against recurrence while roughly halving major bleeding.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines

subtopic_detail: choosing between treatment regimens for latent infection in a person about to start a biologic agent
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in a pre-biologic screening clinic. A 39-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is due to start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor and has been screened as part of that workup.

She moved to Australia from Vietnam at age 22 and has no history of tuberculosis treatment or known contact. She is entirely asymptomatic with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. Her interferon gamma release assay is positive, and her chest radiograph shows no parenchymal abnormality, no cavitation, no pleural thickening and no calcified nodes. Two sputum samples induced for completeness are smear negative and cultures are pending at six weeks with no growth to date. Her liver function and full blood count are within normal limits, she takes methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid, and she is not pregnant and is using reliable contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no lymphadenopathy, weight stable, synovitis in both wrists
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive, liver function and full blood count within normal limits, two induced sputum samples smear negative with cultures showing no growth at six weeks
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph with no parenchymal abnormality, cavitation, pleural thickening or calcified nodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before she starts the biologic?

options.text: Perform a tuberculin skin test to confirm the result before committing her to any treatment
options.rationale: The skin test is less specific than the interferon gamma release assay, particularly after bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination which is routine in Vietnam, so a discordant result would create confusion rather than clarity. The blood assay was chosen for exactly this population for that reason. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Treat for latent infection with isoniazid and pyridoxine, with monthly clinical and liver review
options.rationale: A positive interferon gamma release assay with a normal chest radiograph and no symptoms indicates latent infection, and treatment is required before a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor because that class markedly increases the risk of reactivation and of disseminated disease. Isoniazid with pyridoxine for six to nine months is a standard Australian regimen, and pyridoxine is co-prescribed to prevent peripheral neuropathy. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Treat with a four drug regimen of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for six months
options.rationale: This is the regimen for active disease, and using it for latent infection exposes her to four drugs with their combined hepatotoxicity, ocular toxicity and hyperuricaemia for no additional benefit. The distinction rests on her normal radiograph, absent symptoms and negative cultures, which together define latent rather than active infection. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Proceed with the biologic now and monitor with a chest radiograph every three months
options.rationale: Radiographic surveillance detects reactivation after it has occurred rather than preventing it, and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors are associated with rapid progression including extrapulmonary and disseminated disease. Screening exists precisely so that latent infection can be treated before immunosuppression begins. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Repeat the interferon gamma release assay in three months and treat only if it remains positive
options.rationale: The assay is not used serially to confirm itself, and a positive result in a person from a high incidence country reflects genuine prior exposure rather than a laboratory artefact. Repeating it would delay the biologic by three months without changing the decision. (Source: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection means viable organisms held in check by an intact immune response, with no symptoms, a normal chest radiograph and negative cultures, and it carries a lifetime reactivation risk of around 5 to 10 per cent that rises sharply with immunosuppression. Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors are among the strongest drivers of reactivation because tumour necrosis factor alpha maintains granuloma integrity, so screening before starting one is mandatory and treatment of any latent infection should precede or at least begin before the biologic. Screening in Australia uses an interferon gamma release assay in preference to the tuberculin skin test in people vaccinated with bacille Calmette-Guerin, since prior vaccination does not cause a false positive blood assay. Active disease must be excluded before treating latent infection, because monotherapy in unrecognised active disease generates resistance. Regimen options include isoniazid for six to nine months, rifampicin for four months, or combined isoniazid and rifapentine weekly for twelve weeks, with the choice influenced by drug interactions, hepatotoxicity risk and the likelihood of completion.
key_points: Latent infection means a positive immunological test with no symptoms, normal imaging and negative cultures.
Exclude active disease before treating latent infection, since monotherapy would select resistance.
Interferon gamma release assays are unaffected by prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination.
Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors markedly increase reactivation risk including extrapulmonary disease.
Co-prescribe pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin based regimens induce cytochrome P450 3A4 and render the combined oral contraceptive unreliable for the duration of treatment and for four weeks afterwards, which often decides the regimen choice in a woman of reproductive age.

sources.label: NTAC: Management of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

subtopic_detail: prioritising which of several contributing medicines to withdraw first after recurrent falls in an older adult
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar reviewing an 84-year-old woman referred after three falls in two months, the most recent causing a wrist fracture. She lives alone, uses a stick outdoors, and describes feeling lightheaded when she gets up from the toilet at night.

Her medications are amitriptyline 25 mg at night started eleven years ago for tension headache and never reviewed, temazepam 10 mg most nights for the past six years, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and paracetamol as required. Her vision was corrected with new glasses last month and she has no cataract. Her sitting blood pressure is 142/78 falling to 108/62 after three minutes standing, with a pulse rising from 74 to 78. Her timed up and go test takes 18 seconds. Her vitamin D is 68 nmol/L (greater than 50), her corrected calcium is within normal limits, and her sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 sitting rising to 78 standing, blood pressure 142/78 sitting falling to 108/62 after 3 minutes standing, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go 18 seconds, dry mouth, no focal neurological deficit, no cerebellar signs, gait cautious with a stick
data_table.Investigations: Vitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50), corrected calcium within normal limits, sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Amitriptyline 25 mg at night for 11 years, temazepam 10 mg most nights for 6 years, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, paracetamol as required

lead_in: Which medication change would you prioritise first?

options.text: Cease the atorvastatin, since statins cause myopathy that contributes to falls in older adults
options.rationale: Clinically significant statin myopathy is uncommon and she reports no muscle pain or weakness, so there is no evidence it is contributing here. Removing secondary prevention without a demonstrated harm trades a real benefit for a theoretical one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Add fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily to treat the postural hypotension directly
options.rationale: Adding a drug to counteract the effect of another drug is a prescribing cascade, and fludrocortisone brings supine hypertension, oedema and hypokalaemia in an older patient. Pharmacological treatment of postural hypotension is considered only after the contributing medicines have been removed and non pharmacological measures have failed. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Taper and cease the amitriptyline, since it contributes both anticholinergic burden and postural hypotension
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants are high risk in older adults through anticholinergic effects, sedation, and alpha blockade causing postural hypotension, and at eleven years for a headache indication the benefit is unverified while the harm is now measurable in her postural drop and dry mouth. It contributes to more of her falls mechanisms than any other agent on the list, which is what makes it the priority. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Taper and cease the temazepam, since benzodiazepines are the strongest single risk factor for falls
options.rationale: Stopping the benzodiazepine is genuinely important and will be the next step, but a six year habit requires a slow taper to avoid withdrawal insomnia and rebound anxiety, and it does not explain her postural drop. Sequencing withdrawals one at a time also makes it possible to attribute any change to the drug that was stopped. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Cease the perindopril, since antihypertensives are the usual cause of postural hypotension
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors do contribute to postural drops and her dose may well need reducing, but stopping an agent with cardiovascular and renal benefit before removing a drug with no verified benefit at all inverts the risk to benefit reasoning. Her sitting pressure of 142/78 also does not suggest she is over-treated overall. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Falls in older adults are multifactorial, and a structured assessment covers gait and balance, vision, footwear, cognition, continence, home hazards, postural blood pressure, vitamin D status and above all medications. Fall risk increasing drugs include benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antidepressants including tricyclics and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, opioids, anticholinergics, antihypertensives and hypoglycaemic agents, and risk rises with the total number as much as with any individual agent. Deprescribing works best when it is sequenced rather than simultaneous, starting with the drug that has the weakest ongoing indication and the strongest contribution to the presenting problem, so that any deterioration can be attributed and reversed. Anticholinergic burden deserves specific attention because it accumulates silently across drugs prescribed by different clinicians and contributes to cognitive impairment, urinary retention, constipation and falls. Exercise programs emphasising balance and strength remain the single most effective non pharmacological intervention for preventing further falls.
key_points: Assess postural blood pressure lying and after three minutes standing in every faller.
Prioritise deprescribing the drug with the weakest indication and the strongest contribution to falls.
Withdraw one drug at a time so that effects can be attributed and reversed.
Long term benzodiazepines require a slow taper to avoid withdrawal insomnia and rebound anxiety.
Balance and strength exercise programs are the most effective non pharmacological intervention.
explanation.pearls: A timed up and go test taking longer than 12 seconds identifies a person at increased risk of falling and takes under a minute to perform, which makes it the most practical single bedside screen in a busy clinic.

subtopic_detail: setting oxygenation and carbon dioxide targets in the first hours after return of spontaneous circulation in a comatose survivor
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the intensive care unit taking over care of a 58-year-old man who had a witnessed out of hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest 90 minutes ago with bystander compression only cardiopulmonary resuscitation and two defibrillations before return of spontaneous circulation.

He remains comatose, does not obey commands, and is intubated and ventilated. His coronary angiogram on arrival showed an occluded right coronary artery that has been stented, and he is now on a low dose noradrenaline infusion. His current ventilator settings deliver an inspired oxygen fraction of 1.0 and a minute volume set by the retrieval team. The arterial blood gas taken five minutes ago shows a partial pressure of oxygen of 186 mmHg, a partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 28 mmHg and a pH of 7.46, with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L that is falling from 8.1 mmol/L on arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 in sinus rhythm, blood pressure 102/58 on low dose noradrenaline, respiratory rate 18 ventilated, SpO2 100 per cent, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Comatose and not obeying commands, pupils 3 mm and reactive bilaterally, no spontaneous movement
data_table.Investigations: Arterial partial pressure of oxygen 186 mmHg, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 28 mmHg, pH 7.46, lactate 4.2 mmol/L falling from 8.1 mmol/L
data_table.Ventilator: Inspired oxygen fraction 1.0, minute volume as set by the retrieval team

lead_in: What adjustment to his ventilation would you make now?

options.text: Maintain the inspired oxygen at 1.0 and increase minute volume further to reduce the carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Deliberate hyperventilation was once used to control intracranial pressure but is now avoided because the cerebral vasoconstriction it produces reduces perfusion to injured brain. His carbon dioxide of 28 mmHg is already too low rather than too high. (Source: ANZICS: Post Cardiac Arrest Care)

options.text: Reduce the inspired oxygen to target normal saturation and increase minute volume to clear the lactate
options.rationale: The oxygen adjustment is right but hyperventilating to compensate for a metabolic acidosis treats the number rather than the cause, and his lactate is already falling with restored perfusion. Respiratory compensation driven by the ventilator adds the cerebral vasoconstriction without addressing tissue oxygen delivery. (Source: ANZICS: Post Cardiac Arrest Care)

options.text: Reduce the inspired oxygen to target a saturation of 88 to 92 per cent and leave minute volume unchanged
options.rationale: A saturation target of 88 to 92 per cent belongs to patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and applying it here risks hypoxaemia in a brain that has just sustained a global ischaemic insult. The hypocapnia would also be left uncorrected. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.8: Post-Resuscitation Therapy)

options.text: Reduce the inspired oxygen to target normal oxygen saturation and reduce minute volume to normalise carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Both hyperoxaemia and hypocapnia worsen outcome after cardiac arrest, the first by generating reactive oxygen species during reperfusion and the second by causing cerebral vasoconstriction that reduces blood flow to an already injured brain. Once return of spontaneous circulation is achieved the inspired oxygen is titrated down to a saturation of 94 to 98 per cent and ventilation is adjusted to a normal carbon dioxide of roughly 35 to 45 mmHg. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.8: Post-Resuscitation Therapy)

options.text: Maintain the inspired oxygen at 1.0 and maintain the current minute volume until he wakes
options.rationale: Maximal oxygen is appropriate during the arrest itself when oxygen delivery is the limiting factor, and continuing it afterwards is the anti-pattern this question targets. Sustained hyperoxaemia after return of spontaneous circulation is associated with higher mortality in observational and trial data. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.8: Post-Resuscitation Therapy)

explanation.summary: Post cardiac arrest syndrome comprises brain injury, myocardial dysfunction, a systemic ischaemia and reperfusion response resembling sepsis, and the persisting precipitating pathology, and care in the first hours is aimed at limiting secondary brain injury. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are among the few variables under direct minute to minute control, and both extremes are harmful: hyperoxaemia drives oxidative injury during reperfusion while hypoxaemia deepens the insult, and hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction while hypercapnia raises intracranial pressure. Targeted temperature management is used to avoid fever, with active control of temperature and treatment of any temperature above 37.7 degrees Celsius. Mean arterial pressure is supported to maintain cerebral perfusion, urgent coronary angiography is performed for ST elevation or a strong suspicion of a coronary cause, and seizures are treated but not prophylactically prevented. Neurological prognostication is deliberately deferred to at least 72 hours after return of spontaneous circulation, and longer if sedation confounds the examination, using multiple modalities rather than a single test.
key_points: Titrate inspired oxygen after return of spontaneous circulation to a saturation of 94 to 98 per cent.
Target a normal carbon dioxide of about 35 to 45 mmHg and avoid deliberate hyperventilation.
Actively control temperature and treat fever, which worsens neurological outcome.
Defer neurological prognostication until at least 72 hours after return of spontaneous circulation.
Arrange urgent coronary angiography for ST elevation or a strong clinical suspicion of a coronary cause.
explanation.pearls: Prognostication at 72 hours relies on several independent modalities together, with bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20 somatosensory evoked potentials, a malignant electroencephalogram, and a neuron specific enolase that stays high across serial samples all pointing the same way before any withdrawal decision.

subtopic_detail: sequencing blockade before surgery in a patient with episodic hypertension whose beta blocker was started first
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 44-year-old man referred with hypertension resistant to three agents. He describes episodes two or three times a week lasting about 20 minutes in which he sweats through his shirt, his heart pounds and he develops a severe throbbing headache, and he says he feels a sense of doom during them.

His general practitioner started metoprolol 50 mg twice daily nine days ago and he reports that since then the episodes have felt worse, with higher readings on his home monitor. His plasma free metanephrines are four times the upper reference limit on two separate occasions, and computed tomography shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units. Surgery has been discussed with the endocrine surgeons and he has no chest pain, no cardiac failure and a normal echocardiogram.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 178/104, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and diaphoretic during an episode observed in clinic, no thyroid enlargement, no abdominal bruit, no neurocutaneous stigmata
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines four times the upper reference limit on two occasions, potassium and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass with unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue the metoprolol, add phenoxybenzamine, and proceed to surgery once the blood pressure settles
options.rationale: Adding alpha blockade does address the deficiency but leaving the beta blocker running through the interim continues the unopposed alpha stimulation that has already worsened his episodes. The sequence is what the question tests, and correcting it means stopping the beta blocker rather than layering over it. (Source: Endocrine Society: Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)

options.text: Continue the metoprolol, add amlodipine, and proceed to adrenalectomy within the next week
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are used as adjuncts where alpha blockade alone is insufficient or poorly tolerated, but they do not substitute for it, and operating within a week gives insufficient time for the volume re-expansion that alpha blockade allows. Inadequate preparation is the main driver of intraoperative hypertensive crisis and postoperative hypotension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the metoprolol, arrange metaiodobenzylguanidine scintigraphy, and defer any blockade until it returns
options.rationale: Functional imaging has a role in assessing for metastatic or multifocal disease but does not change the need for preoperative blockade, and deferring treatment leaves him exposed to further paroxysms. Biochemical confirmation with a corresponding adrenal mass has already established the diagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society: Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)

options.text: Cease the metoprolol, arrange adrenal vein sampling, and commence spironolactone while awaiting results
