Continue fluid resuscitation guided by dynamic markers of fluid responsiveness (passive leg raise, stroke volume variation, IVC ultrasound).
key_points: 30 mL/kg crystalloid within first 3 hours in sepsis-related hypotension or lactate above 4.
Start noradrenaline for MAP below 65 during or after initial 30 mL/kg fluid.
Vasopressin added when noradrenaline exceeds 0.25-0.5 microgram/kg/min.
explanation.pearls: Septic shock with MAP below 65 after 30 mL/kg crystalloid gets noradrenaline started immediately targeting MAP 65 mmHg, not more large-volume fluid or dopamine - noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor per Surviving Sepsis 2021.

subtopic_detail: Indication for urgent haemodialysis in acute kidney injury with hyperkalaemia refractory to medical therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old man on the ward on day 4 of admission for community-acquired pneumonia. He has developed acute kidney injury on top of baseline chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline creatinine 148 micromol/L). He takes perindopril, hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; the ACE inhibitor and spironolactone were stopped on day 2 of admission.

This morning he reports increasing shortness of breath and palpitations. On assessment he has pulse rate 58 per minute, blood pressure 152/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute, oxygen saturation 92 percent on 4 L per minute nasal prongs, temperature 36.9 degC. Cardiovascular examination reveals no gallop, elevated jugular venous pressure at 6 cm and bilateral basal crackles. Investigations: potassium 6.8 mmol/L (yesterday 6.2), sodium 130 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, urea 42 mmol/L, creatinine 480 micromol/L (baseline 148), venous pH 7.20, lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Electrocardiogram now shows sinus bradycardia with peaked T waves in V2 to V5, PR interval 240 milliseconds and a widened QRS at 130 milliseconds. In the past 30 minutes he has received intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent, intravenous salbutamol nebulised 10 mg, insulin 10 units with dextrose 50 mL of 50 percent, and intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol. Urine output has been 20 mL in the last 4 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58 /min, blood pressure 152/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 92% on 4 L NP O2, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Fluid status: Elevated JVP 6 cm, bilateral basal crackles, urine output 20 mL in 4 h
data_table.Bloods: K 6.8 mmol/L (yesterday 6.2), Na 130 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, urea 42 mmol/L, creatinine 480 micromol/L (baseline 148), venous pH 7.20, lactate 1.8 mmol/L
data_table.ECG: Sinus bradycardia, peaked T waves V2-V5, PR 240 ms, QRS 130 ms
data_table.Given in last 30 min: Calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% IV, salbutamol 10 mg nebulised, insulin 10 units + dextrose 50 mL 50%, sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol IV
data_table.Medications: Perindopril and spironolactone stopped day 2, still on hydrochlorothiazide

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent renal consult for haemodialysis access via femoral vascular catheter for immediate haemodialysis in the intensive care unit for hyperkalaemia refractory to medical therapy with pulmonary oedema
options.rationale: Refractory hyperkalaemia with widened QRS and ECG changes plus fluid overload plus severe uraemic acidosis meets multiple KDIGO indications for urgent renal replacement. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012))
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012)

options.text: Give further intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent bolus and repeat insulin 10 units with dextrose 50 mL of 50 percent bolus and reassess electrocardiogram at 30 minutes
options.rationale: Further temporising measures do not remove potassium and do not correct fluid overload or acidosis; definitive removal via haemodialysis is required. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012))
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012)

options.text: Give oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g single dose and give intravenous furosemide 80 mg to promote diuresis and potassium excretion with reassessment of potassium at 60 minutes
options.rationale: Polystyrene sulfonate is slow (hours) and furosemide is ineffective in oligoanuric AKI; definitive removal via haemodialysis is required urgently. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012))
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012)

options.text: Commence intravenous sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g three times daily and repeat calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenous bolus and reassess the electrocardiogram at 30 minutes
options.rationale: Sodium zirconium is oral only, has onset over hours, and does not correct fluid overload or acidosis; not suitable for this life-threatening emergency. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012))
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012)

options.text: Give continuous salbutamol nebulisation 10 mg per hour and repeat sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol intravenous with reassessment of potassium and arterial blood gas at 30 minutes after therapy
options.rationale: Repeat bicarbonate and beta-agonist temporise potassium shift but not fluid or uraemia; definitive removal via haemodialysis is required. (Source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012))
source_refs: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012)

explanation.summary: Acute kidney injury requires urgent renal replacement therapy for AEIOU indications: Acidosis (severe metabolic, pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 10 mmol/L refractory to bicarbonate therapy), Electrolyte disturbance (hyperkalaemia above 6.5 mmol/L refractory to medical therapy or with ECG changes), Ingestion (dialysable toxin: methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylate, valproate), Overload (pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics in oligoanuric patient), Uraemia (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding). Medical management of severe hyperkalaemia: calcium gluconate 10 mL 10 percent IV (cardiac membrane stabilisation), insulin 10 units with 50 mL 50 percent dextrose IV (intracellular shift, effect at 15-30 min), salbutamol 10 to 20 mg nebulised (intracellular shift, additive), sodium bicarbonate 50 to 100 mmol IV (if severe acidosis), sodium polystyrene sulfonate 15-30 g PO or PR (gastrointestinal removal, slow onset). None of these definitively remove potassium in oligoanuric patients; dialysis is required. Furosemide is ineffective without residual urine output. Modality: intermittent haemodialysis is preferred if haemodynamically stable; continuous renal replacement therapy for haemodynamic instability.
key_points: AEIOU indications for urgent RRT: Acidosis, Electrolyte, Ingestion, Overload, Uraemia.
Refractory hyperkalaemia with ECG changes and oliguria requires urgent haemodialysis.
Furosemide is ineffective in oligoanuric AKI; medical measures only temporise potassium.
explanation.pearls: AKI with potassium 6.8 mmol/L, widened QRS, oligoanuria, pulmonary oedema and pH 7.20 refractory to full medical hyperkalaemia protocol has multiple KDIGO indications for urgent haemodialysis - further calcium and insulin only buy time.

sources.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012)

subtopic_detail: Adult acute pyelonephritis empirical therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34 year old woman with 2 days of right flank pain, rigors, and vomiting. She reports urinary frequency and dysuria since yesterday. She has no medical history, no known allergies, is not pregnant (urine bhCG negative), and takes only the combined oral contraceptive pill.

On examination she is flushed with right costovertebral angle tenderness. Pulse 108, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C. Urinalysis shows leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 2+. Urine and blood cultures are collected. Full blood count shows white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45 to 90), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). She is able to tolerate oral fluids after antiemetic but still has rigors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 98% RA, temp 38.9
data_table.Bloods: WCC 16.2 x10^9/L; creatinine 82 micromol/L; lactate 1.8 mmol/L
data_table.Cultures: Urine and blood cultures collected before antibiotics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen at this point?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg every 6 hours for 10 days with early GP review at 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral cefalexin is not recommended for empirical pyelonephritis because of poor tissue penetration and unreliable coverage of resistant Enterobacterales (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 14 days without empirical intravenous cover
options.rationale: Trimethoprim resistance in Australian E coli approaches 25 percent and it is not adequate empirical therapy for pyelonephritis; a beta lactam or aminoglycoside is preferred while cultures are awaited (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral fluconazole 200 mg for empirical yeast cover
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone dosing for pyelonephritis is correct, but empirical antifungal is not indicated without evidence of candiduria in a catheterised or immunocompromised patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg per kg with amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours pending culture results
options.rationale: Gentamicin plus amoxicillin is the eTG first-line empirical regimen for hospitalised pyelonephritis in a non pregnant adult without penicillin allergy; the combination covers Enterobacterales and enterococci and can be narrowed once cultures return (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous meropenem 1 g every 8 hours for broad spectrum cover pending culture results
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for confirmed or high risk multidrug resistant infection or severe sepsis in a colonised patient; first line empirical use undermines antimicrobial stewardship (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Australian empirical therapy for hospitalised acute pyelonephritis in a non pregnant adult with no penicillin allergy is intravenous gentamicin 5 mg per kg once daily plus amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours, or ceftriaxone 1 g once daily as monotherapy where an aminoglycoside is contraindicated. Cultures are collected before the first dose, and switch to oral therapy occurs after 24 to 48 hours of clinical improvement, tailored to susceptibility. Trimethoprim, cefalexin, and empirical antifungals are inappropriate for hospitalised pyelonephritis. Carbapenems are reserved for confirmed multidrug resistance or severe sepsis with concerning colonisation.
key_points: First line: gentamicin plus amoxicillin IV, or ceftriaxone IV alone
Cultures before first dose; tailor once susceptibilities available
Total 10 to 14 days including step down to oral therapy
explanation.pearls: Once daily gentamicin at 5 mg per kg gives high peak concentration for gram negative killing and is safer than divided dosing; check level before the second dose.

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection with atypical presentation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with 45 minutes of interscapular pain that woke him from sleep. He describes it as tearing, radiating to the left flank, and he vomited once at home. He has hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily, smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 30 years, and quit 4 years ago. His father died aged 62 of a ruptured aorta.

He is diaphoretic. Vital signs are pulse 96 regular, blood pressure 176/104 mmHg right arm and 138/82 mmHg left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.9. Chest auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. His left radial pulse is diminished compared with the right. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria; no ST elevation. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Bedside troponin is not elevated. High-sensitivity D-dimer is 4.2 mg/L (less than 0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP right arm 176/104, BP left arm 138/82, RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, temp 36.9
data_table.Bedside findings: Diaphoretic; diminished left radial pulse; early diastolic murmur LSE
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm; LVH by voltage; no ST elevation
data_table.Investigations: Widened mediastinum on CXR; troponin negative; D-dimer 4.2 mg/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Trans thoracic echocardiogram at the bedside to look for aortic root dilatation and regurgitation
options.rationale: TTE has limited sensitivity for type A or B dissection (about 60 percent) and cannot delineate the extent needed for surgical planning; CT angiography is the primary diagnostic in a stable patient (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

options.text: Repeat high-sensitivity troponin at 1 hour and reassess for type 2 myocardial infarction cause
options.rationale: Serial troponin has utility for ACS assessment but does not evaluate the primary concern of dissection when clinical features and imaging are highly suggestive; further delay risks rupture (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

options.text: Coronary angiography via right radial access to exclude an unstable ostial coronary lesion
options.rationale: Coronary angiography in an undiagnosed dissection risks catheter entry of the false lumen and delays definitive management; ACS is not the leading differential given asymmetric arm pressures and widened mediastinum (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

options.text: Contrast enhanced computed tomography angiography of the aorta from arch to iliac bifurcation now
options.rationale: CT angiography of the whole aorta is the primary diagnostic in a haemodynamically stable patient with suspected acute aortic dissection; it delineates entry tear, extent, branch vessel involvement, and guides surgical or endovascular decisions (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

options.text: Magnetic resonance angiography of the aorta with gadolinium contrast within the next 24 hours
options.rationale: MR angiography has excellent characterisation but scanner availability and scan duration make it impractical for the initial evaluation of suspected acute dissection; it is reserved for follow up or contrast allergic patients (Source: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline).

explanation.summary: Tearing interscapular pain, asymmetric arm blood pressures (a difference above 20 mmHg), aortic regurgitation, diminished peripheral pulse, and a widened mediastinum in a hypertensive smoker with family history of aortic disease form a high probability presentation of acute aortic dissection. The primary diagnostic in a haemodynamically stable patient is CT angiography of the entire aorta (arch to iliac) to define classification (Stanford A vs B), branch vessel involvement, and surgical or endovascular strategy. Concurrently, target heart rate below 60 with intravenous esmolol or labetalol before adding a vasodilator, and involve cardiothoracic surgery for type A. Serial troponin, TTE, and MR are secondary tools here.
key_points: CT angiography aorta arch to iliac is the primary diagnostic
Rate control first (target HR below 60) then vasodilator
Stanford A requires urgent cardiothoracic surgery
explanation.pearls: A blood pressure difference of more than 20 mmHg between arms in a patient with tearing chest or back pain has a specificity above 80 percent for dissection; get the CT before starting anticoagulant or antiplatelet.

subtopic_detail: Adult sepsis hour-1 bundle sequencing
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old woman transferred from a nursing home with 8 hours of fevers, rigors, and reduced oral intake. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and a permanent indwelling urinary catheter for neurogenic bladder. On arrival her Glasgow Coma Scale is 14, she is confused about place, and she has cool mottled knees.

Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94% on 4 L nasal prong oxygen, temperature 39.2. Point of care venous lactate is 4.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). Bedside creatinine 168 micromol/L (45 to 90) from a rise of 82 last month. Urinalysis of catheter urine is grossly turbid with leucocytes 4+ and nitrites positive. Chest x-ray shows no consolidation. Two intravenous cannulas are in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 82/48, RR 26, SpO2 94% 4L NP, temp 39.2
data_table.qSOFA / signs: Altered mentation; SBP below 100; RR above 22
data_table.Bloods: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (from 82 last month)
data_table.Source clues: Turbid catheter urine; leucocytes 4+; nitrites positive; CXR clear

lead_in: Within the first hour of recognition, which sequence best reflects the ANZICS-endorsed sepsis bundle?

options.text: Give empirical antibiotics, then start intravenous fluids, then collect blood cultures once stable
options.rationale: Cultures should precede antibiotics whenever they do not delay antibiotic administration; collecting after antibiotics reduces yield and undermines antimicrobial stewardship (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

options.text: Measure lactate, give a 500 mL fluid bolus, arrange CT abdomen, then collect blood cultures before antibiotics
options.rationale: Imaging is important for source control but delaying antibiotics for CT in confirmed septic shock breaches the hour-1 bundle; imaging follows initial resuscitation and antibiotics (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

options.text: Measure lactate, collect blood cultures, give empirical broad spectrum antibiotics, and commence 30 mL per kg crystalloid
options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle groups lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics, empirical broad spectrum antibiotics, and 30 mL per kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, delivered within the first hour of recognition (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

options.text: Start noradrenaline infusion immediately then collect cultures and give antibiotics after stabilisation
options.rationale: Vasopressors are indicated after adequate fluid resuscitation for persistent hypotension; starting them before fluid loading is not standard bundle sequencing (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

options.text: Commence 250 mL of 4 percent albumin, transfuse packed red cells for haemoglobin above 100, then give antibiotics
options.rationale: Crystalloid is the recommended initial resuscitation fluid; routine transfusion above 100 is not indicated (target above 70 unless active bleeding or myocardial ischaemia) (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)).
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle, endorsed by ANZICS, groups four actions within the first hour of sepsis recognition: measure lactate, collect blood cultures before antibiotics if this does not cause delay, administer empirical broad spectrum antibiotics, and give 30 mL per kg crystalloid when there is hypotension or a lactate at or above 4 mmol/L. Vasopressors follow if mean arterial pressure remains below 65 mmHg after fluid loading. Imaging for source control (CT abdomen, ultrasound biliary tree) is important but sits after the initial four bundle elements. Catheter removal or exchange for a suspected catheter associated urinary sepsis is a specific source control step for this patient.
key_points: Bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid in the first hour
Vasopressors after fluid loading if MAP remains below 65 mmHg
Source control (catheter exchange, imaging) follows the initial bundle
explanation.pearls: In catheter associated urinary sepsis the indwelling catheter is the reservoir; a fresh catheter change (or removal where feasible) after the first antibiotic dose materially reduces bacterial load.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle (endorsed by ANZICS)

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation criteria
stem:
You are the medical registrar coordinating care for a 58 year old man with cirrhosis brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 4 hour history of vomiting fresh red blood. He has vomited 3 more times since arrival, each estimated 300 to 400 mL. Ambulance recorded blood pressure 82/48 mmHg and pulse 128 with two 16 gauge cannulas placed en route and 1000 mL of Hartmann's solution infused.

On arrival pulse 132, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prong oxygen, temperature 35.4 degrees C. He is confused (GCS 13) and peripheries are cold. Bedside haemoglobin 62 g/L (135 to 175), platelets 68 x10^9/L (150 to 400), INR 2.1, fibrinogen 1.1 g/L (2.0 to 4.0), lactate 6.8 mmol/L. You have called endoscopy and given intravenous terlipressin and ceftriaxone. Two units of emergency O negative packed cells are already infusing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 78/44, RR 26, SpO2 96% 4L NP, temp 35.4, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: Hb 62; platelets 68; INR 2.1; fibrinogen 1.1; lactate 6.8
data_table.Prior resuscitation: 1000 mL Hartmann's; 2 units emergency O negative pRBC infusing

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in his resuscitation?

options.text: Continue two more units of O negative packed cells and reassess response after another 500 mL Hartmann's
options.rationale: Ongoing crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia; empirical continuation of packed cells alone will not correct the fibrinogen or coagulopathy that will drive continued bleeding (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol and target packed cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate
options.rationale: ANZ National Blood Authority guidance recommends MTP activation for critical bleeding likely to require 5 or more units in 4 hours, or a shock index above 1 with ongoing haemorrhage; balanced replacement of pRBC, FFP, platelets, and cryoprecipitate corrects coagulopathy and reduces mortality (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

options.text: Give a single unit of platelets alone since platelet count is only mildly reduced at 68 x10^9/L
options.rationale: Isolated platelet transfusion does not correct the coagulopathy, hypofibrinogenaemia, and ongoing loss; balanced product resuscitation is required (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

options.text: Give intravenous prothrombinex 25 units per kg to correct INR of 2.1 in place of any plasma or platelets
options.rationale: Prothrombinex is a factor concentrate for warfarin or DOAC related bleeding; it does not replace fibrinogen or platelets and is not the correct product for critical bleeding coagulopathy (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

options.text: Delay further transfusion until formal cross match is complete to reduce the risk of a haemolytic reaction
options.rationale: In critical bleeding with ongoing shock, emergency group O red cells and MTP components are given without waiting for cross match; the risk of exsanguination exceeds the risk of an unmatched transfusion (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

explanation.summary: The Australian National Blood Authority defines critical bleeding as major haemorrhage that is life threatening and likely to require massive transfusion (5 or more units of red cells in 4 hours). Activation of the massive transfusion protocol triggers balanced delivery of packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate, aiming for physiological targets (temperature above 35 degrees C, pH above 7.2, ionised calcium above 1.1 mmol/L, fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, platelets above 50 to 100 depending on setting, INR less than 1.5). Tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours reduces mortality in trauma; in upper GI bleeding evidence is less strong but is often used. Definitive source control (endoscopy, angiography, surgery) is the definitive step.
key_points: MTP for 5+ units in 4 hours or shock plus ongoing haemorrhage
Balanced pRBC, FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate
Physiological targets: temp above 35, pH above 7.2, iCa above 1.1
explanation.pearls: Ionised calcium falls rapidly with citrated products; replace with 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate for every 4 units of blood product to prevent bleeding from citrate hypocalcaemia.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Critical Bleeding / Massive Transfusion

subtopic_detail: Unprovoked VTE anticoagulation duration
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52 year old man in outpatients 3 months after a right sided segmental pulmonary embolus. There was no preceding surgery, plaster cast, prolonged immobility, hospitalisation, cancer, oestrogen exposure, or long haul travel. He has no personal or family history of thrombosis. His pulmonary embolism was diagnosed on CT pulmonary angiogram after 3 days of pleuritic chest pain; troponin was negative and echocardiogram normal. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily since diagnosis.

Repeat compression ultrasound of the legs is normal. D-dimer measured today after 4 weeks off treatment (planned trial cessation) is 620 micrograms/L (less than 500). Full blood count, renal function, liver function tests, and coagulation studies are within normal limits. He is a non-smoker, drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, has hypertension controlled with perindopril, and works as a physiotherapist. His HAS-BLED score is 1.

data_table.Anticoagulant: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily since diagnosis
data_table.Post-cessation trial D-dimer: 620 micrograms/L (less than 500) after 4 weeks off treatment

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from this point?

options.text: Stop apixaban permanently now and rely on daily 100 mg aspirin as long term secondary prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for secondary prevention of unprovoked VTE and stopping anticoagulation with a positive post-cessation D-dimer risks recurrence at 5 to 10 percent per year (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely without dose reduction at any point in the future
options.rationale: Extended therapy is warranted, but current evidence supports dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months for unprovoked VTE with acceptable bleeding profile (AMPLIFY-EXT); indefinite full dose is not the preferred plan (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

options.text: Extend apixaban for a further 3 months only then reassess with repeat D-dimer at that time again
options.rationale: A finite additional course does not resolve the ongoing recurrence risk in unprovoked VTE with a positive D-dimer; recurrence risk after any finite duration returns to baseline once anticoagulation stops (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

options.text: Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months as extended low intensity secondary prevention
options.rationale: For unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk and features suggesting persistent risk (positive post-cessation D-dimer), THANZ endorses extended anticoagulation, with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months preferred over full dose per AMPLIFY-EXT data (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

options.text: Switch to warfarin with target INR 2 to 3 for at least 10 years then reassess bleeding risk
options.rationale: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for extended VTE therapy in the absence of specific indications (antiphospholipid syndrome, severe renal impairment); switching without cause adds monitoring burden and bleeding risk (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

explanation.summary: Unprovoked pulmonary embolism carries an annual recurrence risk of about 5 to 10 percent per year once anticoagulation stops after a standard 3 to 6 month course. THANZ recommends extended anticoagulation for unprovoked proximal DVT or PE where bleeding risk is acceptable, and the AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months, which preserves efficacy against recurrence with lower bleeding rates than full dose. A positive post-cessation D-dimer after 4 weeks off treatment strongly favours continued therapy in this scenario. Aspirin is inferior to DOAC. Warfarin is preferred only for antiphospholipid syndrome and severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance below 30).
key_points: Unprovoked VTE recurrence 5 to 10 percent per year after stopping
Extended apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is preferred beyond 6 months
Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for extended secondary prevention
explanation.pearls: A positive D-dimer 4 weeks after stopping anticoagulation carries a hazard ratio of about 2 for recurrent VTE and is a legitimate discriminator when extending therapy is uncertain.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand (THANZ) VTE Guidance

subtopic_detail: Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 46 year old man with 5 days of unsteady gait and double vision. He had 3 days of gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago (self limited, no antibiotics). On examination he is alert with normal cognition. Cranial nerve examination shows bilateral partial abduction failure with limitation of upgaze; pupils are 4 mm and sluggishly reactive. Facial strength and swallow are normal. Limb power is 5 out of 5 throughout with normal tone; deep tendon reflexes are absent at both biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles. Plantar responses are downgoing.

Romberg positive; heel-shin dysmetria bilaterally. Vital signs are pulse 82 regular, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C. Bedside single breath count is 32; forced vital capacity 4.1 L. MRI brain and orbits are unremarkable. CSF from lumbar puncture shows protein 0.9 g/L (0.15 to 0.45), white cell count 3 x10^6/L (less than 5), glucose 3.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Peripheral: Areflexia; power 5/5; sensory loss absent; Romberg positive
data_table.CSF: Protein 0.9 g/L; WCC 3 x10^6/L; glucose 3.8 mmol/L

lead_in: Which single specific antibody test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Anti aquaporin 4 antibody serum titre to distinguish neuromyelitis optica spectrum from other syndromes
options.rationale: Aquaporin 4 antibodies characterise neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, typically with optic neuritis or transverse myelitis, not ophthalmoplegia with areflexia (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Anti acetylcholine receptor antibody assay to confirm myasthenia gravis at a specialised neuroimmunology lab
options.rationale: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies confirm generalised myasthenia gravis, but the areflexia and CSF albuminocytological dissociation here point away from myasthenia (reflexes are preserved) (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Anti myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody to characterise a demyelinating central nervous system syndrome
options.rationale: MOG antibodies mark central demyelinating disease and are not associated with the ophthalmoplegia and areflexia pattern of Miller Fisher syndrome (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Anti GQ1b IgG serum antibody to confirm the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome
options.rationale: Anti GQ1b IgG is present in over 85 percent of Miller Fisher syndrome, characterised by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia after a preceding infection; the triad plus CSF albuminocytological dissociation fits classically (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

options.text: Anti Hu paraneoplastic antibody panel to look for an underlying small cell lung cancer in the setting
options.rationale: Anti Hu antibodies are associated with paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy and encephalomyelitis, not the acute post infective Miller Fisher pattern (Source: BMJ Best Practice Guillain-Barre Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Miller Fisher syndrome is a Guillain-Barre variant defined by the triad of external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia after an infective prodrome, most commonly Campylobacter jejuni or upper respiratory viruses. Anti GQ1b IgG is present in over 85 percent of cases and is the most specific serological confirmation. CSF classically shows albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein with normal white cell count) after the first week. Management is IVIG or plasma exchange with close respiratory monitoring; vital capacity below 20 mL per kg or negative inspiratory force above -30 cmH2O predicts need for ventilation. Miller Fisher generally has a good prognosis with recovery over weeks to months.
key_points: Triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia
Anti GQ1b IgG in more than 85 percent of Miller Fisher cases
Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange with close respiratory monitoring
explanation.pearls: Single breath count under 20 or a falling forced vital capacity in Guillain-Barre spectrum disease warrants ICU review even before oxygen desaturation; respiratory failure is often abrupt.

subtopic_detail: Warfarin over-anticoagulation without bleeding
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 74 year old woman with a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis maintained on warfarin 5 mg on alternate days with 4 mg on the other days for the past 6 years. She takes no other regular medications. She rings you because a routine INR taken today shows 8.9 (target 2.5 to 3.5 for mechanical mitral valve). She feels well, has no bruising, no gum bleeding, no melaena, no haematuria, and no headache. She reports she started a 5 day course of clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily 4 days ago for a chest infection.

Baseline vital signs 2 weeks ago were pulse 72 regular, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, and today she reports feeling the same. She has an appointment available with her cardiologist next week and lives 15 minutes drive from a public hospital emergency department. She asks what to do now.

data_table.Warfarin regimen: 5 mg on alternate days with 4 mg on other days for 6 years
data_table.Recent medication: Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily started 4 days ago
data_table.Bleeding: No overt bleeding or headache reported

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Continue current warfarin dose and repeat INR in 2 weeks after clarithromycin course completes
options.rationale: An INR above 8 carries a high risk of spontaneous bleeding; continuing warfarin without action is unsafe even without overt bleeding (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous vitamin K 10 mg via slow infusion at home to reverse anticoagulation now
options.rationale: IV vitamin K is reserved for major bleeding and can fully reverse anticoagulation, which is undesirable in a patient with a mechanical mitral valve; oral low dose vitamin K is preferred for asymptomatic elevation (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Administer prothrombinex 25 units per kg with fresh frozen plasma at the general practice today
options.rationale: Prothrombinex is reserved for major or life threatening bleeding, or urgent surgery; use in asymptomatic elevation risks over correction and thrombosis around a mechanical valve (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Withhold two warfarin doses only, without vitamin K, and repeat INR in 3 days at the practice
options.rationale: For INR above 8 without bleeding, guidance is to withhold warfarin and give 1 to 2 mg oral vitamin K; withholding alone is inadequate (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Withhold warfarin, give 1 mg oral vitamin K1 (phytomenadione), and repeat INR in 24 hours
options.rationale: For INR above 8 without significant bleeding, National Blood Authority guidance recommends withholding warfarin and giving 1 to 2 mg oral vitamin K; the mechanical valve makes over correction with high dose IV vitamin K undesirable (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

explanation.summary: National Blood Authority warfarin reversal guidance stratifies management by INR level and bleeding. INR above target but below 4.5 with no bleeding: reduce dose or omit next dose. INR 4.5 to 10 with no bleeding: withhold warfarin, consider 1 mg oral vitamin K if bleeding risk is high. INR above 10 with no bleeding: withhold warfarin, give 3 to 5 mg oral vitamin K. Any INR with major bleeding: prothrombinex 25 to 50 units per kg plus fresh frozen plasma 150 to 300 mL plus 5 to 10 mg IV vitamin K. In this scenario with INR 8.9 and no bleeding, oral low dose vitamin K 1 mg with warfarin withholding is the fit. Also stop the interacting antibiotic (clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2C9, raising warfarin levels).
key_points: INR 4.5 to 10 no bleeding: withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg
INR above 10 no bleeding: withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K 3 to 5 mg
Major bleeding: prothrombinex plus FFP plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg
explanation.pearls: Clarithromycin, erythromycin, metronidazole, fluconazole, and amiodarone all raise INR through CYP inhibition; check INR within 3 to 5 days of starting or stopping them if patient is on warfarin.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guidance

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection recognition and surgical urgency
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63 year old man admitted 6 hours ago with a red painful right lower leg after minor gardening trauma 24 hours earlier. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin. Since arrival his pain has escalated from 4 out of 10 to 9 out of 10 despite oral oxycodone 15 mg and paracetamol 1 g given 90 minutes ago. He now has a tense, waxy area of swelling above the ankle with 2 haemorrhagic bullae, and the skin overlying appears anaesthetic to pinprick testing.

Vital signs deteriorate: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C. Bloods: white cell count 22 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), sodium 129 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 178 micromol/L (from 92 last month), glucose 14.2 mmol/L, CRP 348 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 4.4 mmol/L. His LRINEC score is calculated at 9.

data_table.Local findings: Tense waxy swelling; 2 haemorrhagic bullae; skin anaesthesia to pinprick
data_table.Pain trajectory: Escalated from 4/10 to 9/10 despite opioid analgesia
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 96% RA, temp 39.4

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate step in management?

options.text: Give intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and admit for 48 hours of observation before reassessment
options.rationale: Empirical monotherapy for streptococcal cellulitis alone underdoses necrotising fasciitis and delays the essential surgical review; broader empirical cover plus urgent surgery is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Arrange a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the leg to confirm fascial involvement before surgical review
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical diagnosis; MRI can delay definitive debridement and false negatives occur early. Imaging must not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Elevate the limb, apply topical dressings, and mark the erythematous margin for reassessment in 4 hours
options.rationale: Standard cellulitis nursing measures are inadequate for suspected necrotising fasciitis; delay of a few hours can be lethal and progression is rapid (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Urgent surgical referral for operative exploration with concurrent broad spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation
options.rationale: LRINEC score 9 with anaesthetic skin, haemorrhagic bullae, and pain out of proportion has very high probability of necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical debridement with concurrent broad spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin) is the definitive first step (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Refer to hyperbaric oxygen therapy after intravenous antibiotics have been running for 24 hours
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen may be an adjunct after debridement in some centres but is not the immediate step and must not delay surgery (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency where every hour of delay increases mortality (which reaches 25 to 30 percent overall). Clinical clues that separate it from severe cellulitis are pain out of proportion to visible findings, anaesthetic skin over the affected area, haemorrhagic or dusky bullae, rapid progression, and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose to stratify risk; a score of 6 or more is intermediate risk and 8 or more high risk. Empirical antibiotics are piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin (for antitoxin effect against group A strep) plus vancomycin (for MRSA). Definitive management is urgent operative debridement; imaging must not delay surgical review.
key_points: Surgical debridement is definitive and time critical
LRINEC score 6 to 8 intermediate risk, 8 or more high risk
Empirical: piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin
explanation.pearls: Anaesthesia over the affected skin from cutaneous nerve destruction is a late but highly specific sign; if you find it, the patient is going to theatre now.

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis first line pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 72 year old postmenopausal woman 8 weeks after a wrist fracture sustained from a fall from standing height. She has no significant medical history, no current medications, and is a lifelong non smoker. Her mother had a hip fracture aged 75. DXA scan shows lumbar spine T score -2.1 and femoral neck T score -2.6.

Vitamin D was 62 nmol/L (above 50), corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60), TSH within normal limits, and eGFR 74 mL/min/1.73m2. Coeliac serology is negative and full blood count and myeloma screen are unremarkable. She has good dentition and no recent dental work planned. She drinks 1 standard drink weekly and walks 30 minutes daily. She asks what medication is best to reduce her risk of another fracture.

data_table.Fracture history: Left distal radius fracture 8 weeks ago from fall from standing height
data_table.DXA: Lumbar spine T -2.1; femoral neck T -2.6
data_table.Bloods: Vitamin D 62 nmol/L; corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L; eGFR 74; TSH within normal limits
data_table.Secondary screen: Coeliac serology negative; myeloma screen normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy to recommend now?

options.text: Calcium 1000 mg with vitamin D 1000 IU daily as a single agent for 12 months and reassess DXA scan
options.rationale: Calcium plus vitamin D alone does not adequately reduce fracture risk in established osteoporosis with a minimal trauma fracture; specific antiresorptive therapy is required (Source: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide).
source_refs: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide

options.text: Subcutaneous romosozumab 210 mg monthly for 12 months as anabolic agent for very high risk profile
options.rationale: Romosozumab is reserved for very high fracture risk profiles (multiple fractures, very low T score); first line here is oral bisphosphonate, and romosozumab carries cardiovascular caution (Source: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide).
source_refs: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms daily for 24 months as an anabolic agent first line
options.rationale: Teriparatide is a second line PBS restricted anabolic for severe osteoporosis where bisphosphonate has failed or is contraindicated; it is not first line here (Source: PBS Teriparatide Listing).

options.text: Oestrogen with progestogen menopausal hormone therapy for prevention of further fragility fracture
options.rationale: Menopausal hormone therapy is reserved for symptomatic postmenopausal women in the first 10 years after menopause; it is not first line for osteoporosis in a 72 year old (Source: RACGP Menopausal Hormone Therapy Guidance).

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation as first line therapy
options.rationale: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is first line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture in an ambulant patient with normal renal function and good dentition; PBS covers it after a minimal trauma fracture (Source: PBS Alendronate Listing).

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman with T score below -2.5 defines osteoporosis and mandates specific antiresorptive therapy in addition to calcium and vitamin D. Oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly (or risedronate 35 mg weekly) is first line where renal function is preserved (eGFR above 30 for oral, above 35 for zoledronic acid) and gastro-oesophageal reflux is not prohibitive. Zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenous annually is an alternative for adherence or reflux concerns. Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous six monthly is second line and requires uninterrupted therapy (rebound fractures on cessation). Teriparatide and romosozumab are reserved for severe or very high risk cases via PBS restriction. Vitamin D above 50 nmol/L should be maintained and calcium intake at 1200 to 1300 mg daily supported by diet plus supplementation where needed.
key_points: Fragility fracture plus T below -2.5 defines pharmacotherapy indication
Oral alendronate weekly is first line with normal renal function
Denosumab must not be stopped without transition to bisphosphonate
explanation.pearls: Vitamin D should be at or above 50 nmol/L before initiating a bisphosphonate; hypocalcaemia after zoledronic acid is common if vitamin D is deficient at baseline.

sources.label: Osteoporosis Australia Consumer Medicine Reference Guide

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition on prednisolone taper
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man who was tapered off prednisolone 4 weeks ago after 18 months of 15 to 20 mg daily for pemphigus vulgaris. He was reduced from 5 mg every second day to zero over 3 weeks. He is now on day 4 of an upper respiratory tract infection with fevers to 38.6 and rigors. Today he attended the emergency department after collapsing at home when he stood up quickly.

Examination: he is drowsy but rousable, mucosal pallor, deeply tanned in sun exposed areas. Vital signs are pulse 118, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg (unresponsive to a 500 mL saline bolus already given), respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C. Bloods: sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), glucose 3.1 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest x-ray shows early right lower zone consolidation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 76/44 (unresponsive to 500 mL saline), RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, temp 38.9
data_table.Steroid history: Prednisolone 15 to 20 mg daily x 18 months, tapered off 4 weeks ago
data_table.Bloods: Na 128; K+ 5.4; glucose 3.1 mmol/L; urea 12.4; creatinine 148
data_table.Skin: Deeply tanned in sun exposed areas; mucosal pallor

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g and doxycycline 100 mg for community acquired pneumonia as primary treatment
options.rationale: Antibiotics are appropriate for the pneumonia, but they do not address the underlying adrenal crisis that is producing the refractory hypotension; hydrocortisone must be given first (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline infusion titrated to mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg via central line access
options.rationale: Vasopressors will fail without cortisol replacement in adrenal crisis; noradrenaline is not a substitute for hydrocortisone here (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Intravenous 3 percent sodium chloride 100 mL bolus to correct hyponatraemia before other interventions
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia is secondary to cortisol deficiency and corrects with hydrocortisone plus isotonic saline; hypertonic saline is not indicated without neurological symptoms (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Send a short synacthen test now and defer any glucocorticoid until baseline and 30 minute cortisol return
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis and any diagnostic delay is dangerous; hydrocortisone should be given immediately and a stimulation test performed later, or a random cortisol drawn just before dosing (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately with concurrent normal saline resuscitation and glucose
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical emergency; intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours) with isotonic saline and glucose correction is the primary treatment; delay for testing worsens outcomes (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in a patient recently withdrawn from long term supraphysiological glucocorticoid therapy is a clinical diagnosis: hypotension unresponsive to fluid, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and precipitating stressor (here, sepsis and pneumonia). Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg over 24 hours as continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours, plus isotonic saline resuscitation and dextrose for hypoglycaemia are the immediate mainstay. Treatment must not wait for cortisol testing (a random pre-treatment cortisol can be drawn if easily done). Antibiotics for the precipitant follow. Once stable, transition to oral hydrocortisone with a written sick day plan, medic alert bracelet, and self-injection education.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours
Isotonic saline resuscitation and glucose correction concurrently
Do not delay treatment for the short synacthen test
explanation.pearls: Any patient on more than 5 mg prednisolone equivalent daily for more than 3 weeks has HPA axis suppression risk; sick day rules and a hydrocortisone emergency kit prevent crisis.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia intravenous iron choice
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 45 year old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids. She has 6 months of fatigue and shortness of breath climbing stairs. She has trialled two oral iron products (ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily and iron polymaltose 100 mg elemental daily) but stopped both within 2 weeks because of intolerable epigastric pain and constipation. She is on the waitlist for a Mirena insertion in 8 weeks.

Bloods: haemoglobin 82 g/L (115 to 165), MCV 74 fL (80 to 100), ferritin 4 micrograms/L (30 to 200), transferrin saturation 6 percent (16 to 45), CRP 3 mg/L (less than 5). Coeliac serology and faecal occult blood are negative. She has no history of severe allergy or asthma, is not pregnant, and is otherwise well. She weighs 68 kg, and her calculated iron deficit (Ganzoni formula) is approximately 1200 mg.

data_table.Iron studies: Hb 82; MCV 74; ferritin 4; transferrin saturation 6 percent
data_table.Oral iron trial: Ferrous sulfate and iron polymaltose both stopped within 2 weeks for GI intolerance
data_table.Cause of loss: Heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids; Mirena in 8 weeks

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step for iron replacement?

options.text: Single dose intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes with 15 minutes post infusion monitoring
options.rationale: Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV over at least 15 minutes with 30 minutes post infusion monitoring is standard for oral iron intolerance in the PBS-listed indication of iron deficiency anaemia; a single dose covers a deficit up to 1000 mg (Source: PBS Ferric Carboxymaltose Listing).

options.text: Restart oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily with a proton pump inhibitor 40 mg to reduce epigastric pain
options.rationale: PPI reduces gastric acid and impairs iron absorption; it is not a fix for oral iron intolerance and does not address her existing anaemia in a timely way (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

options.text: Transfuse 2 units of packed red blood cells now to correct haemoglobin above 100 g/L rapidly
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia not manageable by iron replacement or with haemoglobin below 70 g/L (or 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease); this patient warrants iron replacement first (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Prescribe intramuscular iron dextran 100 mg alternate days for 12 weeks in the general practice setting
options.rationale: IM iron dextran is largely superseded by IV iron polymaltose or ferric carboxymaltose which are faster, better tolerated, and safer; IM dosing carries staining and slower correction (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

options.text: Delay all iron replacement until the Mirena insertion in 8 weeks resolves the ongoing menstrual loss
options.rationale: Waiting 8 weeks in a symptomatic patient with haemoglobin 82 and severe iron deficiency is unsafe; correction is done in parallel with definitive management of the cause (Source: RACGP Iron Deficiency Position).

explanation.summary: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose has largely replaced iron polymaltose in Australia for oral iron intolerance and rapid correction. A single 1000 mg dose given over at least 15 minutes with 30 minutes of monitoring afterwards suffices for a deficit up to 1000 mg; larger deficits are made up 1 week later. Hypersensitivity is rare but staff must be trained in anaphylaxis management and pre-treatment history must screen for prior hypersensitivity reactions and severe atopy. Watch for hypophosphataemia after high dose FCM (check phosphate at 2 to 4 weeks if repeat dosing planned). Definitive management of the cause (Mirena for menorrhagia, endoscopy in men or postmenopausal women) proceeds in parallel.
key_points: Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV single dose over at least 15 minutes
Repeat 1 week later if deficit exceeds 1000 mg
Manage the cause in parallel; do not delay for definitive treatment
explanation.pearls: Extravasation of ferric carboxymaltose causes long lasting brown skin staining; large bore cannula in a straight vein above the wrist minimises this risk.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Pleural effusion Light's criteria interpretation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old man with progressive breathlessness on exertion over 8 weeks and left sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a 40 pack year smoking history, quit 2 years ago. On examination he has stony dull percussion and reduced breath sounds over the left lower zone. Chest x-ray shows a moderate left pleural effusion. Bedside ultrasound guided pleurocentesis is performed and 40 mL of straw coloured pleural fluid is aspirated.

Pleural fluid analysis: protein 38 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 320 U/L, glucose 4.1 mmol/L, pH 7.36. Serum protein 62 g/L, serum lactate dehydrogenase 210 U/L (upper limit of normal 240 U/L). Cytology and culture are pending. Bloods: full blood count and creatinine within normal limits, NT-proBNP 82 ng/L (less than 125). Echocardiogram shows normal biventricular function.

data_table.Imaging: Moderate left pleural effusion on CXR

lead_in: How should the pleural fluid be classified using Light's criteria and what is the next step?

options.text: Transudate; initiate loop diuretic therapy and repeat chest x-ray in 2 weeks without further evaluation
options.rationale: Fluid protein 38 g/L (ratio 0.61, above 0.5) meets Light's criteria for an exudate, not a transudate; loop diuretic without cause is inappropriate (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

options.text: Exudate; arrange contrast enhanced CT chest and consider pleural biopsy given smoking history and unilateral effusion
options.rationale: Pleural protein to serum protein ratio 0.61 (above 0.5) and pleural LDH to serum LDH ratio 1.52 (above 0.6) meet 2 of 3 Light's criteria for exudate; contrast CT and pleural biopsy are indicated to exclude malignancy given age, smoking history, and unilateral effusion (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

options.text: Exudate; initiate empirical broad spectrum antibiotics and arrange chest drain insertion for empyema treatment
options.rationale: The fluid has pH 7.36 and glucose 4.1 mmol/L with no purulence, which does not meet criteria for empyema; empirical antibiotics and drain are not indicated without those features (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

options.text: Transudate; commence NT-proBNP based heart failure workup and add angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor immediately
options.rationale: NT-proBNP is normal and echocardiogram normal; the fluid meets exudate criteria not transudate; heart failure is not the cause (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

options.text: Indeterminate; repeat pleurocentesis in 4 weeks with albumin gradient to establish the effusion aetiology later
options.rationale: The Light's criteria are met for exudate; workup should proceed now with CT and biopsy rather than await repeat tap (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline).

explanation.summary: Light's criteria classify a pleural effusion as exudate if any one of pleural to serum protein ratio above 0.5, pleural to serum LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH is met. This patient's protein ratio is 0.61 and LDH ratio 1.52 (both criteria met). Common exudative causes are malignancy, parapneumonic effusion, empyema, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, and connective tissue disease. Unilateral exudative effusion in a smoker over 50 warrants contrast CT chest and image guided pleural biopsy (or medical thoracoscopy) to exclude malignancy including mesothelioma. Fluid pH below 7.2, glucose below 3.3 mmol/L, or frank pus indicate complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema and require chest drain.
key_points: Light's criteria (any 1 of 3) define exudate
Unilateral exudate in a smoker over 50: CT chest and biopsy
Fluid pH below 7.2 or glucose below 3.3 mmol/L: drain empyema
explanation.pearls: If diuretic therapy has been given before the tap, the pleural to serum albumin gradient (above 12 g/L implies transudate) is more reliable than Light's criteria, which can falsely classify diuretic-treated transudates as exudates.

subtopic_detail: NSTEMI antiplatelet regimen selection in an older patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 78 year old man with new-onset chest pain lasting 4 hours and a high-sensitivity troponin I of 78 ng/L (99th percentile 34) that rose to 220 ng/L 3 hours later. He has known chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73 m2, hypertension on perindopril, and takes no antiplatelet at baseline. He weighs 74 kg. He is not on anticoagulation and has no history of intracranial haemorrhage or recent bleeding.

On examination he is comfortable in bed with resolved chest discomfort. Vital signs: pulse 78/min, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. ECG shows sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST depression in leads V4 to V6 that has resolved on the current tracing. He has been given aspirin 300 mg and sublingual GTN and the cardiology team has planned a coronary angiogram within 24 hours.

data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm; 1 mm ST depression V4 to V6, resolved on current
data_table.Given so far: Aspirin 300 mg; sublingual GTN; angiography planned within 24 hours
data_table.Bleeding risk: No ICH history; no recent bleeding; not on anticoagulant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional antiplatelet to add now?

options.text: Continue aspirin monotherapy without adding a P2Y12 inhibitor before angiography
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy is standard for NSTEMI to reduce recurrent ischaemic events; single antiplatelet under-treats when angiography is planned within 24 hours (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).

options.text: Oral prasugrel 60 mg loading dose then 10 mg daily as second antiplatelet
options.rationale: Prasugrel is contraindicated in patients over 75 years and in those with previous stroke or TIA; it is not appropriate here (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).

options.text: Oral ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose then 90 mg twice daily as second antiplatelet
options.rationale: Ticagrelor is more potent but has a higher bleeding rate in older patients and its dyspnoea and bradycardia adverse effects are more troublesome in this age group; clopidogrel is preferred over 75 (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).

options.text: Commence oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily as an anticoagulant addition to aspirin
options.rationale: DOAC monotherapy is not indicated in NSTEMI without atrial fibrillation and adds bleeding without ACS benefit; P2Y12 inhibitor is the standard second antiplatelet (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).

options.text: Oral clopidogrel 300 mg loading dose then 75 mg daily as part of dual antiplatelet therapy
options.rationale: In NSTEMI planned for angiography in a patient over 75 with reduced renal function, clopidogrel is preferred over ticagrelor and prasugrel because both carry higher bleeding risk in older patients (prasugrel contraindicated over 75 kg cut-off aside, and ticagrelor has higher intracranial haemorrhage in over 75s); clopidogrel is the CSANZ-preferred agent when bleeding risk is high (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).

explanation.summary: For NSTEMI in a patient over 75 with reduced renal function, dual antiplatelet therapy is standard alongside heparin bridging to angiography. CSANZ prefers clopidogrel over ticagrelor or prasugrel in older patients because both alternatives carry higher rates of intracranial and gastrointestinal bleeding in over-75s; prasugrel is explicitly contraindicated over 75 years, in patients under 60 kg, and after prior stroke or TIA. Ticagrelor also has dyspnoea and bradycardia effects that are less well tolerated in older patients. Aspirin monotherapy is not adequate before planned coronary angiography for NSTEMI.
key_points: Clopidogrel is preferred P2Y12 inhibitor over 75 years or with high bleeding risk
Prasugrel is contraindicated over 75 years, under 60 kg, or after prior stroke or TIA
Dual antiplatelet plus anticoagulant bridge is standard for NSTEMI before angiography
explanation.pearls: Older patients are the group where the theoretical superiority of ticagrelor is most likely to be undone by bleeding; the CSANZ default is clopidogrel unless there is a specific reason to escalate.

subtopic_detail: SGLT2 inhibitor indication in chronic kidney disease with albuminuria
stem:
You are the nephrology registrar reviewing a 62 year old man in the CKD clinic with type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension, and a background of chronic kidney disease. His HbA1c is 7.6 percent on metformin 2 g daily and gliclazide 60 mg daily. He is on perindopril 8 mg daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg. His weight has been stable and his blood pressure is controlled.

Investigations today: eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 (stable over 12 months), urinary albumin-creatinine ratio 62 mg/mmol (up from 42 six months ago), sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, HbA1c 7.6 percent (target under 7 for this patient). He has never had diabetic ketoacidosis and has no history of recurrent genital or urinary infections. Ophthalmology screening at 6 months was normal.

data_table.Current meds: Metformin 2 g/day; gliclazide 60 mg/day; perindopril 8 mg; rosuvastatin 20 mg
data_table.Renal function: eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 stable; uACR 62 mg/mmol rising from 42
data_table.Screening: No DKA history; no recurrent genital or urinary infection; ophthalmology normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medication change?

options.text: Reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily because of the reduced eGFR
options.rationale: Metformin can be continued at reduced dose down to eGFR 30 (500 mg twice daily), but the eGFR here is 38 and standard dose is acceptable with ongoing monitoring; this is not the priority medication change (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

options.text: Add oral empagliflozin 10 mg daily as an SGLT2 inhibitor for cardiorenal protection
options.rationale: Australian KHA and CSANZ guidance recommends SGLT2 inhibitors in T2DM with eGFR 20 or above with albuminuria (uACR at least 2.5 in men or 3.5 in women) for cardiorenal benefit; empagliflozin can be initiated down to eGFR 20 and continued to dialysis (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

options.text: Increase gliclazide to 120 mg daily to further lower HbA1c to under 7 percent
options.rationale: Sulfonylurea intensification adds hypoglycaemia risk in reduced eGFR without cardiorenal benefit; SGLT2 inhibitor is the intervention that improves both glycaemia and kidney outcomes (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

options.text: Cease perindopril because of the reduced eGFR and switch to amlodipine
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are renoprotective in albuminuric CKD and continued unless serum creatinine rises more than 30 percent or hyperkalaemia develops; switching to a calcium channel blocker loses the renal-protection benefit (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

options.text: Add oral dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly injection as a GLP-1 receptor agonist for weight loss
options.rationale: GLP-1 agonists provide cardiovascular and modest renal benefit but the specific gap here is a proven kidney-protective agent for progressive albuminuric CKD, which is the SGLT2 inhibitor class (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors are now the first-line addition for T2DM with albuminuric CKD because of consistent cardiorenal benefit (slower eGFR decline, reduced hospitalisation for heart failure, reduced cardiovascular death). Australian guidance from KHA-CARI accepts initiation down to eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73 m2 and continuation to dialysis. The main risks are volume depletion, mycotic genital infection, and euglycaemic DKA (particularly if metformin or insulin is reduced peri-operatively). ACE inhibitors are continued unless creatinine rises more than 30 percent or hyperkalaemia develops; metformin is continued at 500 mg twice daily if eGFR falls to 30.
key_points: SGLT2 inhibitors: add for T2DM with eGFR 20 or above with albuminuric CKD
Empagliflozin licensed in AU down to eGFR 20 and continued to dialysis
Watch for euglycaemic DKA and mycotic infection; hold before major surgery
explanation.pearls: SGLT2 inhibitors cause a small expected acute eGFR dip in the first 4 weeks; do not stop the drug for this drop unless it exceeds 30 percent or is accompanied by other markers of AKI.

sources.label: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease
CSANZ Position Statement on SGLT2 Inhibitors

subtopic_detail: Adrenal insufficiency stress-dose glucocorticoid during acute illness
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 48 year old woman with known Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg midday plus fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily. She has worn a MedicAlert bracelet for 6 years. She presents with 24 hours of vomiting, cramping abdominal pain, and non-bloody diarrhoea after a work barbecue; her husband has similar mild symptoms. She has taken sips of water and has vomited both her morning and midday hydrocortisone doses.

On examination she is tired but alert with dry mucous membranes. Vital signs: pulse 108/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg with a postural drop to 82/50 mmHg on standing, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds. Point-of-care electrolytes show sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L. She has not yet used her home emergency hydrocortisone injection.

data_table.Diagnosis: Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20/10 mg and fludrocortisone 100 microgram
data_table.Illness: 24 hours vomiting, cramping abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhoea; vomited scheduled doses
data_table.Vitals: HR 108; BP 96/58 supine, 82/50 standing; RR 18; SpO2 99 percent; T 37.6
data_table.POC bloods: Na 132 mmol/L; K 4.5 mmol/L; glucose 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Emergency plan: MedicAlert bracelet worn; home emergency hydrocortisone not used

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give ondansetron 8 mg intravenous alone and reassess before considering any change to steroid
options.rationale: Antiemetic without stress-dose steroid leaves the underlying adrenal insufficiency untreated; even if vomiting settles the ongoing physiological stress requires hydrocortisone escalation (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous now followed by 200 mg over 24 hours as continuous or 6 hourly boluses
options.rationale: Vomiting with postural hypotension in a woman on chronic replacement steroids is impending adrenal crisis; the AU protocol is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately, then 200 mg/24 hours (as infusion or 50 mg 6 hourly) with saline resuscitation (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Double the fludrocortisone dose to 200 microgram daily and continue routine hydrocortisone
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not the primary sick-day drug; higher-dose hydrocortisone at stress-dose provides both glucocorticoid and adequate mineralocorticoid effect through cross-reactivity, and fludrocortisone dose doubling is not part of the crisis pathway (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Administer intramuscular dexamethasone 4 mg while awaiting adrenal function tests
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is used when a Synacthen test is planned within hours because it does not cross-react with cortisol assays, but it lacks mineralocorticoid activity; hydrocortisone is the correct crisis drug for a woman already known to have Addison's (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

options.text: Give oral hydrocortisone 40 mg as a double dose and observe in the emergency department for 4 hours
options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is not reliably absorbed in a vomiting patient with impending crisis and the sick-day rule is to switch to parenteral hydrocortisone once oral is not tolerated (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

explanation.summary: In a patient with known primary adrenal insufficiency who is vomiting, febrile, or haemodynamically unstable, the correct action is immediate hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (as an infusion or 50 mg 6 hourly), plus normal saline resuscitation. Fludrocortisone is not the acute drug and does not need dose adjustment when hydrocortisone doses are already at stress level. Dexamethasone is used only when a Synacthen test is planned within the next few hours and cortisol assay interference must be avoided. Patients should carry a home emergency hydrocortisone injection kit and a MedicAlert bracelet.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM stat, then 200 mg over 24 hours plus saline
Fludrocortisone not the sick-day drug; stress-dose hydrocortisone has enough mineralocorticoid effect
Dexamethasone only if imminent Synacthen test needed to preserve cortisol assay
explanation.pearls: The doubling sick-day rule for oral hydrocortisone stops working once the patient is vomiting; switch to parenteral without waiting for shock.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

subtopic_detail: COPD exacerbation antibiotic indication and choice
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 71 year old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 42 percent predicted) presenting with 4 days of worsening breathlessness, increased sputum volume, and change in sputum colour from clear to green. She uses tiotropium and a fluticasone-vilanterol preventer with salbutamol as needed. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily. She has no penicillin allergy and is not on immunosuppression.

On examination she is speaking in short sentences with pursed-lip breathing. Vital signs: pulse 108/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 90 percent on 1 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius. Chest examination reveals widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally. CXR shows hyperinflation without focal consolidation. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.38, PaCO2 48 mmHg (35 to 45), PaO2 62 mmHg (75 to 100), HCO3 30 mmHg (22 to 32). She has already received nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium and oral prednisolone 50 mg.

data_table.Baseline: Severe COPD, FEV1 42 percent predicted; tiotropium plus fluticasone-vilanterol plus salbutamol
data_table.Symptoms: 4 days worsening breathlessness; increased sputum volume; change from clear to green sputum
data_table.Vitals: HR 108; BP 138/82; RR 26; SpO2 90 percent on 1 L/min NP; T 37.2
data_table.Imaging: CXR hyperinflation without focal consolidation
data_table.Given so far: Nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium; oral prednisolone 50 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding antibiotic therapy?

options.text: Commence oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days as first-line antibiotic agent
options.rationale: Azithromycin is not first-line for AU COPD exacerbations and has QT prolongation and macrolide resistance concerns; amoxicillin has better activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus in local ecology (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Commence intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours for broad-spectrum cover
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum antibiotics are reserved for severe exacerbations needing ICU, structural lung disease, or Pseudomonas risk factors; a hospital-managed but non-ICU exacerbation without those features does not need this cover (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Withhold antibiotics because CRP and white cell count have not returned to guide need
