options.rationale: Antibiotic decision in COPD exacerbation is clinical (Anthonisen criteria), not laboratory-driven; withholding antibiotics with all three cardinal features is inconsistent with the guideline (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Antibiotics are indicated in COPD exacerbations meeting 2 of 3 Anthonisen criteria (increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, purulent sputum) or requiring mechanical ventilation; amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days is the AU first-line for non-severe hospital-managed exacerbation without ICU need (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Commence oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line antibiotic agent
options.rationale: Doxycycline is the eTG second-line COPD exacerbation antibiotic (used in penicillin allergy or amoxicillin intolerance); amoxicillin remains first-line in non-allergic patients (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Antibiotics in a COPD exacerbation are indicated when two or more Anthonisen criteria are met (increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, sputum purulence) or when the patient is sick enough to need mechanical ventilation. The AU first-line agent is oral amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days, with doxycycline 100 mg BD for 5 days as an alternative in penicillin allergy. Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 50 mg for 5 days) run alongside bronchodilators. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are reserved for structural lung disease, Pseudomonas colonisation, ICU-level illness, or documented resistance.
key_points: Anthonisen 2 of 3 triggers antibiotics in COPD exacerbation
Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days is AU first-line
Doxycycline second-line in penicillin allergy or intolerance
explanation.pearls: Purulent sputum is the single most useful of the three Anthonisen criteria and independently predicts bacterial cause; changed sputum colour alone can carry the decision.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

subtopic_detail: Hyperacute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis window and blood pressure threshold
stem:
You are the medical registrar on the stroke team called to a 68 year old woman brought in by ambulance with sudden onset right-sided weakness and expressive dysphasia noted by her husband. Symptom onset was 2 hours and 20 minutes ago as timed by his phone. She has hypertension on amlodipine and is on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, last taken 14 hours ago. She has no history of intracranial haemorrhage and has not had recent major surgery.

On examination her NIHSS is 12, GCS 15. Vital signs: pulse 84/min irregular, blood pressure 192/102 mmHg (repeated 190/104 five minutes later), respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Point-of-care glucose is 6.8 mmol/L. Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct core. CT angiography demonstrates a left middle cerebral artery M1 occlusion. Apixaban level is not available and idarucizumab is not stocked; andexanet alfa is available.

data_table.Time and severity: Onset 2 h 20 min ago; NIHSS 12; GCS 15
data_table.Vitals: HR 84 irregular; BP 192/102 then 190/104; RR 16; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.7
data_table.Bloods: POC glucose 6.8 mmol/L; apixaban level unavailable
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast CT no haemorrhage or infarct core; CTA left MCA M1 occlusion
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD (last dose 14 hours ago); amlodipine
data_table.Reversal availability: Andexanet alfa available; idarucizumab not stocked

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Proceed directly to mechanical thrombectomy without thrombolysis and target blood pressure under 180/105 mmHg
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is contraindicated when apixaban has been taken in the last 48 hours without a validated low drug level; mechanical thrombectomy for a large-vessel occlusion is not contraindicated by DOAC use and blood pressure target is below 180/105 mmHg to reduce reperfusion haemorrhage (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Administer intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg after reversing apixaban with andexanet alfa pre-treatment
options.rationale: AU Stroke Foundation guidance does not endorse routine DOAC reversal to enable thrombolysis; the safer strategy is to proceed to thrombectomy in a large-vessel occlusion rather than to reverse anticoagulation for lytic therapy (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Give intravenous tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg without waiting for the apixaban level result today
options.rationale: Recent DOAC ingestion within 48 hours without a low drug level is a contraindication to thrombolysis (tenecteplase included) because of intracranial haemorrhage risk (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Lower blood pressure to under 140/90 mmHg with intravenous labetalol before any reperfusion therapy
options.rationale: Over-aggressive blood pressure lowering in an acute large-vessel occlusion can worsen penumbral perfusion; target is under 180/105 for thrombectomy, not the strict antihypertensive target for haemorrhagic stroke (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Commence intravenous heparin infusion to prevent thrombus extension while awaiting thrombectomy
options.rationale: Heparin has no role in acute ischaemic stroke and increases haemorrhagic transformation without improving outcomes; standard therapy is thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

explanation.summary: Mechanical thrombectomy is indicated for anterior circulation large-vessel occlusion within 6 hours of onset (or up to 24 hours with imaging selection) and is not contraindicated by DOAC use. Intravenous thrombolysis is contraindicated when a DOAC has been taken in the last 48 hours unless a validated drug level is low or specific reversal (idarucizumab for dabigatran) is used per protocol. Andexanet alfa is used mainly for DOAC-related haemorrhage rather than to unlock thrombolysis. Blood pressure target during thrombectomy is under 180/105 mmHg. Heparin has no role in acute ischaemic stroke.
key_points: DOAC in the last 48 hours contraindicates thrombolysis without validated low level
Mechanical thrombectomy is not contraindicated by DOAC use
BP under 180/105 mmHg during thrombectomy; do not over-aggressively lower
explanation.pearls: Dabigatran has a specific fast reversal (idarucizumab) that permits thrombolysis; the anti-Xa DOACs do not have this pathway in Australian stroke guidance so thrombectomy is the primary reperfusion route.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
CSANZ Position Statement on Direct Oral Anticoagulants

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia discrimination SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting post-SAH
stem:
You are the medical registrar consulted on a 58 year old woman on day 5 of admission to the neurosurgical ward after coiling of a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm. She has developed a serum sodium of 124 mmol/L (135 to 145) over 48 hours. She is drowsy but rousable and has had 2 loose stools today. Fluid intake over 24 hours has been 2.8 L of oral water plus 1 L intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride. Her weight is 62 kg, down from 66 kg on admission.

On examination she has dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. Vital signs: pulse 108/min, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg supine falling to 88/54 mmHg after 1 minute of standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 percent, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Investigations: serum osmolality 258 mOsm/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 640 mOsm/kg (300 to 900), urine sodium 92 mmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, cortisol 480 nmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L (45 to 90), and urine output over 24 hours 3200 mL.

data_table.Post-op day: Day 5 after coiling of ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm
data_table.Vitals: HR 108; BP 106/62 supine, 88/54 standing; RR 16; SpO2 98 percent; T 36.7
data_table.Bloods: Na 124 mmol/L; osmolality 258 mOsm/kg; TSH 1.8 mIU/L; cortisol 480 nmol/L; creatinine 88 micromol/L
data_table.Urine: Osmolality 640 mOsm/kg; sodium 92 mmol/L; 24 hour output 3200 mL
data_table.Fluid balance: Oral intake 2.8 L water plus 1 L 0.9 percent saline in the last 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 to 2 mL/kg/h intravenously and monitor daily weight and urine output
options.rationale: The clinical picture (hyponatraemia with high urine sodium, high urine output, weight loss, and postural hypotension after subarachnoid haemorrhage) fits cerebral salt wasting; treatment is isotonic saline replacement, not fluid restriction as in SIADH (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

options.text: Fluid restrict to 800 mL per 24 hours with daily serum sodium monitoring and postural check
options.rationale: SIADH is euvolaemic or mildly hypervolaemic and fluid restriction is its treatment; here the patient is hypovolaemic with weight loss and postural hypotension, so restriction would worsen hypovolaemia and cerebral perfusion (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

options.text: Commence oral tolvaptan 15 mg daily to correct the hyponatraemia by aquaresis
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is a vaptan used for euvolaemic or hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (SIADH) and is not indicated in cerebral salt wasting where sodium and volume must be replaced (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

options.text: Administer 3 percent hypertonic saline 100 mL bolus over 10 minutes and repeat the dose as needed
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) with a rate cap; drowsy but rousable with no seizure does not meet threshold and standard isotonic replacement is safer at this sodium (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide 40 mg to promote diuresis of free water and correct hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Furosemide is contraindicated in a hypovolaemic patient with hyponatraemia and would worsen sodium and volume loss (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

explanation.summary: SIADH and cerebral salt wasting both cause hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and high urine sodium after subarachnoid haemorrhage but differ in volume status: SIADH is euvolaemic or mildly hypervolaemic, while cerebral salt wasting is hypovolaemic with weight loss, postural hypotension, and negative fluid balance. Treatment diverges: SIADH is treated with fluid restriction (and second-line tolvaptan or urea), while cerebral salt wasting is treated with isotonic sodium chloride replacement and sometimes fludrocortisone. Confusing the two is dangerous because restricting fluid in cerebral salt wasting worsens cerebral perfusion and delayed ischaemic deficit after subarachnoid haemorrhage.
key_points: Volume status distinguishes SIADH (euvolaemic) from CSW (hypovolaemic)
Post-SAH sodium disorders often need saline replacement, not fluid restriction
Fluid restriction in CSW worsens cerebral perfusion and delayed ischaemic deficit
explanation.pearls: Daily weight and postural blood pressure discriminate SIADH from CSW more reliably than urine sodium alone; a 3 to 4 kg fall in weight is the CSW signal.

sources.label: Neurocritical Care Society Consensus on Sodium Disorders after Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: Warfarin over-anticoagulation with active bleeding reversal strategy
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 76 year old man on chronic warfarin for mechanical mitral valve replacement (target INR 2.5 to 3.5) who has been brought in by ambulance with 3 hours of melaena and lightheadedness. He takes no other antiplatelet or NSAID. Endoscopy has been requested and will be available within 4 hours.

On arrival he is pale and cool peripherally. Vital signs: pulse 118/min regular, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on 2 L/min nasal prongs, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds. Investigations: haemoglobin 82 g/L (baseline 138), platelets 210 x 10^9/L, INR 6.4, urea 14.8 mmol/L (2.5 to 7.5), creatinine 108 micromol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L. Group and hold has been done and 2 units of cross-matched red cells will be available in 15 minutes.

data_table.Indication: Chronic warfarin for mechanical mitral valve, target INR 2.5 to 3.5
data_table.Vitals: HR 118; BP 92/58; RR 22; SpO2 98 percent on 2 L/min NP; T 36.6
data_table.Bloods: Hb 82 (baseline 138); platelets 210; INR 6.4; urea 14.8; creatinine 108
data_table.Bleeding: 3 hours of melaena; lightheaded; endoscopy in 4 hours
data_table.Blood products: 2 units cross-matched red cells in 15 minutes; group and hold done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate strategy to correct anticoagulation?

options.text: Withhold warfarin now and repeat the INR in 4 hours before deciding on any specific reversal step
options.rationale: Repeat INR in 4 hours delays treatment while active bleeding continues in a patient with a mechanical valve who cannot tolerate anaemia; immediate reversal is required (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Guidelines).

options.text: Administer fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg alone without prothrombin complex concentrate to reverse warfarin
options.rationale: FFP is slower to prepare and requires large volumes to correct high INR, and lacks the concentrated factor replacement of PCC; PCC is preferred for immediate correction in life-threatening bleeding (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Guidelines).

options.text: Give oral vitamin K 10 mg and hold the next warfarin dose without giving factor replacement now
options.rationale: Oral vitamin K takes 12 to 24 hours to correct INR and is inappropriate for a haemodynamically unstable bleed; parenteral vitamin K and factor replacement are required (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Guidelines).

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 25 to 50 IU/kg now
options.rationale: Warfarin-associated major bleeding requires immediate factor replacement with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K; PCC works within 15 to 30 minutes, and vitamin K maintains reversal beyond the half-life of the factors (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Guidelines).

options.text: Give recombinant activated factor VII 90 microgram/kg as the primary reversal agent for the bleed
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not the standard warfarin reversal agent, is off-label, and carries thrombotic risk; PCC is the specific replacement therapy for vitamin K dependent factor deficiency (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Warfarin-associated major bleeding is reversed with intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (25 to 50 IU/kg by INR band); PCC corrects INR within 15 to 30 minutes and vitamin K maintains reversal beyond the short half-life of the replaced factors. FFP is a slower, larger-volume alternative reserved for when PCC is not available. Oral vitamin K is used for non-bleeding INR elevations (INR 5 to 9 without bleeding). In a mechanical valve patient, once bleeding is controlled the patient is bridged back to therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin then warfarin under haematology guidance.
key_points: Warfarin major bleed: IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus PCC 25 to 50 IU/kg
PCC works within 15 to 30 minutes; vitamin K maintains reversal beyond factor half-life
FFP is a fallback when PCC not available; oral vitamin K is for non-bleeding INR elevation
explanation.pearls: In a mechanical valve patient, over-reversal risks valve thrombosis; the plan after bleeding control is early heparin bridge back to warfarin, not indefinite withdrawal.

subtopic_detail: Hour one sepsis bundle timing
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 68 year old man is brought in by ambulance with 12 hours of fever, cough with rusty sputum and confusion. His temperature at triage is 39.4 degrees C. He has a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and type 2 diabetes on metformin.

On examination he is drowsy but rousable and confused about the date. He has right basal crackles and dullness to percussion. Peripheries are warm with capillary refill 3 seconds.

Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg after a 500 mL fluid bolus, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 92% on 4 L per minute via nasal prong, temperature 39.4 degrees C. Lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). Blood cultures have been drawn and a portable chest radiograph shows a right lower lobe consolidation. His weight is 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122/min; BP 88/54 mmHg after 500 mL bolus; RR 28/min; SpO2 92% on 4 L/min nasal prong; T 39.4 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; confused about the date; right basal crackles; dull to percussion; capillary refill 3 sec; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); CXR: right lower lobe consolidation; blood cultures drawn
data_table.History: COPD; T2DM on metformin; 82 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step within the hour one bundle?

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g and azithromycin 500 mg orally, and reassess response after 2 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone at 1 g is under dosed for severe community acquired pneumonia and oral azithromycin is inappropriate in a septic drowsy patient; the correct regimen for severe pneumonia with septic shock is broader with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus intravenous azithromycin or intravenous ceftriaxone at higher dose plus intravenous azithromycin (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg within the hour, plus further fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: In septic shock the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour one bundle requires antibiotics within one hour together with 30 mL/kg crystalloid; the eTG antibiotic guideline for severe community acquired pneumonia is intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence noradrenaline peripherally at 5 micrograms per minute before further fluid resuscitation is complete
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation to 30 mL/kg is completed first while vasopressors are prepared; starting noradrenaline without adequate fluid loading is not first line unless there is contraindication to further fluids (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Perform urgent computed tomography scan of the chest to characterise the consolidation before starting antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotics are not delayed for imaging in septic shock; a portable chest radiograph is sufficient to guide first line antimicrobial therapy and further imaging can follow after resuscitation (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021).

options.text: Give intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g monotherapy and add atypical cover only if the patient deteriorates
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin monotherapy does not cover atypical pathogens or resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae; severe pneumonia in Australia requires both third generation cephalosporin cover and atypical cover concurrently (Source: TG Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: In septic shock the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour one bundle mandates measurement of lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, 30 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid, broad spectrum antibiotics within one hour, and vasopressors if the mean arterial pressure remains below 65 mmHg after fluids. For severe community acquired pneumonia the eTG antibiotic guideline recommends intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily. Vasopressors are commenced after or during fluid resuscitation, not before it. Imaging beyond a portable chest radiograph is deferred until after resuscitation.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour of septic shock recognition.
Severe community acquired pneumonia: ceftriaxone 2 g plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenously.
30 mL/kg crystalloid before or with vasopressors.
explanation.pearls: For severe community acquired pneumonia in Australia default to intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily; the atypical cover matters even when the radiograph looks lobar because Legionella can present with dense consolidation.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice for pyelonephritis
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 42 year old woman with 24 hours of loin pain, rigors and dysuria. She is nauseated but tolerating small sips. She has no vomiting and no drug allergies. She takes no regular medications and has not been in hospital recently.

On examination she looks unwell but not septic. She has right loin tenderness on percussion. Abdomen is otherwise soft.

Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 122/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C. Urine dipstick leucocytes 3 plus, nitrites positive, blood 1 plus. She is 12 weeks post partum from a first pregnancy and is not currently breastfeeding. She has no known renal impairment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96/min; BP 122/72 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Unwell but not septic; right loin tenderness on percussion; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick leucs 3+, nitrites positive, blood 1+
data_table.History: 12 weeks post partum; not breastfeeding; no drug allergies; no regular medications; no recent hospital

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally once daily for 3 days and outpatient review and safety netting for any worsening loin pain or systemic symptoms
options.rationale: Trimethoprim monotherapy is inadequate for pyelonephritis because tissue penetration and coverage of E coli in Australia is limited; a longer course and different agent are required (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid 875 plus 125 mg orally twice daily for 10 days and general practitioner review at 48 hours
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid is a second line oral option; it is used when there is beta lactam allergy exclusion and local sensitivities support it, but the current eTG first line for pyelonephritis at home is oral trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole or cefalexin depending on culture (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 to 14 days after a urine sample is sent for culture and susceptibility
options.rationale: For non pregnant, non septic pyelonephritis that can be managed as an outpatient with reliable oral intake the eTG first line is oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 to 14 days with urine culture guiding subsequent choice, plus safety netting and 48 hour review (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg once and admit for further doses for further intravenous antibiotic therapy on the ward round
options.rationale: Intravenous gentamicin is used for hospitalised patients with severe pyelonephritis; this woman meets criteria for outpatient oral treatment given absence of sepsis, tolerating oral intake and no comorbidity (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days after a urine sample is sent for further review with the general practitioner in 48 hours
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin has poor tissue penetration and is not recommended for pyelonephritis; it is reserved for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (Source: TG Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Pyelonephritis in a non pregnant adult who is not septic and tolerates oral intake can be managed at home with a 10 to 14 day course of oral antibiotics guided by a pre treatment urine culture. The eTG antibiotic first line oral options are trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole or cefalexin. Trimethoprim monotherapy and nitrofurantoin are inadequate because of poor tissue penetration. Admission for intravenous therapy is indicated for severe illness, pregnancy, inability to tolerate oral intake, or failure of outpatient therapy at 48 hours.
key_points: Outpatient pyelonephritis: 10 to 14 days oral, culture guided.
First line oral: trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole or cefalexin.
Admit for pregnancy, sepsis, vomiting or failure to improve at 48 hours.
explanation.pearls: Send a mid stream urine for culture before starting any antibiotic for pyelonephritis, then switch to a narrow spectrum agent once susceptibilities are known; empirical cefalexin covers most E coli in Australia while sparing higher generation agents.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis
stem:
You are the surgical registrar on call reviewing a 62 year old man with a 24 hour history of a red painful right lower leg after a scratch from a garden hedge. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. His pain has escalated over the last 6 hours and is now out of keeping with the appearance of the skin.

On examination the right calf is diffusely red, warm and tense over 20 cm of skin. There is exquisite tenderness beyond the erythematous margin and a small area of dusky discolouration. Sensation is intact but blistering is starting to form.

Pulse rate 116/min, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C. Bloods show white cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 380 mg/L (less than 5), sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 12.4 mmol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L. Point of care lactate 3.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). LRINEC score is calculated at 8.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 116/min; BP 102/60 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Right calf diffusely red; warm; tense; tenderness beyond the erythematous margin; small dusky area; early blistering
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); CRP 380 mg/L (<5); Na 132 mmol/L; creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110); glucose 12.4 mmol/L; Hb 128 g/L; lactate 3.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); LRINEC 8
data_table.History: T2DM; hypertension; scratch from garden hedge 24 h ago; escalating pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g and observe the response overnight before further imaging
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy is inadequate for a suspected necrotising fasciitis with pain out of keeping and LRINEC score of 8; observation delays surgical source control and increases mortality (Source: TG Antibiotic; eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

options.text: Contrast enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the leg to confirm the diagnosis before any surgical involvement
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay operative source control in suspected necrotising fasciitis; a high LRINEC score together with the clinical picture is enough to proceed directly to theatre (Source: eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

options.text: Aspirate any blister fluid for microscopy and culture and reassess in 4 hours before making any treatment decision
options.rationale: Aspiration and observation delay urgent operative treatment; the intraoperative findings and cultures at debridement are the definitive investigation (Source: eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

options.text: Urgent surgical referral for debridement now, plus broad spectrum antibiotics including meropenem, vancomycin and clindamycin
options.rationale: The combination of pain out of proportion, dusky skin, systemic toxicity and a LRINEC score of 6 or more is a surgical emergency; the treatment is immediate debridement combined with broad spectrum antibiotics including meropenem or piperacillin tazobactam, vancomycin for methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus cover and clindamycin for toxin suppression (Source: TG Antibiotic; eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

options.text: Elevate the limb, mark the erythematous margin with a pen and reassess after 6 hours of intravenous fluids
options.rationale: This is a treatment of simple cellulitis, not necrotising fasciitis; deferring surgical care by 6 hours in a septic patient with a high LRINEC score is inappropriate (Source: eMJA necrotising soft tissue infection).

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency in which pain out of proportion to skin appearance, systemic toxicity, dusky discolouration, crepitus or blistering distinguish it from cellulitis. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis score integrates C reactive protein, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; a score of 6 or more raises suspicion and 8 or more strongly supports the diagnosis. The treatment is immediate operative debridement plus broad spectrum antibiotics with meropenem or piperacillin tazobactam, vancomycin and clindamycin for toxin suppression. Imaging should not delay surgical source control.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, systemic toxicity: necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise.
LRINEC at least 6 raises suspicion; 8 or more strongly supports the diagnosis.
Immediate debridement plus meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin.
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added to the empirical regimen for necrotising fasciitis regardless of susceptibility because it suppresses streptococcal exotoxin production and reduces mortality independent of the antibiotic sensitivity result.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic differentiation of DKA and HHS
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman brought in by her son for 4 days of increasing lethargy, thirst and confusion. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide, and hypertension. She has had reduced oral intake since her chest infection started a week ago.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable, with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. There is no Kussmaul breathing. Chest reveals right basal crackles.

Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C. Glucose 42 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), venous pH 7.32 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-30), ketones 0.6 mmol/L (less than 0.6), sodium 152 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 180 micromol/L (60-110), calculated osmolality 348 mOsm/kg (285-295).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 96% RA; T 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; rousable; dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; no Kussmaul breathing; right basal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 42 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); venous pH 7.32 (7.35-7.45); bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-30); ketones 0.6 mmol/L (<0.6); Na 152 mmol/L (135-145); K 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 180 micromol/L (60-110); osmolality 348 mOsm/kg (285-295)
data_table.History: T2DM on metformin and gliclazide; hypertension; reduced intake for 1 week; chest infection

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state precipitated by pneumonia requiring careful fluid resuscitation and delayed low dose insulin infusion
options.rationale: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is defined by hypovolaemia, glucose above 30 mmol/L, arterial or venous pH above 7.30, bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L, ketones under 3 mmol/L and effective osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg; the profile here fits and pneumonia is the classical precipitant (Source: JBDS hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state guideline; TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by pneumonia requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation and a fixed rate insulin infusion
options.rationale: DKA requires ketones at or above 3 mmol/L, pH below 7.30 and bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L; her ketones are only 0.6 mmol/L, pH is 7.32 and bicarbonate is 20 mmol/L, so DKA is excluded (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis from SGLT2 inhibitor use requiring cessation of the SGLT2 inhibitor and dextrose plus insulin infusion
options.rationale: Euglycaemic DKA presents with glucose usually under 14 mmol/L and elevated ketones with acidosis, and requires an SGLT2 inhibitor which this woman is not taking; the profile is not consistent (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Alcohol induced ketoacidosis requiring supportive care, thiamine and dextrose infusion under monitoring with regular monitoring in a high dependency bed
options.rationale: Alcohol induced ketoacidosis presents with low or normal glucose, elevated ketones and a history of chronic alcohol use; there is no alcohol history and glucose is markedly elevated (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Lactic acidosis due to metformin accumulation in acute kidney injury requiring supportive care, cessation of metformin and possible haemodialysis
options.rationale: Metformin lactic acidosis produces a low pH with an elevated lactate; her pH is 7.32 and there is no reported lactic acidosis in the profile, and it does not explain the marked hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality (Source: TG Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is a hyperglycaemic emergency in older patients with type 2 diabetes precipitated by infection or intercurrent illness. It is defined by hypovolaemia, glucose above 30 mmol/L, arterial or venous pH above 7.30, bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L, ketones under 3 mmol/L, and effective serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg. Treatment is slower fluid replacement than DKA using 0.9% sodium chloride at 500 to 1000 mL per hour with careful sodium monitoring, and low dose insulin infusion added once glucose stops falling with fluids alone. Sudden osmotic shifts risk cerebral oedema and central pontine myelinolysis, so aim for a sodium fall of no more than 10 mmol per 24 hours.
key_points: Glucose above 30 mmol/L, osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, ketones under 3 mmol/L.
DKA needs pH below 7.30 and ketones at or above 3 mmol/L.
Correct sodium slowly, no more than 10 mmol per 24 hours.
explanation.pearls: In hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state fluids alone will drop the glucose by 5 mmol/L per hour, so hold insulin until the fall slows below 5 mmol/L per hour to avoid rapid osmolar shifts and central pontine myelinolysis.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice in infective endocarditis by valve type
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with 3 weeks of fever, night sweats and weight loss. He had a mechanical mitral valve replacement 3 years ago for chronic rheumatic disease. He is on warfarin with an INR at target of 3.0. He has had no recent dental or surgical procedures.

On examination he has a splenomegaly of 3 cm below the costal margin, splinter haemorrhages on his fingers and a new pansystolic murmur at the apex.

Pulse rate 102/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn from separate venepunctures. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a 12 mm vegetation on the mitral prosthetic valve with moderate paravalvular regurgitation. Bloods show haemoglobin 108 g/L, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L, CRP 128 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 92 micromol/L. He has no beta lactam allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102/min; BP 118/76 mmHg; RR 20/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 38.6 C
data_table.Examination: Splenomegaly 3 cm; splinter haemorrhages; new pansystolic murmur at apex
data_table.Investigations: TTE: 12 mm vegetation on mitral prosthesis with moderate paravalvular regurgitation; Hb 108 g/L; WCC 12.4 x10^9/L; CRP 128 mg/L (<5); creatinine 92 micromol/L; 3 sets of blood cultures drawn
data_table.History: Mechanical mitral valve 3 years ago; warfarin INR 3.0; no recent procedures; no beta lactam allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours and gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for 4 to 6 weeks with regular clinical and echocardiographic review
options.rationale: This regimen covers viridans streptococci for native valve endocarditis but does not cover Staphylococcus aureus adequately or coagulase negative staphylococci which are the dominant organisms in prosthetic valve endocarditis (Source: TG Antibiotic; ESC infective endocarditis guideline).

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin, intravenous gentamicin and intravenous rifampicin, adjusted to trough levels once available with cardiothoracic surgical review for consideration of prosthetic valve replacement
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires empirical cover for methicillin resistant staphylococci and coagulase negative staphylococci; the eTG combination is vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin, with rifampicin added after the first 3 to 5 days for prosthetic material penetration once blood cultures are cleared (Source: TG Antibiotic; ESC infective endocarditis guideline).

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours and intravenous gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for 4 to 6 weeks with regular clinical and echocardiographic review
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin covers only methicillin sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and misses coagulase negative staphylococci and methicillin resistant organisms that are common in prosthetic valve endocarditis (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy for streptococcal cover for 4 to 6 weeks with regular clinical and echocardiographic review with clinical review and repeat echocardiography
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy is used for penicillin susceptible viridans streptococcal native valve endocarditis; it is inadequate for empirical prosthetic valve cover where staphylococcal disease dominates (Source: TG Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous daptomycin as monotherapy for staphylococcal cover in prosthetic valve endocarditis with cardiothoracic surgical review for consideration of valve replacement
options.rationale: Daptomycin is inactivated by lung surfactant and is not used as sole empirical therapy for prosthetic valve endocarditis; combination therapy with vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin is standard (Source: TG Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Prosthetic valve infective endocarditis is dominated by staphylococcal disease, in particular coagulase negative staphylococci and methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and requires broader empirical cover than native valve disease. The eTG antibiotic regimen is intravenous vancomycin plus intravenous gentamicin plus intravenous rifampicin, with rifampicin often added at day 3 to 5 once blood cultures are clear because of the biofilm penetration required for prosthetic material. Native valve infective endocarditis is treated empirically with benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, or flucloxacillin and gentamicin depending on the suspected organism, and adjusted once cultures return. Surgical review is indicated for large vegetations, heart failure, uncontrolled infection or perivalvular extension.
key_points: Prosthetic valve empirical therapy: vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin.
Native valve empirical therapy: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin.
Rifampicin added at day 3 to 5 for biofilm penetration.
explanation.pearls: For prosthetic valve endocarditis rifampicin is added 3 to 5 days after other antibiotics have cleared bloodstream bacteraemia to reduce the risk of rifampicin resistance emerging in a large bacterial load.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and management of adrenal crisis on chronic steroids
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman brought in by her husband with 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and increasing weakness. She has been on prednisolone 15 mg daily for the last 4 years for polymyalgia rheumatica. She stopped her tablets 3 days ago because of the vomiting. She has no diabetes and no known cardiac history.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. She has mild epigastric tenderness. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill 4 seconds.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg after 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C. Bloods show sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), urea 10.4 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L, cortisol pending, TSH within normal limits. ECG sinus tachycardia. She has a chest infection which has been treated with amoxicillin over the last 5 days by her general practitioner.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 78/44 mmHg after 1 L saline; RR 22/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 37.4 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; rousable; mild epigastric tenderness; capillary refill 4 sec; cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L (135-145); K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); urea 10.4 mmol/L; creatinine 128 micromol/L; cortisol pending; TSH within normal limits; ECG sinus tachycardia
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 15 mg daily for 4 years; stopped 3 days ago; recent amoxicillin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 50 mg orally once glucose is corrected and reassess before further steroid and repeat the sodium, potassium and glucose measurements in 1 hour
options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is inappropriate in a vomiting hypotensive patient; parenteral hydrocortisone is required (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Wait for the cortisol result before commencing steroid replacement to avoid interfering with the diagnostic test and reassess the blood pressure and level of consciousness in 1 hour
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis treatment is not delayed for confirmatory testing; a random cortisol is drawn before steroid is given but treatment proceeds immediately (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously and continue aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride and 10 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis in a patient on chronic corticosteroid with intercurrent illness who has stopped their medication is a life threatening emergency; the immediate treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg with continued 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation and correction of hypoglycaemia with 10 percent dextrose (Source: TG Endocrinology; Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline).

options.text: Give fludrocortisone 0.1 mg orally to correct the hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia and repeat the sodium, potassium and glucose measurements in 1 hour
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid used for chronic maintenance in primary adrenal insufficiency; it is not first line in acute adrenal crisis, where high dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity (Source: TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg to avoid interfering with cortisol assay and admit to the ward for handover to the general medical team once she is stable
options.rationale: Dexamethasone does not provide mineralocorticoid activity, which matters when hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia are present; hydrocortisone is preferred and cortisol can be drawn before administration (Source: TG Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis develops in patients on chronic corticosteroids or with primary adrenal insufficiency when an intercurrent illness increases cortisol requirements and endogenous production cannot rise. It presents with hypotension refractory to fluids, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock. The immediate treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride, correction of hypoglycaemia and treatment of the precipitant. Any patient on the equivalent of more than 5 mg of prednisolone daily for more than 3 weeks is at risk and needs a sick day plan with double or triple dosing during acute illness.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously as first line in adrenal crisis.
Prednisolone above 5 mg daily for over 3 weeks needs sick day dosing.
Draw random cortisol before steroid but never delay treatment.
explanation.pearls: Any patient on chronic corticosteroids should double their oral steroid on the first sick day and switch to intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg every 8 hours if vomiting or unable to swallow, delivered from a home sick day pack.

subtopic_detail: Screening test choice for Cushing's syndrome
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 42 year old woman with 18 months of weight gain, new hypertension, and violaceous abdominal striae. She has type 2 diabetes diagnosed 6 months ago that is difficult to control on metformin plus dapagliflozin. She takes no steroids and does not use inhaled corticosteroids. She drinks less than 4 standard drinks per week.

On examination she has central obesity, a dorsocervical fat pad, thin skin with easy bruising and proximal muscle weakness. She has striae up to 2 cm wide on her abdomen. She has 3 hospital admissions with vertebral compression fractures in the last year.

Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 158/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.4 percent (less than 5.7), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), TSH within normal limits. She does not have a shift work pattern or any recent stress that would perturb her circadian rhythm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84/min; BP 158/98 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Central obesity; dorsocervical fat pad; thin skin with easy bruising; proximal muscle weakness; 2 cm violaceous abdominal striae
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L; HbA1c 8.4% (<5.7); K 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); TSH within normal limits
data_table.History: 18 months symptoms; new T2DM 6 months on metformin plus dapagliflozin; 3 vertebral fractures in 1 year; no exogenous steroids; no shift work

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial screening test?

options.text: Random serum cortisol drawn at any time of day, with confirmatory ACTH if elevated
options.rationale: A single random cortisol is not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome; cortisol is pulsatile and stress reactive and a single value has poor sensitivity or specificity (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline).

options.text: Insulin tolerance test with hypoglycaemia challenge to demonstrate cortisol response
options.rationale: The insulin tolerance test is a second line dynamic test used to assess adrenal reserve or pituitary function, not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome; it is contraindicated in patients with ischaemic heart disease or seizures (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline).

options.text: Serum ACTH concentration and inferior petrosal sinus sampling to distinguish source
options.rationale: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is a second line localisation test used to distinguish pituitary from ectopic ACTH after Cushing's syndrome is confirmed biochemically; it is not a screening test (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline).

options.text: 24 hour urinary free cortisol collected on at least two occasions
options.rationale: For adult Cushing's screening the Endocrine Society recommends any one of 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two occasions, late night salivary cortisol on two nights, or the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test as first line; her stable circadian rhythm and lack of shift work make urinary free cortisol reliable and it avoids the false positives of stress activated cortisol from a single measurement (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline; TG Endocrinology).

options.text: Adrenal computed tomography scan with contrast to identify a cortisol producing adenoma
options.rationale: Imaging is a localisation study performed after biochemical confirmation; imaging before biochemistry produces incidentaloma related distraction and is not first line (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline).

explanation.summary: The Endocrine Society Cushing's syndrome guideline recommends one of three screening tests as first line: 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two occasions, late night salivary cortisol on two nights, or the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Choice depends on patient factors: shift work invalidates salivary and 24 hour urinary tests based on a standard rhythm, and adherence issues limit dexamethasone suppression. Serum ACTH, imaging and inferior petrosal sinus sampling are localisation tests performed only after biochemical confirmation. Bilateral vertebral compression fractures, hypokalaemia and difficult to control diabetes in a young adult should trigger a screening test.
key_points: First line screening: 24 hour urinary free cortisol, late night salivary cortisol or 1 mg dexamethasone suppression.
Perform at least two of the same test to reduce false positives.
Imaging is a localisation test, performed after biochemical confirmation.
explanation.pearls: A red flag combination for Cushing's is difficult to control diabetes plus new hypertension plus fragility fracture plus hypokalaemia in an adult under 50; screen with 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two occasions before any imaging.

subtopic_detail: Reversal of dabigatran in life threatening bleeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department. A 78 year old man is brought in by ambulance after a witnessed collapse followed by right sided weakness. He takes dabigatran 150 mg orally twice daily for non valvular atrial fibrillation; last dose was 6 hours ago. He also takes ramipril and atorvastatin. He has no other bleeding history and no known renal impairment.

On examination he has a dense right hemiparesis, aphasia and left sided gaze deviation. NIHSS is 22.

Pulse rate 92/min irregular, blood pressure 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C. Non contrast computed tomography of the brain shows a 45 mL left temporo parietal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with intraventricular extension and 4 mm midline shift. Bloods show haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 234 x10^9/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), INR 1.4, aPTT 42 seconds (25-35), point of care dilute thrombin time is prolonged.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92/min irregular; BP 168/94 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 96% RA; T 36.7 C; NIHSS 22
data_table.Examination: Dense right hemiparesis; aphasia; left gaze deviation
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: 45 mL left temporo parietal intracerebral haemorrhage with intraventricular extension and 4 mm midline shift; Hb 128 g/L; platelets 234 x10^9/L; creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110); INR 1.4; aPTT 42 sec (25-35); dilute thrombin time prolonged
data_table.Medications: Dabigatran 150 mg BD, last dose 6 h ago; ramipril; atorvastatin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?

options.text: Give 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units/kg intravenously as a single infusion and admit to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations
options.rationale: 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate is the reversal for factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban when andexanet is unavailable and is used off label for warfarin bleeding; it is not the first line reversal for dabigatran because a specific antibody exists (Source: TG Haematology).

options.text: Give vitamin K 10 mg intravenously and fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg and admit to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations for the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma reverse warfarin; they do not reverse dabigatran, which is a direct thrombin inhibitor unaffected by clotting factor replacement (Source: TG Haematology).

options.text: Give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously and platelet transfusion and admit to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid may be adjunctive but does not reverse dabigatran; platelets do not restore thrombin activity blocked by a direct thrombin inhibitor (Source: TG Haematology).

options.text: Perform urgent haemodialysis to remove dabigatran without giving pharmacological reversal while admitting to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations
options.rationale: Haemodialysis can remove dabigatran but is used as an adjunct or when idarucizumab is unavailable; when specific reversal is available it is preferred because dialysis is slower and less complete (Source: TG Haematology).

options.text: Give idarucizumab 5 g intravenously as two consecutive 2.5 g boluses and admit to a monitored bed with hourly neurological observations for the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor and idarucizumab is its specific monoclonal antibody reversal agent; it is given as two 2.5 g intravenous doses less than 15 minutes apart, and it fully reverses the anticoagulant effect within minutes in patients with life threatening bleeding (Source: TG Haematology; Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC reversal 2020).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC reversal 2020

explanation.summary: Direct oral anticoagulants require agent specific reversal in life threatening bleeding. Dabigatran is reversed with idarucizumab 5 g intravenously given as two 2.5 g doses less than 15 minutes apart; factor Xa inhibitors are reversed with andexanet alfa where available, or 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units/kg where andexanet is unavailable or unaffordable. Warfarin is reversed with intravenous vitamin K plus 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma, guided by INR. Haemodialysis can remove dabigatran but is slower and less effective than idarucizumab, so it is used only as an adjunct or when idarucizumab is not available.
key_points: Dabigatran reversal: idarucizumab 5 g intravenously in two doses.
Factor Xa inhibitor reversal: andexanet alfa or 4 factor prothrombin complex concentrate.
Warfarin reversal: intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate.
explanation.pearls: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran within minutes and is stocked in Australian emergency departments; two consecutive 2.5 g intravenous doses less than 15 minutes apart give complete reversal for life threatening bleeding.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC reversal 2020

subtopic_detail: SMART-COP triage decision for a patient failing outpatient CAP therapy
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 68 year old man presenting with a 4 day history of productive cough, fevers and progressive shortness of breath. He was started 48 hours ago on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily by his general practitioner for suspected community acquired pneumonia. He has ongoing symptoms and now describes pleuritic right chest pain.

He has a background of well controlled hypertension. He is a lifelong non smoker with no chronic lung disease. He has not travelled overseas in the past year and there are no known unwell contacts.

Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C. He is oriented to time, place and person. Chest x ray shows dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with no pleural effusion. Bloods: white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 168 mg/L (less than 5), sodium 130 mmol/L (135-145), urea 8.2 mmol/L, albumin 34 g/L. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.44, pO2 62 mmHg, pCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 30/min; SpO2 91% RA; T 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Oriented; dense right basal signs; no rash
data_table.Investigations: CXR right lower lobe consolidation no effusion; WCC 16.8; CRP 168; Na 130; urea 8.2; albumin 34; ABG pH 7.44 pO2 62 pCO2 32 HCO3 24
data_table.Treatment so far: 48 h oral amoxicillin 1 g TDS; no improvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management pathway based on the Australian severity score?

options.text: Discharge home on oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline and community follow up in 48 hours for reassessment of the response of his respiratory symptoms to the additional oral therapy today
options.rationale: His SMART-COP score is at least 4 (SBP under 90 scores 2, RR at least 30 scores 1, hypoxia scores 2) so intensive care support risk is significant; discharge home is unsafe (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic; Charles PGP SMART-COP).

options.text: Admit under general medicine for intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline and titrated oxygen; escalate to intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin if there is no improvement
options.rationale: His severity score places him at risk of needing intensive respiratory or vasopressor support and mandates intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin now, not step up later; benzylpenicillin monotherapy misses atypical cover (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic; Charles PGP SMART-COP).

options.text: Admit to a high acuity or intensive care bed with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg and titrated oxygen to a saturation target of 92 to 96 percent
options.rationale: His SMART-COP score is at least 4 (SBP under 90 scores 2, RR at least 30 scores 1, hypoxia at his age scores 2) predicting need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support; TG antibiotics are ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic; Charles PGP SMART-COP).

options.text: Admit to the ward for intravenous meropenem plus oral azithromycin and titrated oxygen; escalate to a high acuity bed if there is no improvement within the first 24 hours after commencement
options.rationale: Meropenem is not first line for community acquired pneumonia even severe; ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the TG regimen for severe CAP requiring intensive support (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit under general medicine for oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily as respiratory quinolone monotherapy and titrated oxygen with review by the medical registrar within 2 hours of the transfer
options.rationale: Moxifloxacin monotherapy is not first line CAP therapy in AU; TG first line for severe CAP is intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and quinolones are reserved for penicillin allergy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: SMART-COP is an Australian severity score for community acquired pneumonia predicting need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support. Points are scored for systolic blood pressure under 90 (2), multilobar involvement (1), albumin under 35 (1), respiratory rate 30 or above at any age (1), tachycardia 125 or above (1), confusion (1), oxygen (2 if age adjusted hypoxia), and pH under 7.35 (2). A score of 3 or more predicts intensive support risk and mandates admission with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin per Therapeutic Guidelines.
key_points: SMART-COP score 3 or more equals high risk severe CAP.
TG first line severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin.
Titrate oxygen to 92 to 96 percent in non hypercapnic patient.
explanation.pearls: SBP under 90 scores 2 points in SMART-COP even if isolated; a hypotensive patient with tachypnoea already has 3 points and should not be sent home from an emergency department review.

subtopic_detail: Rate versus rhythm control in AF of unknown duration
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 72 year old man with new palpitations and mild breathlessness on arrival. He is a lifelong non smoker with hypertension well controlled on perindopril 5 mg daily and type 2 diabetes on metformin 500 mg twice daily. He has no chest pain, no syncope, and no signs of decompensated heart failure.

He is unsure how long his symptoms have been present because he only noticed them last night when trying to sleep. He denies previous documented AF episodes; his last general practitioner review 6 months ago documented a regular pulse and sinus rhythm on ECG.

Pulse rate 138/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 138 bpm and no ischaemic changes. Bloods: haemoglobin 138 g/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, magnesium 0.82 mmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), high sensitivity troponin 8 ng/L (less than 14). Bedside echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular function and mild left atrial enlargement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138/min irregular; BP 132/78 mmHg; RR 20/min; SpO2 97% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable at rest; no chest pain; JVP not raised; no crepitations
data_table.Investigations: ECG AF ventricular rate 138 bpm no ischaemic changes; K 4.2; Mg 0.82; TSH 1.8; hs troponin 8; TTE preserved LV function; mild LA enlargement
data_table.History: Palpitations noticed overnight; last documented sinus rhythm 6 months ago; hypertension on perindopril; T2DM on metformin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous heparin infusion, arrange direct current cardioversion within 4 hours of presentation, and start apixaban 5 mg twice daily immediately after the successful cardioversion procedure
options.rationale: AF of unknown duration (potentially over 48 hours) requires either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or a transoesophageal echocardiogram to exclude atrial thrombus before elective cardioversion; immediate DCCV would risk stroke (Source: CSANZ atrial fibrillation guideline).

options.text: Commence intravenous amiodarone loading dose 300 mg over 60 minutes for pharmacological cardioversion and start apixaban 5 mg twice daily immediately after conversion to sinus rhythm today
options.rationale: Pharmacological cardioversion in AF of unknown duration also carries stroke risk without prior anticoagulation or TOE; amiodarone toxicity profile makes it a rarely used first line option in stable AF (Source: CSANZ atrial fibrillation guideline).

options.text: Commence oral aspirin 100 mg daily and rate control with oral metoprolol 25 mg twice daily titrated to a target ventricular rate under 110 bpm and arrange outpatient cardiology follow up
options.rationale: Aspirin is no longer recommended for stroke prevention in AF; a DOAC is required for CHA2DS2 VA at least 2, and his score is at least 3 (Source: CSANZ atrial fibrillation guideline).

options.text: Commence oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily and rate control with oral metoprolol 25 mg twice daily titrated to a target ventricular rate under 110 bpm and arrange outpatient cardiology follow up
options.rationale: CHA2DS2 VA at least 3 (age 65 to 74 plus 1, hypertension plus 1, diabetes plus 1) mandates DOAC; AF of unknown duration is rate controlled first with metoprolol to under 110 bpm and elective rhythm decision made outpatient (Source: CSANZ AF guideline).

options.text: Commence oral warfarin loading with heparin bridging, arrange transoesophageal echocardiogram tomorrow, and cardiovert if no atrial thrombus is seen; long term rate control with atenolol
options.rationale: DOAC is preferred over warfarin bridging in non valvular AF; TOE guided cardioversion is an option but requires initial rate control and shared decision making, not necessarily tomorrow (Source: CSANZ atrial fibrillation guideline).

explanation.summary: AF of unknown duration in a stable patient is managed by initial rate control (metoprolol titrated to under 110 bpm) plus DOAC anticoagulation if CHA2DS2 VA at least 2 (any woman scores 1, men score 1 for hypertension, diabetes, age 65 to 74, congestive heart failure, prior stroke or vascular disease). Elective rhythm control decision is deferred to outpatient cardiology after 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or TOE guided cardioversion. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF. Warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves and mitral stenosis; DOAC is first line in non valvular AF.
key_points: CHA2DS2 VA at least 2 equals DOAC.
Rate control target under 110 bpm.
Immediate cardioversion needs TOE or 3 weeks anticoagulation if AF over 48 hours.
explanation.pearls: CHA2DS2 VA replaced CHA2DS2 VASc in Australia in 2022 by removing the female sex point; recalculate historical scores because some patients previously on aspirin will now need DOAC or vice versa.

subtopic_detail: Immediate management of suspected adrenal crisis in a patient on chronic prednisolone
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 58 year old woman who presented with 24 hours of vomiting, diarrhoea and increasing lethargy after a family gastroenteritis outbreak. She has a background of polymyalgia rheumatica for 18 months on prednisolone 7.5 mg orally daily, which she has been unable to keep down since yesterday morning. She has no other chronic medications and no known drug allergies.

On examination she looks unwell, has cool peripheries with mottled skin, and dry mucous membranes. She has no abdominal tenderness on palpation. She has no focal chest signs and no rash.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C. Bloods: sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L (baseline 72), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.9-11.1), venous blood gas pH 7.29 with lactate 3.8 mmol/L and HCO3 16 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 82/48 mmHg; RR 22/min; SpO2 97% RA; T 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Unwell; cool peripheries; mottled; dry mucous membranes; no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Na 128; K 5.4; urea 12.4; creatinine 148 (baseline 72); glucose 3.2; VBG pH 7.29 lactate 3.8 HCO3 16
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 7.5 mg daily 18 months for PMR; missed 24 hours of doses due to vomiting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Await a serum cortisol result before giving any parenteral corticosteroid to avoid confounding a subsequent short synacthen test that will inform her long term steroid replacement plan
options.rationale: Do NOT delay hydrocortisone in adrenal crisis; take a cortisol sample first if possible and give hydrocortisone immediately (Source: ESA adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal insufficiency

options.text: Give oral prednisolone 15 mg as a double dose, commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 1 hour, and give intravenous 10 percent dextrose 100 mL for the hypoglycaemia she has today
options.rationale: Oral steroid is not absorbed reliably in a vomiting shocked patient; parenteral hydrocortisone is required for adrenal crisis (Source: ESA adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal insufficiency

options.text: Give intramuscular dexamethasone 4 mg as a stat dose, commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 1 hour, and give intravenous 10 percent dextrose 100 mL for the hypoglycaemia today
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has minimal mineralocorticoid activity, has slow onset compared to hydrocortisone, and is a second choice reserved for when hydrocortisone is unavailable or a short cort test is planned (Source: ESA adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal insufficiency

options.text: Give intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microg as a stat dose, commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 1 hour, and give intravenous 10 percent dextrose 100 mL for the hypoglycaemia today
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is oral only and not needed acutely; hydrocortisone 100 mg IV provides adequate mineralocorticoid activity at that dose (Source: ESA adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal insufficiency

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as a stat dose, commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 1 hour, and give intravenous 10 percent dextrose 100 mL for the hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg per 24 hours infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours; fluid resuscitation with saline addresses hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia; dextrose corrects hypoglycaemia (Source: ESA adrenal insufficiency; Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal insufficiency

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency in patients on chronic corticosteroids who develop intercurrent illness that prevents oral absorption. Presentation is hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis in a patient on chronic prednisolone or hydrocortisone. Treatment is immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (or IM), then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours, plus rapid fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline and correction of hypoglycaemia. Do not delay for a cortisol result; take the sample and give hydrocortisone.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately; do not wait for cortisol.
Fluid resuscitate with 0.9 percent saline.
Correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose.
explanation.pearls: Any patient on the equivalent of over 5 mg of prednisolone daily for more than 3 weeks is at risk of adrenal suppression; issue sick day rules and a hydrocortisone emergency kit for parenteral use at home during vomiting illness.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Escalating stable COPD therapy after a recent exacerbation per COPD X
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in outpatient clinic reviewing a 68 year old man with confirmed moderate COPD (post bronchodilator FEV1 55 percent predicted; FEV1/FVC 0.62). He is an ex smoker of 12 months with a 40 pack year history. He has been on tiotropium 18 microg inhaled daily as a long acting muscarinic antagonist monotherapy for the last 18 months.

He was admitted 4 weeks ago with an infective exacerbation requiring oral prednisolone and doxycycline and was discharged home after 5 nights. He has had 2 further exacerbations managed by his general practitioner in the previous 12 months. His mMRC dyspnoea score is 2 (short of breath walking up an incline).

He is well between exacerbations and his examination today is unremarkable with SpO2 96% in room air, chest clear, and no peripheral oedema. Blood eosinophil count today is 220 cells per microL. Chest x ray shows hyperinflation with no consolidation. Inhaler technique has been reviewed and is correct with an aerochamber spacer for MDI use.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO2 96% RA; comfortable at rest
data_table.Examination: Chest clear; no oedema; correct inhaler technique
data_table.Investigations: Post bronchodilator FEV1 55 percent predicted; FEV1/FVC 0.62; blood eosinophils 220 cells per microL; CXR hyperinflated no consolidation
data_table.History: Ex smoker 12 months; 40 pack year; on tiotropium 18 microg daily for 18 months; 3 exacerbations in 12 months (1 hospitalised)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate step up in therapy today?

options.text: Substitute his tiotropium for a fixed dose combination of long acting beta 2 agonist plus long acting muscarinic antagonist and reassess exacerbation frequency in 3 months from today
options.rationale: Frequent exacerbations on LAMA monotherapy warrant escalation to LABA plus LAMA; ICS is added only if eosinophils are 300 or more or there are further exacerbations despite LABA plus LAMA (Source: COPD X guideline).

options.text: Add an inhaled corticosteroid to his current tiotropium as a fixed dose combination of inhaled corticosteroid plus long acting muscarinic antagonist inhaler for maintenance today
options.rationale: COPD X advises against ICS plus LAMA alone; if adding ICS the standard is triple therapy (ICS plus LABA plus LAMA), and LABA addition is required first at this stage (Source: COPD X guideline).

options.text: Add azithromycin 250 mg orally three times weekly as a maintenance immunomodulator to reduce future exacerbation frequency and continue current tiotropium monotherapy for maintenance
options.rationale: Azithromycin prophylaxis is reserved for patients on optimal inhaled therapy (triple therapy) with ongoing exacerbations; QT and hearing monitoring required (Source: COPD X guideline).

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 10 mg daily as maintenance therapy to prevent further exacerbations and continue current tiotropium monotherapy for background management of his airflow limitation
options.rationale: Long term oral corticosteroid is NOT recommended for stable COPD maintenance because of adverse effect burden without clear reduction in mortality or exacerbations (Source: COPD X guideline).

options.text: Commence oral roflumilast 500 microg daily as an anti inflammatory therapy for chronic bronchitis with recurrent exacerbation profile and continue current tiotropium monotherapy for maintenance
options.rationale: Roflumilast is a niche add on for severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and repeated exacerbations despite triple therapy; it is not the first escalation from LAMA monotherapy (Source: COPD X guideline).

explanation.summary: COPD X escalation follows an eosinophil aware ladder. After long acting muscarinic antagonist monotherapy, patients with frequent exacerbations or persistent breathlessness are escalated to LAMA plus LABA. Triple therapy (LAMA plus LABA plus ICS) is added if there are further exacerbations or if the blood eosinophil count is 300 cells per microL or more. Azithromycin prophylaxis and roflumilast are reserved for patients on optimal inhaled therapy with ongoing exacerbations. Long term oral corticosteroid is not recommended.
key_points: LAMA plus LABA is standard escalation after LAMA monotherapy.
Triple therapy with ICS if eosinophils 300 or more, or ongoing exacerbations.
Long term oral prednisolone is not recommended for maintenance.
explanation.pearls: Review inhaler technique before escalation because up to 70 percent of patients use their device incorrectly; a well fitted spacer with an MDI often outperforms a poorly used dry powder device without the need for a therapy step up.

subtopic_detail: Bisphosphonate selection after low trauma vertebral fracture on background CKD
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in outpatient clinic reviewing a 74 year old woman referred by her general practitioner after her second low trauma vertebral compression fracture in 12 months. Her first fracture 12 months ago was managed conservatively with analgesia. She has not been on bone therapy previously.

She has a background of chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 32 mL/min per 1.73 square metre, well controlled hypertension on perindopril 5 mg daily, and osteoarthritis. She is otherwise independent, uses a stick outdoors, and lives with her husband. She has never had breast cancer, has no history of oesophageal disease, and has intact dentition with regular dental care.

Bone mineral density T score at the lumbar spine is minus 2.9 and at the femoral neck is minus 2.7. Serum calcium is 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D is 68 nmol/L (over 50), phosphate 1.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.82 mmol/L, parathyroid hormone 5.8 pmol/L, corrected for calcium and eGFR reference. Alkaline phosphatase 128 U/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg; comfortable at rest
data_table.Examination: Kyphotic; no long bone tenderness; intact dentition
data_table.Investigations: BMD LS T minus 2.9; FN T minus 2.7; Ca 2.34; 25 OH vit D 68; phosphate 1.0; Mg 0.82; PTH 5.8; ALP 128; TSH 2.1; eGFR 32
data_table.History: Two low trauma vertebral fractures in 12 months; CKD stage 3b; no oesophageal disease; regular dental care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate bone active therapy today?

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and follow up in 3 months to review symptoms and repeat bone mineral density in 2 years
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates are contraindicated at eGFR below 35 mL/min per 1.73 square metre; alendronate is not safe at her renal function (Source: Osteoporosis Australia; AMH).

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and follow up in 3 months to review symptoms and repeat bone mineral density measurement in 2 years
options.rationale: Denosumab is not renally excreted and is preferred over bisphosphonates when eGFR is below 35 mL/min per 1.73 square metre; monitor calcium as hypocalcaemia risk rises in CKD (Source: Healthy Bones Australia guideline; AMH).

options.text: Intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg annually with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and follow up in 3 months to review symptoms and repeat bone mineral density measurement in 2 years
options.rationale: Zoledronic acid is also contraindicated at eGFR below 35 mL/min per 1.73 square metre; denosumab is the preferred bone active therapy in this CKD range (Source: Healthy Bones Australia guideline; AMH).

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 microg daily for 18 months with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and follow up in 3 months to review symptoms and repeat bone mineral density in 2 years
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis with ongoing fractures despite antiresorptive therapy and is a subsidised second line option after failed first line therapy (Source: Healthy Bones Australia guideline).

options.text: Oral raloxifene 60 mg daily with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and follow up in 3 months to review symptoms and repeat bone mineral density measurement in 2 years time
options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not non vertebral fractures and carries a venous thromboembolism risk; denosumab has broader fracture reduction and is safer in CKD (Source: Healthy Bones Australia guideline).
