explanation.summary: Bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid) are contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 to 35 mL/min per 1.73 square metre due to accumulation and adverse effects. Denosumab is not renally excreted and is the preferred antiresorptive therapy in patients with CKD stage 3b or 4. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation is added because hypocalcaemia risk rises with denosumab in CKD. Teriparatide (anabolic) is reserved for severe osteoporosis with ongoing fractures despite antiresorptive therapy. Never miss or delay a denosumab dose by more than 4 weeks due to rebound vertebral fracture risk.
key_points: Bisphosphonates avoided at eGFR under 35.
Denosumab is preferred antiresorptive in CKD stage 3b or 4.
Do not miss denosumab doses due to rebound fracture risk.
explanation.pearls: Check corrected calcium and vitamin D BEFORE each denosumab dose and correct hypocalcaemia first; a delayed or missed denosumab dose can cause a rebound of vertebral fractures within 6 to 12 months of interruption.

subtopic_detail: Refractory adult anaphylaxis on beta blocker requiring adjunct pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 62 year old man brought in by ambulance with anaphylaxis after a wasp sting in his garden. He has known bee venom allergy on an ASCIA action plan and has been on regular atenolol 50 mg daily for hypertension for the last 10 years. Paramedics gave him intramuscular adrenaline 500 microg on arrival and again 5 minutes later before transport to hospital.

On arrival to the resuscitation bay he has ongoing hypotension with a persistent expiratory wheeze and generalised urticaria despite two prehospital adrenaline doses. He has no chest pain. Two large bore intravenous cannulae have been established. A 1 L bolus of 0.9 percent saline has been given.

Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 76/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 91% on 15 L via non rebreather mask, temperature 36.5 degrees C. Point of care venous blood gas: pH 7.32, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, base excess minus 4. Bedside echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular function.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82/min; BP 76/48 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 91% on 15 L NRB; T 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; expiratory wheeze; audible stridor absent; peripheries cool
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.32; lactate 4.2; base excess minus 4; TTE preserved LV function
data_table.Treatment so far: Prehospital IM adrenaline 500 microg x 2; 1 L IV 0.9 percent saline bolus
data_table.History: On atenolol 50 mg daily 10 years; bee venom allergy on ASCIA plan

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next specific pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline infusion at 0.05 microg/kg/min via a central line and continue supplemental oxygen with ongoing fluid resuscitation while awaiting arrival of the intensive care team
options.rationale: Noradrenaline is a reasonable second line vasopressor but adrenaline is the first line pressor of choice in anaphylaxis because of the beta 2 bronchodilator effect; glucagon is added for beta blocked patients (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis).

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg and intravenous promethazine 25 mg with ongoing fluid resuscitation and supplemental oxygen therapy while awaiting arrival of the intensive care team for admission
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone and antihistamines have no immediate haemodynamic effect and are not first line for refractory anaphylaxis; adrenaline infusion plus glucagon (in beta blocker exposure) is the primary intervention (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis).

options.text: Intravenous glucagon 1 to 2 mg over 5 minutes and commence adrenaline infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 microg/kg/min while continuing fluid resuscitation and administering supplemental oxygen therapy
options.rationale: Beta blockade reduces adrenaline responsiveness; intravenous glucagon 1 to 2 mg over 5 minutes provides direct chronotropic and inotropic effect independent of beta receptors, and adrenaline infusion is added for ongoing hypotension (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis; AMH).

options.text: Intravenous vasopressin 4 units bolus followed by 0.02 unit per minute infusion via central access and continue supplemental oxygen with ongoing fluid resuscitation while awaiting arrival of the ICU team
options.rationale: Vasopressin is a third line option in refractory shock; adrenaline infusion plus glucagon (in beta blocked patients) is the standard first line (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis).

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g and intravenous ranitidine 50 mg with ongoing fluid resuscitation and supplemental oxygen therapy while awaiting arrival of the intensive care team for admission
options.rationale: High dose methylprednisolone and H2 blocker have no immediate haemodynamic effect and do not address beta blocker refractoriness; adrenaline infusion plus glucagon is required now (Source: ASCIA anaphylaxis).

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis after adequate intramuscular adrenaline should be escalated to an intravenous adrenaline infusion starting at 0.05 to 0.1 microg/kg/min titrated to blood pressure. In patients on chronic beta blocker therapy, adrenaline responsiveness is reduced and intravenous glucagon 1 to 2 mg over 5 minutes provides positive chronotropic and inotropic effect independent of beta receptors. Corticosteroids and antihistamines are adjuncts that address late phase reactions but should not delay adrenaline escalation. Volume resuscitation with crystalloid runs in parallel because vasodilatation is major.
key_points: Refractory anaphylaxis needs adrenaline infusion 0.05 to 0.1 microg/kg/min.
Beta blocker exposure equals add glucagon 1 to 2 mg IV.
Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts, not first line for shock.
explanation.pearls: When paramedics have already given two doses of intramuscular adrenaline without effect, look for beta blocker exposure or occult haemorrhage such as ruptured aortic aneurysm mimicking anaphylaxis; both change the management pathway completely.

subtopic_detail: Priority intervention in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 68 year old man on the acute medical ward who was admitted 48 hours ago with community acquired pneumonia. He has a background of chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline eGFR 22 mL/min per 1.73 square metre), type 2 diabetes and hypertension. His usual medications include ramipril 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily, which were continued on admission.

Overnight urine output has been 30 mL over 8 hours. He is oliguric today. Nurses report he seems more lethargic and are worried about a routine morning blood test.

Pulse rate 42/min regular, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, temperature 37.2 degrees C. Bloods this morning: sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 320 micromol/L (baseline 240), bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, magnesium 0.86 mmol/L. Bedside ECG shows tall peaked T waves in V2 to V5, PR interval 240 ms, and QRS complex 130 ms with sine wave morphology emerging.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 42/min regular; BP 108/72 mmHg; RR 20/min; SpO2 96 percent on 2 L; T 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic; euvolaemic; peripheries warm; oliguric 30 mL in 8 h
data_table.Investigations: Na 138; K 7.4; urea 22; creatinine 320 (baseline 240); HCO3 16; Mg 0.86
data_table.ECG: Tall peaked T waves V2 to V5; PR 240 ms; QRS 130 ms with sine wave morphology emerging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg via a mask over 10 minutes to shift potassium intracellularly and prevent further ECG deterioration during the workup of his underlying acute kidney injury
options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly but does not stabilise the myocardium; ECG changes with sine wave morphology require immediate cardiac membrane stabilisation with calcium (Source: KDIGO acute kidney injury; Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular).

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 100 mL bolus over 15 minutes to shift potassium intracellularly via correction of metabolic acidosis and to reduce ionised calcium levels acutely today
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is second line in acidotic hyperkalaemia and does not stabilise the myocardium; calcium gluconate first then insulin dextrose is standard (Source: KDIGO acute kidney injury).

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 80 mg for diuretic potassium loss; commence sodium polystyrene sulfonate 15 g orally every 6 hours to remove potassium from the body over the following 24 hours after admission
options.rationale: Furosemide requires urine output which is very limited given his oliguria; sodium polystyrene sulfonate has slow onset and does not address the immediate cardiac risk from ECG changes (Source: KDIGO acute kidney injury).

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 minutes for myocardial membrane stabilisation, then intravenous insulin actrapid 10 units with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose to shift potassium
options.rationale: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes requires immediate calcium gluconate for myocardial membrane stabilisation, then insulin dextrose to shift potassium; salbutamol is added as adjunct and dialysis considered if refractory or on renal replacement (Source: KDIGO; TG Cardiovascular).

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis today via an urgent tunnelled dialysis line and observe with cardiac monitoring while awaiting availability of the renal team and dialysis facility for the treatment
options.rationale: Dialysis is definitive but takes time to organise; ECG changes require immediate myocardial protection with calcium gluconate now while dialysis is arranged (Source: KDIGO acute kidney injury).

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves, PR prolongation, QRS widening, sine wave) is a medical emergency. The priority sequence is myocardial membrane stabilisation with intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 minutes (calcium chloride via central access), then intracellular potassium shift with insulin actrapid 10 units plus 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose, plus nebulised salbutamol 10 mg. Potassium removal is achieved by loop diuretic if urine output allows, potassium binder (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate), or dialysis. Stop the causative drugs (RAS inhibitor, spironolactone, NSAID).
key_points: ECG changes equal give IV calcium gluconate immediately.
Insulin dextrose shifts K intracellularly.
Dialysis for refractory or established renal failure.
explanation.pearls: Repeat ECG within 5 minutes of calcium gluconate to confirm resolution of the QRS widening; if changes recur repeat calcium gluconate and expedite dialysis, and always stop the ACE inhibitor and potassium sparing diuretic causing the hyperkalaemia.

subtopic_detail: First line vasopressor after fluid resuscitation in septic shock
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar leading resuscitation of a 62 year old man with community acquired pneumonia and severe sepsis. He has received 30 mL/kg of intravenous crystalloid over the last hour after his initial lactate was 4.8 mmol/L. He has received the first dose of intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g plus azithromycin 500 mg per Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic. Blood cultures were drawn before antibiotic administration.

After fluid resuscitation his mean arterial pressure remains 58 mmHg despite the initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid. He continues to have cool peripheries and oliguria. He has no known cardiac disease and no history of adrenal insufficiency.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, mean arterial pressure 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 94 percent on 8 L via Hudson mask, temperature 39.2 degrees C. Repeat venous blood gas: pH 7.28, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, base excess minus 5. Bedside echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular function with a small underfilled left ventricle and a compliant right ventricle. A central venous catheter has just been inserted in the right internal jugular vein.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 82/48 mmHg; MAP 58 mmHg; RR 28/min; SpO2 94 percent on 8 L; T 39.2 C
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries; oliguric; delayed capillary refill; awake but drowsy
data_table.Investigations: Repeat VBG pH 7.28 lactate 4.6 base excess minus 5; TTE preserved LV underfilled; small LV; compliant RV
data_table.Treatment so far: 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid over 1 h; IV ceftriaxone 2 g plus azithromycin 500 mg; blood cultures pre antibiotic
data_table.Access: Central venous catheter right internal jugular vein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous vasopressin 0.03 units per minute infusion via the central line titrated to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg with hourly urine output monitoring and lactate reassessment
options.rationale: Vasopressin is used as an adjunct or catecholamine sparing agent added to noradrenaline rather than as first line vasopressor in septic shock (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; VASST trial).

options.text: Commence intravenous dopamine infusion at 10 microg/kg/min via the central line titrated to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg with hourly urine output monitoring and lactate reassessment in 2 hours
options.rationale: Dopamine is associated with more arrhythmias and is not first line in septic shock; noradrenaline is preferred with better outcomes (SOAP II trial) (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign).

options.text: Commence intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microg/kg/min via the central line titrated to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg with hourly urine output monitoring and lactate reassessment in 2 hours
options.rationale: Adrenaline is reserved for septic shock refractory to noradrenaline or when there is myocardial depression; it is second line rather than first line (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign).

options.text: Give a further 30 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid bolus over the next hour and reassess mean arterial pressure and lactate; commence vasopressor only if the mean arterial pressure remains under 65 mmHg
options.rationale: Further fluid without haemodynamic reassessment risks fluid overload; his bedside echocardiogram shows adequate filling and the next step is vasopressor rather than more crystalloid (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; FEAST trial cautions).

options.text: Commence intravenous noradrenaline infusion via the central line titrated to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg with hourly urine output monitoring and lactate reassessment in 2 hours
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis and ANZICS advise noradrenaline as first line vasopressor in septic shock once fluid resuscitation has been given (30 mL/kg) and MAP remains under 65 mmHg; titrate to MAP of at least 65 mmHg (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; ANZICS sepsis).
source_refs: ANZICS Statement on care of the critically ill

explanation.summary: Septic shock management follows the Surviving Sepsis hour 1 bundle: measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad spectrum antibiotics within the first hour, resuscitate with 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 or above, and commence noradrenaline as first line vasopressor to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg. Vasopressin 0.03 units per minute is added as a catecholamine sparing adjunct. Adrenaline is reserved for refractory shock or myocardial depression. Ongoing assessment includes lactate, urine output, capillary refill and dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness.
key_points: First vasopressor in septic shock is noradrenaline.
MAP target is at least 65 mmHg.
Add vasopressin as adjunct; adrenaline for refractory shock.
explanation.pearls: Reassess fluid responsiveness with a passive leg raise or a small fluid bolus before giving further crystalloid after 30 mL/kg; static central venous pressure alone is a poor guide to fluid responsiveness in critically ill patients.

sources.label: ANZICS Statement on care of the critically ill

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds at new HIV diagnosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 41 year old man in the ambulatory clinic two weeks after a new diagnosis of human immunodeficiency virus infection made on serology and confirmed by a second assay. He feels well, has gained no weight recently and has no cough, fever or oral lesions.

He has never taken antiretroviral therapy. He has no allergies, in particular no sulfonamide allergy, and his liver function is within normal limits. His chest radiograph is clear and his cryptococcal antigen is negative. His baseline results are now available and he is keen to begin treatment today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 124/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 140 cells/microlitre (500-1500); HIV viral load 82000 copies/mL; cryptococcal antigen negative; chest radiograph clear
data_table.Blood tests: Full blood count, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to commence today?

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy alone, with prophylaxis added only if the CD4 count falls further
options.rationale: The CD4 count is already below the 200 cells per microlitre threshold at which Pneumocystis prophylaxis is indicated, so waiting for a further fall leaves the highest risk period uncovered (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy plus azithromycin weekly for disseminated mycobacterial prophylaxis
options.rationale: Azithromycin prophylaxis against Mycobacterium avium complex applies below 50 cells per microlitre, and this near pair threshold is the point of the distinction (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy plus daily co-trimoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis
options.rationale: Antiretroviral therapy is started at diagnosis regardless of CD4 count, and a CD4 below 200 cells per microlitre triggers co-trimoxazole prophylaxis until immune reconstitution is sustained (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Deferred antiretroviral therapy until the CD4 count recovers above 350 cells per microlitre
options.rationale: Deferring treatment reflects superseded practice; immediate therapy at diagnosis improves survival and reduces transmission irrespective of CD4 count (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines).

options.text: Antiretroviral therapy plus fluconazole daily for prevention of cryptococcal meningitis
options.rationale: Primary antifungal prophylaxis is not routine in Australia and the cryptococcal antigen screen is negative, so this adds toxicity and interactions without benefit (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Antiretroviral therapy is now started at diagnosis in every person with human immunodeficiency virus infection regardless of CD4 count, which was a substantial change from earlier deferred strategies. Opportunistic infection prophylaxis is layered on top according to CD4 thresholds, and the two decisions are made independently at the same visit. The main thresholds worth memorising are 200 cells per microlitre for Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis prophylaxis and 50 cells per microlitre for Mycobacterium avium complex. Prophylaxis is stopped once the CD4 count has been sustained above threshold on suppressive therapy, typically for at least three to six months.
key_points: Start antiretroviral therapy at diagnosis irrespective of CD4 count
CD4 below 200 cells per microlitre triggers co-trimoxazole prophylaxis
CD4 below 50 cells per microlitre triggers azithromycin for Mycobacterium avium complex
Cease prophylaxis once the CD4 count is sustained above threshold on suppressive therapy
explanation.pearls: Screen for cryptococcal antigen when the CD4 count is below 100 cells per microlitre before starting antiretroviral therapy; unmasking an occult cryptococcal infection as immune reconstitution syndrome carries a far higher mortality than treating it first.

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment selection after a positive interferon gamma release assay
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the refugee health clinic. A 26 year old man who arrived from Nepal 11 months ago has been referred after a positive interferon gamma release assay performed during a pre employment health check for aged care work.

He is entirely asymptomatic with no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. Two sputum samples collected for completeness were negative on smear and on culture at six weeks. His chest radiograph reported today shows clear lung fields with no apical scarring, cavitation or hilar lymphadenopathy. He takes no medication, drinks no alcohol, and has normal liver function with a negative human immunodeficiency virus serology. He asks how long treatment will take because he is due to start work.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive; chest radiograph clear; sputum smear and culture negative; HIV serology negative
data_table.Blood tests: Liver function and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months then continuation phase
options.rationale: Four drug therapy treats active disease, which has been excluded by symptoms, a clear chest radiograph and negative cultures, and it exposes him to unnecessary hepatotoxicity (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Guidelines).

options.text: No treatment at present, with a repeat interferon gamma release assay in twelve months
options.rationale: The assay does not distinguish latent from past infection and does not revert usefully, so repeating it adds nothing while leaving a treatable reactivation risk in an aged care worker (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Guidelines).

options.text: Bacille Calmette Guerin vaccination now with annual symptom review by the general practitioner
options.rationale: Vaccination has no role after infection has already occurred and does not reduce reactivation risk from established latent infection (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Rifampicin daily for four months with baseline and interval liver function monitoring
options.rationale: Four months of daily rifampicin is a recommended Australian latent tuberculosis regimen with completion rates and hepatotoxicity superior to nine months of isoniazid, which suits a young man with normal liver function starting work (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Pyrazinamide with rifampicin for two months and fortnightly liver function monitoring throughout
options.rationale: The two month rifampicin and pyrazinamide combination was abandoned because of severe hepatotoxicity and fatalities and is no longer recommended for latent infection (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection is diagnosed when an immunological test is positive and active disease has been excluded clinically, radiologically and where indicated microbiologically. Excluding active disease first is not a formality, because treating active tuberculosis with a single drug generates resistance. Australian regimen options are isoniazid for six to nine months, rifampicin for four months, or weekly rifapentine and isoniazid for three months, with the shorter rifamycin based regimens preferred for completion and hepatic safety. Rifampicin induces cytochrome P450 enzymes, so a medication review for interactions with oral contraceptives, anticoagulants and antiretrovirals is part of prescribing.
key_points: Exclude active disease before treating latent infection to avoid generating resistance
Four months of daily rifampicin is preferred over nine months of isoniazid for completion and hepatic safety
Interferon gamma release assays do not distinguish latent from treated past infection
Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer and needs a full interaction check
explanation.pearls: Warn any patient starting rifampicin that it turns urine, tears and sweat orange and permanently stains soft contact lenses; unexplained discolouration is the commonest reason for self cessation in the first fortnight.

subtopic_detail: Antiviral indication and agent choice in influenza with chronic airways disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old woman during an influenza season. She describes 36 hours of fever, myalgia and a dry cough that began abruptly. A point of care nucleic acid test taken this morning is positive for influenza A.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with a forced expiratory volume in one second of 52 per cent predicted and uses a long acting muscarinic antagonist and a long acting beta agonist daily. She has had two exacerbations in the last 12 months. She is not hypoxic, her chest is clear of focal crackles and her sputum has not changed colour or volume. Her creatinine and eGFR are within normal limits and she received the seasonal vaccine four weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 132/78, RR 20, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A nucleic acid test positive; chest auscultation clear with no focal crackles
data_table.Blood tests: Creatinine and eGFR within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Symptomatic treatment only, since antivirals are of benefit only within 24 hours of onset
options.rationale: The evidence based window for starting a neuraminidase inhibitor is 48 hours from symptom onset, and this presentation at 36 hours falls comfortably inside it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral oseltamivir twice daily for five days alongside her usual inhaled maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is recommended for confirmed influenza in patients at high risk of complications, which includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and age over 65, when started within 48 hours of onset (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Influenza Guidelines).

options.text: Inhaled zanamivir twice daily for five days as the preferred agent in chronic airways disease
options.rationale: Inhaled zanamivir is the near pair but is specifically cautioned in asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because it can precipitate bronchospasm (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for five days to cover secondary bacterial infection risk
options.rationale: There is no change in sputum volume or purulence and no focal findings, so empirical antibacterial therapy is not indicated at this point (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for five days as treatment for an infective exacerbation
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are for an exacerbation defined by increased breathlessness, sputum volume or purulence, none of which is present, and they may prolong viral shedding (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Antiviral therapy for influenza is targeted rather than universal, and the decision rests on the presence of risk factors for complications rather than on symptom severity alone. Australian risk groups include people aged 65 and over, pregnant women, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and those with chronic cardiac, respiratory, renal, neurological or metabolic disease or immunosuppression. Benefit is greatest when treatment starts within 48 hours of symptom onset, though therapy is still offered beyond that window to hospitalised or deteriorating patients. Vaccination reduces but does not eliminate risk, so a recent vaccine does not change the treatment decision once infection is confirmed.
key_points: Treat confirmed influenza in high risk groups within 48 hours of symptom onset
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and age over 65 are both independent risk criteria
Zanamivir is avoided in obstructive airways disease because of bronchospasm risk
Recent vaccination does not remove the indication for antiviral therapy
explanation.pearls: Oseltamivir needs renal dose adjustment once creatinine clearance falls below 60 mL/min, and this is the commonest prescribing error in the older patients who most need the drug.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice in acute pyelonephritis requiring admission
stem:
You are the emergency registrar admitting a 34 year old woman with 24 hours of fever, rigors and right loin pain. She has vomited three times this morning and cannot keep down oral fluids.

She is not pregnant on a beta human chorionic gonadotrophin test, and has had no urinary catheter, hospitalisation or antibiotic exposure in the last six months. She has no known drug allergies and takes no regular medication. She has right renal angle tenderness on examination. Her urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes and a specimen has gone for culture. Her creatinine and potassium are within normal limits and a bedside ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 104/64, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick nitrites and leucocytes positive; urine culture pending; bedside ultrasound no hydronephrosis
data_table.Blood tests: White cell count 16.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine and potassium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for fourteen days with early general practitioner review
options.rationale: She is vomiting and cannot absorb oral therapy, and trimethoprim resistance rates in Australian urinary isolates are too high for empirical use in systemic infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for seven days with oral rehydration in the department
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin is the classic near pair error here because it concentrates in urine but does not achieve therapeutic renal parenchymal or serum levels, so it never treats pyelonephritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for seven days once the vomiting has been controlled
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved in Australia for resistant isolates or specific allergy situations because of resistance stewardship and tendinopathy and neuropathy risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with a loading dose calculated on actual body weight and level monitoring
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers Gram positive organisms and misses the Gram negative Enterobacterales that cause the overwhelming majority of pyelonephritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin with intravenous amoxicillin and review at 48 hours with the culture
options.rationale: Australian empirical therapy for pyelonephritis requiring admission is intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin, covering Enterobacterales and enterococci, with narrowing once susceptibilities return (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis is distinguished from lower urinary tract infection by systemic features such as fever, rigors and loin pain, and this distinction determines both the antibiotic and its route. Agents that concentrate in urine without achieving tissue levels, notably nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin, are effective for cystitis and useless for upper tract disease. Australian empirical therapy uses gentamicin with amoxicillin, with a single daily gentamicin dose and level monitoring if therapy continues beyond 48 hours. Imaging is reserved for those failing to improve at 48 to 72 hours, for suspected obstruction, or for a known stone history, since obstruction with infection is a urological emergency.
key_points: Fever, rigors and loin pain define upper tract infection and change the drug and the route
Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin never treat pyelonephritis despite good urinary concentrations
Empirical Australian therapy is intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin
Reimage at 48 to 72 hours if there is no clinical improvement
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin in this setting is given as a single daily dose of 4 to 7 mg/kg using ideal body weight, and a trough level is only required if therapy extends beyond 48 hours or renal function is impaired.

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis pharmacotherapy selection with impaired renal function
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 72 year old woman four weeks after she sustained a T12 vertebral compression fracture while lifting a shopping bag. The fracture was confirmed on plain radiography and her back pain is now settling with simple analgesia.

She is postmenopausal since age 51, has never smoked, and takes no corticosteroid. Her corrected calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone are within normal limits and her serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D is 68 nmol/L after supplementation. A myeloma screen is negative. Her bone mineral density shows a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.8. Her renal function has been stable at this level for two years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Lumbar spine T score minus 2.8; T12 vertebral compression fracture on radiography; myeloma screen negative
data_table.Blood tests: eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73m2; corrected calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone within normal limits; 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab six monthly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation continued
options.rationale: Denosumab is cleared by the reticuloendothelial system rather than the kidney and needs no dose adjustment, making it the antiresorptive of choice when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly taken fasting with calcium and vitamin D supplementation continued
options.rationale: Oral bisphosphonates are renally cleared and are contraindicated once eGFR falls below 30 to 35 mL/min/1.73m2, which is the single discriminator between this and the correct agent (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Intravenous zoledronic acid five milligrams annually with calcium and vitamin D continued
options.rationale: Zoledronic acid shares the same renal clearance limitation as oral bisphosphonates and is contraindicated below an eGFR of 35 mL/min/1.73m2 (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Calcium 1200 mg and colecalciferol 1000 international units daily as the sole ongoing therapy
options.rationale: Supplementation is adjunctive and does not reduce refracture risk after a minimal trauma vertebral fracture, which mandates specific antiresorptive or anabolic therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide daily for eighteen months with calcium and vitamin D continued
options.rationale: Teriparatide is an anabolic option for very severe or treatment refractory disease and carries restricted Australian subsidy criteria that this presentation does not yet meet (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma vertebral fracture establishes osteoporosis regardless of bone mineral density and mandates pharmacological therapy, since the risk of a further fracture in the following year is substantially raised. Agent selection is driven by renal function, by whether an oral route is tolerated, and by prior treatment. Bisphosphonates are renally cleared and become unsuitable below an eGFR of roughly 30 to 35 mL/min/1.73m2, whereas denosumab is not renally cleared. Secondary causes must be excluded before committing to therapy, which is why myeloma screening, calcium, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D belong in the initial workup.
key_points: A minimal trauma vertebral fracture diagnoses osteoporosis irrespective of T score
Bisphosphonates are contraindicated below an eGFR of about 30 to 35 mL/min/1.73m2
Denosumab is not renally cleared and requires no dose adjustment
Correct vitamin D and calcium before starting any antiresorptive to avoid hypocalcaemia
explanation.pearls: Denosumab must never simply be stopped, because bone turnover rebounds and multiple vertebral fractures can follow within a year; a bisphosphonate is given at the time of cessation to consolidate the gains.

subtopic_detail: Interpretation of pleural fluid biochemistry using Light criteria
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 64 year old man admitted with three weeks of progressive breathlessness. A chest radiograph shows a moderate left pleural effusion and you have performed a diagnostic pleural aspiration.

He is a former smoker with a 30 pack year history and takes no diuretic. His jugular venous pressure is not elevated, there is no peripheral oedema, and his echocardiogram yesterday reported normal left and right ventricular function with no valvular abnormality. His serum albumin, liver function and creatinine are within normal limits. The pleural fluid is straw coloured, and Gram stain shows no organisms with a pH of 7.38.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 128/76, RR 22, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid protein 42 g/L; serum protein 68 g/L; pleural fluid LDH 310 U/L; serum LDH 380 U/L; pleural fluid pH 7.38; Gram stain no organisms
data_table.Blood tests: Serum albumin, liver function and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence furosemide 40 mg daily and repeat the chest radiograph after five days of treatment
options.rationale: Diuresis treats a transudate from cardiac or hepatic failure, but the protein ratio of 0.62 and the LDH ratio of 0.82 both exceed the transudate thresholds (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Insert an intercostal catheter for drainage of a complicated parapneumonic collection today
options.rationale: Drainage is indicated for a pleural fluid pH below 7.20, frank pus or positive microbiology, none of which is present with a pH of 7.38 and a negative Gram stain (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Arrange a contrast enhanced computed tomography of the chest before further pleural intervention
options.rationale: An unexplained exudate in a former smoker requires imaging of the pleura, lung parenchyma and mediastinum to direct subsequent biopsy, and contrast computed tomography is the standard next investigation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory; Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand pleural disease guidance).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand pleural disease guidance

options.text: Repeat the diagnostic pleural aspiration in six weeks and send further fluid for cytology
options.rationale: A second aspiration adds little diagnostic yield over the first and delays imaging that will guide targeted pleural biopsy in an unexplained exudate (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand pleural disease guidance).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand pleural disease guidance

options.text: Repeat the transthoracic echocardiogram with contrast to reassess for occult diastolic dysfunction
options.rationale: The echocardiogram was normal and, more importantly, the fluid is biochemically an exudate, so a cardiac cause has already been excluded by the fluid itself (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

explanation.summary: The first decision in any pleural effusion is transudate or exudate, because the two lists of causes barely overlap and the subsequent workup differs completely. Light criteria classify fluid as an exudate if the pleural to serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, the pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio exceeds 0.6, or the pleural lactate dehydrogenase exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of the serum reference range. Meeting any single criterion is sufficient, which makes the criteria deliberately sensitive at the cost of misclassifying some diuresed heart failure patients as exudates. An unexplained exudate in a smoker raises malignancy and requires imaging then tissue, since fluid cytology alone misses roughly 40 per cent of malignant effusions.
key_points: Any one of the three Light criteria being met defines an exudate
Protein ratio above 0.5 or lactate dehydrogenase ratio above 0.6 are the two commonly used ratios
Pleural fluid pH below 7.20 is the threshold for drainage in a parapneumonic effusion
Cytology alone misses a large proportion of malignant effusions, so tissue is often required
explanation.pearls: Send pleural fluid pH in a blood gas syringe analysed within an hour, because air exposure and delay both falsely raise the pH and can turn a drainable empyema into an apparently simple effusion.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand pleural disease guidance

subtopic_detail: Management of supratherapeutic warfarin anticoagulation without bleeding
stem:
You are the general practitioner contacted by the pathology laboratory about a 76 year old man on warfarin for a mechanical aortic valve replacement performed six years ago. His target international normalised ratio range is 2.5 to 3.5 and his last three readings were in range.

He completed a course of trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole four days ago for a urinary tract infection. He reports no bruising, mucosal bleeding, dark stool, haematuria or headache. He has had no falls or recent trauma. His blood pressure and pulse are unchanged from his baseline and his haemoglobin today is 138 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 134/80, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 8.6 (target 2.5-3.5); haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180); platelets within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No bruising, no mucosal bleeding, no abdominal tenderness, no neurological deficit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold warfarin and recheck the international normalised ratio in three days with no other action
options.rationale: Simple omission is appropriate for an international normalised ratio between 4.5 and 8 without bleeding, but above 8 the risk of spontaneous haemorrhage warrants active reversal (Source: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give vitamin K1 one to two milligrams orally, rechecking in 24 hours
options.rationale: For an international normalised ratio above 8 with no bleeding, Australian guidance is to withhold warfarin and give low dose oral vitamin K, which corrects over about 24 hours without causing warfarin resistance (Source: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give prothrombin complex concentrate at fifty units per kilogram now
options.rationale: Prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for life threatening or critical site bleeding, and giving it without bleeding exposes a mechanical valve patient to unnecessary thrombotic risk (Source: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal

options.text: Withhold warfarin and transfuse two units of fresh frozen plasma with post transfusion coagulation studies
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma reverses incompletely and carries volume and transfusion reaction risk, and it has been superseded by factor concentrate for urgent reversal (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give vitamin K1 ten milligrams intravenously with repeat testing in six hours
options.rationale: A ten milligram dose is the near pair error; it over corrects and produces warfarin resistance lasting up to a week, which is hazardous with a mechanical valve (Source: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal decisions are driven by two variables together, the international normalised ratio and whether the patient is bleeding, and the same ratio calls for entirely different action depending on bleeding status. Without bleeding, an international normalised ratio of 4.5 to 8 is managed by withholding doses, while above 8 low dose oral vitamin K is added. Any clinically significant bleeding moves management to intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate irrespective of the ratio. The dose of vitamin K matters as much as the decision to give it, because high doses render the patient warfarin resistant for days, which is dangerous in a mechanical valve where undertreatment risks valve thrombosis.
key_points: International normalised ratio 4.5 to 8 without bleeding: withhold warfarin only
International normalised ratio above 8 without bleeding: withhold plus vitamin K 1 to 2 mg orally
Any critical bleeding: intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate
High dose vitamin K causes warfarin resistance lasting up to a week
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is among the most potent warfarin interactions, inhibiting CYP2C9 and displacing protein binding at once; check the international normalised ratio within three to five days of starting it rather than waiting for the routine interval.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand guidelines on warfarin reversal
National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Blood pressure targets in hypertensive emergency with retinal and renal involvement
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 52 year old man who presented with three days of headache and blurred vision. He ran out of his perindopril and amlodipine eight weeks ago when he moved interstate.

He has no chest pain, focal neurological deficit or dyspnoea. Fundoscopy shows bilateral flame haemorrhages and disc swelling. His creatinine was 92 micromol/L when checked nine months ago. His electrocardiogram shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy without ischaemic change, his troponin is not raised and his chest radiograph shows a normal cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Computed tomography of the brain is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 224/128, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Fundoscopy: bilateral flame haemorrhages with disc swelling; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110); urinalysis protein 2+ and blood 1+; troponin not raised; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial blood pressure management?

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg repeated as needed until the systolic pressure falls below 160 mmHg
options.rationale: Sublingual short acting nifedipine causes uncontrolled precipitous falls and has been associated with stroke and myocardial infarction, making it an abandoned practice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Restart oral perindopril and amlodipine at previous doses with general practitioner review in one week
options.rationale: Oral outpatient management is appropriate for hypertensive urgency without organ damage, but retinal haemorrhage with disc swelling and a rising creatinine define an emergency needing controlled parenteral therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Intravenous antihypertensive therapy titrated to reach a blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg within one hour
options.rationale: This is the right route with the wrong target; rapid normalisation exceeds cerebral and renal autoregulatory limits in chronic hypertension and precipitates watershed ischaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to reduce mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25 per cent
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency is treated with a titratable intravenous agent aiming to lower mean arterial pressure by no more than 20 to 25 per cent in the first hour, preserving autoregulation while halting ongoing organ injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 10 mg by bolus repeated every twenty minutes until symptoms have settled
options.rationale: Bolus hydralazine produces an unpredictable and prolonged fall that cannot be titrated or stopped, which is precisely what a controlled reduction requires (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: The distinction between hypertensive emergency and urgency is the presence of acute target organ damage, not the absolute blood pressure figure. Retinal haemorrhages with disc swelling, an acute rise in creatinine with proteinuria and haematuria, encephalopathy, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary oedema and aortic dissection all define emergency. Chronic hypertension shifts cerebral and renal autoregulation curves upward, so an abrupt fall to a normal blood pressure causes hypoperfusion at pressures a normotensive person would tolerate. The exceptions to the gradual reduction rule are aortic dissection, where systolic pressure is lowered rapidly toward 100 to 120 mmHg, and thrombolysis eligible stroke.
key_points: Emergency versus urgency is defined by acute target organ damage, not by the number
Reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 20 to 25 per cent in the first hour
Use a titratable intravenous infusion rather than boluses or sublingual agents
Aortic dissection is the exception requiring rapid reduction toward a systolic of 100 to 120 mmHg
explanation.pearls: Flame haemorrhages with disc swelling on fundoscopy convert a high reading into an emergency on the spot, and the finding is missed unless fundoscopy is actually performed rather than deferred to the morning ophthalmology round.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

subtopic_detail: Cortisol testing confounded by oestrogen containing contraception
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman referred with weight gain, purple abdominal striae wider than one centimetre, proximal muscle weakness on standing from a chair, and new hypertension at 152/96 mmHg.

She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol and has done so continuously for four years. She takes no corticosteroid in any form, including inhaled, topical and intra articular preparations, and drinks no alcohol. Her general practitioner performed a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test which returned a morning cortisol of 78 nmol/L, above the suppression threshold of 50 nmol/L. Her potassium and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 152/96, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test: morning cortisol 78 nmol/L (suppression threshold below 50); potassium and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Purple abdominal striae greater than 1 cm wide; proximal weakness on sit to stand testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary to identify a corticotroph adenoma
options.rationale: Imaging before the biochemical diagnosis is secure risks acting on an incidental pituitary lesion, which is present in around one in ten of the population (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Measure plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone now to determine whether the excess is dependent
options.rationale: Determining dependence is the correct second stage but only after hypercortisolism is confirmed, and the current result cannot confirm it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Repeat the same overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test in six weeks for confirmation
options.rationale: Repeating the identical test while the confounder continues will reproduce the same uninterpretable result, since the problem is assay interference rather than random variation (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Arrange inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise the source of the cortisol excess
options.rationale: Petrosal sinus sampling is an invasive tertiary test used to separate pituitary from ectopic sources long after confirmation of hypercortisolism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Measure 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two separate collections while she continues the pill
options.rationale: Oestrogen raises cortisol binding globulin and therefore total serum cortisol, producing false non suppression, whereas urinary free cortisol measures unbound hormone and is unaffected by binding globulin (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

explanation.summary: Screening for Cushing syndrome uses three first line tests, the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24 hour urinary free cortisol and late night salivary cortisol, and at least two abnormal results are needed before proceeding. Oestrogen containing preparations raise cortisol binding globulin by roughly 50 per cent, which inflates total serum cortisol and causes apparent failure of dexamethasone suppression in healthy women. The alternatives are to cease oestrogen for six weeks and repeat the suppression test, or to use a test that measures free rather than total cortisol. Other important confounders are enzyme inducing drugs such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and rifampicin, which accelerate dexamethasone metabolism and also cause false non suppression.
key_points: Oestrogen raises cortisol binding globulin and inflates total serum cortisol
Urinary free cortisol and late night salivary cortisol measure free hormone and avoid this confounder
Two abnormal first line tests are required before proceeding to determine dependence
Enzyme inducing anticonvulsants and rifampicin also cause false non suppression
explanation.pearls: If a suppression test is to be repeated off oestrogen, six weeks of cessation is required for cortisol binding globulin to normalise; four weeks is a common shortcut that still leaves the result uninterpretable.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

subtopic_detail: Interfering antihypertensives in aldosterone to renin ratio testing
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the hypertension clinic seeing a 44 year old woman whose blood pressure remains 168/102 mmHg despite three agents at maximum tolerated doses. She has been on perindopril, amlodipine and spironolactone for the last five months.

Her potassium has been persistently low at 3.1 mmol/L on three occasions and she takes no diuretic other than the spironolactone and no liquorice or over the counter preparations. Her renal function and thyroid function are within normal limits, her urinary metanephrines are not raised and a renal artery duplex shows no stenosis. Her general practitioner has sent an aldosterone to renin ratio which came back below the screening threshold. She asks why her potassium keeps dropping.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 168/102, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Investigations: Aldosterone to renin ratio below screening threshold; urinary metanephrines not raised; renal artery duplex no stenosis
data_table.Blood tests: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); sodium 142 mmol/L (135-145); creatinine and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease spironolactone for six weeks, substitute verapamil and prazosin, then repeat the ratio
options.rationale: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists raise renin and suppress the aldosterone to renin ratio, producing false negatives, so they must be withdrawn for at least six weeks with blood pressure covered by agents that do not interfere (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Accept the negative ratio and add a fourth agent such as hydralazine to control the pressure
options.rationale: Accepting an uninterpretable result leaves a potentially curable cause unexamined in a patient with the classic combination of resistant hypertension and spontaneous hypokalaemia (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Proceed directly to adrenal vein sampling to lateralise aldosterone production before any imaging
options.rationale: Adrenal vein sampling is a lateralisation test performed after biochemical confirmation, and doing it first exposes the patient to an invasive procedure without an established diagnosis (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the adrenal glands and act on any adenoma that is identified
options.rationale: Non functioning adrenal incidentalomas are common and acting on imaging without biochemical confirmation leads to inappropriate adrenalectomy (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Perform a saline suppression test now while the current antihypertensive regimen is continued
options.rationale: The saline suppression test is the near pair confirmatory step, but it is invalidated by exactly the same drug interference that invalidated the screening ratio (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the commonest secondary cause of hypertension and is substantially underdiagnosed, largely because screening tests are performed on drugs that invalidate them. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone and eplerenone raise renin and produce false negative ratios, and beta blockers do the reverse by suppressing renin and producing false positives. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and diuretics all interfere to a lesser degree, whereas verapamil, prazosin, hydralazine and moxonidine are considered ratio neutral. Confirming the diagnosis matters because unilateral disease can be cured surgically and bilateral disease is treated with a targeted mineralocorticoid antagonist rather than escalating generic therapy.
key_points: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia should always prompt screening
Spironolactone and eplerenone cause false negatives and need six weeks of withdrawal
Beta blockers cause false positives by suppressing renin
Verapamil, prazosin, hydralazine and moxonidine are ratio neutral cover during washout
explanation.pearls: Correct hypokalaemia to above 4.0 mmol/L before sampling for an aldosterone to renin ratio, because potassium depletion suppresses aldosterone secretion and can mask the diagnosis it is supposed to reveal.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

subtopic_detail: Myasthenic crisis with respiratory compromise
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward for a 63 year old woman with acetylcholine receptor antibody positive myasthenia gravis. She was admitted yesterday for a chest infection and started on azithromycin.

Over eight hours her voice has become nasal, she is pooling saliva and cannot count past 12 in one breath. Her pupils are 3 mm and reactive, with no abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, bronchorrhoea or fasciculation. Her forced vital capacity has fallen from 2.6 litres on admission to 1.1 litres this afternoon. Her oxygen saturation remains 96 per cent on room air and her chest radiograph shows a right basal consolidation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 142/84, RR 26, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Investigations: Forced vital capacity 1.1 L, fallen from 2.6 L on admission; arterial pH 7.36 with pCO2 46 mmHg; chest radiograph right basal consolidation
data_table.Examination: Nasal speech, pooled secretions, single breath count 12, pupils 3 mm reactive, no fasciculation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the pyridostigmine dose and frequency and reassess the vital capacity in four hours
options.rationale: Escalating an anticholinesterase in crisis increases secretions and aspiration risk without restoring ventilation, and the absence of miosis, cramps and fasciculation already excludes the cholinergic crisis this dose change would treat (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance

options.text: Commence high dose oral prednisolone 60 mg daily as monotherapy and continue ward observation
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid alone causes a transient worsening of weakness in up to half of patients in the first two weeks, which is dangerous when vital capacity is already 1.1 litres (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance

options.text: Transfer to intensive care for airway support and commence plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin
options.rationale: A falling vital capacity with bulbar weakness defines myasthenic crisis and requires critical care monitoring with rapid acting immunotherapy, since normal oxygen saturation does not exclude imminent respiratory failure (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance

options.text: Perform an edrophonium test at the bedside to distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic crisis
options.rationale: Edrophonium testing has been abandoned because of bradyarrhythmia risk, and the clinical picture without miosis or fasciculation already answers the question it was intended to settle (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance

options.text: Commence azathioprine as a steroid sparing agent and arrange thiopurine methyltransferase testing
options.rationale: Azathioprine takes months to produce clinical benefit and has no role in the acute management of a crisis unfolding over hours (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is defined by weakness severe enough to threaten the airway or ventilation, and it is monitored with forced vital capacity and single breath count rather than with oxygen saturation. Saturation and arterial carbon dioxide remain normal until very late because neuromuscular respiratory failure is a pump problem rather than a gas exchange problem, so waiting for desaturation means intubating a patient in extremis. A vital capacity below 15 mL/kg or roughly one litre, an inability to count past 20 in one breath, and bulbar weakness with pooled secretions are the triggers for intensive care transfer. Precipitants must be sought and removed, and macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium and beta blockers are among the drugs that unmask or worsen the disease.
key_points: Monitor with forced vital capacity and single breath count, not oximetry
Cholinergic crisis is distinguished by miosis, fasciculation, cramps and bronchorrhoea
Plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin are the rapid acting therapies in crisis
Macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones and magnesium can precipitate crisis
explanation.pearls: Start corticosteroids only after the airway is secured or immunotherapy is underway, because up to half of patients transiently worsen in the first one to two weeks of high dose prednisolone.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists myasthenia guidance

subtopic_detail: Early Guillain Barre syndrome with normal initial cerebrospinal fluid protein
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 38 year old man with five days of progressive leg weakness that has now reached his thighs and is affecting his grip. He had a diarrhoeal illness three weeks ago that settled without treatment.

He has areflexia at the knees and ankles with preserved sensation to pinprick and mild distal paraesthesia. There is no sensory level on the trunk, no back pain, and bladder and bowel function are normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine performed this morning is unremarkable. His lumbar puncture shows a protein of 0.38 g/L with one white cell per microlitre, and his forced vital capacity is 3.1 litres. His electrolytes, glucose and inflammatory markers are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 138/82, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal and distal lower limb weakness, absent knee and ankle reflexes, no sensory level, normal anal tone
data_table.Investigations: CSF protein 0.38 g/L (0.15-0.45) with 1 white cell per microlitre; MRI whole spine unremarkable; forced vital capacity 3.1 L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the lumbar puncture in one week and withhold treatment until the protein is elevated
options.rationale: Cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal in a substantial minority of patients during the first week, so a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis and waiting wastes the treatment window (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin over five days with four hourly vital capacity monitoring
options.rationale: Treatment is started on clinical grounds in a progressing patient because benefit is greatest within two weeks of onset, and serial vital capacity rather than oximetry detects impending respiratory failure (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone one gram daily for three days with proton pump cover
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have been shown in randomised trials to provide no benefit in this condition, which is the key difference from most other inflammatory neuropathies (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance

options.text: Commence plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin together to maximise the treatment effect
options.rationale: The two therapies are equally effective but sequential or combined use confers no additional benefit and adds the risks of both, so one is chosen (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast before starting any therapy
options.rationale: Areflexia with an ascending symmetrical pattern and no sensory level localises to peripheral nerve rather than to brain, and spinal imaging has already excluded cord compression (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance

explanation.summary: Guillain Barre syndrome is a clinical diagnosis supported rather than defined by investigations, and both cerebrospinal fluid protein and nerve conduction studies are frequently normal in the first week. Albuminocytological dissociation develops in most patients by the second week, so a normal early protein is expected rather than reassuring. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange is most effective when started within two weeks of symptom onset, and the two are equivalent and not combined. Respiratory monitoring is the single most important ward task, since roughly one in four patients needs ventilation, and autonomic instability with arrhythmias and labile blood pressure is the other major cause of deterioration.
key_points: Cerebrospinal fluid protein is often normal in the first week and does not exclude the diagnosis
Corticosteroids are ineffective in this condition unlike in other inflammatory neuropathies
Intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange are equivalent and are not combined
Monitor forced vital capacity serially and watch for autonomic instability
explanation.pearls: Use the 20/30/40 rule for escalation: vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure weaker than minus 30 cmH2O, or maximum expiratory pressure below 40 cmH2O each predict the need for ventilation before any change in oximetry.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists neuromuscular guidance

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulant selection in cancer associated venous thromboembolism
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 61 year old man with a newly diagnosed right femoral deep vein thrombosis confirmed on compression ultrasound. He was diagnosed six weeks ago with a locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma and started palliative chemotherapy last week.

His endoscopy at diagnosis described a large ulcerated antral tumour that oozed on contact with the scope. His haemoglobin has drifted from 128 to 106 g/L over four weeks and his faecal occult testing was positive. He has no chest pain and no dyspnoea. His platelet count is 168 x10^9/L, his creatinine clearance is 74 mL/min and his liver function is within normal limits. He takes no antiplatelet agent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Compression ultrasound: occlusive right femoral vein thrombus; endoscopy: ulcerated antral tumour with contact oozing
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (130-180), down from 128; platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine clearance 74 mL/min; liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Oral apixaban at treatment dose for six months with three monthly haemoglobin monitoring
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are reasonable for many cancer associated thromboses but carry excess major gastrointestinal bleeding when an intact luminal gastrointestinal tumour is present (Source: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance

options.text: Oral rivaroxaban at treatment dose for six months with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban shares the same luminal gastrointestinal bleeding signal as apixaban and acid suppression does not mitigate bleeding from a friable tumour surface (Source: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance

options.text: Oral warfarin bridged with enoxaparin until the international normalised ratio reaches the target range
options.rationale: Warfarin performs poorly in malignancy because chemotherapy, vomiting and variable intake destabilise the international normalised ratio, and it is inferior to low molecular weight heparin here (Source: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance

options.text: Subcutaneous enoxaparin at treatment dose for six months with periodic reassessment of the bleeding risk
options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin remains preferred when there is a luminal gastrointestinal malignancy with recent or ongoing bleeding, since it avoids the excess gastrointestinal haemorrhage seen with direct oral agents in this specific group (Source: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance

options.text: Insertion of a retrievable inferior vena cava filter with no systemic anticoagulation commenced
options.rationale: Filters are reserved for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation, and occult gastrointestinal oozing without overt haemorrhage does not meet that bar (Source: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance

explanation.summary: Cancer associated thrombosis carries both a higher recurrence risk and a higher bleeding risk than thrombosis in the general population, so anticoagulant choice is a balance rather than a default. Direct oral anticoagulants have largely replaced low molecular weight heparin for most patients on the strength of trials showing equivalent recurrence prevention with better convenience. The important exception is luminal gastrointestinal and genitourinary malignancy, where those trials showed a consistent excess of major bleeding with direct oral agents. Anticoagulation continues for at least six months and then for as long as the cancer is active or treatment continues, with the choice revisited as the tumour and bleeding risk change.
key_points: Direct oral anticoagulants are first line for most cancer associated thrombosis
Luminal gastrointestinal and genitourinary tumours are the exception favouring low molecular weight heparin
Warfarin is inferior in malignancy because of unstable international normalised ratios
Continue anticoagulation for at least six months and while cancer remains active
explanation.pearls: When platelets fall between 25 and 50 x10^9/L during chemotherapy, halve the low molecular weight heparin dose rather than stopping it; full cessation below 25 x10^9/L is the accepted threshold and recurrence risk climbs sharply during any interruption.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia and eviQ cancer associated thrombosis guidance

subtopic_detail: Severe cutaneous adverse reaction with eosinophilia and organ involvement
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34 year old woman with a widespread rash and fever. She started lamotrigine 24 days ago for bipolar disorder and takes no other new medication.

Her rash is a confluent morbilliform eruption over roughly 60 per cent of her body surface with marked facial swelling. Nikolsky sign is negative, there are no target lesions, no skin detachment and her oral, ocular and genital mucosae are entirely spared. She has palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Her blood film shows an eosinophil count of 1.9 x10^9/L and her alanine aminotransferase is 284 U/L. Her creatinine is 96 micromol/L and blood cultures taken on arrival are negative at 48 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106, BP 118/70, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.7
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption 60% body surface area with facial oedema; Nikolsky sign negative; mucosae spared; cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); alanine aminotransferase 284 U/L (5-35); creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90); blood cultures negative at 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and commence intravenous immunoglobulin at two grams per kilogram over five days
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is used in toxic epidermal necrolysis where keratinocyte apoptosis drives skin detachment, and the negative Nikolsky sign with spared mucosae excludes that diagnosis here (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists severe cutaneous adverse reaction guidance).
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists severe cutaneous adverse reaction guidance

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and commence ciclosporin three milligrams per kilogram daily for seven days
options.rationale: Ciclosporin is a treatment option in Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis rather than in an eosinophilic reaction with visceral involvement (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists severe cutaneous adverse reaction guidance).
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists severe cutaneous adverse reaction guidance

options.text: Continue lamotrigine at a reduced dose with daily liver function testing and topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug at any dose risks progression to fulminant hepatitis, and rechallenge with the same agent carries a high mortality (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and commence oral cetirizine with emollients and outpatient dermatology review
options.rationale: Antihistamines address itch alone and outpatient management is unsafe with transaminases at eight times the upper limit and ongoing fever (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists severe cutaneous adverse reaction guidance).
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists severe cutaneous adverse reaction guidance

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and commence systemic prednisolone with thyroid function monitoring for six months
options.rationale: Fever, morbilliform rash with facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and hepatitis two to eight weeks after an aromatic anticonvulsant defines a hypersensitivity syndrome treated with drug withdrawal and systemic corticosteroid, with late autoimmune thyroid disease requiring prolonged follow up (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists severe cutaneous adverse reaction guidance).
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists severe cutaneous adverse reaction guidance
